Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Shree Karni Electrovision Vs Union of India (Rajasthan High Court) Summary: The Rajasthan High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by M/s Shree Karni Electrovision challenging the validity of Section 16(2)(c) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 read with the Rajasthan Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 and seeking quashing of an order dated 24.11.2022. The petitioner, engaged in supplying electronic goods, had procured goods from M/s Techno Kart India Limited, a retail arm of the Videocon Group, for Rs.59,42,860.91/-. Tax of Rs.13,00,000/-, comprising Rs.6,50,000/- CGST and Rs.6,50,000/- RGST, arose on transactions during December 2017 to January 2018. The petitioner claimed Input Tax Credit on the basis that the supplier was responsible for depositing the corresponding tax with the Government. The supplier subsequently became insolvent and proceedings were initiated under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1} The petitioner contended that the respondents had failed to lodge their tax claim against the supplier in the insolvency proceedings and could not thereafter impose the unpaid tax liability upon the purchaser under Section 16(2)(c). Reliance was placed upon Ghanashyam Mishra & Sons (P.) Ltd. Vs. Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Co. Ltd., [2021] 126 taxmann.com 132 (SC), on the effect of approval of a resolution plan and extinguishment of claims not forming part of the plan. The respondents, however, argued that Section 16(2)(c) imposes an absolute condition requiring the tax charged on a supply to have actually been paid to the Government and that wrongly availed ITC could consequently be recovered from the purchaser. :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2} The respondents also relied upon Maruti Enterprise through its authorized partner, Jigneshbhai Bharatbhai Tarpara Vs. Union of India & Ors., decided by the Gujarat High Court on 01.05.2026. That decision considered the constitutional challenge to Section 16(2)(c), the doctrine of lex non cogit ad impossibilia and the statutory interaction between Sections 16(2)(c), 41 and 155 and Rule 37A. The Gujarat High Court had held, inter alia, that the conditions in Section 16(2) must be read conjointly, the claimant bears the burden of proving eligibility for ITC, and Section 16(2)(c) does not suffer from constitutional or legal infirmity. :contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3} The Rajasthan High Court held that Section 16(2)(c), subject to Section 41 of the CGST/RGST Act, constitutes a mandatory condition requiring the tax charged in respect of the supply to be actually paid to the Government. Unless that condition is fulfilled, availment of ITC is prohibited. According to the Court, a purchaser who avails ITC without ascertaining whether the supplier has paid the tax becomes liable to recovery in accordance with law where the supplier has not discharged the liability. :contentReference[oaicite:4]{index=4} The Court further held that the Supreme Court judgment in Ghanashyam Mishra & Sons (P.) Ltd., dealing with the consequences of an approved resolution plan under the IBC, did not dispense with the statutory condition governing the petitioner’s entitlement to ITC under Section 16(2)(c). Finding no ground to interfere with the impugned order dated 24.11.2022, the High Court dismissed the writ petition and disposed of the pending applications. :contentReference[oaicite:5]{index=5} Cases Discussed Ghanashyam Mishra & Sons (P.) Ltd. Vs. Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Co. Ltd.; [2021] 126 taxmann.com 132 (SC), decided on April 13, 2021 — relied upon by the petitioner regarding the effect of an approved resolution plan under the IBC; held not to dispense with the statutory condition governing entitlement to ITC under Section 16(2)(c). Maruti Enterprise through its authorized partner, Jigneshbhai Bharatbhai Tarpara Vs. Union of India & Ors. (R/Special Civil Application No.18080 of 2023 and other connected matters), decided on 01.05.2026 — relied upon by the respondents and considered by the Court on the constitutional validity of Section 16(2)(c), the burden of proving ITC eligibility and the interplay of Sections 16(2)(c), 41 and 155 with Rule 37A. FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF RAJASTHAN HIGH COURT 1. The instant writ petition has been preferred seeking the following reliefs: “It is, therefore, most respectfully prayed that this Hon’ble Court may graciously be pleased to issue an appropriate writ of Mandamus, certiorari and prohibition or any other appropriate order/ direction and kindly: a) To hold tha
rows.summary: Rajasthan High Court said buyers can lose GST input tax credit if their supplier fails to pay the tax to the government.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Delhi High Court Dismisses NSE Divestment PIL for Forum Shopping
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12344 Case Name Parinay Sharma Vs Union of India & Ors. (Delhi High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Delhi High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Parinay Sharma Vs Union of India & Ors. (Delhi High Court) Summary: The Delhi High Court dismissed with exemplary costs of ₹5,00,000/- a Public Interest Litigation filed by Parinay Sharma under Article 226 of the Constitution of India concerning IFCI Limited’s divestment of its shareholding in the National Stock Exchange of India Limited (“NSE”). The PIL sought, inter alia, preservation and production of records, disclosure of ownership, ultimate beneficial ownership and source of funds of DVI Fund (Mauritius) Ltd., Soach Global Opportunities Fund and similarly placed entities, restraint on their participation in NSE’s proposed Offer for Sale, deposit of transfer proceeds in escrow, examination by SEBI of the transfers and transferees, and consideration of the petitioner’s complaint dated 05.06.2026 by SEBI and CBI. The petition stated that IFCI held 24,97,750 equity shares of NSE as on 31.03.2015, representing 5.55% of its paid-up equity share capital, and during FY 2015-16 divested 11,25,000 shares in four tranches for aggregate consideration of ₹440.93 crores. The petitioner alleged that the shares transferred between 15.09.2015 and 01.07.2016 were sold at a valuation lower than a comparable June 2013 transaction and contended that, compared with NSE’s present unlisted-market valuation of approximately ₹5,00,000 crores, the impugned divestment caused a notional loss of approximately ₹12,121.13 crores to IFCI and consequently the public exchequer. NSE opposed the PIL at the threshold, pointing out that the petitioner had already filed W.P. No. 2408/2026, Parinay Sharma v. Securities and Exchange Board of India & Anr., before the Bombay High Court on 02.05.2026, before instituting the Delhi PIL on 05.08.2026, and had not disclosed that proceeding. The Delhi High Court held that suppression of the Bombay writ and the contrary averment made on oath in Paragraph 41 of the PIL were serious. Rule 9(i)(h) of the Delhi High Court (Public Interest Litigation) Rules, 2010 required disclosure of previously filed PILs or letter petitions, including their number, status and outcome. Comparing the two proceedings, the Court found a direct and substantial overlap in the reliefs concerning NSE shareholding, shareholders and ultimate beneficial ownership. The Court held that the petitioner appeared to have resorted to clever drafting to camouflage substantially similar prayers and accepted NSE’s submission that the petitioner had indulged in forum shopping. Relying on State of Uttaranchal v. Balwant Singh Chaufal, (2010) 3 SCC 402; State of M.P. v. Narmada Bachao Andolan, (2011) 7 SCC 639; and State of Jharkhand v. Shiv Shankar Sharma, (2022) 19 SCC 626, the Court reiterated that PIL jurisdiction requires complete candour, full and true disclosure and clean hands, and that suppression of material facts can justify refusal of relief at the threshold. The Court declined to examine the merits of the allegations concerning IFCI’s NSE divestment, held that the petitioner had approached the Court with unclean hands and abused the process through forum shopping, and imposed exemplary costs of ₹5,00,000/- payable to the Delhi High Court Bar Clerks’ Association within two weeks. The request for reduction of costs was rejected and the writ petition was dismissed. :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2} Cases Discussed State of Uttaranchal v. Balwant Singh Chaufal, (2010) 3 SCC 402 — cited on preventing misuse of PIL jurisdiction and discouraging petitions instituted with oblique motives. State of M.P. v. Narmada Bachao Andolan, (2011) 7 SCC 639 — cited on the obligation of a PIL petitioner to make full and true disclosure of material facts and approach the Court with clean hands, clean mind, clean heart and clean objective. State of Jharkhand v. Shiv Shankar Sharma, (2022) 19 SCC 626 — cited on non-disclosure of prior similar proceedings and rejection of PILs suppressing material facts. FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF DELHI HIGH COURT 1. The present Writ Petition, stated to be a Public Interest Litigation (“PIL”) under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, 1950 (“Constitution”), seeks directions concerning the divestment of IFCI Limited (“IFCI”) of its shareholding in the National Stock Exchange of India Limited (“NSE”). The Petitioner seeks preservation and production of the complete record; disclosure by DVI Fund (Mauritius) Ltd. (“DVI Fund”), Soach Global Opportunities Fund (“Soach Global”) and similarly placed entities of their ownership, ultimate beneficial ownership and source of funds; restraint on their participation in NSE’s
rows.summary: Delhi High Court rejected a PIL on NSE stake divestment, calling it forum shopping and imposing ₹5 lakh costs.

rows.title: Custom Duty | Customs SCN Cannot Be Reopened After Settlement Election: Delhi HC
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12342 Case Name NITCO Ltd. And Anr. Vs Customs (Delhi High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Delhi High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); NITCO Ltd. And Anr. Vs Customs (Delhi High Court) Summary: The Delhi High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by M/S NITCO Ltd. and another challenging Clause (e) of Paragraph No.51(ii) of the order dated 14.11.2019 passed by the Customs, Central Excise & Service Tax Settlement Commission, Principal Bench, New Delhi. The controversy was confined to the petitioners’ liability to pay interest on the amount determined pursuant to the Settlement Commission’s order. The proceedings arose from investigations by the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence concerning, inter alia, alleged misuse of EPCG Authorisations. In respect of one EPCG Authorisation issued by DGFT, New Delhi, a Show Cause Notice dated 18.06.2018 demanded duty of Rs.10,29,81,146/- along with interest. The Commissioner of Customs (Export), Mumbai Customs Zone-I adjudicated the SCN on 13.03.2019. Meanwhile, the petitioners approached the Settlement Commission, which by order dated 14.11.2019 settled the duty liability at Rs.6,69,57,333/-. After credit of Rs.1,41,49,366/- already paid, the balance duty liability was Rs.5,28,07,967/-. The petitioners themselves had quantified interest at Rs.1,10,04,634/-, while the Settlement Commission directed the jurisdictional Commissioner to verify and quantify the interest liability and intimate any further amount payable. The jurisdictional Commissioner subsequently recalculated interest at Rs.15,16,65,821/-. The petitioners argued that the SCN dated 18.06.2018 was barred by limitation under Section 28 of the Customs Act, 1962. They contended that the relevant date under Clause (d) of Explanation 1 to Section 28 should be reckoned from 06.11.2006, when duty was paid, or alternatively from 2009, when the alleged short-payment and fraud came to the knowledge of DRI. The respondent relied upon the conclusiveness attached to a Settlement Commission order under Section 127J of the Customs Act, 1962 and contended that, having voluntarily chosen settlement rather than pursuing adjudication proceedings, the petitioners could not reopen the SCN forming the subject matter of that settlement. Examining the limited scope of judicial review over Settlement Commission orders, the High Court relied upon Jyotendrasinhji v. S.I. Tripathi and Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited v. Commissioner of Income Tax, Bangalore & Ors. The Court noted that judicial interference with a Settlement Commission order is confined to limited grounds such as contravention of the statute, prejudice, fraud, bias or malice, and that the High Court cannot scrutinise such an order as an appellate court. The Court held that the petitioners had consciously elected to approach the Settlement Commission rather than pursue the statutory appellate remedy against the adjudication order dated 13.03.2019. Having themselves submitted an interest computation and obtained settlement of the proceedings, they could not isolate the direction concerning interest and use it to reopen the validity of the underlying SCN on limitation. The Court clarified that whether the jurisdictional Commissioner had correctly quantified interest at Rs.15,16,65,821/- was a distinct issue which would have to be examined independently, if otherwise maintainable, with reference to the relevant statutory provision governing interest. However, that issue could not be enlarged into an indirect challenge to the validity of the SCN. The High Court further held that interest is a statutory consequence of liability to pay duty and does not stand extinguished merely because the quantum of duty is settled by the Settlement Commission. The fact that the jurisdictional Commissioner ultimately quantified a substantially higher amount of interest than the petitioners’ own computation could not, by itself, furnish a ground for interference with the Settlement Commission’s order. No material was shown to establish that Clause (e) of Paragraph No.51(ii) was contrary to the Customs Act or that the Settlement Commission had exceeded its jurisdiction. Accordingly, the Court found no ground to interfere with the order dated 14.11.2019; held that the limitation challenge to the SCN dated 18.06.2018 could not be reopened in these proceedings; found no infirmity in the consequential direction for quantification of interest; and dismissed the writ petition along with the pending application. Cases Discussed Jyotendrasinhji v. S.I. Tripathi, 1993 Supp (3) SCC 389 — relied upon for the limited scope of judicial review of Settlement Commission orders. Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited v. Commissioner of Income Tax, Bangalore & Ors., MANU/SC/1
rows.summary: Delhi High Court ruled customs authorities cannot reopen a settled show-cause notice after a settlement election, though interest liability remained disputed.

rows.title: Custom Duty | CESTAT Sets Aside Chapter 78 Classification for Imported Lead-Bearing Material
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12332 Case Name Mittal Pigments Pvt. Ltd. Vs C.C. Mundra (CESTAT Ahmedabad) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Ahmedabad Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Mittal Pigments Pvt. Ltd. Vs C.C. Mundra (CESTAT Ahmedabad) Summary: The Customs, Excise & Service Tax Appellate Tribunal, West Zonal Bench at Ahmedabad, considered the second round of litigation concerning the classification of imported lead-bearing material declared as “Lead Concentrate” under CTH 26070000. The Revenue contended that the goods were Lead Waste/Scrap classifiable under CTH 7802, more particularly CTI 78020090, and that powdered lead scrap/waste was restricted for import under the applicable Foreign Trade Policy. The matter had earlier been decided by the Tribunal in favour of the party, but the Supreme Court, in Commissioner of Customs, Mundra vs Mittal Pigments Private Limited, reported at 2022 (380) ELT 243 (SC), set aside the earlier Tribunal order because the rival submissions had not been considered and the order contained virtually no reasons. The appeal was restored for fresh disposal, with all rights and contentions on merits kept open. The record contained conflicting laboratory reports. Customs Laboratory, Kandla reported material having characteristics consistent with lead concentrate, whereas Customs Laboratory, CH Nhava Sheva reported that the goods were other than Lead Concentrate and had characteristics of used lead battery scrap. CRCL, New Delhi issued reports concerning the powder and also separately examined metallic/plastic pieces. Other reports concerning factory samples and remnant samples were not uniform. The Tribunal ultimately examined the reports and the composition of the samples in determining whether the Revenue could sustain classification under heading 7802. The Department relied upon the statement of Shri Ramesh Kumar Agarwal; load-port customs export documents; Pre-Shipment Inspection Certificates; Country of Origin Certificates; Form 9 under the Hazardous Wastes (Management, Handling and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2008; the nature of the importers’ secondary metallurgical plants; their use of rotary furnaces; the absence of silver production; correspondence from the Central Pollution Control Board; and technical literature concerning primary and secondary lead production. The Department also relied upon judicial precedents concerning classification, redemption fine and confiscation. The appellants relied upon the chemical composition shown in the laboratory reports, common parlance, tariff provisions, HSN material, the conflicting reports and the decision in Gravitas India Ltd. v. Commissioner of Customs, Mundra. While analysing the conflicting reports, the Tribunal referred to the principle that, where scientific reports conflict, the basis of scientific investigation is to be preferred over an opinion without basis. It considered precedents including Jenson Enterprises vs Collector of Customs, Cochin and Another, Gastrade International vs CC Kandla, Hewlett Pack and India Sales Pvt. Ltd. vs Comm. Of Cus. (Import) Nhava Sheva, C.C., Mumbai vs Dilip Kumar and Co. and CC Mundra vs Sunrise Traders. The Tribunal also considered the earlier decision in Gravitas India Ltd. v. Commissioner of Customs, Mundra, which arose from the same investigation and concerned materially similar classification and evidentiary issues. The Tribunal examined the tariff headings and noted that “concentrate” was not defined in the tariff. It contrasted heading 2607, covering lead ores and concentrates, with heading 7802, covering lead waste and scrap. On the reports before it, the Tribunal found that the material was primarily composed of lead oxide and lead sulphate, with lead in metallic form present only in very small or minuscule quantities. It observed that lead oxide was specifically covered under heading 2824 and sulphates under heading 2833, whereas Chapter 78 applied to lead in metallic/primary form. On this reasoning, the Tribunal held that the Revenue’s proposed classification under heading 78020090 could not be sustained. It further recorded that, since the Revenue’s classification was not applicable to the goods, it was unnecessary to pronounce upon various grounds concerning the sample-drawing process, the conflicting reports, the benefit of doubt and whether the Department could independently seek retesting on the ground that a particular laboratory was not competent. The Tribunal accordingly set aside the impugned order classifying the goods under Chapter 78 and allowed the appeals. It concluded that the case of the Department could not be sustained and that the classification indicated by the party deserved to be undisturbed. Cases Discussed Commissioner of Customs, Mundra
rows.summary: CESTAT again backed the importer, rejecting Customs’ lead-scrap classification and the related import restriction, after a Supreme Court remand.

rows.title: Custom Duty | CESTAT Bangalore Upholds Customs Duty & Interest, Reduces Redemption Fine on Smuggled Bike
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12331 Case Name Anuj John Vs Commissioner of Customs (CESTAT Bangalore) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Bangalore Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Anuj John Vs Commissioner of Customs (CESTAT Bangalore) Summary: The appellant, Shri Anuj John, had purchased a Yamaha R-1 motorbike bearing registration No. MH 06 AR 8899 from Shri Mohammad on 10.04.2013. Acting on specific intelligence, the bike was recovered from a workshop. Verification from the RTO authorities showed that the address of the recorded owner was fake, while verification of the Bill of Entry disclosed that Bill of Entry No. 110190 dated 29.05.2008 was fake/fabricated and no customs duty had been paid. The original authority therefore ordered confiscation and imposed redemption fine of Rs. 50,000/- and penalty of Rs. 20,000/- under Section 112 of the Customs Act, 1962. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order but dropped the penalty under Section 112. The appellant challenged the order before the Bench. The appellant contended that the bike had been imported through Indira Gandhi International Airport and that he had possessed the Bill of Entry, insurance policy documents, challan No.99975892 dated 30.05.2008 and a sale letter signed by M/s. Galaxy Trading. He stated that he purchased the bike from Mr. Mohammad in Bangalore for Rs. 5,00,000/- in 2013 under bona fide belief that the documents were genuine. He therefore argued that duty could not be collected from him and redemption fine could not be imposed. He relied on Commissioner of Customs (Import), Bombay vs. VXL India Ltd., Shanoob M.S. vs. Commissioner of Customs, Cochin and HCL HP Ltd. Vs. Commissioner of Customs on limitation. The Revenue submitted that the documents were fake and the import was fraudulent, so limitation did not arise. Reliance was placed on Commissioner of Customs (Preventive) vs. AAFLOAT Textiles (I) Pvt. Ltd. and Mercedes Benz India Pvt. Ltd. Vs. Commissioner of Customs, Delhi. The Revenue also submitted that, since duty had not been paid at import, the appellant was liable to duty and redemption fine. The Tribunal found it admitted that the motorbike had been smuggled illegally without payment of duty, that the RTO owner was fictitious and that the Bill of Entry was fake/fabricated. It held that the goods were liable to confiscation under Section 123(5) of the Customs Act, 1962. The principal challenge was limitation and the appellant’s claimed bona fide belief. The Tribunal found that the Revenue came to know of the fraudulent illegal import only on 17.04.2013 and that the show-cause notice dated 19.08.2013 was therefore within time. In addressing limitation, the Tribunal relied on the Supreme Court’s discussion in Commissioner of Customs (Preventive) vs. AAFLOAT Textiles (I) Pvt. Ltd. concerning fraud, forged documents and caveat emptor. The Tribunal treated the forged/fake nature of the documents as sufficient to extend the limitation period and rejected the appellant’s time-bar objection. The Tribunal then considered the liability to pay duty and interest when confiscated goods are redeemed on payment of fine. It relied on the Supreme Court’s decision in Navayuga Engineering Co. Ltd. vs. Union of India, which explains the relationship between confiscation, redemption under Section 125, and the assessment and determination of duty and interest. The Tribunal noted the Supreme Court’s principles that customs duty liability arises in connection with redemption under Section 125(2), that the duty obligation is distinct from the confiscation fine, and that Section 28 operates for assessment and determination of the duty and other charges. The Tribunal also considered Union of India v. M/s Security and Finance (P.) Ltd., which distinguished the obligation to pay import duty from the separate liability arising from confiscation, penalty and fine. It noted that Parliament subsequently introduced Section 125(2) to clarify that, in addition to fine, the owner or person referred to in Section 125(1) is liable to duty and charges payable in respect of the goods. The Tribunal further considered Fortis Hospital Ltd. v. Commr. of Customs, Import, where the Supreme Court held that the Section 125(2) duty liability is triggered when the option to pay fine and redeem the goods is actually exercised. The Tribunal concluded that the liability to pay duty and other charges under Section 125(2) arises when the owner exercises the redemption option and the Department accepts it. It further held that the decision in Jagdish Cancer and Research Centre does not establish that calculation, determination or assessment of duty arising under Section 125 cannot be made under Section 28. On interest, the Tribunal relied on the Supreme Court’s reasoning
rows.summary: CESTAT Bangalore upheld customs duty and interest on a smuggled bike, but reduced the redemption fine despite finding the import documents fake.

rows.title: Service Tax | Lease Premium and Ground Rent Received by DDA Liable to Service Tax: CESTAT Delhi
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12328 Case Name Delhi Development Authority Vs Commissioner of Service Tax (CESTAT Delhi) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Delhi Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Delhi Development Authority Vs Commissioner of Service Tax (CESTAT New Delhi) Summary: The CESTAT New Delhi disposed of two appeals filed by Delhi Development Authority (DDA) arising from orders concerning service tax liability on activities involving Renting of Immovable Property and Club Services. The first appeal was Service Tax Appeal No. 50278 of 2017, arising from Order-in-Original No. DLI-SVTAX-002/COM-020/2016-17 dated 30.09.2016. The second was Service Tax Appeal No. 50191 of 2021, arising from Order-in-Original No. 11-14/TPS/PC/CGST/DSC/2020-21 dated 16.09.2020. The periods and amounts involved in the two appeals included substantial demands relating to lease/premium receipts and other activities. DDA was registered with the Service Tax department for services including Mandap Keeper Service, Health and Fitness Service, Architect Service and Club or Association Service. Audit proceedings revealed that DDA was receiving amounts from Renting of Immovable Property for commercial use without registration under that service and without payment of service tax. Show cause notices were consequently issued proposing demand and recovery of service tax, and the proposals were confirmed through the respective orders-in-originals. At the hearing on 13.05.2026, none appeared for DDA. The Departmental Representative argued that DDA is a corporate body managed under Section 3(3) of the Delhi Development Authority Act, 1957, but that the statutory character of an authority does not by itself exclude its taxable commercial activities. Reliance was placed on a Chennai Bench decision concerning a municipality, as well as the Larger Bench decision in RIICO Ltd. The Revenue contended that lease premium/salami and ground-rent related receipts were liable to service tax even though DDA claimed to be merely a custodian of Nazul land belonging to the Government of India. The Tribunal considered the Supreme Court decision in Krishi Upaj Mandi Samiti, New Mandi Yard, Alwar Vs. Commissioner of Central Excise & Service Tax, Alwar, which dealt with the distinction between statutory/sovereign functions and activities undertaken for consideration. The Tribunal also considered Circular No. 89/7/2006 dated 18.12.2006, under which statutory functions performed by sovereign/public authorities for compulsory statutory levies deposited into the Government treasury were distinguished from services undertaken for consideration. For the relevant pre-negative-list period, the Tribunal examined Section 65(105)(zzzz) of the Finance Act, 1994, defining the taxable service of Renting of Immovable Property. For the post-01.07.2012 period, it examined Section 65B(44) of the Finance Act, 1994, defining “service”, and Section 66D, containing the negative list. The Tribunal observed that DDA was letting/giving the Nazul lands on rent or lease on behalf of the Central Government and receiving ground rent and one-time premium. Although the object of the DDA Act was development of Delhi, the Tribunal held that if DDA earned profits while discharging functions under the statute, such amounts could be liable to tax. The receipts were not established to be statutory levies or fees deposited into the Government treasury; rather, they were admitted to be amounts received against Renting of Immovable Property. The Tribunal further considered the Larger Bench decision concerning RIICO Ltd., under which lease premium or salami was held liable to service tax under Renting of Immovable Property for the relevant period. It also noted an earlier DDA appeal, Service Tax Appeal No. 58914 of 2013, in which the matter had been remanded for consideration of the commercial or non-commercial nature of the property and the taxability of vacant land prior to 01.07.2010 in light of the decision in Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority Vs. CCE & ST, Noida. Following remand, one of the orders under challenge had held that leasing or Renting of Immovable Property constituted a taxable service, while renting of vacant land prior to 01.07.2010 was excluded from the service tax demand. The activity of charging membership and subscription for DDA’s sports complex was also held not to constitute a sovereign activity and was treated as commercial and taxable. The Tribunal found no infirmity in the findings of the original adjudicating authorities. It also noted that DDA had not appeared to make submissions and had failed to produce documents supporting its claim that the leasing of Government lands against rent, lease or premium constituted a sovereign function. Consequently
rows.summary: CESTAT Delhi held DDA’s lease premium and ground rent receipts are taxable, reinforcing service tax exposure on commercial property rentals.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GST Applies to Highway Annuity as Works Contract: Rajasthan High Court
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12327 Case Name Nagaur Mukundgarh Highways Pvt. Ltd. Vs Central Board of Indirect Taxes And Customs (Rajasthan High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Rajasthan High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Nagaur Mukundgarh Highways Pvt. Ltd. Vs Central Board of Indirect Taxes And Customs (Rajasthan High Court) Summary: The Rajasthan High Court considered a bunch of writ petitions led by D.B. Civil Writ Petition No. 10055/2024 filed by M/s Nagaur Mukundgarh Highways Pvt. Ltd. challenging the validity and applicability of Circular No.150/06/2021-GST dated 17.06.2021, a show cause notice dated 09.12.2022 and recovery order dated 07.07.2023 relating to levy of GST on annuity payments received under highway concession agreements. The petitioner contended that Entry 23A of Notification No.12/2017-Central Tax (Rate) dated 28.06.2017, issued under Section 11 of the CGST Act, exempted “service by way of access to a road or a bridge on payment of annuity” under Heading 9967. It was further contended that an advance ruling dated 12.02.2019 had already held Entry 23A applicable and, having not been challenged by Revenue, continued to bind the applicant and departmental authorities under Section 103 of the CGST Act. The petitioner argued that CBIC could not, through an administrative circular issued under Section 168, override, modify, dilute or retrospectively withdraw a statutory exemption. Reliance was placed upon DPJ Bidar-Chincholi (Annuity) Road Project Private Limited & Anr. Vs. Union of India & Ors., 2022 SCC OnLine Kar 1829. Revenue, on the other hand, maintained that Circular No.150/06/2021-GST merely clarified the statutory distinction between services by way of access to roads falling under Heading 9967 and construction services falling under Heading 9954. Revenue also relied upon CG Tollway Ltd. Vs. Union of India & Ors., Jorabat Shillong Expressway Ltd. Vs. Union of India and GMR Pochanpalli Expreessways Limited Vs. Additional Director, Directorate General of GST Intelligence & Ors. Revenue further invoked Section 103(2), arguing that an advance ruling remains binding only so long as the relevant law, facts and circumstances remain unchanged. The High Court principally relied upon the Coordinate Bench ruling in CG Tollway Ltd. v. The Union of India & Others, decided on 22.05.2026. That decision had examined Sections 2(31), 2(119) and Section 7 of the CGST Act, Schedule II and Rules 27 and 28 of the CGST Rules, 2017, and held that construction and maintenance obligations performed in return for valuable contractual rights constituted taxable works-contract services. It had also held that road-construction services fall under Heading 9954 rather than Heading 9967 and referred to Commissioner of Customs v. Dilip Kumar & Co. and Commissioner (CGST) v. Safari Retreats (P) Ltd. concerning interpretation of exemption notifications. Examining the petitioner’s concession agreement with NHAI, the Court noted that 50% of the Project Cost was payable in five equal instalments during the construction period while the remaining 50% was payable in twenty biannual instalments commencing from the 180th day of COD. The agreement described these deferred payments, together with interest, as “Annuity Payments”. The Court observed that the arrangement was essentially a design, build, operate and transfer project. Unlike CG Tollway, where the concessionaire bore the entire investment risk under the BOT arrangement, the petitioner had invested approximately 50% of the required funds while the remaining 50% was payable by NHAI on an annuity basis. Nevertheless, the Court held that this distinction did not change the essential nature of the services. The Court held that the concession agreement constituted “works contract services” and was taxable. The petitioner’s services were not confined merely to providing access to a road or bridge on payment of annuity; the contractual obligations included construction, design and maintenance of roads. Entry 23A related to transport services and did not exempt works-contract construction services. The Bench followed CG Tollway and declined to adopt the different view taken by the Single Bench of the Telangana High Court in GMR Pochanpalli Expreessways Limited, noting that CG Tollway had expressly distinguished that decision. The Court also rejected the challenge that Circular No.150/06/2021-GST impermissibly amended the exemption notification. According to the Court, the circular clarified terminology and prevented misinterpretation by authorities implementing the CGST Act, which fell within the Board’s domain under Section 168. It further rejected the petitioner’s reliance upon the earlier advance ruling, observing that an erroneous interpretation
rows.summary: Rajasthan High Court ruled highway annuity under concession agreements is taxable as a works contract, not exempt road access service.

rows.title: Income Tax | Actuarial Deficit Fund Contributions Fully Deductible: Calcutta High Court
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12325 Case Name PCIT Vs Syama Prasad Mookherjee Port Kolkata (Calcutta High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2018-19 Courts All High Courts, Calcutta High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); PCIT Vs Syama Prasad Mookherjee Port Kolkata (Calcutta High Court) Summary: The Calcutta High Court considered a Revenue appeal under Section 260A of the Income Tax Act, 1961 against the ITAT Kolkata order dated 18.11.2024 for AY 2018-19 in the case of Syama Prasad Mookherjee Port Kolkata, formerly known as Kolkata Port Trust. The assessee had filed its original return on 27.09.2018 and revised return on 28.03.2019. Assessment under Section 143(3) read with Section 144B was completed on 24.09.2021 at total income of Rs.876,16,93,450, including disallowances of Rs.710,68,55,297 towards Superannuation Fund contributions, Rs.33,11,01,366 towards approved Gratuity Fund contributions and Rs.8,38,35,219 towards alleged belated employees’ PF/ESI contributions under Section 36(1)(va). The CIT(A) deleted the additions and the ITAT confirmed that decision. On the Superannuation Fund issue, the Assessing Officer had applied the 27% ceiling under Rule 87 of the Income-tax Rules, 1962. Salary for the relevant computation was Rs.446,33,18,867 and the AO calculated the permissible contribution at Rs.120,50,96,094, whereas the assessee had debited Rs.831,20,51,391 to its Profit & Loss account. The assessee explained that the payment was necessitated by a severe actuarial deficit caused by funding constraints over preceding years and represented an extraordinary ad hoc interim contribution intended to bridge the gap between the fund’s assets and its actuarial liabilities. The CIT(A) and ITAT treated the payment as neither an ordinary annual contribution under Rule 87 nor an initial contribution under Rule 88 and relied upon PCIT-1 Vs Exide Industries Limited. The Revenue sought to distinguish Exide Industries on the ground that funding of deficits had occurred regularly over several years and therefore could not be treated as an exceptional one-time contribution. The High Court rejected this argument. It held that the legal nature of the contribution depended upon its purpose, namely remedying an actuarial deficit, and not upon the number of years required to eliminate that deficit. A persistent deficit arising from earlier funding constraints could not convert ad hoc gap-filling payments into ordinary annual contributions. The Court further observed that applying the Rule 87 ceiling to necessary actuarially-backed funding of an approved fund would compromise the fund’s solvency and run contrary to the scheme of Section 36(1)(iv). It therefore upheld deletion of the disallowance of Rs.710,68,55,297 and answered substantial questions (1) and (3) against the Revenue. On the Gratuity Fund contribution of Rs.33,11,01,366, the Revenue relied upon the 8.33% ceiling prescribed by Rule 103. The Court held that a fundamental distinction existed between ordinary annual contributions and payments specifically made to bridge an actuarial valuation deficit. The payment was intended to bridge the shortfall between actuarial liability and actual availability in the approved Gratuity Fund maintained with LIC and therefore did not fall within the restrictive category of an ordinary annual contribution under Rule 103. The Court also noted that Section 36(1)(v) itself did not impose an 8.33% ceiling and allowed contributions to an approved gratuity fund created under an irrevocable trust for the exclusive benefit of employees. Relying upon CIT v. Eastern Equipment & Sales Limited, the Court held that once the Commissioner had approved the fund, the Assessing Officer could not sit in judgment over that approval or use Rule 103 to disregard the approved status of the fund. The second substantial question was accordingly answered against the Revenue. On the Rs.8,38,35,219 disallowance of employees’ PF/ESI contributions under Section 36(1)(va), the Court noted that the assessee was governed by the Kolkata Port Trust (Non-contributory Provident Fund) Regulations, 1988, notified under the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963, and those regulations prescribed no due date for depositing employees’ contributions. The 15th of the following month shown in Serial No.20(b) of Form 3CD had been entered because the e-filing software compulsorily required a date. The Court held that the general deadline under Clause 38 of the Employees’ Provident Fund Scheme did not apply to the respondent. In the absence of a legally prescribed due date under the applicable regulatory framework, there could be no “delay” capable of triggering Section 36(1)(va). The Court therefore upheld deletion of this disallowance also. Finally, the Court reject
rows.summary: The Calcutta High Court upheld that contributions to an actuarial deficit fund are fully deductible, reducing the tax disallowance for the port trust.

rows.title: Excise Duty | CESTAT Ahmedabad Sets Aside Excise Recovery Beyond Five-Year Limitation
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12320 Case Name Panasonic Life Solutions India Private Limited Vs Commissioner of CGST & and Central Excise (CESTAT Ahmedabad) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Ahmedabad Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Panasonic Life Solutions India Private Limited Vs Commissioner of CGST & and Central Excise (CESTAT Ahmedabad) Summary: The CESTAT Ahmedabad allowed the appeal filed by Panasonic Life Solutions India Private Limited, Kutch, concerning recovery of Rs. 54,00,034/- taken as suo moto credit in the account current under Notification No. 39/2001-CE dated 31.07.2001. The appellant manufactures Glass Shell, Wires & Cables, Ceiling Fan, Switch Gear and other goods at its Kutch unit and was availing the area-based exemption under the Notification No. 39/2001-CE, as amended. The audit noticed that the appellant had taken suo moto credit of Rs. 54,00,034/- in April 2010 by endorsing it as “Re-credit (08-09 annual)”. A show cause notice dated 29.02.2016 proposed recovery under Section 11A read with Notification No. 39/2001-CE, together with interest under Section 11AA and penalty under Section 11AC read with Rule 25 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002. The Joint Commissioner confirmed the recovery, interest and equal penalty on 25.01.2018. The Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the appellant’s appeal, resulting in the present proceedings. The appellant principally contended that the demand was barred by limitation because the credit was taken in April 2010 whereas the show cause notice was issued on 29.02.2016. It was also submitted that an application/statement for the annual differential refund for financial year 2008-09 had been filed with the Jurisdictional Assistant Commissioner on 11.05.2009, but no decision had been communicated. The appellant relied on various judicial decisions, including Parle Product Pvt. Ltd., Government of India Vs. Citedal Fine Pharmaceuticals, Valley Valvet P. Ltd., SAL Steels Limited, Sun Pharma Laboratories Ltd., Reckitt Benckiser, Saurashtra Cement Ltd. and Amrit Foods. The appellant further contended that Para 2.2 of the notification permitted annual differential refund and that the amount of Rs. 54,00,038/- represented the differential between the duty paid and the amount already sanctioned through re-credit orders. It was also argued that there was no suppression, wilful misstatement, collusion or fraud because the appellant had disclosed the matter to the jurisdictional Assistant Commissioner in May 2009. The Revenue submitted that suo moto credit without waiting for the Assistant Commissioner’s order violated the notification and amounted to suppression of facts, justifying the extended limitation period. Reliance was placed on Garden Silk Mills Ltd., BDH Industries Ltd. and Krishna Electrical Industries Ltd. The Revenue also informed the Bench that the status of the refund application could not be ascertained. The Tribunal examined the relevant provisions of Notification No. 39/2001-CE, including Paras 2, 2A, 2B, 2C, 2.1 and 2.2. Para 2C permitted the manufacturer, subject to prescribed conditions, to take credit of the amount calculated under Para 2 in its account current. Para 2C required submission of a statement to the Assistant Commissioner, who was to determine the amount correctly refundable. Para 2C(g) provided for recovery of irregular or excess credit as if it were recovery of duty of excise erroneously refunded. Para 2.2(1) provided for annual differential refund where the total refund paid or payable during the financial year was less than the total duty paid, subject to the prescribed ceiling, while Para 2.2(2) required the Assistant Commissioner or Deputy Commissioner to refund the differential amount not later than 15 May of the subsequent financial year. On limitation, the Tribunal held that the notification read with Section 11A of the Central Excise Act, 1944 permitted recovery proceedings for erroneous refund within the applicable limitation period. Since the appellant had taken the suo moto credit in April 2010 and the notice was issued on 29.02.2016, the Tribunal held that the proceedings emanated from a time-barred show cause notice and were therefore unsustainable. The Tribunal also examined the merits. It noted that the appellant had submitted its annual differential duty statement on 11.05.2009, but the application had not been decided. During the proceedings, the department was unable to categorically state whether the refund claim was pending or had been disposed of. The Tribunal criticised the functioning of the Division Office and directed the Jurisdictional Chief Commissioner to enquire into the reasons for the prolonged inaction. The Tribunal held that the appellant had acted in accordance with the notification afte
rows.summary: CESTAT Ahmedabad held excise recovery was time-barred, setting aside demand, interest and penalty on Panasonic’s self-credited area-based exemption amount.

rows.title: Custom Duty | Rajasthan HC Quashes Drawback Recovery Made Without Prior Customs Reassessment
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12319 Case Name Bhati & Company Vs Union of India (Rajasthan High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Rajasthan High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Bhati & Company Vs Union of India (Rajasthan High Court) Summary: The Rajasthan High Court at Jodhpur allowed two connected writ petitions concerning recovery of excess duty drawback paid to exporters following misclassification of exported handicrafts and artistic wooden furniture. The principal petition was filed by M/s Bhati & Company in D.B. Civil Writ Petition No. 19673/2022, and the connected petition concerned Latiyal Handicrafts Pvt. Ltd. The common order was pronounced on 12.08.2026 by Hon’ble Mr. Justice Munnuri Laxman and Hon’ble Mrs. Justice Sangeeta Sharma. In the case of M/s Bhati & Company, six shipping bills covering exports between 13.05.2011 and 20.05.2011 were involved, while Latiyal Handicrafts Pvt. Ltd. had exported under seven shipping bills commencing from 13.10.2009 to 25.05.2011. The petitioners had self-assessed the exported goods under Drawback Schedule Nos. 9401 and 940399. The respondents subsequently took the view that the appropriate classification was Drawback Schedule No. 442101. The resulting classification difference led to excess drawback payments. The petitioners had carried out self-assessment under Section 17 of the Customs Act, 1962. Following an audit objection, show cause notices dated 25.03.2013 were issued seeking recovery of the alleged excess drawback by invoking Section 142(1) read with Section 75A of the Act and Rule 16 of the Customs and Central Excise Duties and Service Tax Drawback Rules, 1995. The original orders determining the excess drawback were challenged in appeal. The revisional authority subsequently set aside the original and appellate orders and remanded the matters for fresh consideration. The principal issue before the High Court was whether, after self-assessment of export goods, the authorities could directly invoke Section 75A for recovery of drawback without first undertaking reassessment under Section 17. The petitioners contended that where the proper officer disagrees with self-assessment, the statutory mechanism requires verification and reassessment, and recovery can follow only after the liability is crystallised through that process. 3The Court examined Sections 17, 18, 50 and 51 of the Customs Act. It observed that an exporter entering export goods under Section 50 is required to self-assess the duty, if any, leviable on such goods. Where the proper officer does not agree with the self-assessment, the officer is required to proceed with reassessment under Section 17(4). Where the reassessment is not accepted by the exporter, a speaking order is required. The Court also considered Section 18 concerning provisional assessment and Section 75A(2), which deals with recovery of drawback that has been paid erroneously or has otherwise become recoverable under the Act or rules. The Court held that the present proceedings had proceeded on the assumption that the drawback payments were erroneous, whereas the payments had been made pursuant to the petitioners’ self-assessments. According to the Court, even if the self-assessment subsequently turns out to involve misdeclaration or misclassification, the authorities cannot directly proceed under Section 75A(2) while the self-assessment remains in force and has not been reassessed. If the misclassification results in excess drawback, the authority may have recourse to Section 17(4) or Section 18 for further inquiry, as applicable. The High Court therefore held that Section 75A could be invoked in the facts of the case only after the amount had been crystallised as a consequence of reassessment. Since the authorities had not invoked Sections 17 and 18 and had proceeded directly under Section 75A(2), the proceedings were held to be a misapplication of law. The Court consequently set aside the impugned orders dated 05.01.2015 and 24.10.2021. It allowed the writ petitions while giving liberty to the respondents to have recourse to Sections 17 and 18 of the Customs Act, if law permits them. Pending applications, if any, were also disposed of. FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF RAJASTHAN HIGH COURT 1. The issue involved in these two writ petitions is common. Therefore, both the writ petitions are being taken up for disposal by this common order. 2. The facts of the cases disclose that in the case of M/s Bhati & Company, the petitioner had exported handicrafts/artistic wooden furniture items under six shipping bills commencing from 13.05.2011 to 20.05.2011 and in the case of Latiyal Handicrafts Pvt. Ltd., the petitioner had exported handicrafts/artistic wooden furniture items under seven shipping bills commen
rows.summary: Rajasthan High Court ruled customs cannot recover excess duty drawback for exporters without first issuing a proper reassessment of the export classification.

rows.title: Corporate Law | MP HC Holds Benami Suit Not Barred for Father’s Purchase in Minor Sons’ Names
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12317 Case Name Lateef Qureshi And Others Vs Ajeem Qureshi And Others (Madhya Pradesh High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Madhya Pradesh HC Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Lateef Qureshi And Others Vs Ajeem Qureshi And Others (Madhya Pradesh High Court) Summary: The Madhya Pradesh High Court at Jabalpur, in Lateef Qureshi and Others Versus Ajeem Qureshi and Others, considered whether a civil suit concerning properties purchased by a father in the names of his minor sons in 1968 and 1972 was barred by Section 4 of the Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988. The revision petition under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure challenged the Trial Court’s order dated 25 September 2025, by which the defendants’ application seeking rejection of the plaint had been dismissed. The Trial Court had held that the suit was not barred under the 1988 Act, taking into account the amended definition of “benami transaction” under Section 2(9). The plaintiffs and defendants were members of the same family. According to the plaint, the father of defendants Nos. 9 and 10 had purchased the suit property in their names through two sale deeds, first in 1968 and again in 1972. At that time, the plaintiffs and defendants Nos. 11 and 12 had not been born. The defendants sought rejection of the plaint under Order VII Rule 11 CPC on the ground that the suit was barred by Section 4 of the 1988 Act. Before the High Court, the applicants argued that the Trial Court had wrongly relied upon Section 2(9), since that provision was introduced by the 2016 amendment and could not have retrospective operation. It was submitted that the unamended provisions had to be considered because the transactions pre-dated the 1988 Act itself. The applicants further contended that the Hindu Undivided Family coparcenary exception under the unamended Section 4(3)(a) was unavailable because the parties were Muslims, while the purchases in the names of the sons did not constitute purchases by a trustee or person standing in a fiduciary capacity. The plaintiffs, on the other hand, argued that the amended provisions should apply because the transactions occurred in 1968–1972, before enactment of the 1988 Act, whereas the suit was instituted in 2025 after the 2016 amendment. They further contended that the father had purchased the properties in the names of his minor sons and that the relationship between guardian and ward constituted a fiduciary relationship, thereby bringing the transaction within the protection of unamended Section 4(3)(b) as well. The High Court considered the Supreme Court’s decision in Manjula And Others Vs D.A. Srinivas, (2026) 488 ITR 407. The Supreme Court, as quoted in the order, held that the 2016 amendments, insofar as they were declaratory, procedural, curative and machinery-oriented, operated retrospectively/retroactively, whereas penal provisions creating new offences or enhancing punishment could operate only prospectively. The High Court therefore held that the provisions relied upon in the present case, being declaratory, would apply retrospectively. The High Court then examined amended Section 2(9), under which an exception is carved out where an individual acquires property in the name of a spouse or child. Since the transaction in the present case was alleged to have been made by the father in the names of his minor sons, the Court held that it fell within the exception under Section 2(9) and was therefore not hit by the 1988 Act. The Court further held that even if the pre-amended provisions were considered, the transaction would still be protected by Section 4(3)(b). That provision excluded transactions where the person in whose name property was held was a trustee or another person standing in a fiduciary capacity and the property was held for the benefit of another person towards whom such fiduciary capacity existed. For this purpose, the High Court relied upon Pawan Kumar v. Babulal, (2019) 4 SCC 367, in which the Supreme Court considered fiduciary relationships in the context of father and children and discussed the earlier decision in Marcel Martins v. M. Printer, (2012) 5 SCC 342. The quoted discussion explains that “fiduciary capacity” is not precisely defined in the 1988 Act but carries a recognised legal significance and encompasses relationships founded upon trust, confidence, good faith and an obligation to act for another’s benefit. The Supreme Court had also referred to CBSE v. Aditya Bandopadhyay, (2011) 8 SCC 497, for the meaning of fiduciary relationship. Applying that principle, the High Court observed that the transaction in favour of minor children involved the relationship between guardian and ward, which was undisputedly fiduciary. It ther
rows.summary: The Madhya Pradesh High Court allowed a family benami-property suit to proceed, finding a father’s 1960s purchases in his minor sons’ names may not be barred.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Supreme Court Upholds Arbitration Despite Full and Final Discharge Voucher
rows.desc: 1 REPORTABLE IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION CIVIL APPEAL No. 8550 OF 2019 (ARISING OUT OF SLP (C) NO. 34186 OF 2015) THE ORIENTAL INSURANCE CO. LTD. & ANR. ...APPELLANTS VERSUS DICITEX FURNISHING LTD. ...RESPONDENT J U D G M E N T S. RAVINDRA BHAT, J. 1.Leave granted. With the consent of counsel, the appeal was heard finally. The Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd (hereafter “the insurer” or “the appellant”) appeals the decision of a single judge of the Bombay High Court, who allowed the respondent’s application under Section 11(6) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (hereafter “the Act”) and appointed an 2 arbitrator. The insurer’s objection about maintainability of the application on the ground that the respondent (hereafter “Dicitex”) had signed the discharge voucher and accepted the amount offered, thus, signifying accord and satisfaction, which in turn meant that there was no arbitrable dispute, was rejected. 2.The relevant facts in this appeal are that on 17.09.2011, Dicitex obtained a Standard Fire and Special Peril Policy; it was issued by the appellant to cover the stocks of goods lying in its three separate godowns located at Thane, Maharashtra, by three separate endorsements. The total sum insured was @ 13 crores.₹ Clause 13 of the terms and conditions of the said policy contained an arbitration clause. On 25.05.2012, a fire broke out at night on the ground floor of the building occupied by RFCL, which fire spread to the first floor of the building and completely engulfed all of the appellant’s three godowns which had stored its goods. All the stocks in all the three godowns were completely destroyed. Dicitex informed the appellant on 26.05.2012, about the fire and the consequential loss. The appellant appointed M/s. C.P. Mehta & Co. as Surveyors and Assessors to survey the loss suffered by Dicitex and to report on the claim to be lodged upon 3 the insurer­appellant, by the said company. Dicitex lodged a total and final claim upon the appellant for a sum of 14,88,14,327/­₹ comprising 13,52,85,752/­ towards cost of the materials₹ destroyed and 1,35,28,575/­ as overheads. Dicitex claims also₹ to have submitted comprehensive documentary evidence and detailed work sheets in support of the claim made to the insurer. On 14.08.2012, after visiting Dicitex’s factory and the godowns, and after scrutinizing the materials submitted by it in support of its claim, the Surveyor appointed by the insurer filed a Final Survey Report recommending that the claim be settled for an amount of 12,93,26,704.98/­ and that after deducting an₹ amount of 5% towards compulsory deduction for excess, a net amount of 12,28,60,369/­ be paid over to Dicitex. The latter₹ alleged that a copy of this survey report was not supplied to it, by the insurer, or the surveyor. 3.On 20.09.2012, Dicitex addressed a letter to the appellant’s chairman, informing him of the financial distress that it was facing, requesting for settlement of the claim on priority basis. Dicitex also informed him about a temporary loan obtained ­to the tune of 10 crores­ from Union Bank of India for 3 months at₹ 4 a high rate of interest which was due for repayment in September 2012 and requested him that it would be a great financial help if its claim could be settled on priority basis which would mitigate their hardship. Again, on 25.10.2012, Dicitex informed the insurer that the sale value of the goods destroyed was above 19₹ crores and that it had not only lost its goods but also its profits. Dicitex informed that it had already submitted all the documentary evidence supporting the claim to the Surveyor, M/s. C.P. Mehta & Co., yet another letter was addressed to the appellant’s chairman on 31.10.2012 placing on record that it had understood from the surveyor M/s. C.P. Mehta & Co. that the Head Office of the appellant asked for some more information in connection with the claim. Dicitex stated that compiling, organizing and sending various documents totalling around 35,000 in number, entailed voluminous work. It was stated that the surveyor had already gone through those documents and had picked up at random, sample of various concerned records. Dicitex stated that it was arranging to compile the documents and agreed to send them to the surveyor as soon as possible. In other letters (dated 10.01.2012, 28.01.2013), again requests were 5 made to the insurer to release the amounts. Apparently, the appellant appointed a Chartered Accountant (M/s Naveen Jhand & Associates) to carry out a resurvey of the claim made by it (Dicitex). The latter had already furnished 37,700 documents physically, which showed the exact quantity of furnishing fabrics in meters. Dicitex brought to the notice of the Chairman­cum­ Managing Director that the new surveyors had asked for large number of documents again and such documents could not be supplied. On 09.02.2013, addressing the new surveyor M/s Naveen Jhand, Dicitex submitted 37,700 documents and submi
rows.summary: The Supreme Court allowed arbitration to proceed despite a signed full-and-final discharge voucher, saying the insurer’s “settled” claim did not end the dispute.

rows.title: Corporate Law | SC Bars Courts from Excluding Claims at Section 11 Arbitration Stage
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12309 Case Name Office for Alternative Architecture Vs Ircon Infrastructure and Services Ltd. (Supreme Court of India) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts Supreme Court of India Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Office for Alternative Architecture Vs Ircon Infrastructure and Services Ltd. (Supreme Court of India) Summary: The Supreme Court considered whether a court exercising jurisdiction under Section 11 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 can exclude particular claims from arbitration by holding them to be non-arbitrable or to fall within an excepted category, after finding that an arbitration agreement exists. The appeal arose from the judgment and order dated September 6, 2023 of the High Court of Delhi at New Delhi. While appointing an arbitral tribunal under Section 11 of the 1996 Act, the High Court had excluded certain claims referred to in paragraphs 48(ii), (iii) and (iv) of the claim petition, treating them as non-arbitrable/excepted matters in view of Clauses 50 and 50.2 of the agreement. The appellant, Office for Alternative Architecture, contended that once the Court found an arbitration agreement to exist, its enquiry under Section 11 had to remain confined to that question. According to the appellant, whether particular claims fell within an excepted category was a matter for the arbitral tribunal. The appellant therefore sought setting aside of the impugned order to the extent it excluded the specified claims, leaving all such pleas open before the arbitral tribunal. The respondent relied upon the Supreme Court’s decision in Emaar India Limited vs. Tarun Aggarwal Projects LLP and Anr., (2023) 13 SCC 661, to contend that the High Court was empowered to exclude non-arbitrable claims at the stage of appointment. The Supreme Court examined Section 11(6A) of the 1996 Act, which was inserted by Act 3 of 2016 with effect from October 23, 2015. The provision requires the Supreme Court or High Court, while considering an application under Section 11(4), (5) or (6), to confine its examination to the existence of an arbitration agreement. The Court noted that although Act 33 of 2019 omitted Section 11(6A), that amendment had not been notified and consequently Section 11(6A) continued to remain in the statute book. The Court also considered the statement of objects and reasons accompanying the 2015 amendment, which stated that while considering an application for appointment of an arbitrator, the Court should examine the existence of a prima facie arbitration agreement and “not other issues”. The significance of those words had been considered by the seven-Judge Bench in In Re: Interplay Between Arbitration Agreements under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 and the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, 2023 INSC 1066. The Supreme Court in that decision observed that the issues beyond the existence of a prima facie arbitration agreement included matters arising from unnecessary judicial interference in arbitration proceedings. The Court further relied upon the three-Judge Bench decision in SBI General Insurance Co. Ltd. vs. Krish Spinning, 2024 INSC 532, which had considered the seven-Judge Bench decision in In Re: Interplay and held that the enquiry at the stage of appointment of an arbitrator is limited to scrutiny of the prima facie existence of the arbitration agreement. The Court also noted that the observations in Vidya Drolia vs. Durga Trading Corporation, (2021) 2 SCC 1, and NTPC vs. SPML Infra Limited, (2023) 9 SCC 385, concerning the extent of enquiry at the referral stage could not continue to apply in a manner inconsistent with the subsequent decision in In Re: Interplay. On that basis, the Supreme Court held that the High Court had erred in bisecting the appellant’s claims into arbitrable and non-arbitrable portions after finding that an arbitration agreement existed. The proper course was to leave the question of non-arbitrability of particular claims to the arbitral tribunal. The Court therefore allowed the appeal and set aside the High Court’s order insofar as it excluded the claims mentioned in paragraph 48(ii), (iii) and (iv), as referred to in paragraph 8 of the impugned order. The parties were left at liberty to raise the plea of non-arbitrability of particular claims before the arbitral tribunal, which was directed to decide that issue without being prejudiced by the observations contained in the High Court’s order. There was no order as to costs. Cases Discussed Emaar India Limited Vs. Tarun Aggarwal Projects LLP and Anr., (2023) 13 SCC 661 — referred to on the respondent’s contention that the High Court was empowered to exclude non-arbitrable claims while exercising jurisdiction under Section 11. In Re: Interplay Between Arbitration Agreements under the Arbi
rows.summary: The Supreme Court said Section 11 courts should only decide if arbitration exists, not exclude specific claims as non-arbitrable or excepted.

Clause 28 of the agreement provided that any dispute or difference between the parties, including regarding the validity or interpretation of the agreement, would be referred to the sole arbitration of the District Magistrate, Murshidabad. A dispute arose following a letter dated January 11, 2022 issued by Murshidabad Zilla Parishad alleging neglect and failure to pay rent. The respondent also raised suspicion regarding the actual amount collected by the petitioner in running the hospital and the figures disclosed to it. The petitioner challenged the termination notice by filing a suit before the Civil Judge (Senior Division), First Court, Murshidabad at Berhampore. In that suit, the respondent invoked Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, contending that the dispute arising from the termination letter was required to be decided through arbitration. The Trial Court rejected the Section 8 application and granted an injunction until disposal of the suit. The orders were challenged before the High Court in FMA 816 of 2025. By judgment dated July 15, 2025, the Division Bench allowed the appeal and held that the dispute ought to have been referred to arbitration under Section 8. The Division Bench also held that the injunction granted by the Trial Court was without jurisdiction because the Trial Court was required to refer the entire dispute to arbitration instead of entertaining the suit and deciding the prayer for injunction. According to the petitioner, the Division Bench had already held that the disputes raised in the suit were governed by the arbitration clause. Following disposal of the appeal, the petitioner issued a notice under Section 21 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, enumerating disputes including termination, arrear rent, audit discrepancies, eviction proceedings, denial of rents and extension. The petitioner also alleged that it had invested more than Rs.20 crores in running the hospital and claimed that such amount was recoverable from the respondent. The petitioner relied upon the Supreme Court decision in Central Warehousing Corporation and Another vs. Sidhartha Tiles & Sanitary Pvt. Ltd., reported at 2024 SCC OnLine SC 2983. The reliance was placed on the distinction between contractual disputes falling within an arbitration agreement and proceedings under a special statute governing eviction. The petitioner contended that even if the special statute governed eviction proceedings, the area of operation of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act and the West Bengal Public Land (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1962 were different and arbitration could not be refused merely because proceedings under the 1962 Act had been initiated. The respondent contended that the issues of eviction and termination were included in the notice invoking arbitration. It argued that its right to proceed against the petitioner under the 1962 Act was not an arbitrable issue and that the referral court should therefore resist referring the dispute concerning eviction and termination to arbitration. It was further submitted that the lease had expired by efflux of time on July 9, 2025 and that the petitioner had thereafter become an authorised occupant. According to the respondent, nothing prevented it from evicting the petitioner under the 1962 Act. The notice under that Act had been issued on July 22, 2025, before the notice invoking arbitration. The High Court noted that the respondent had accepted the existence of the arbitration clause. It further noted that, on the respondent’s own appeal, the dispute arising in the suit had already been referred to arbitration and that the principal dispute in the suit concerned termination of the tenancy prior to expiry of the lease. The Court also found from the notice invoking arbitration that there were claims and allegations apart from eviction. While considering the issue, the Court reproduced paragraphs 13 and 14 of the Supreme Court judgment in Central Warehousing Corporation.
