rows.summary: Calcutta High Court said pending eviction action under the 1962 Act does not stop arbitration of related contract disputes.

rows.title: Corporate Law | SC Upholds Arbitration for Contractual Disputes Despite Public Premises Act
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12307 Case Name Central Warehousing Corporation & Anr. Vs Sidhartha Tiles & Sanitary Pvt. Ltd. (Supreme Court of India) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts Supreme Court of India Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Central Warehousing Corporation & Anr. Vs Sidhartha Tiles & Sanitary Pvt. Ltd. (Supreme Court of India) Summary: The Supreme Court considered whether the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971 overrides the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, and whether the High Court erred in appointing an arbitrator under Section 11 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. Central Warehousing Corporation, a statutory body under the Warehousing Corporations Act, 1962 and under the administrative control of the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Government of India, had provided 1295 sq. mtrs. of storage space to M/s Sidhartha Tiles & Sanitary Pvt. Ltd. Possession was handed over on 12.09.2012. A lease agreement dated 26.09.2012 provided for a three-year period commencing from 12.09.2012 and expiring on 11.09.2015, with renewal by mutual consent. The storage rate was fixed at Rs. 131 per square metre per month. Clause 16 contained an arbitration clause. During the subsistence of the agreement, the Corporation communicated revisions to the storage charges. A demand for enhanced payment with effect from 01.11.2012 was raised, followed by further communications dated 10.05.2013 and 31.12.2014. The storage charges were subsequently revised with effect from 01.04.2015, and the respondent was informed that the tariff would be Rs.177 per sq. mtr. per month. The respondent indicated its interest in continuing the facility and sought renewal of the agreement, while undertaking to clear arrears due under the original agreement. On 16.09.2015, the appellant rejected the request for renewal and raised a demand of Rs.16,10,004/-. Since the respondent had not vacated the premises after expiry of the lease on 11.09.2015, the appellant invoked the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971. The respondent subsequently vacated the premises on 13.11.2015 before an order of the Estate Officer could be passed. The Estate Officer nevertheless passed an order on 31.12.2015 holding that the respondent was in unauthorised possession from 11.09.2015 to 13.11.2015 and directing payment of certain dues. The respondent invoked arbitration by filing an application under Section 11(6) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, relying upon the subsisting arbitration clause. The disputes concerned the right of renewal of the contract and the legality and propriety of the revision of storage rates during the subsistence of the agreement. The High Court concluded that the claims raised in the notice and Section 11 application were covered by Clause 16 of the agreement and referred the disputes to arbitration. The appellant challenged that decision before the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court held that the submission concerning the overriding effect of the Public Premises Act had to fail. It observed that the disputes raised in the Section 11 application related to promises and reciprocal promises arising from the agreement dated 26.09.2012. The right of renewal and the legality and propriety of the enhanced demand arose during the subsistence of that agreement and depended upon its interpretation, construction and contractual obligations. The Court distinguished these contractual disputes from proceedings under the Public Premises Act, which authorises ejectment of a tenant in unauthorised occupation of public premises and consequential directions. Since the original lease validly subsisted until 11.09.2015, the Public Premises Act did not affect the contractual dispute relating to the period from 12.09.2012 to 11.09.2015. The Court further held that the Public Premises Act neither barred nor overlapped with the arbitration proceedings initiated under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act. On the appointment of the arbitrator, the Supreme Court held that the revision of storage charges occurred during the subsistence of the contract and that its legality and propriety would depend upon the terms of the agreement. The right of renewal likewise depended upon the construction of that agreement. Both disputes therefore arose out of the agreement and were covered by Clause 16. In considering the scope of Section 11(6), the Court relied upon its decision in SBI General Insurance Co. Ltd. vs. Krish Spinning, 2024 SCC OnLine SC 1754, and reproduced paragraphs 110, 111 and 114 concerning the limited enquiry at the referral stage. The Court stated that the referral court was required to examine the existence of an arbitration agreement and that the enquiry was confined to a prima facie scr
rows.summary: The Supreme Court said contractual disputes can still go to arbitration, even where public-premises eviction laws also apply.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Breach of Contract Not Cheating Without Initial Fraudulent Intent: SC
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12303 Case Name Sarabjit Kaur Vs State of Punjab & Anr. (Supreme Court of India) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts Supreme Court of India Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Sarabjit Kaur Vs State of Punjab & Anr. (Supreme Court of India) The appellant approached the Supreme Court after the High Court dismissed her petition seeking quashing of F.I.R. No. 430 dated 16.10.2017 registered under Sections 420, 120-B and 506 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. The dispute arose from an Agreement to Sell concerning a one-kanal plot. The appellant had entered into an agreement to purchase the property from Malkit Kaur on 27.05.2013 and thereafter entered into an Agreement to Sell the same property to Sarabjit Kaur, wife of respondent No. 2, on 18.11.2013. The agreement specifically stated that the appellant was not then the owner of the property and was entitled to the property on the basis of the earlier agreement in her favour. An amount of ₹5,00,000/- was received as earnest money and the date for execution of the sale deed was initially fixed as 25.06.2014. The date was subsequently extended to 24.12.2014 upon receipt of an additional ₹75,000/-. Respondent No. 2, Darshan Singh, had earlier lodged a complaint on 30.09.2015 concerning the same alleged transaction, but the complaint was directed against property dealers Manmohan Singh and Ranjit Singh alias Billa. The complaint referred to two other transactions and sought recovery of ₹29,39,500/- from the property dealers. Following investigation by the Economic Offences Wing, a report was submitted and the District Attorney opined that no criminal offence was made out and that the complainant was at liberty to approach the civil court. The opinion was accepted by the Senior Superintendent of Police on 18.05.2016. A further complaint was made by Darshan Singh on 05.10.2016 with substantially the same allegations. That complaint was also enquired into and, having regard to the earlier complaint and finding that no criminal offence was made out, was consigned to record. The Supreme Court noted that the second complaint did not disclose the fate of the earlier complaint. Thereafter, further complaints were made and ultimately the F.I.R. in question was registered on the basis of the complaint dated 15.06.2017 against the appellant, Manmohan Singh and Ranjit Singh. The appellant contended that the dispute was purely civil in nature and that, if the sale deed had not been executed by the last date of 24.12.2014, the appropriate remedy was to seek specific performance of the Agreement to Sell or return of the earnest money. It was also submitted that no civil proceedings had been instituted and that the criminal complaint was filed nearly three years after the last date fixed for execution of the sale deed. The State opposed the appeal on the ground that the chargesheet had already been filed and that the appellant could raise her pleas before the trial court. Respondent No. 2 did not appear despite service of notice. On examining the material, the Supreme Court found that the Agreement to Sell itself specifically recorded the appellant’s position regarding title to the property. The Court also noted that neither the complainant nor the vendee had initiated civil proceedings seeking execution of the sale deed or, in the alternative, return of the earnest money. There was also no material showing that notice had been issued to the appellant either immediately before expiry of the extended date or thereafter demanding execution of the sale deed. The Supreme Court held that a breach of contract does not give rise to criminal prosecution for cheating unless fraudulent or dishonest intention is shown right at the beginning of the transaction. Mere failure to keep a promise is insufficient to initiate criminal proceedings. On the facts before it, the Court found that the case had progressively been improved in subsequent complaints: the first complaint did not allege cheating against the appellant and was directed only against the property dealers, whereas the appellant was subsequently implicated. The Court concluded that the apparent object of the criminal proceedings was to convert a civil dispute into a criminal case and exert pressure upon the appellant for return of the money allegedly paid. It emphasised that criminal courts are not meant to be used for settling scores or pressurising parties to settle civil disputes. Since continuation of the proceedings would amount to an abuse of the process of the Court, interference under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 was warranted. Accordingly, the Supreme Court set aside the impugned order of the High Court and allowed the appellant’s petition for quashing. F.I.R. No. 430 dated 16.10.2017 and
rows.summary: The Supreme Court said a breach of contract is not cheating unless there was fraud from the start, limiting criminal exposure in property deals.

rows.title: Income Tax | ESOP Discount Is Deductible Revenue Expenditure Under Section 37(1): Delhi HC
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12300 Case Name PVR LTD Vs CIT (Delhi High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Delhi High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); PVR LTD Vs CIT (Delhi High Court) The Delhi High Court considered whether the difference between the price at which stock options were offered to employees under the Employee Stock Option Plan (ESOP) and Employee Stock Purchase Scheme (ESPS), and the prevailing market price of the stock on the date of grant, was allowable as revenue expenditure under Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961. The appeal had been admitted by the Court on 30 April 2013 on this question of law. During the pendency of the appeal, the Karnataka High Court in Commissioner of Income Tax vs. Biocon Ltd., [2020] 121 taxmann.com 351 (Karnataka) upheld the Special Bench decision of the Tribunal on the issue in favour of the assessee. The Delhi High Court reproduced the relevant reasoning from that judgment. The reasoning in Biocon Ltd., as reproduced by the Delhi High Court, was that Section 37(1) permits deduction for expenditure laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for business purposes and does not require an actual cash pay-out. In an ESOP, employees receive an option to acquire shares at a predetermined price lower than the prevailing market price. The discount represents the difference between the market price at the time of grant and the offer price. Employees are required to render services during the vesting period, and upon completion of the vesting period the options vest with them. The Karnataka High Court held that where an ESOP vests over a period of four years at 25% per year, the employee obtains a definite right to the relevant portion at the end of each year and the assessee becomes bound to allow such vesting. Relying on the principles stated in Bharat Movers and Rotork Controls India P. Ltd., the Court held that a business liability arising during the accounting year remains deductible even though its exact quantification and discharge may take place at a future date. The eventual determination of the actual benefit upon exercise of the option was treated as quantification of an existing liability rather than a contingent liability. The Karnataka High Court further held that the expression “expenditure” in Section 37(1) includes a loss. Therefore, where shares are issued at a discount and the assessee absorbs the difference between the issue price and the market value, the difference constitutes expenditure for the purposes of Section 37(1). The object of the arrangement was considered to be securing consistent employee services and earning profits, rather than wasting or diminishing capital. The Delhi High Court also noted that it had previously followed the Special Bench decision in Principal Commissioner of Income-tax vs. New Delhi Television Ltd., [2018] 99 taxmann.com 401 (Delhi). The Court further recorded that subsequent appeals, ITA 107/2015 and ITA 214/2019, filed by the Commissioner of Income Tax on similar issues, had been dismissed by it following the Karnataka High Court’s decision in Biocon Ltd.. Consequently, following the Karnataka High Court’s judgment in Biocon Ltd., the Delhi High Court decided the question of law in favour of the assessee. It held that the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal had erred in law in holding that the difference between the price at which stock options were offered to employees under ESOP and ESPS and the prevailing market price on the date of grant was not allowable revenue expenditure under Section 37(1). The impugned Tribunal judgment was set aside and the appeal was disposed of. Cases Discussed Commissioner of Income Tax vs. Biocon Ltd., [2020] 121 taxmann.com 351 (Karnataka) — followed; the Delhi High Court adopted the Karnataka High Court’s ruling that ESOP discount is allowable under Section 37(1) and is not merely a contingent liability. Principal Commissioner of Income-tax vs. New Delhi Television Ltd., [2018] 99 taxmann.com 401 (Delhi) — referred to because this Court had followed the Special Bench decision in Biocon Ltd. on the ESOP expenditure issue. FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF DELHI HIGH COURT 1. Present appeal had been admitted by this Court on 30th April, 2013 on the following question of law:- “Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal erred in law in holding that the difference between the price at which stock options were offered to employees of the appellant company under ESOP and ESPS and the prevailing market price of the stock on the date of grant of such options was not allowable revenue expenditure underSection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1961.?” 2.During the pendency of the present appeal, the Karnataka High Court inC
rows.summary: Delhi High Court said ESOP discount can be deducted as business expense under Section 37(1), reducing taxable income.

rows.title: Company Law | Delhi HC Dismisses SFIO Investigation Writ for Lack of Territorial Jurisdiction
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12294 Case Name Anil Laxminarayan Biyani Vs Union of India and Anr. (Delhi High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Delhi High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Anil Laxminarayan Biyani Vs Union of India and Anr. (Delhi High Court) Summary: The Delhi High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by Anil Laxminarayan Biyani challenging the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) order dated 31.10.2025 directing the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) to investigate the affairs of Future Retail Limited (FRL) and Future Consumer Retail Private Limited (FCRPL). The petition was dismissed on the ground of territorial jurisdiction, with the Court holding that the High Court of Bombay was the appropriate and convenient forum. The Court expressly clarified that it had not examined the merits of the challenge or any other issue relating to the investigation. FRL and FCRPL were incorporated in 2007. The judgment records the restructuring discussions concerning the Future Group’s HomeTown and FabFurnish businesses during 2016–2017 and the proposed demerger into Praxis Home Retail Private Limited. Amazon acquired a 49% stake in Future Coupons Private Limited in 2019. SEBI subsequently initiated proceedings concerning alleged insider trading in FRL shares during the period from 10.03.2017 to 20.04.2017. The SEBI order dated 03.02.2021 was challenged before the Securities Appellate Tribunal, which on 20.12.2023 quashed the SEBI order and exonerated the appellants, holding, inter alia, that the trading was not based on UPSI. FRL was admitted into CIRP before the NCLT, Mumbai, and was subsequently ordered to be liquidated on 29.07.2024 after expiry of the maximum CIRP period without approval of a resolution plan. Insolvency proceedings against FCRPL were initiated on 24.09.2024. The judgment notes that, unlike FRL, no application under Section 66 of the IBC was filed against FCRPL and no transaction audit report was furnished in its insolvency proceedings. On 20.11.2024, IBBI made a reference to MCA concerning alleged avoidance transactions involving approximately ₹15,856.68 crore in relation to FRL and FCRPL. On 31.10.2025, MCA passed the impugned order under Section 212(1)(c) of the Companies Act, 2013, directing SFIO to investigate FRL and FCRPL. The petitioner challenged the order before the Delhi High Court on 19.01.2026. The respondents raised a preliminary objection that Delhi lacked territorial jurisdiction. They submitted that the companies under investigation had their registered offices in Mumbai; their statutory, financial and compliance records were maintained there; ROC Mumbai was the concerned Registrar; insolvency and avoidance proceedings were pending before the NCLT, Mumbai Bench; and any consequential prosecution would be before the competent Special Court having jurisdiction in Mumbai under Section 436 of the Companies Act, 2013. Reliance was placed upon Oil and Natural Gas Commission v. Utpal Kumar Basu, (1994) 4 SCC 711, and Kusum Ingots & Alloys Ltd. v. Union of India, (2004) 6 SCC 254. The respondents contended that the mere situs of the authority passing an order could not, by itself, establish territorial jurisdiction and that the doctrine of forum conveniens required the Court to consider the forum having the closest connection with the dispute. The petitioner, on the other hand, argued that the impugned order had been issued by MCA from New Delhi and that SFIO’s investigation machinery was operating from Delhi. It was submitted that SFIO’s Delhi office had issued notices to the petitioner and that the investigation was being controlled from Delhi. The petitioner also contended that Article 226(2) of the Constitution governed the territorial jurisdiction of the writ proceedings and that Section 2(29) of the Companies Act had no bearing on such constitutional jurisdiction. The Court rejected the petitioner’s contention. It held that merely because MCA was situated in New Delhi and had passed the investigation order there, territorial jurisdiction could not automatically be conferred upon the Delhi High Court. The Court observed that the expression “may” in Article 226(2), as opposed to “shall”, indicates that even where part of the cause of action arises within a High Court’s territorial jurisdiction, the Court is required to consider whether it is the appropriate and convenient forum. The Court also rejected the contention that the posting of an SFIO officer at its Delhi headquarters established that the investigation itself had its principal nexus with Delhi. Merely because an officer stationed at headquarters filed an affidavit on behalf of SFIO could not constitute a substantial part of the cause of action. On the contrary, the Court found consid
rows.summary: Delhi High Court threw out a challenge to an SFIO probe order on jurisdictional grounds, saying the Bombay High Court was the proper forum.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Hindustan Distributors Vs Commissioner of Customs (CESTAT Chandigarh) Summary: The Chandigarh Regional Bench of the Customs, Excise and Service Tax Appellate Tribunal allowed both appeals filed by M/s Hindustan Distributors and held that the appellant was entitled to interest at 12% per annum from the date of the revenue deposit until actual payment of the refund. The appeals concerned interest on amounts deposited as redemption fine for redeeming imported goods. The two appeals arose from separate orders of the Commissioner (Appeals), Ludhiana. The issue in both matters was identical, and the Tribunal therefore treated Customs Appeal No. 60490 of 2025 as the lead case. The refund amounts involved were Rs. 18,00,000/- in Appeal No. C/60490/2025 and Rs. 27,00,000/- in Appeal No. C/60519/2025. The appellant was a proprietorship firm engaged in importing iron and steel products falling under the freely importable category. The Director General of Foreign Trade, through Notification No. 38/2015-2020 dated 05.02.2016, imposed a Minimum Import Price restriction. The appellant filed three Bills of Entry on 26.02.2016 and responded to an EDI query on 01.03.2016 by contending that the restrictive notification did not apply. Following the initial adjudication, the appellant appealed before the Commissioner (Appeals). By Order-in-Appeal dated 27.07.2023, the confiscation and redemption fine of Rs. 18 lakh were set aside, although the penalty was upheld. The appellant consequently filed a refund claim on 23.08.2023 for the Rs. 18 lakh redemption fine. The respondent sanctioned the refund by Order-in-Original dated 30.01.2024 but rejected interest under Section 27A of the Customs Act, 1962, reasoning that the refund had been sanctioned within three months from the application. The appellant contended that Section 27A applied to refunds of duty or interest, whereas the present matter concerned a redemption fine that was never legally payable. According to the appellant, the Department had retained money which was ultimately found not to be payable, and interest was therefore compensatory for the period during which the Department enjoyed the appellant’s funds. The appellant relied upon Commissioner of C.Ex. Chennai-II Vs. Ucal Fuel System Ltd. and M/s Parle Agro Pvt. Ltd. Vs. Commissioner of CGST, Noida. The Department defended the impugned order by submitting that the Customs Act contained no provision for interest except Section 27A and that interest under that provision became payable only where a refund was not granted within three months from receipt of the refund application. The Department relied upon M/s HLG Trading Vs. Principal Commissioner of Customs, M/s Ajay Industrial Corporation Ltd. Vs. Deputy Commissioner of Customs, M/s Union of India Vs. Orient Enterprises, Commissioner of Customs (Preventive) Vs. Daleep Kumar Verma and India Carbon Ltd. Vs. State of Assam. The Tribunal identified the sole issue as whether interest could be granted on the refund of a redemption fine when Section 27A did not specifically provide for such interest. It noted that the Commissioner (Appeals) had also denied interest because the appellant had not specified the statutory provision under which interest was claimed. The Tribunal relied particularly upon the Division Bench decision in M/s Parle Agro Pvt. Ltd., where the provisions of Section 11B of the Central Excise Act and Section 27A of the Customs Act were considered pari materia. In that decision, the Tribunal had distinguished a refund of duty from refund of a revenue deposit and, relying upon Sandvik Asia Ltd. Vs. Commissioner of Income Tax-I, Pune and Riba Textiles Pvt. Ltd., held that interest could be granted on a revenue deposit. The Tribunal had considered the interest provisions under Sections 11AA, 11BB and 11DD of the Central Excise Act for guidance and granted interest at 12% per annum from the date of deposit until payment. That decision was stated to have been upheld by the Allahabad High Court in 2025 (37) Centax 217. The Tribunal further relied upon the Allahabad High Court decision in M/s Pace Marketing Specialties Vs. Commissioner of Central Excise, which followed Sandvik Asia Ltd. and granted interest at 12% per annum on amounts deposited during investigation and adjudication. It also relied upon M/s Riba Textiles, where 12% interest was granted on amounts deposited during investigation and at the stage of entertaining the stay application. The Punjab and Haryana High Court had upheld that decision and affirmed entitlement to 12% annual interest on delayed
rows.summary: CESTAT ordered 12% annual interest on refunded redemption fines from the deposit date until payment, increasing Customs refund exposure.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Madras High Court Directs ITC Unblocking After Rule 86A One-Year Period
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12290 Case Name Metal Trade Incorporation Vs State Tax Officer (Madras High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Madras High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Metal Trade Incorporation Vs State Tax Officer (Madras High Court) Summary: The Madras High Court considered a writ petition filed by M/s Metal Trade Incorporation challenging proceedings dated 11.05.2023 and 13.09.2023 under which the petitioner’s Input Tax Credit in the Credit Ledger had been blocked under Rule 86A of the Tamil Nadu Goods and Services Tax Rules, 2017. The petitioner was a trader in Iron and Steel Products and possessed valid GST registration. The judgment records that, from 01.07.2017, the petitioner had filed the specified returns and paid GST collected on its supplies under the CGST and SGST Acts. On 18.10.2022, the first respondent issued summons under Section 70(1) of the Acts. The petitioner subsequently challenged the summons in WP.No.3033 of 2023, which was disposed of with a direction to appear before the first respondent and present objections concerning simultaneous prosecution by Central and State authorities. The petitioner appeared and statements were recorded. An intimation dated 03.02.2023 proposed a penalty demand for assessment years 2017-18 to 2022-23. Based on intelligence and initial findings, the third respondent issued a communication dated 11.05.2023 to Joint Commissioners (ST) of Chennai, stating that the petitioner was found to be a non-existent dealer and directing reversal of Input Tax Credit claimed by beneficiaries under Rule 86A of the GST Rules, 2017. Proceedings were thereafter issued to block the Input Tax Credit of beneficiaries of the bill trader. The petitioner had been treated as a beneficiary and bill trader without adjudication. Although various grounds had originally been raised, the petitioner’s counsel restricted the claim before the Court to continuation of the ITC blockage beyond the one-year period prescribed under Rule 86A. The petitioner submitted that the ITC had been blocked as early as 27.01.2023. The Court noted that the ITC had in fact been blocked on 27.01.2023, before the impugned communication dated 11.05.2023, and that the restriction continued. Referring to Rule 86A(3) of the TNGST Rules, the Court held that the restriction imposed under Rule 86A(1) ceases to have effect after expiry of one year from the date on which the restriction is imposed. The Credit Ledger reflected the denial of debit as “blocked”. Since the restriction had been imposed on 27.01.2023 and more than 2 ½ years had elapsed, the Court held that the restriction had ceased to have effect after one year and could not continue merely because the third respondent subsequently issued the communication dated 13.09.2023. The Court emphasised that the language of Rule 86A(3) makes the one-year period mandatory and that the restriction must automatically cease upon expiry of that period. The Court observed that the purpose of the restriction is to enable assessment proceedings to be completed at the earliest, since indefinite blockage or denial of Input Tax Credit in a dealer’s Credit Ledger can have drastic civil consequences. It further noted that, in practice, authorities do not always remove the blockage after one year, resulting in writ petitions challenging continued restrictions. The Court stated that regular recovery proceedings based on assessment are contemplated under Section 79 and that the appropriate course for State Tax Authorities would be to initiate regular recovery proceedings under Section 79 after completing assessment. The Court therefore directed the authorities to act promptly. The Court also observed that the proceedings challenged in the writ petition were only an internal communication and that such communication alone could not form the basis for invoking Section 86A. The appropriate authority was required to ensure that the requirements under Section 86A were satisfied before denying debit from the Credit Ledger. Accordingly, the writ petition was disposed of with a direction to the fourth respondent to forthwith unblock the Input Tax Credit lying in the petitioner’s Credit Ledger. At the same time, the respondents were left free to complete pending assessment proceedings and initiate recovery proceedings in accordance with law, if necessary. No costs were imposed and the connected miscellaneous petitions were closed. FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF MADRAS HIGH COURT The present Writ Petition has been filed challenging the impugned proceedings dated 11.05.2023 and the consequential proceedings dated 13.09.2023, whereby the Input Tax Credit of the petitioner in the Credit Ledger has been blocked under Rule 86A of the Tamil Nadu Goods and Ser
rows.summary: Madras High Court said blocked GST input tax credit must be unblocked after Rule 86A’s one-year limit expires.

rows.title: Custom Duty | SC Upholds Port Trust Custodian Notification Under Section 45(1) for Pilfered Goods
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12285 Case Name Union of India & Others Vs Board of Trustees of The Port of Bombay (Supreme Court of India) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts Supreme Court of India Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Union of India & Others Vs Board of Trustees of The Port of Bombay (Supreme Court of India) Summary: The Supreme Court considered whether the Commissioner of Customs could validly approve the Mumbai Port Trust as custodian of imported goods under Section 45(1) of the Customs Act, 1962, despite the Port Trust’s custody arising under the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963, and whether the Section 45(3) liability for customs duty on pilfered goods could consequently attach to it. The respondent, a Major Port Trust, had received show cause-cum-demand notices dated 18.06.1996, 02.04.1997, 28.04.1997 and 24.05.2000 seeking recovery of customs duty under Section 45(3) in respect of goods pilfered while in its custody during 1996–2000. Orders-in-original dated 06.11.1997, 02.10.1997, 06.10.1997 and 17.05.2001 confirmed the demands. The Commissioner of Customs (Appeals), by common order dated 30.07.2002, dismissed the Port Trust’s appeals. The Bombay High Court thereafter allowed Writ Petition No.1278/2003 by order dated 28.07.2009, holding that the recovery could not be made from the statutory Port Trust and quashing the Notification dated 11.10.2000 as without jurisdiction and ultra vires Section 45(1). The parties’ submissions narrowed the controversy. The appellants contended that the saving words in Section 45(1) did not prevent the Commissioner from approving a person already having custody under another statute and that Section 45(3), with its non obstante clause, imposed the duty liability on the approved custodian. The respondent contended that its custody flowed from the Major Port Trusts Act and that the Commissioner therefore lacked jurisdiction to approve it under Section 45(1). It also submitted that the 11.10.2000 Notification could not retrospectively support demands for earlier pilferage. The appellants fairly accepted that, without approval under Section 45(1), the pre-notification demands could not be sustained, leaving the validity of the Notification as the principal controversy. The Court examined the saving clause in Section 45(1) against the non obstante clause in Section 45(3), referring to Aswini Kumar Ghosh vs. Arabinda Bose, AIR 1952 SC 369 and Dominion of India vs. Shrinbai A. Irani, AIR 1954 SC 596. It held that a non obstante clause cannot ordinarily cut down clear statutory language, but its operation depends upon the enacting provision and the inconsistency it is intended to overcome. On the Major Port Trusts Act, the Court examined Sections 42 to 45 and the Port Trust’s responsibility as a bailee. That responsibility is conditional upon the statutory requirements, including the issue of a receipt under Section 42(2), and is a civil responsibility towards the owner of goods. The Court distinguished this from Section 45(3) of the Customs Act, which creates a statutory liability to pay customs duty to the Revenue when imported goods are pilfered while in the custody of a person approved under Section 45(1). The Court also considered Section 13 of the Customs Act, under which the importer is not liable to pay duty on pilfered goods in the specified circumstances, and held that Section 45(3) addresses the resulting revenue gap by fastening duty liability on the approved custodian. The Court emphasised that Section 45(2) imposes statutory duties on the custodian, irrespective of the legal source of custody, including maintaining records and preventing removal or other dealing with the goods except with the proper officer’s permission. The Court concluded that there was no conflict requiring reconciliation between the Customs Act and the Major Port Trusts Act. The latter governs the Board’s civil liability as a bailee, whereas Section 45(3) imposes a distinct statutory liability to the Revenue. Since the Major Port Trusts Act did not itself impose a customs-duty liability on pilferage, the non obstante clause in Section 45(3) operated notwithstanding that Act. The Commissioner of Customs (Import) was therefore justified in issuing the Notification dated 11.10.2000 approving Mumbai Port Trust as custodian under Section 45(1). Accordingly, the Supreme Court held the Notification dated 11.10.2000 valid and set aside the Bombay High Court’s contrary finding and quashing of that Notification. However, the Court did not interfere with the quashing of the show cause-cum-demand notices dated 18.06.1996, 02.04.1997, 28.04.1997 and 24.05.2000, because those demands related to the period before 11.10.2000 and no Section 45(3) liability could arise without prior approval under Section 45(1). Th
rows.summary: Supreme Court held a port trust can be approved as customs custodian, so it may be liable for duty on pilfered imported goods.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GSTAT Quashes Section 129 Penalty on Same-GSTIN Stock Transfer Without E-Way Bill
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12284 Case Name M S Steels Vs Commissioner of Kerala State GST (GSTAT Thiruvananthapuram Bench) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts GST Appellate Authority Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); M S Steels Vs Commissioner of Kerala State GST (GSTAT Thiruvananthapuram Bench) Summary: The Goods and Services Tax Appellate Tribunal, Thiruvananthapuram Bench, considered whether penalty under Section 129 of the CGST/KGST Act, 2017 could be imposed where goods were transported without an e-way bill on account of an internal stock transfer between registered premises of the same assessee. M/s M.S. Steels, a partnership firm dealing in steel goods, transported steel goods on 13.06.2022 under Delivery Challan No. M120 from its own premises to its own godown. The movement was between registered premises of the appellant under the same GSTIN. The vehicle was intercepted by Mobile Squad No. II, Thiruvananthapuram, and the goods were detained under Section 129(1) on the ground that no e-way bill was available. A penalty of Rs.1,34,640, comprising CGST of Rs.67,320 and SGST of Rs.67,320, was imposed under Section 129(3), without any tax demand. The appellant paid the full penalty to secure release of the goods. Its first appeal before the Joint Commissioner of State Tax (Appeals), Thiruvananthapuram, was dismissed by Order-in-Appeal No. GSTA No. 77/2022 dated 02.11.2022. Before the Tribunal, the appellant contended principally that the movement was an internal movement between locations of the same GSTIN, supported by a delivery challan, and did not constitute an outward taxable supply. It argued that the expression “tax payable” in Section 129(1) could not be considered independently of the charging provisions. According to the appellant, Section 9 applies to intra-State supplies and a taxable event must first exist under Section 7. Since the movement involved only the appellant, with no second person or entity and no consideration, there was no supply and consequently no tax payable on the movement. The appellant relied, among others, on Fabricship Pvt. Ltd. v. Union of India, 2024 (90) G.S.T.L. 302 (Bom.) / (2024) 20 Centax 84 (Bom.), and on the decisions in Vacmet India Ltd. v. Additional Commissioner Grade-2 (Appeal), 2024 (81) G.S.T.L. 149 (All.) / (2023) 12 Centax 156 (All.), and Goverdhan Oil Mill v. Additional Commissioner, (2025) 32 Centax 368 (All.). It also relied upon Kamal Envirotech Pvt. Ltd. v. Commissioner of GST, 2025 (94) G.S.T.L. 345 (Del.) / (2025) 26 Centax 332 (Del.) in relation to minor procedural breaches and the principles under Section 126. The Revenue, on the other hand, submitted that Rule 138(1) requires an e-way bill for movement of goods exceeding Rs.50,000 not only in relation to a supply but also “for reasons other than supply”. It contended that Section 129 is a self-contained, non-obstante machinery provision and that “tax payable on such goods” is merely a measure for quantifying the penalty by reference to the value and ordinarily applicable rate of tax. The Revenue also argued that the decision in Fabricship was distinguishable because the goods involved there were exempt, whereas the TMT bars in the present case were not exempt. It further contended that the absence of any e-way bill made the default qualitatively different and that Section 129 did not require proof of intent to evade tax. The Tribunal rejected the Revenue’s central contention concerning the meaning of “tax payable”. It reproduced Section 129(1)(a), which provides for penalty equal to two hundred per cent of the tax payable on the goods where the owner comes forward for payment. The Tribunal held that any penalty under the provision is leviable only in terms of the tax payable on the goods. It then examined the charging provision in Section 9, under which tax is levied on intra-State supplies of goods or services or both, and considered the definition of intra-State supply through Section 2(64) of the CGST/KGST Act and Section 8 of the IGST Act. The Tribunal thereafter examined Section 7(1), which includes forms of supply such as sale, transfer, barter, exchange, licence, rental, lease or disposal made or agreed to be made for a consideration by a person in the course or furtherance of business. On the facts before it, the Tribunal held that a transaction falling within Section 7 necessarily involved two persons or entities constituting the parties to the sale, transfer, exchange or other transaction. In the present case, there was only one party—the appellant—and there was no second party and no consideration. It therefore concluded that the stock transfer was not a supply under Section 7. Since it was not a supply, it could not be an intra-State supply and consequently fell outside the charging provisi
rows.summary: GSTAT ruled no Section 129 penalty applies to same-GSTIN stock transfers without an e-way bill when goods move between the taxpayer’s own registered premises.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | AP HC Quashes GST Order Passed Against Deceased Proprietor Without Hearing Legal Heir
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12283 Case Name SSS Agro Foods Vs Assistant Commissioner ST (Andhra Pradesh High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Andhra Pradesh HC Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); SSS Agro Foods Vs Assistant Commissioner ST (Andhra Pradesh High Court) Summary: The Andhra Pradesh High Court allowed the writ petition filed by SSS Agro Foods and set aside the assessment proceedings dated 31.12.2024 and the rejection endorsement dated 28.03.2026. The Court held that the assessment order passed against the deceased proprietor had no legal efficacy and that the proceedings were also vitiated by failure to comply with Section 75(4) of the GST Act concerning opportunity of personal hearing. The petitioner’s husband, who was the proprietor of M/s. S.S.S. Agro Foods, died on 03.05.2024, prior to the assessment order dated 31.12.2024. According to the petitioner, the husband had been looking after the financial affairs of the business and the assessment proceedings were therefore not within her knowledge. A statutory appeal against the assessment order was subsequently rejected on the ground that it was filed beyond the condonable period prescribed under the A.P. GST Act. Before the High Court, the petitioner contended that the appellate authority had failed to consider the circumstances arising from the proprietor’s death. It was further submitted that the assessment proceedings had been completed without affording an opportunity of personal hearing as contemplated under Section 75(4) of the GST Act. Reliance was placed on the Coordinate Bench decision in W.P. No. 6029 of 2025 dated 24.12.2025. The Revenue defended the appellate rejection on the ground of delay and contended that the writ petition was not sustainable without availing the statutory remedies. The Court examined the death certificate dated 01.06.2024, which indicated that Balusu Surya Prathap Chowdary, purportedly the proprietor of the writ petitioner, had died on 03.05.2024. The Court observed that the death had occurred much before the assessment order dated 31.12.2024. It held that an order passed against a dead person does not have any legal efficacy. The Court further found that the impugned proceedings had not adverted to the relevant statutory provision, particularly Section 75(4), which contemplates an opportunity of personal hearing before an assessment order is passed. The Court relied upon the Coordinate Bench decision in W.P. No. 6029 of 2025, identified in TaxGuru as Baratam Satish v. The Joint Commissioner of Central Tax. In that decision, the Court had considered Section 93 of the GST Act and held that proceedings could not be sustained against a deceased person, while dues could be recovered through the statutory mechanism involving the appropriate representative or estate. Following that reasoning, the High Court held that the proceedings dated 31.12.2024 were liable to be set aside. Since the original order itself was non est in law, the rejection endorsement dated 28.03.2026 emanating from that assessment proceeding was also declared invalid. The writ petition was accordingly allowed. However, the first respondent was granted liberty to issue appropriate notice to Smt. Balusu Bhuvaneswari Devi and proceed with the assessment after giving her due opportunity of hearing. The Court also directed that the period from the date of passing of the impugned order until receipt of the High Court’s order would be excluded for limitation purposes. There was no order as to costs. Cases Discussed Baratam Satish v. The Joint Commissioner of Central Tax, W.P. No. 6029 of 2025, dated 24.12.2025 — the Coordinate Bench decision relied upon for the proposition that assessment proceedings cannot be sustained against a deceased person and that fresh assessment must involve the legal representative. FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF ANDHRA PRADESH HIGH COURT Heard Mr.Anurag Sampath, learned counsel representing the petitioner, who appeared through online and Mr.S.A.V. Sai Kumar, learned Assistant Government Pleader for Commercial Tax, representing respondent Nos.1 to 3. With their consent, the writ petition is disposed of at the stage of admission. 2. Aggrieved by the assessment order dated 31.12.2024 passed against proprietary concern M/s. S.S.S. Agro Foods, the present writ petition is filed. 3. As per the averments made in the affidavit, the husband of the deponent is proprietor of M/s. S.S.S. Agro Foods and he expired on 03.05.2024. Respondent authorities passed impugned adjudication order on 31.01.2024 and since the husband of the petitioner was proprietor looking after the financial activities of the business, passing of assessment order was not within the knowledge of the deponent. Be that as it may. 4. Against the asse
rows.summary: Andhra Pradesh HC invalidated a GST assessment against a deceased proprietor because the legal heir was not heard, violating mandatory hearing rules.

rows.title: Service Tax | CENVAT Credit on RCM Service Tax Eligible Under Rule 9(1)(e): CESTAT Chennai
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12281 Case Name Madura Micro Finance Ltd. Vs Commissioner of GST & Central Excise (CESTAT Chennai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Chennai Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Madura Micro Finance Ltd. Vs Commissioner of GST & Central Excise (CESTAT Chennai) Summary: The Customs, Excise & Service Tax Appellate Tribunal, Chennai allowed the appeal filed by Madura Micro Finance Ltd. against rejection of its refund claim concerning Service Tax paid under the Reverse Charge Mechanism. The appellant, a non-banking financial company, had paid Rs.40,13,483/- towards Service Tax following audit objections for April 2012 to June 2017, including Rs.20,11,196/- under reverse charge. It claimed 50% of the latter amount, i.e. Rs.10,05,598/-, as eligible CENVAT credit/refund after being unable to avail or carry forward the credit into the GST regime. The Department rejected the claim by invoking Rule 9(1)(bb) of the CENVAT Credit Rules, 2004. The Tribunal held that Rule 9(1)(e), and not Rule 9(1)(bb), was the relevant provision because the appellant had paid Service Tax under reverse charge and the prescribed document was a challan evidencing payment by the person liable to pay Service Tax. Relying on Polygenta Technologies Ltd., the Tribunal held that Rule 9(1)(bb) concerned supplementary invoices, bills or challans issued by a provider of output service and could not be applied to deny credit to a recipient paying tax under reverse charge. On transition into GST, the Tribunal found that Section 142 of the CGST Act, 2017 permitted the eligible amount to be refunded in cash where the credit could not be availed after the GST regime commenced. It noted that the Service Tax was paid on 18.12.2017, after GST came into force, and that the appellant had applied within the stipulated period for TRAN-1 credit. No fraud, collusion, wilful misstatement, suppression or intent to evade Service Tax had been alleged through a show cause notice. The Tribunal therefore held that the rejection on the ground of non-declaration in Service Tax returns was hyper-technical. It also relied on Adfert Technologies Pvt. Ltd. and the Supreme Court order concerning Adfert Technologies in support of the principle that transitional credit could not be denied on procedural or technical grounds. The impugned order was set aside and the appeal was allowed with consequential relief, as per law. Cases Discussed M/s. Asiatic Drugs and Pharmaceuticals Pvt. Ltd. Vs. Commissioner, CGST, Alwar dated 25.7.2022 — cited by the appellant in support of eligibility for credit. M/s. Global Analytics India Pvt. Ltd. Vs. CGST & CE dated 22.7.2019 — cited by the appellant in support of eligibility for credit. Polygenta Technologies Ltd. Vs. Commissioner of Central Excise, Nasik-I, 2018 (2) TMI 804-CESTAT, Mumbai — relied upon for holding that Rule 9(1)(e), rather than Rule 9(1)(bb), governs credit based on Service Tax paid under reverse charge. Adfert Technologies Pvt. Ltd. Vs. UOI, 2020 (32) GSTL 726 (P&H) — relied upon concerning transitional credit and procedural or technical grounds. UOI & Ors. Vs. Adfert Technologies Pvt. Ltd., 2020 (34) GSTL J138 (S.C.) — cited as the Supreme Court decision concerning Adfert Technologies. FULL TEXT OF THE ORDER OF CESTAT, CHENNAI This appeal is filed by Madura Micro Finance Ltd. against Order in Appeal No. 22/2022 (CTA – II) dated 12.5.2022 passed by the Commissioner of GST & Central Excise (Appeals – II), Chennai (impugned order). 2. Brief facts of the case are that the appellant is engaged in the business of Non-banking Financial Services. During the course of audit by the Audit – II Commissionerate for the period from April 2012 to June 2017, the audit raised certain objections involving non/short payment of service tax by the appellant totaling to Rs.40,13,483/- which was paid by the appellant on 18.12.2017. Out of the above amount, Rs.20,11,196/- was paid as service tax under reverse charge mechanism. The appellant submitted in their letter dated 26.9.2018 that they being a non-banking financial company, they are eligible for CENVAT credit of 50% of the amount paid as service tax. As they could neither take CENVAT credit of the same nor carry forward in TRAN-1, they wrote to the Range Superintendent for refund of Rs.10,05,598/- being 50% of the service tax paid under reverse charge mechanism. Department rejected the refund claim vide communication dated 26.4.2021 to the appellant. Since the appellant requested for personal hearing, the same was granted and vide Order in Original dated 25.6.2021 the lower authority rejected the refund claim. In appeal, the Ld. Appellate Authority upheld the adjudication order. Hence the present appeal. 3. Shri K. Manimaran, learned Chartered Accountant app
rows.summary: CESTAT Chennai held that service tax paid under reverse charge can qualify for CENVAT credit/refund when supported by the payment challan.

rows.title: Custom Duty | CESTAT Chennai Upholds Reclassification of Imported Lauric Acid Under Tariff Item 29159090
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12279 Case Name Hindustan Unilever Ltd. Vs Commissioner of Customs (CESTAT Chennai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Chennai Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Hindustan Unilever Ltd. Vs Commissioner of Customs (CESTAT Chennai) Summary: The three appeals were heard together by the CESTAT Chennai as they involved an identical issue. Appeal Nos. C/41635/2015 and C/41636/2015 challenged Order-in-Appeal Nos. 432/2015 and 433/2015, both dated 24.04.2015, which upheld Order-in-Original Nos. 2/2014 and 1/2014, both dated 14.10.2014. Appeal No. C/41986/2015 challenged Order-in-Appeal No. 566/2015 dated 26.06.2015, which upheld Order-in-Original No. 35347/2015 dated 25.02.2015 confirming demand of duty along with penalty. The appellant had filed Bills of Entry for import of “Lauric Acid”, classifying the goods under Tariff Item 29157090 and seeking clearance on payment of applicable duties. Revenue took the view that the goods were classifiable under Tariff Item 29159090 under “Other”. Revenue further considered the goods assessable to Basic Customs Duty at 7.5% vide Sl. No. 553 of Notification No. 21/2002-Customs, with Additional Duty of Customs at 10% and SAD at 4%. According to Revenue, the incorrect classification had resulted in short levy of duty. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0} Show cause notices were accordingly issued proposing reclassification under Tariff Item 29159090 under “Other”. The appellant filed replies and was afforded opportunities of personal hearing. The Original Authority noted that the importer had filed written submissions and an opinion of a retired Professor, but had not furnished technical details when called upon to do so. The Original Authority therefore considered the competing tariff headings and rejected the declared classification, confirming the proposed reclassification under Tariff Item 29159090 through the respective Orders-in-Original. The appellant thereafter approached the First Appellate Authority against the reclassification and consequential differential duty demands. The Tribunal recorded that the importer did not participate in the appellate proceedings despite opportunity and that the Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed the appeals through Order-in-Appeal Nos. 432/2015, 433/2015 and 566/2015, thereby upholding the Orders-in-Original. Before the CESTAT, the common issue was whether rejection of the declared classification and reclassification of the imported goods by the authorities below was correct. The Tribunal examined the reasoning contained in the Orders-in-Original. The crux of that reasoning was that the imported goods could not be classified under Tariff Item 29157090 because subheading 2915.70 specifically dealt with “Palmitic Acid and Stearic Acid, their salts and esters”. The Original Authority considered Tariff Item 29157090 to be specific and limited to those two fatty acids and their salts and esters and held that it could not be extended to other saturated fatty acids such as Lauric Acid, particularly when the imported goods were neither a salt nor an ester. The Tribunal observed that the appellant had relied upon an opinion but that a copy of the opinion had not been filed before the Tribunal. It also found no other documentary evidence supporting the appellant’s classification claim. The Tribunal therefore found that the appellant’s case consisted of claims and arguments without supporting material. On examining the tariff heading, the Tribunal found that it specifically covered “Palmitic Acid and Stearic Acid, their salts and esters”. Since the appellant did not contend that the imported Lauric Acid was either a salt or ester of Palmitic Acid or Stearic Acid, the Tribunal held that the impugned orders did not call for interference. Accordingly, the CESTAT Chennai dismissed all three appeals and upheld the impugned orders concerning classification and the consequential demands. Revenue felt that the said goods imported wa

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Delhi HC Relegates GST Writ Petition to Statutory Appeal Under Section 107
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12277 Case Name Marginmart Ifosystems Private Limited Vs Assistant Commissioncr CGST (Delhi High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Delhi High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Marginmart Ifosystems Private Limited Vs Assistant Commissioncr CGST (Delhi High Court) Summary: The Delhi High Court considered W.P.(C) 9013/2026 filed by MarginMart IFOSYSTEMS Private Limited, along with CM APPL. 42192/2026 and CM APPL. 42193/2026, challenging a Show Cause Notice dated 27.09.2025 and the consequential order dated 24.03.2026 passed pursuant thereto. The impugned order recorded that proceedings under Section 122(1)(ii) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 were initiated against the Petitioner on the allegation that invoices had been issued without actual supply of goods and inadmissible Input Tax Credit had been passed on to M/s Enriche Retail Private Limited. The order further recorded that, during the investigation, M/s Enriche Retail Private Limited was found to be non-existent at its registered place of business, following which the proceedings culminated in the impugned order. The judgment therefore concerned a challenge to GST proceedings arising from allegations of invoices issued without actual supply and passing on of inadmissible ITC. The Petitioner contended that the Show Cause Notice and consequential order had been issued and passed mechanically and in a predetermined manner, without independent examination qua the Petitioner. It was further submitted that the proceedings were without jurisdiction and violative of the principles of natural justice. On these grounds, the Petitioner urged the High Court to exercise its extraordinary writ jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. The Court noted that the Petitioner admittedly had an efficacious statutory remedy of appeal under Section 107 of the CGST Act. The Court held that the contentions raised by the Petitioner, including the challenges concerning the manner in which the proceedings were initiated and decided, could appropriately be examined by the Appellate Authority in proceedings under Section 107. Accordingly, the Delhi High Court declined to entertain the writ petition in view of the availability of the statutory appellate remedy. The Court expressly stated that it was not expressing any opinion on the merits of the contentions raised by the Petitioner. The Petitioner was relegated to avail the remedy of appeal before the competent Appellate Authority, if so advised. The Writ Petition was consequently disposed of with liberty to the Petitioner to avail the statutory remedy in accordance with law. The Court further clarified that it had not expressed any opinion on the merits of the controversy and that all questions were left open for consideration by the Appellate Authority. The order therefore does not finally adjudicate the allegations concerning invoices, actual supply, inadmissible ITC, jurisdiction or natural justice. Those issues were expressly left open for consideration by the statutory Appellate Authority. The Court’s disposition was confined to declining writ intervention because an efficacious statutory appeal under Section 107 was available. FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF DELHI HIGH COURT 1. Through the present Petition, the Petitioner seeks issuance of a writ in the nature of certiorari for quashing the Impugned Show Cause Notice dated 27.09.2025, and the consequential Impugned Order dated 24.03.2026 passed pursuant thereto. 2. The Impugned Order records that proceedings under Section 122(1)(ii) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 [„the Act‟] were initiated against the Petitioner on the allegation that invoices were issued without actual supply of goods and that inadmissible Input Tax Credit was passed on to M/s Enriche Retail Private Limited. It further records that, during the course of investigation, M/s Enriche Retail Private Limited was found to be non-existent at its registered place of business, and on that basis the proceedings culminated in the passing of the Impugned Order. 3. Admittedly, the Petitioner has an efficacious statutory remedy of appeal under Section 107 of the Act. 4. Learned counsel representing the Petitioner submits that the Impugned Show Cause Notice as well as the consequential Impugned Order have been issued and passed in a mechanical and pre-determined manner, without any independent examination qua the Petitioner. It is further submitted that the proceedings are without jurisdiction and are also violative of the principles of natural justice. On these grounds, it is urged that this Court ought to exercise its extraordinary writ jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. 5. The aforesaid content
rows.summary: Delhi High Court sent a GST challenge back to the statutory appeal process, where the taxpayer was accused of fake invoicing and wrongful input tax credit.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Dibyajyoti Mishra Vs State of Odisha (Orissa High Court) Summary: The petitioner, Dibyajyoti Mishra, approached the High Court of Orissa at Cuttack apprehending arrest in connection with alleged violation of provisions of the GST Act. The petitioner submitted that he was working as a priest in a temple at Rourkela and had been falsely implicated. He had received summons and, on that basis, apprehended that he might be taken into custody. He therefore sought protection by way of pre-arrest bail. The matter was heard by Justice V. Narasingh on 21.08.2026. Learned counsel for the petitioner reiterated the apprehension of arrest. On behalf of the State, learned counsel appeared before the Court. Mr. A. Kedia, learned Junior Standing Counsel, Central GST and Central Excise, on instruction, submitted that in the case at hand assessment had been made raising a demand of Rs.33,05,562/- on account of Financial Year 2018-19. It was further submitted on instruction that the apprehension of the petitioner being taken into custody was misconceived. Upon considering the rival submissions, the High Court did not find force in the petitioner’s submission that there was even any perceptible threat of arrest. The Court accordingly did not grant the requested pre-arrest protection and disposed of the ABLAPL. The Court, however, granted liberty to the petitioner to renew his prayer if there was any fresh cause of action. FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF HIGH COURT OF ORISSA AT CUTTACK 1. Heard learned counsel for the Petitioner and learned counsel for the State. 2. It is submitted that the Petitioner, who is working as a priest in a temple at Rourkela, has been falsely implicated for violation of provisions of GST Act. He has received summons. Therefore, he apprehends arrest and, hence, may be protected by pre-arrest bail. 3. Mr. Kedia, learned Junior Standing Counsel, Central GST and Central Excise, on instruction, submits that in the case at hand assessment has been made raising a demand of Rs.33,05,562/- on account of Financial Year 2018-19. It is further submitted by the learned Junior Standing Counsel, Central GST and Central Excise, on instruction, that the apprehension of the Petitioner being taken into custody is misconceived. 4. On considering the rival submissions, this Court does not find force in the submissions made by the learned for the Petitioner that there is even any perceptible threat of arrest. 5. Accordingly, the ABLAPL stands disposed of. 6. Liberty is given to the Petitioner to renew his prayer if there is any fresh cause of action. rows.title: Income Tax | Gujarat HC Quashes Section 148 Notice for Lack of Live Link with Seized Material
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12363 Case Name Gaurav Santramdas Varma Vs ACIT (Gujarat High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Gujarat High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Gaurav Santramdas Varma Vs ACIT (Gujarat High Court) Summary: The Gujarat High Court considered a writ petition challenging the notice dated 30.03.2025 issued under Section 148 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 for Assessment Year 2021-22. The petitioner had filed his return on 10.03.2022 declaring total income of Rs. 92,80,990/-. He, along with joint purchasers Shri Mrunal Santarambhai and Shri Tarunbhai Santarambhai, purchased land at Moje Adalaj bearing Survey Nos. 184 and 182 through registered sale deeds dated 01.03.2021 for considerations of Rs. 93,00,000/- and Rs. 63,00,000/- respectively. :contentReference[oaicite:0]{index=0} A search under Section 132 was conducted on 28.09.2021 at the premises of B Safal Group and City Estate Management India, a real estate broker providing brokerage services to the B Safal Group. Inquiry registers were seized from the broker. The Revenue relied upon an entry dated 18.06.2020 concerning land at Moje Adalaj, recording Survey Nos. 182, 183, 184, 189 and 190, total area of 8.34 bigha, a rate of 2.70 Q and the name “Krupeshbhai Gajipara”. On the basis of that entry, the Assessing Officer formed the opinion that the petitioner had paid on-money on the purchase of Survey No. 182 and alleged escaped income of Rs. 3,73,56,434/-. A satisfaction note was recorded on 18.03.2025 and approved by the Principal Commissioner of Income Tax-3, Ahmedabad on 22.03.2025. The notice under Section 148 was thereafter issued on 30.03.2025. The petitioner filed objections on 09.01.2026, but no order disposing of those objections was passed, leading to the writ petition. The petitioner contended that the seized register entry substantially predated the actual purchase. The entry was dated 18.06.2020, whereas the land was purchased on 01.03.2021, approximately nine months later. Reliance was also placed on the statement of Shri Pravin Nagjibhai Bavadiya recorded under Section 131, according to which the inquiry registers contained details of land/plots available for sale at different locations near Ahmedabad and did not record concluded transactions or the parties to such transactions. The petitioner further pointed out that the seized entry covered five survey numbers and 8.34 bigha, whereas he and the co-purchasers acquired only Survey Nos. 184 and 182, measuring 2.38 bigha and 1.62 bigha respectively. The entry therefore covered three additional survey numbers and more than double the area actually purchased. The name “Krupeshbhai Gajipara” appearing in the register was also stated to be entirely unconnected with the petitioner, and no inquiry had been made by the Department from that person. Neither the register nor Shri Bavadiya’s statement referred to the petitioner or the co-purchasers. The Revenue opposed the petition contending that the inquiry registers were structured business records maintained by a professional real estate broker and were not dumb documents. It relied on the broker’s statement and the statutory presumptions under Sections 132(4A) and 292C. According to the Revenue, verification of revenue records through the AnyROR portal established an asset-based nexus because the survey numbers in the register corresponded with the petitioner’s purchase. It relied on Explanation 2(iv) to Section 148, under which documents seized from another person that “pertain to” or contain information that “relates to” the assessee may constitute information suggesting escapement of income. The Revenue submitted that discrepancies in dates, area and names concerned the merits and should be examined during assessment proceedings. The Revenue also relied upon Raymond Woollen Mills Ltd. vs. ITO, CIT vs. Rajesh Jhaveri Stock Brokers (P.) Ltd. and Anshul Jain vs. PCIT to contend that, at the notice stage, the Court should not examine the merits or sufficiency of the material in the manner applicable at final assessment. The High Court, however, examined the seized inquiry register itself and found that the entry dated 18.06.2020 predated the petitioner’s actual purchase by approximately nine months. In the circumstances, the Court held that the entry could, at best, be viewed as a market survey reflecting the asking rate for land available for sale at Moje Adalaj on that date. The statement of Shri Bavadiya also confirmed that the registers contained details of land/plots available for sale. The Court therefore held that the entry could not be treated as a record of a transaction executed by the petitioner. The Court further considered the evidentiary value of the seized register in light of Shri Bavadiya’s own
rows.summary: Gujarat High Court struck down a tax reassessment notice, ruling the seized documents did not clearly connect to the taxpayer’s property purchase.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Mohmedmunaf Noormohmed Cambaywala Vs ITO (Gujarat High Court) Summary: The Gujarat High Court allowed the writ petition filed by Mohmedmunaf Noormohmed Cambaywala and quashed the notices issued under Section 148 of the Income Tax Act, 1961, along with the subsequent proceedings and reassessment order. The petition arose from reassessment proceedings initiated by the Income Tax Department by invoking the pre-01.04.2021 provisions of Section 148 of the Income Tax Act. Subsequently, notices were issued under Section 148A(b) of the amended Act, which came into force with effect from 01.04.2021. An order under Section 147 read with Sections 250 and 144B was thereafter passed on 21.03.2026. Before the Gujarat High Court, it was demonstrated that the issue concerning notices issued under Section 148 prior to 01.04.2021 and notices under Section 148A(b) under the amended reassessment regime had been considered by the Supreme Court in Union of India & Ors. Vs Rajeev Bansal, reported in 2024 SCC OnLine SC 2693. The judgment records that, in relation to Assessment Year 2015-2016, the Revenue had conceded before the Supreme Court that all notices issued on or after 01.04.2021 would have to be dropped because they would not fall within the period prescribed under the Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation and Amendment of Certain Provisions) Act, 2020 (TOLA). The Revenue’s submission before the Supreme Court was that, under the amended provisions including Section 148A(b), notices could have been issued only up to 31.03.2022 and that notices issued thereafter under the new regime were also time-barred. The Gujarat High Court noted that the consequential proceedings, including the order passed under Section 147 read with Sections 250 and 144B dated 21.03.2026, would consequently be bad in law. After hearing both sides, the Court recorded that the legal position placed before it could not be disputed by the learned Senior Standing Counsel appearing for the Revenue. Since the issue was squarely covered by the Supreme Court’s decision in Rajeev Bansal as well as by various decisions of the Gujarat High Court, it quashed all notices challenged in the writ petition and all consequential proceedings, including the reassessment order. Accordingly, the writ petition was allowed in terms of the Supreme Court’s decision in Rajeev Bansal and Rule was made absolute to that extent. Cases Discussed Union of India & Ors. Vs Rajeev Bansal, 2024 SCC OnLine SC 2693 — considered on the validity and limitation of reassessment notices issued under the pre-01.04.2021 regime and the application of TOLA in the context of the amended reassessment provisions. The subsequent notices are issued by invoking Section 148A(b) of the amended Act, which came into force with effect from 01.04.2021. Subsequently, the order under Section 147 read with Section 250 read with Section 144B of the Act has been passed on 21.03.2026. 3. It is demonstrated before us that the issue pertaining to the notices invoking section 148 of the Act (prior to 01.04.2021) and Section 148A(b) of the Act, amended by the Finance Act, 2021 with effect from 01.04.2021, came up for consideration before the Apex Court in case of Union of India and others Vs. Rajeev Bansal reported in 2024 SCC OnLine SC 2693. 4. For the Assessment Year 2015-2016, the Revenue conceded before the Apex Court that all the notices issued on or after 01.04.2021 will have to be dropped as they will not fall during the period prescribed under the Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation and Amendment of Certain Provisions) Act, 2020 (for short “the TOLA”). Consequently, the subsequent proceedings including the order passed under Section 147 read with Section 250 read with Section 144B of the Act, dated 21.03.2026, is also bad in law. 5. Heard both the sides. The position

rows.title: Income Tax | Delhi HC sets aside pre-CIRP demands after IBC resolution plan approval
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12360 Case Name Garg Inox Ltd. & Anr. Vs Union of India & Ors. (Delhi High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Delhi High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Garg Inox Ltd. & Anr. Vs Union of India & Ors. (Delhi High Court) Summary: The Delhi High Court considered a writ petition filed by Garg Inox Ltd & Anr. challenging various demand and payment notices issued in respect of liabilities allegedly arising prior to the initiation of the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) on 25.07.2017. The petitioners sought quashing of demands relating to income tax, provident fund, customs, GST and local authority dues pertaining to periods preceding the CIRP commencement date. Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process had been initiated against Petitioner No. 1 under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC) by an order dated 25.07.2017 passed by the National Company Law Tribunal, New Delhi. Petitioner No. 2 was the Successful Resolution Applicant. The resolution plan submitted by Petitioner No. 2 was approved by the NCLT on 04.12.2018 under Section 31 of the IBC. The petitioners specifically challenged demand notices issued by the Income Tax Department, including a notice dated 29.05.2020 concerning financial year 2009-10 and an assessment order dated 31.03.2016 concerning assessment year 2013-14. The first demand related to Rs.6,83,244/-, comprising demand of Rs.3,38,280/- and interest of Rs.3,44,964/-, with adjustment against TDS refund. The petitioners also referred to other departmental demands arising from periods preceding the CIRP. The Court noted that an earlier order dated 22.07.2021 had captured the central controversy: after approval of the resolution plan by the NCLT, whether demands relating to dues payable for a period preceding commencement of CIRP could subsequently be raised against the successful resolution applicant. The petitioners relied upon the Supreme Court judgment in Ghanshyam Mishra & Sons Private Limited Vs. Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Limited, particularly paragraph 95. The Supreme Court had held that once a resolution plan is duly approved by the Adjudicating Authority under Section 31, claims provided in the resolution plan become binding, while claims not forming part of the resolution plan stand extinguished and cannot subsequently be pursued. Reliance was also placed on the Supreme Court judgment in Essar Steel India Ltd. Committee of Creditors v. Satish Kumar Gupta, where the Court emphasised that a successful resolution applicant cannot be confronted with undecided claims after approval of the resolution plan. The Court observed that all claims should be submitted to and decided by the resolution professional so that the successful resolution applicant knows the liabilities it is taking over and can operate the corporate debtor on a fresh slate. The Delhi High Court further considered its own Division Bench decisions in Ireo Fiverriver Pvt. Ltd. v. Income Tax Department & Anr. and National Sewing Thread Company Limited v. Deputy Commissioner. In the former, the Court had taken note of Essar Steel and Ghanshyam Mishra and held that a successful resolution applicant cannot be saddled with liabilities other than those specified and factored into the resolution plan. In the latter, the Court reiterated that once a resolution plan is approved, the successful resolution applicant takes over the business on a fresh slate. On a combined reading of these authorities, the Court held that once a resolution plan has been approved by the Adjudicating Authority under the IBC, any claim which was not part of that resolution plan stands extinguished and cannot be enforced at a later stage. The Court described the rationale as the “Clean Slate Theory”, intended to provide the resolution applicant with a fresh start free from prior liabilities and to prevent further litigation concerning claims which should have been dealt with during the insolvency resolution process. Applying that principle, the Court found that the impugned claims had arisen prior to 25.07.2017, the date on which CIRP commenced. The demand notice dated 30.09.2019 issued by Respondent No. 4 related to the year 2009-10, while the demand notice dated 18.11.2015 issued by Respondent No. 5 related to 2009-10 and May 2010 to January 2015. The Court therefore held that the “Clean Slate Theory” squarely applied. Accordingly, the writ petition was allowed and the impugned demand notices issued by the respondents concerning claims arising prior to approval of the resolution plan were set aside. rows.summary: Delhi HC held pre-CIRP tax and other government dues are extinguished once an IBC resolution plan is approved.
