Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Shree Karni Electrovision Vs Union of India (Rajasthan High Court) Summary: The Rajasthan High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by M/s Shree Karni Electrovision challenging the validity of Section 16(2)(c) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 read with the Rajasthan Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 and seeking quashing of an order dated 24.11.2022. The petitioner, engaged in supplying electronic goods, had procured goods from M/s Techno Kart India Limited, a retail arm of the Videocon Group, for Rs.59,42,860.91/-. Tax of Rs.13,00,000/-, comprising Rs.6,50,000/- CGST and Rs.6,50,000/- RGST, arose on transactions during December 2017 to January 2018. The petitioner claimed Input Tax Credit on the basis that the supplier was responsible for depositing the corresponding tax with the Government. The supplier subsequently became insolvent and proceedings were initiated under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1} The petitioner contended that the respondents had failed to lodge their tax claim against the supplier in the insolvency proceedings and could not thereafter impose the unpaid tax liability upon the purchaser under Section 16(2)(c). Reliance was placed upon Ghanashyam Mishra & Sons (P.) Ltd. Vs. Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Co. Ltd., [2021] 126 taxmann.com 132 (SC), on the effect of approval of a resolution plan and extinguishment of claims not forming part of the plan. The respondents, however, argued that Section 16(2)(c) imposes an absolute condition requiring the tax charged on a supply to have actually been paid to the Government and that wrongly availed ITC could consequently be recovered from the purchaser. :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2} The respondents also relied upon Maruti Enterprise through its authorized partner, Jigneshbhai Bharatbhai Tarpara Vs. Union of India & Ors., decided by the Gujarat High Court on 01.05.2026. That decision considered the constitutional challenge to Section 16(2)(c), the doctrine of lex non cogit ad impossibilia and the statutory interaction between Sections 16(2)(c), 41 and 155 and Rule 37A. The Gujarat High Court had held, inter alia, that the conditions in Section 16(2) must be read conjointly, the claimant bears the burden of proving eligibility for ITC, and Section 16(2)(c) does not suffer from constitutional or legal infirmity. :contentReference[oaicite:3]{index=3} The Rajasthan High Court held that Section 16(2)(c), subject to Section 41 of the CGST/RGST Act, constitutes a mandatory condition requiring the tax charged in respect of the supply to be actually paid to the Government. Unless that condition is fulfilled, availment of ITC is prohibited. According to the Court, a purchaser who avails ITC without ascertaining whether the supplier has paid the tax becomes liable to recovery in accordance with law where the supplier has not discharged the liability. :contentReference[oaicite:4]{index=4} The Court further held that the Supreme Court judgment in Ghanashyam Mishra & Sons (P.) Ltd., dealing with the consequences of an approved resolution plan under the IBC, did not dispense with the statutory condition governing the petitioner’s entitlement to ITC under Section 16(2)(c). Finding no ground to interfere with the impugned order dated 24.11.2022, the High Court dismissed the writ petition and disposed of the pending applications. :contentReference[oaicite:5]{index=5} Cases Discussed Ghanashyam Mishra & Sons (P.) Ltd. Vs. Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Co. Ltd.; [2021] 126 taxmann.com 132 (SC), decided on April 13, 2021 — relied upon by the petitioner regarding the effect of an approved resolution plan under the IBC; held not to dispense with the statutory condition governing entitlement to ITC under Section 16(2)(c). Maruti Enterprise through its authorized partner, Jigneshbhai Bharatbhai Tarpara Vs. Union of India & Ors. (R/Special Civil Application No.18080 of 2023 and other connected matters), decided on 01.05.2026 — relied upon by the respondents and considered by the Court on the constitutional validity of Section 16(2)(c), the burden of proving ITC eligibility and the interplay of Sections 16(2)(c), 41 and 155 with Rule 37A. FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF RAJASTHAN HIGH COURT 1. The instant writ petition has been preferred seeking the following reliefs: “It is, therefore, most respectfully prayed that this Hon’ble Court may graciously be pleased to issue an appropriate writ of Mandamus, certiorari and prohibition or any other appropriate order/ direction and kindly: a) To hold tha
rows.summary: The Rajasthan High Court held that a buyer can lose GST input tax credit if the supplier fails to pay the tax to the government.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Delhi High Court Dismisses NSE Divestment PIL for Forum Shopping
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12344 Case Name Parinay Sharma Vs Union of India & Ors. (Delhi High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Delhi High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Parinay Sharma Vs Union of India & Ors. (Delhi High Court) Summary: The Delhi High Court dismissed with exemplary costs of ₹5,00,000/- a Public Interest Litigation filed by Parinay Sharma under Article 226 of the Constitution of India concerning IFCI Limited’s divestment of its shareholding in the National Stock Exchange of India Limited (“NSE”). The PIL sought, inter alia, preservation and production of records, disclosure of ownership, ultimate beneficial ownership and source of funds of DVI Fund (Mauritius) Ltd., Soach Global Opportunities Fund and similarly placed entities, restraint on their participation in NSE’s proposed Offer for Sale, deposit of transfer proceeds in escrow, examination by SEBI of the transfers and transferees, and consideration of the petitioner’s complaint dated 05.06.2026 by SEBI and CBI. The petition stated that IFCI held 24,97,750 equity shares of NSE as on 31.03.2015, representing 5.55% of its paid-up equity share capital, and during FY 2015-16 divested 11,25,000 shares in four tranches for aggregate consideration of ₹440.93 crores. The petitioner alleged that the shares transferred between 15.09.2015 and 01.07.2016 were sold at a valuation lower than a comparable June 2013 transaction and contended that, compared with NSE’s present unlisted-market valuation of approximately ₹5,00,000 crores, the impugned divestment caused a notional loss of approximately ₹12,121.13 crores to IFCI and consequently the public exchequer. NSE opposed the PIL at the threshold, pointing out that the petitioner had already filed W.P. No. 2408/2026, Parinay Sharma v. Securities and Exchange Board of India & Anr., before the Bombay High Court on 02.05.2026, before instituting the Delhi PIL on 05.08.2026, and had not disclosed that proceeding. The Delhi High Court held that suppression of the Bombay writ and the contrary averment made on oath in Paragraph 41 of the PIL were serious. Rule 9(i)(h) of the Delhi High Court (Public Interest Litigation) Rules, 2010 required disclosure of previously filed PILs or letter petitions, including their number, status and outcome. Comparing the two proceedings, the Court found a direct and substantial overlap in the reliefs concerning NSE shareholding, shareholders and ultimate beneficial ownership. The Court held that the petitioner appeared to have resorted to clever drafting to camouflage substantially similar prayers and accepted NSE’s submission that the petitioner had indulged in forum shopping. Relying on State of Uttaranchal v. Balwant Singh Chaufal, (2010) 3 SCC 402; State of M.P. v. Narmada Bachao Andolan, (2011) 7 SCC 639; and State of Jharkhand v. Shiv Shankar Sharma, (2022) 19 SCC 626, the Court reiterated that PIL jurisdiction requires complete candour, full and true disclosure and clean hands, and that suppression of material facts can justify refusal of relief at the threshold. The Court declined to examine the merits of the allegations concerning IFCI’s NSE divestment, held that the petitioner had approached the Court with unclean hands and abused the process through forum shopping, and imposed exemplary costs of ₹5,00,000/- payable to the Delhi High Court Bar Clerks’ Association within two weeks. The request for reduction of costs was rejected and the writ petition was dismissed. :contentReference[oaicite:2]{index=2} Cases Discussed State of Uttaranchal v. Balwant Singh Chaufal, (2010) 3 SCC 402 — cited on preventing misuse of PIL jurisdiction and discouraging petitions instituted with oblique motives. State of M.P. v. Narmada Bachao Andolan, (2011) 7 SCC 639 — cited on the obligation of a PIL petitioner to make full and true disclosure of material facts and approach the Court with clean hands, clean mind, clean heart and clean objective. State of Jharkhand v. Shiv Shankar Sharma, (2022) 19 SCC 626 — cited on non-disclosure of prior similar proceedings and rejection of PILs suppressing material facts. FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF DELHI HIGH COURT 1. The present Writ Petition, stated to be a Public Interest Litigation (“PIL”) under Article 226 of the Constitution of India, 1950 (“Constitution”), seeks directions concerning the divestment of IFCI Limited (“IFCI”) of its shareholding in the National Stock Exchange of India Limited (“NSE”). The Petitioner seeks preservation and production of the complete record; disclosure by DVI Fund (Mauritius) Ltd. (“DVI Fund”), Soach Global Opportunities Fund (“Soach Global”) and similarly placed entities of their ownership, ultimate beneficial ownership and source of funds; restraint on their participation in NSE’s
rows.summary: The Delhi High Court threw out a PIL on IFCI’s NSE share sale, calling it forum shopping and imposing ₹5 lakh in costs.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GST Notice Without Digital or Physical Signature Invalid: Rajasthan HC
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12343 Case Name Deena Paints Limited Vs Assistant Commissioner (Rajasthan High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Rajasthan High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Deena Paints Limited Vs Assistant Commissioner (Rajasthan High Court) Summary: The Rajasthan High Court allowed the writ petition filed by Deena Paints Limited challenging the recovery notice dated 26.12.2025 issued pursuant to an Order-in-Original dated 28.06.2022 and Show Cause Notice dated 19.02.2021, whereby a demand of Rs.1,51,198/- had been raised under Section 73 of the CGST/RGST Act, 2017 towards CGST for the tax period July 2017 to March 2018. The petitioner contended that the recovery proceedings were void ab initio because the Show Cause Notice, Order-in-Original and corresponding summaries uploaded on the GST portal under Rule 142(1)(a) and Rule 142(5) were unsigned and therefore could not constitute valid statutory proceedings. It was further argued that neither the Show Cause Notice nor the Order-in-Original had been served upon the petitioner and that they were merely uploaded on the GSTN portal under the “Additional Notices/Orders” tab. The petitioner also alleged that the documents were vague and cryptic and that the adjudication had been undertaken in breach of statutory procedure and principles of natural justice. The respondents opposed the petition, contending that the Order-in-Original had been duly issued and dispatched to the petitioner’s principal place of business and was also available on the GSTN Portal. They further submitted that proceedings under Sections 78 and 79 of the CGST/RGST Act, 2017 read with Rule 142B were lawful and within the jurisdiction of the competent authority. The High Court, however, noted that the controversy had already been dealt with by it in M/s Mayur Timber Vs. State of Rajasthan & Ors., D.B. Civil Writ Petition No. 14232/2025. The issue was whether a show-cause notice which was neither digitally signed nor physically signed but merely uploaded on the website could be sustained in law. Reproducing its reasoning in M/s Mayur Timber, the Court emphasised Rule 26(3) of the CGST Rules, 2017, which requires notices, certificates and orders to be issued electronically through digital signature certificate, E-signature under the Information Technology Act, 2000, or another notified mode of signature or verification. The Court held that Rule 26(3) uses mandatory language and that electronic issuance and authentication are distinct and cumulative requirements. Mere electronic generation of a document on the portal satisfies issuance but does not satisfy authentication. According to the Court, the signature authenticates the document, fixes responsibility upon the issuing officer and operates as a safeguard against arbitrariness by evidencing application of mind. Applying that view, the High Court held that the Show Cause Notice dated 19.02.2021 was neither digitally nor physically signed and therefore deserved to be quashed. Consequently, the recovery notice dated 26.12.2025 and Order-in-Original dated 28.06.2022 were also quashed. However, the Court granted liberty to the respondents to proceed afresh in accordance with law by issuing a fresh show cause notice and passing such further orders as may be deemed appropriate. All pending applications were also disposed of. Cases Discussed M/s Mayur Timber Vs. State of Rajasthan & Ors., D.B. Civil Writ Petition No. 14232/2025, 2026:RJ-JP:31584-DB — followed on the proposition that a show cause notice and adjudication order bearing neither digital nor physical signature cannot be sustained and that authentication under Rule 26(3) is mandatory. FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF RAJASTHAN HIGH COURT 1. Petitioner approaches this Court seeking quashing and setting aside of the recovery notice dated 26.12.2025, issued pursuant to the Order-in-Original dated 28.06.2022 and Show Cause Notice dated 19.02.2021, whereby a demand of Rs.1,51,198/- was raised under Section 73 of the CGST/RGST Act, 2017 towards CGST for the tax period July 2017 to March 2018. 2. Learned counsel for the petitioner argues that the impugned recovery proceedings are void ab initio, having been founded upon non-existent and unauthenticated documents. He contends that the show cause notice dated 19.02.2021, Order-in-Original dated 28.06.2022 and the corresponding summaries uploaded on the GST portal under Rule 142(1)(a) and Rule 142(5) were unsigned and, therefore, could not constitute valid statutory proceedings. Consequently, in the absence of any valid demand, the consequential recovery notice dated 26.12.2025 issued under Section 79 is wholly unsustainable. 2.1 Learned counsel for the petitioner further argues that the respondent No. 1 issu
rows.summary: Rajasthan HC held a GST notice and related recovery action invalid because they were uploaded unsigned, without proper digital or physical signatures.

rows.title: Custom Duty | Customs SCN Cannot Be Reopened After Settlement Election: Delhi HC
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12342 Case Name NITCO Ltd. And Anr. Vs Customs (Delhi High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Delhi High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); NITCO Ltd. And Anr. Vs Customs (Delhi High Court) Summary: The Delhi High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by M/S NITCO Ltd. and another challenging Clause (e) of Paragraph No.51(ii) of the order dated 14.11.2019 passed by the Customs, Central Excise & Service Tax Settlement Commission, Principal Bench, New Delhi. The controversy was confined to the petitioners’ liability to pay interest on the amount determined pursuant to the Settlement Commission’s order. The proceedings arose from investigations by the Directorate of Revenue Intelligence concerning, inter alia, alleged misuse of EPCG Authorisations. In respect of one EPCG Authorisation issued by DGFT, New Delhi, a Show Cause Notice dated 18.06.2018 demanded duty of Rs.10,29,81,146/- along with interest. The Commissioner of Customs (Export), Mumbai Customs Zone-I adjudicated the SCN on 13.03.2019. Meanwhile, the petitioners approached the Settlement Commission, which by order dated 14.11.2019 settled the duty liability at Rs.6,69,57,333/-. After credit of Rs.1,41,49,366/- already paid, the balance duty liability was Rs.5,28,07,967/-. The petitioners themselves had quantified interest at Rs.1,10,04,634/-, while the Settlement Commission directed the jurisdictional Commissioner to verify and quantify the interest liability and intimate any further amount payable. The jurisdictional Commissioner subsequently recalculated interest at Rs.15,16,65,821/-. The petitioners argued that the SCN dated 18.06.2018 was barred by limitation under Section 28 of the Customs Act, 1962. They contended that the relevant date under Clause (d) of Explanation 1 to Section 28 should be reckoned from 06.11.2006, when duty was paid, or alternatively from 2009, when the alleged short-payment and fraud came to the knowledge of DRI. The respondent relied upon the conclusiveness attached to a Settlement Commission order under Section 127J of the Customs Act, 1962 and contended that, having voluntarily chosen settlement rather than pursuing adjudication proceedings, the petitioners could not reopen the SCN forming the subject matter of that settlement. Examining the limited scope of judicial review over Settlement Commission orders, the High Court relied upon Jyotendrasinhji v. S.I. Tripathi and Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited v. Commissioner of Income Tax, Bangalore & Ors. The Court noted that judicial interference with a Settlement Commission order is confined to limited grounds such as contravention of the statute, prejudice, fraud, bias or malice, and that the High Court cannot scrutinise such an order as an appellate court. The Court held that the petitioners had consciously elected to approach the Settlement Commission rather than pursue the statutory appellate remedy against the adjudication order dated 13.03.2019. Having themselves submitted an interest computation and obtained settlement of the proceedings, they could not isolate the direction concerning interest and use it to reopen the validity of the underlying SCN on limitation. The Court clarified that whether the jurisdictional Commissioner had correctly quantified interest at Rs.15,16,65,821/- was a distinct issue which would have to be examined independently, if otherwise maintainable, with reference to the relevant statutory provision governing interest. However, that issue could not be enlarged into an indirect challenge to the validity of the SCN. The High Court further held that interest is a statutory consequence of liability to pay duty and does not stand extinguished merely because the quantum of duty is settled by the Settlement Commission. The fact that the jurisdictional Commissioner ultimately quantified a substantially higher amount of interest than the petitioners’ own computation could not, by itself, furnish a ground for interference with the Settlement Commission’s order. No material was shown to establish that Clause (e) of Paragraph No.51(ii) was contrary to the Customs Act or that the Settlement Commission had exceeded its jurisdiction. Accordingly, the Court found no ground to interfere with the order dated 14.11.2019; held that the limitation challenge to the SCN dated 18.06.2018 could not be reopened in these proceedings; found no infirmity in the consequential direction for quantification of interest; and dismissed the writ petition along with the pending application. Cases Discussed Jyotendrasinhji v. S.I. Tripathi, 1993 Supp (3) SCC 389 — relied upon for the limited scope of judicial review of Settlement Commission orders. Kotak Mahindra Bank Limited v. Commissioner of Income Tax, Bangalore & Ors., MANU/SC/1
rows.summary: Delhi High Court held customs duty disputes settled by the Commission cannot be reopened later, and the importer must pay the settled interest.

rows.title: Income Tax | ₹20.33 Crore Income Tax Refund to Be Credited Within Two Weeks: Delhi HC
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12341 Case Name Clix Capital Services Private Limited Vs DCIT (Delhi High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Delhi High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Clix Capital Services Private Limited Vs DCIT (Delhi High Court) Summary: The Delhi High Court disposed of the writ petition filed by Clix Capital Services Private Limited, as successor to Clix Finance India Private Limited, after the Department informed the Court that the Assessing Officer had undertaken the requisite exercise and, by a manual order dated 18.08.2026, calculated an amount of Rs.20,33,42,656/- as payable to the petitioner. The Assessing Officer had recently joined on 13.08.2026. The Department submitted that although there had been substantial delay, the delay arose because the company’s legal status and name had changed multiple times pursuant to mergers and amalgamations, requiring tax deducted details and assessment orders standing in the names of various companies to be verified and reconciled. The Department assured the Court that the calculated amount would be credited to the petitioner’s account within two weeks. Senior Counsel for the petitioner pointed out that there was a small error in the refund amount shown as payable. Since the petitioner’s grievance had substantially been redressed, the High Court did not consider it necessary to examine that discrepancy at that stage. Instead, it directed the Assessing Officer, Mr. Nirdesh Gangwar, to meet the petitioner’s representative on 31.08.2026 at a time convenient to him. The purpose of the meeting was to permit the representative to explain the discrepancy, facilitate verification of the record and address issues arising from the intimation under Section 245 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 concerning the proposed withholding/adjustment of refund. The Court accordingly disposed of the petition while expressly reserving the petitioner’s rights to pursue appropriate remedies concerning calculation of the refund and interest. It further clarified that, if necessary, the petitioner would remain free to seek revival of the writ petition and/or appropriate directions. The pending application was also disposed of. FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF DELHI HIGH COURT 1. Mr. Indruj Singh Rai, learned Senior Standing Counsel for Department informed that on 18.08.2026, the respondent-Assessing Officer, who has recently joined (on 13.08.2026) has undertaken the requisite exercise and passed a manual order on 18.08.2026 and calculated an amount of Rs. 20,33,42,656/- payable to the petitioner. 2. While inviting the court’s attention towards the affidavit of the AO which has been filed pursuant to our order of previous date, Mr. Rai submitted that although the delay was substantial, it was caused because of the fact that the company’s legal status changed multiple times and its name also changed on account of mergers and amalgamations, due to which, the details of tax deducted and assessment orders in the name of various companies were to be verified and reconciled. He assured that now the amount has been calculated and the same will be credited within two weeks in the petitioner’s account. 3. While complimenting the officer (who has joined recently) for the efforts he has taken, Mr. Jolly, learned Senior Counsel, pointed out that there is a small error in the amount of the refund shown to have been payable to the petitioner, qua which, we do not deem necessary to dilate upon, at this juncture. 4. While disposing of the petition as petitioner’s grievance in substance has been redressed, we direct the Assessing Officer-Mr. Nirdesh Gangwar, to meet the representative of the petitioner-company on 31.08.2026 at any time as per his convenience, so that the representative can explain the discrepancy, and also facilitate the verification of the record and address the issues arising out of the intimation under Section 245 of the Income Tax Act of 1961, for the proposed withholding/adjustment of refund. 5. With these observations, the petition stands disposed of. 6. Needless to observe that petitioner’s rights to take up its remedy in relation to the calculation of refund/interest shall stand reserved and in case of necessity, the petitioner shall be free to apply for revival of the writ petition and /or for appropriate direction. 7. Pending application stands disposed of. Vs State of Rajasthan (Rajasthan High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Rajasthan High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Cirrus Chemicals Pvt Ltd. Vs State of Rajasthan (Rajasthan High Court) Summary: The Rajasthan High Court allowed the writ petition filed by Cirrus Chemicals Pvt Ltd. challenging the ex-parte Order-in-Original dated 24.02.2025, whereby a demand of Rs.8,28,888/- had been raised, as well as consequential recovery proceedings initiated through notice dated 25.06.2025 under Section 79(1)(c) of the RGST Act, 2017, pursuant to which Rs.15,16,141/- had been recovered from the petitioner’s bank account. The petitioner, engaged in production of liquefied hydrogen gas, challenged the Order-in-Original issued in Form GST DRC-07, which was based upon an alleged mismatch between Input Tax Credit availed in GSTR-3B and credit reflected in GSTR-2A. The petitioner contended that the Show Cause Notice dated 21.11.2024 and reminder-cum-personal-hearing notice dated 06.02.2025 were neither received nor made available on the GST portal in a manner enabling it to respond. It therefore filed no reply and attended no hearing. According to the petitioner, it discovered those notices only when the Order-in-Original dated 24.02.2025 was uploaded. It further contended that the alleged ITC discrepancy was capable of documentary reconciliation, but no opportunity had been provided to place such material on record. After the order, it filed a rectification application dated 01.03.2025 and reminder dated 17.07.2025. During pendency of rectification, Rs.15,16,141/- was recovered from its bank account on 25.06.2025. The petitioner also stated that no copy of the notice in Form GST DRC-13 issued to the bank had been furnished to it. The petitioner argued that the proceedings violated principles of natural justice because no Show Cause Notice was validly served and no personal hearing was granted. Reliance was placed on Section 75(4) of the RGST/CGST Act, which mandates hearing where an adverse decision is contemplated, and Section 169, which prescribes the manner of service. Reliance was also placed on Saral Wire Craft Pvt. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Central Excise & Service Tax, 2017 (50) STR 237 (SC), for the proposition that where a statute prescribes a manner of doing an act, it must be done in that manner or not at all. The respondents, however, maintained that recovery had been lawfully initiated under Sections 78 and 79 of the CGST/RGST Act, 2017 and that efficacious appellate remedies were available under Section 107 and Section 112. The High Court confined its examination to violation of natural justice and statutory notice requirements, expressly declining to enter into merits of the Order-in-Original. It noted that the respondents’ reply contained only a general assertion that adequate opportunity had been granted, while the petitioner’s specific plea that the notices were not uploaded under the correct portal tab had not been specifically answered. On examining the record, the Court found that the Show Cause Notices annexed to the respondents’ reply bore neither physical nor digital signatures. The Court applied Rule 26(3) of the Rules, which mandates electronic issuance and authentication of notices, certificates and orders through digital signature, E-signature or another notified mode. Following its earlier decision in M/s Mayur Timber v. State of Rajasthan & Ors., the Court reiterated that issuance and authentication are distinct cumulative requirements and that mere electronic generation or portal upload does not satisfy authentication. An unsigned notice does not acquire legal existence or binding character and the defect goes to the root of the authority to proceed. Accordingly, the High Court set aside the Order-in-Original dated 24.02.2025 and granted liberty to the respondents to proceed afresh after intimating the petitioner and affording it a personal hearing upon advance notice of the date fixed. The Court cautioned the respondents to strictly comply with procedural requirements in future, observing that failure to do so invites suspicion even where a notice may genuinely have been issued. It further directed that any amount recovered pursuant to the order dated 24.02.2025 be refunded to the petitioner, subject to the passing of a fresh order as directed above. All pending applications were disposed of. Cases Discussed Saral Wire Craft Pvt. Ltd. v. Commissioner of Central Excise & Service Tax, 2017 (50) STR 237 (SC) — relied upon for the proposition that where a statute prescribes a particular manner for performing an act, it must be done in that manner or not at all. M/s Mayur Timber v. State of Rajasthan & Ors
rows.summary: Rajasthan High Court held unsigned GST notices invalid and ordered refund of Rs.15.16 lakh recovered from the company’s bank account.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Abhishek Pathak Vs State of Chhattisgarh (Chhattisgarh High Court) Summary: The Chhattisgarh High Court allowed the first bail application filed by Abhishek Pathak under Section 483 of the Bhartiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, seeking regular bail in connection with Crime No.AD220526005259A of GST/2026, a complaint case of D.G.G.I., Raipur, concerning an alleged offence under Section 69 of the GST Act. The applicant had been in custody since 01.06.2026. According to the prosecution case recorded in the order, DGGI Raipur had sent a show cause notice to the applicant on 07.02.2025 regarding GST Registration rejection under section 21(A) of GST Act. The applicant did not submit a reply at that stage and instead sent an application stating that his mother was sick and admitted to hospital in Uttar Pradesh, supported by a medical prescription. He subsequently sent a reply in March 2025, but the Superintendent was not satisfied. On 03.04.2025, GST registration-related documents, bank statement, computer and other equipment were seized and an amount of Rs.5,46,00,000/- in the bank was stated to have been “fridged”. The applicant thereafter filed WPC No.3364/2025 before the High Court on 12.06.2025, which remained pending. The order records that the applicant was arrested on 01.06.2026 pursuant to an arrest warrant under Section 69 of GST. DGGI Raipur obtained transit remand from CJM Shajapur, Uttar Pradesh and produced the applicant before CJM Raipur on 02.06.2026 for regular remand. The applicant remained in jail thereafter. The order further records that the investigation was pending and no charge sheet had been filed. Learned counsel for the applicant argued that the applicant was innocent and had been falsely implicated on the basis of memorandum statements of accused persons. It was contended that the ingredients of Section 69 of GST Act were not attracted, sufficient material relating to GST and the amount referred to by the prosecution had not been collected, WPC No.3364/2025 remained pending, and the applicant had no criminal antecedents. The State/non-applicant opposed the bail application and submitted that the complaint had already been filed against the applicant. After hearing the parties and perusing the case diary, the High Court took into consideration that the complaint had already been submitted, the applicant had no criminal antecedents as stated in the bail application, he had remained in jail since 01.06.2026, and conclusion of the trial was likely to take some time. The Court therefore held that the applicant was entitled to be released on bail. It directed that Abhishek Pathak be released upon furnishing a personal bond of Rs.1,00,000/- with one solvent surety to the satisfaction of the concerned Court. The bail order was directed to remain in force till disposal of the case. FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF CHHATTISGARH HIGH COURT 1. This is the first bail application filed under Section 483 of the Bhartiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 for grant of regular bail to the applicant who has been arrested in connection with Crime No.AD220526005259A of GST/2026, Complaint case of D.G.G.I, Raipur (C.G.) for the offence under Section 69 of GST Act. 2. The prosecution case, in brief, is that on 07/02/2025 the concerned DGGI Raipur sent a show cause notice to the applicant for GST Registration rejection under section 21(A) of GST Act issued by Superintendent Range -1, Nivideta Pilik sent on signature of Notice to applicant. The applicant at that time not presenting any part of reply. The applicant sent only one application for mother sick and admitted hospital in U.P. and they have to attend the mother and support the medical prescription. After passing of one month the applicant sent the reply of Notice in the month of March 2025 but Superintendent Range-1, was not satisfied with the reply sent by the applicant. On 03/04/2025 all GST registration and Bank statement and amount and computer and another equipment seized and bank amount 5,46,00,000/- has been fridged by the Superintendent and DGGI Raipur. Thereafter applicant filed WPC before this Court which is registered as WPC No.3364/2025 on 12/06/2025 which is pending before this Court. After fridging all documents and equipment the applicant not filed GST in the year of 2024-25 in the month of March. The DGGI Raipur Range has knowledge in WPC No. 3364/2025 dated 12/06/2025 which is pending before this Court as per knowledge of DGGI Raipur Range sent the arrest warrant under section 69 of GST and the applicant was arrested on 01/06/20
rows.summary: The Chhattisgarh High Court granted regular bail to a GST accused, citing prolonged custody and slow trial progress.

rows.title: Corporate Law | NCLT Rejects ₹7 Crore Resolution Plan and Orders Liquidation of Worlds Window Exim
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12338 Case Name Central Bank of India Vs Worlds Window Exim Pvt. Ltd. (NCLT New Delhi) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts NCLT Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Central Bank of India Vs Worlds Window Exim Pvt. Ltd. (NCLT New Delhi) Summary: The captioned petition was preferred by the Resolution Professional in respect of M/s Worlds Window Exim Pvt. Ltd. seeking approval of the Resolution Plan. Central Bank of India had initiated CIRP against the Corporate Debtor alleging default of Rs. 175,96,47,674/- as on 22.03.2024. Following admission of IB-108/PB/2025, the CIRP commenced and Dickey Special Situation Investment Trust, through its Investment Manager Dickey Asset Management Private Limited, submitted the Resolution Plan and emerged as the successful Resolution Applicant. Worlds Window Exim Private Limited was incorporated on 19.01.2006. Although its business was stated as sale and purchase of goods, the Resolution Plan also recorded that the company had been incorporated as an asset-holding company of its group companies and was not operative. The Tribunal noted from the record that the Corporate Debtor had been incorporated only to hold a land bank. Its 99.9999% equity shares were held by Worlds Window Infrastructure and Logistics Pvt. Ltd., while 0.0001% shares were held by Mr. Sandesh, a nominee of Worlds Window Infrastructure & Logistics Pvt. Ltd. The Corporate Debtor had no workers or employees. As on 31.07.2025, claims of the Financial Creditors aggregated to INR 9,97,44,98,649. Against these claims, the Resolution Plan proposed a total payment of only INR 7 crore as upfront payment. The Plan stated that the amount had been arrived at on the basis of the commercial evaluation undertaken by the Resolution Applicant after diligence and examination of the information memorandum. The Tribunal further noted that the Form H certificate recorded the Fair Value of the Corporate Debtor at Rs. 21,30,53,919/- and its Liquidation Value at Rs. 9,42,25,758/-, whereas the Plan Value was only Rs. 7 crore. Punjab National Bank, one of the Financial Creditors, did not vote in favour of the Resolution Plan and therefore emerged as a dissenting creditor. The Tribunal observed that while it may not interfere with valuation of the Corporate Debtor’s assets or reject a Resolution Plan merely because its value is below the liquidation value, a Plan value below liquidation value creates a specific issue concerning the amount payable to a dissenting secured Financial Creditor. The Tribunal considered Section 30(2)(b) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, including Explanation 1, which requires distribution to dissenting Financial Creditors to be fair and equitable and provides that their payment cannot be less than the amount payable under Section 53(1) in liquidation. The Tribunal rejected the contention advanced on behalf of the Resolution Professional that distribution of Rs. 7 crore amongst secured Financial Creditors might nevertheless result in PNB receiving the amount available to it under Section 53. It held that such a situation would result in the amount payable to another secured creditor being contrary to Explanation 1 to Section 30(2). Accordingly, the Tribunal held that the Resolution Plan was violative of Section 30(2)(b) of the Code and could not be approved. The Tribunal also examined Regulation 38(3) of the IBBI (Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016, under which the Resolution Plan is expected to address the cause of default. It found from clause 2.14 of the Plan that the Resolution Applicant was not fully aware of the cause of default. The Plan proposed utilisation of the land securitised with lenders after settlement of their dues and stated that a viable business proposition would be attempted to generate positive returns. The Tribunal expressed its inability to appreciate how such a viable business proposition could be attempted when the Corporate Debtor itself had been created as an asset-holding company. The Tribunal further observed that although creation of an asset-holding company may be legally permissible, the circumstances involving the financial facility availed by such an asset-holding company, assignment of debt by a public bank to an ARC, and a Resolution Plan offering an amount that did not provide the share which a secured Financial Creditor could receive in liquidation had to be viewed with suspicion. The learned counsel representing the Suspended Promoters conceded the Plan. The Tribunal rejected the Resolution Plan for violation of Section 30(2)(b) of the Code as well as Regulation 39(3)(a) of the IBBI (Resolution Process for Corporate Persons) Regulations, 2016. In accordance with Section 33(1)(b), it directed liquidation of the Corporate
rows.summary: NCLT rejected a ₹7 crore resolution plan for Worlds Window Exim and ordered liquidation after finding the company was only a land-holding entity.

rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12337 Case Name State Bank of India Vs Mangalagiri Textile Mills Private Limited (NCLT Amaravati Bench) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts NCLT Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); State Bank of India Vs Mangalagiri Textile Mills Private Limited (NCLT Amaravati Bench) Summary: The National Company Law Tribunal, Amaravati Bench, considered IA (IBC) (LIQ)/3/2026 filed by Mr. Immaneni Eswara Rao, Resolution Professional of Mangalagiri Textiles Mills Private Limited, under Sections 33, 34(1) and 60(5) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, seeking liquidation of the Corporate Debtor and appointment of the Applicant as Liquidator. The application was filed following the failure of the resolution process after the Resolution Applicant did not furnish the Performance Bank Guarantee required under the Request for Resolution Plan. The Corporate Debtor had been admitted into Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 7 of the Code by order dated 25.07.2024. The Resolution Professional thereafter conducted the CIRP, constituted the Committee of Creditors with State Bank of India as its sole member, and undertook the process for inviting and evaluating resolution plans. Five prospective resolution applicants submitted expressions of interest. Following several extensions, negotiations and revisions, the resolution plan submitted by Dr. Goli Nagasaina Rao, the suspended director, was ultimately found to be the only compliant plan and was approved by the CoC through voting dated 09.12.2025. Despite the approval, the Performance Bank Guarantee required under the RFRP was not submitted. The Resolution Applicant repeatedly sought extensions, but failed to furnish the PBG within the additional time granted. During the 25th CoC meeting and its adjourned meeting, the CoC recorded that the failure to submit the PBG rendered the Resolution Plan non-responsive. The CoC subsequently considered whether to restart the resolution process or proceed with liquidation and, through e-voting dated 30.01.2026, decided with 100% voting share to liquidate the Corporate Debtor and approved the appointment of the Applicant as Liquidator. The Corporate Debtor had also remained non-functional and non-operational since December 2021. The Applicant had appointed two IBBI-registered valuers, who reported an average fair value of Rs.75.74 crore and an average liquidation value of Rs.56.89 crore. However, while considering the application, the Tribunal observed that it was not clear whether all assets had been considered by the valuers, particularly because financial statements as on the CIRP commencement date were not available with the RP. The Tribunal also examined the issue of preferential, undervalued, fraudulent and extortionate transactions. The Transaction Auditor had identified fraudulent transactions to the tune of Rs.20.67 crore as probable fraudulent transactions. The RP stated that he was unable to form a conclusive opinion, and the CoC had resolved not to file an application concerning PUFE transactions. However, the Tribunal noted that the Transaction Auditor had categorically given its finding on fraudulent transactions under Section 66 of the Code. The Tribunal observed that it appeared that the RP had delayed discussions on the PUFE transactions in the CoC and consequently delayed filing the PUFE application to accommodate the resolution plan of the suspended director. The Tribunal noted that, being an MSME, the suspended director would otherwise become ineligible under Section 29A(g) of the IBC. Without finally adjudicating the avoidance transactions, the Tribunal directed the Liquidator to examine the Transaction Audit Report, subsequent financial statements supplied by the suspended directors and other information available on record, and take a decision regarding filing appropriate applications under Sections 43, 45, 49, 50 and 66 of the Code within one month. The Liquidator was further directed to examine avoidance transactions and fraudulent or wrongful trading within two months. A further issue arose regarding appointment of the Liquidator. The application had initially sought appointment of the existing RP. However, following the amended provisions of the Code and Regulation 3A of the Liquidation Regulations, the Tribunal required the CoC to recommend a Liquidator from the IBBI panel. The CoC initially recommended Mr. Naga Bhushan Bhagawati and thereafter Mr. Rajesh Chillale, but both names were found not to appear in the IBBI panel for the East Zone for the relevant period. The CoC consequently recommended Mr. Golla Ramakantha Rao, whose name appeared in the IBBI panel for the East Zone for 01.07.2026 to 31.12.2026. The CoC made the recommendation with 100% voting share and enclosed his writt
rows.summary: NCLT ordered Mangalagiri Textile Mills into liquidation after its resolution applicant failed to provide the required performance bank guarantee.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Belated Revaluation Challenge Cannot Reopen Approved CIRP: NCLAT Delhi
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12336 Case Name Santosh R. Shetty Vs Rajan Deshraj Agarwal (NCLAT Delhi) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts NCLAT Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Santosh R. Shetty Vs Rajan Deshraj Agarwal (NCLAT Delhi) Summary: The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, Principal Bench, New Delhi considered two appeals filed by Santosh R. Shetty, suspended Director and promoter of Sristi Hospitality Private Limited, under Section 61 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 against orders of NCLT Mumbai Bench-V. The first appeal challenged dismissal of an application seeking fresh valuation and declaration that the CIRP was void; the second challenged approval of the resolution plan. The Corporate Debtor, an MSME engaged in hospitality, owned Liberty Lodge at Vile Parle West, Mumbai. Saraswat Co-operative Bank Ltd. had extended secured facilities aggregating Rs.21.50 crore in 2017. After defaults and SARFAESI action, the Bank filed a Section 7 application claiming Rs.28,30,42,444.42, which was admitted on 27.02.2023. The Appellant alleged serious procedural irregularities, including short notice for CoC meetings, denial of minutes and the resolution plan, inflated creditor claims, collusion between the Resolution Professional and Successful Resolution Applicant, and substantial undervaluation of Liberty Lodge. He relied on earlier valuations of Rs.57.65 crore in 2017 and Rs.76.72 crore in 2020 and argued that the approved plan consideration was far below the property’s actual value. He further contended that, as promoter of an MSME and personal guarantor, he had a direct stake in the CIRP and was ready to offer a superior proposal. The Resolution Professional, sole financial creditor and Successful Resolution Applicant disputed these allegations. They stated that notices and CIRP documents had been shared, the Appellant attended only the first CoC meeting, did not cooperate with the Resolution Professional, never submitted an EOI or resolution plan, and approached the Adjudicating Authority only after the CoC had approved the plan. They maintained that valuation was conducted by independent IBBI-registered valuers under Regulations 27 and 35 of the CIRP Regulations and that the successful plan, approved with 100% CoC voting share, provided for payment of admitted claims in accordance with the Code. NCLAT first held that the Appellant had locus standi. His status as suspended director coupled with exposure as a personal guarantor created a direct legal and financial stake, and he was a “person aggrieved” under Section 61(1). Relying on Vijay Kumar Jain Vs Standard Chartered Bank & Ors., the Tribunal recognized his right to participation in the CIRP. On delay, however, NCLAT upheld dismissal of the revaluation application. The Appellant was aware of the CIRP, CoC meetings and pendency of the plan-approval application but filed his challenge more than eight months after CoC approval and after orders on the approval application had been reserved. Such a belated challenge was inconsistent with the time-bound framework of the IBC. On alleged CIRP violations, NCLAT noted that IBBI had treated non-supply of the seventh CoC minutes as a procedural lapse rather than material irregularity, and that the IBBI order had attained finality. Although the Tribunal held that the Appellant ought to have received the seventh CoC minutes and was entitled to participate in CoC meetings, it found no material irregularity sufficient to invalidate the CIRP. The allegations of inflated claims and misconduct were also not substantiated by contemporaneous evidence. On valuation, NCLAT held that valuation undertaken by IBBI-registered valuers appointed after commencement of CIRP, in accordance with Regulations 27 and 35, is the relevant valuation for the CoC. Pre-CIRP valuations do not govern the statutory process. Valuation is intended to guide the CoC, which is not bound to approve a plan at or above liquidation value. Once the CoC accepts the statutory valuation and approves a resolution plan, a suspended director cannot reopen the valuation merely on allegations of commercial inadequacy. The Tribunal relied inter alia on Maharashtra Seamless Limited Vs Padmanabhan Venkatesh & Ors., Ramkrishna Forgings Limited, M.K. Rajagopalan, K. Sashidhar Vs Indian Overseas Bank & Ors. and Committee of Creditors of Essar Steel India Limited Vs Satish Kumar Gupta & Ors.. NCLAT further rejected the contention that the Appellant was denied an opportunity to submit a competing plan. The statutory process required an EOI and a resolution plan compliant with Section 25(2)(h), Regulation 36A, Form G and Section 30. An investor commitment letter or informal willingness could not substitute for a resolution plan submitted within the prescribed proc
rows.summary: NCLAT held a belated valuation challenge cannot undo an approved insolvency resolution process, even if the promoter alleges procedural irregularities.

rows.title: Corporate Law | NCLAT Restores Right to File Reply in Section 9 IBC Proceedings Despite Counsel’s Procedural Default
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12335 Case Name Hannu Steels Private Limited Vs Rathi Powertech Global Private Limited (NCLAT Delhi) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts NCLAT Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Hannu Steels Private Limited Vs Rathi Powertech Global Private Limited (NCLAT Delhi) Summary: The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, Principal Bench, New Delhi, allowed the appeal filed by Hannu Steels Private Limited against the order dated 08.12.2025 passed by the National Company Law Tribunal, New Delhi Bench-IV, in CP (IB) No. 567/ND/2025. The NCLT had closed the Appellant’s right to file reply in proceedings initiated under Section 9 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. The dispute arose from a License User Agreement dated 01.03.2022 between Hannu Steels Private Limited and Rathi Powertech Global Private Limited. Rathi Powertech, owner of the “POWERTECH” trademark for manufacture and marketing of TMT Bars, had granted Hannu Steels a licence to use the trademark against a monthly licence fee of Rs.23,00,000/- plus applicable GST. The agreement was subsequently extended by an Addendum dated 28.02.2023 until 28.02.2025, with the monthly royalty/licence fee increased to Rs.30,00,000/- plus applicable GST. Clause 20 of the agreement permitted Hannu Steels to terminate the arrangement by giving three months’ advance written notice in the event of breach, non-feasibility, non-viability or any other unforeseen reason, while continuing royalty payments during the notice period. On 03.06.2024, the Commission for Air Quality Management directed closure of Hannu Steels’ manufacturing unit under Section 12(2)(xi) of the Commission for Air Quality Management in National Capital Region and Adjoining Areas Act, 2021. Hannu Steels thereafter issued a termination notice dated 10.06.2024 invoking Clause 20 and stating that the agreement would terminate with effect from 10.09.2024. Rathi Powertech subsequently alleged non-payment of royalty/licence fee for part of September 2024 and for October 2024 to February 2025 and filed a Section 9 application before the Adjudicating Authority claiming operational debt arising from unpaid licence fees. The Company Petition was filed on 19.10.2025 and registered on 29.10.2025. On 19.11.2025, a proxy counsel appeared for Hannu Steels, accepted notice and was granted one week to file a reply. When the matter was taken up on 08.12.2025, the Adjudicating Authority declined the request for adjournment and closed Hannu Steels’ right to file reply. A subsequently engaged counsel appeared on 05.01.2026 and sought an opportunity to place the defence on record, but the request was declined. Before the NCLAT, Hannu Steels sought condonation of a seven-day delay in filing the appeal. It submitted that it became aware of the impugned order only on 26.12.2025 after independently checking the Adjudicating Authority’s website and after unsuccessful attempts to contact its erstwhile counsel. It contended that the delay was attributable to the previous counsel and was neither deliberate nor intentional. The Appellant relied, among others, on Ramchandra Dallaram Choudhary v. Adani Infrastructure & Developers Pvt. Ltd., Rafiq & Anr. v. Munshilal & Anr. and Dwarika Prasad (Dead) through LRs v. Prithvi Raj Singh. The Respondent opposed the appeal, contending that the Appellant had been duly served, had appeared through counsel, had received one week to file its reply and had failed to comply with the direction. It argued that no sufficient cause had been demonstrated and that the Appellant could not shift responsibility to its counsel. Reliance was placed on Salil Dutta v. T.M. & M.C. (P) Ltd., Rajneesh Kumar v. Ved Prakash, Moddus Media Private Ltd. v. Scone Exhibition Pvt. Ltd., R Mall Developers Pvt. Ltd. v. Lemon Chilli Veg Gourmet Foods LLP and SCB Steels Pvt. Ltd. v. —-. The NCLAT first considered the limitation issue. It noted that the appeal was filed seven days beyond the prescribed thirty-day period but that the delay fell within the additional fifteen-day period contemplated by the proviso to Section 61(2) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. Considering the explanation furnished by the Appellant and the fact that the delay was only seven days, the Tribunal was satisfied that sufficient cause had been shown and condoned the delay. On the substantive procedural issue, the NCLAT observed that regulation of proceedings and case management ordinarily fall within the procedural discretion of the Adjudicating Authority and such discretion should not be lightly interfered with. However, that discretion must remain consistent with natural justice and a fair and meaningful opportunity to present a case. The Tribunal agreed that the contractual disputes underlying the Section 9 proceedings we
rows.summary: NCLAT held a company should not lose its chance to respond in an IBC claim because of its lawyer’s procedural lapse.

rows.title: Corporate Law | NCLT Guwahati Admits Section 7 IBC Petition Over Rs.55.45-Crore Default
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12334 Case Name IL&FS Financial Services Limited Vs Adhunik Meghalaya Steels Private Limited (NCLT Guwahati) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts NCLT Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); IL&FS Financial Services Limited Vs Adhunik Meghalaya Steels Private Limited (NCLT Guwahati) Summary: The National Company Law Tribunal, Guwahati Bench, considered a petition filed by IL&FS Financial Services Limited under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 read with Rule 4 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy (Application to Adjudicating Authority) Rules, 2016, seeking initiation of Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process against Adhunik Meghalaya Steels Private Limited. The Financial Creditor claimed an unresolved financial debt of Rs. 55,45,97,395/- as on 15.11.2023 arising from a term loan facility sanctioned up to Rs. 30 crore under a Loan Agreement dated 27.02.2015, of which Rs. 24,44,44,456/- was disbursed on 17.03.2015 after adjustment of upfront interest. The Corporate Debtor had failed to repay the quarterly instalments. Its account was classified as NPA on 01.03.2018, followed by an Event of Default Notice dated 10.07.2018 and a Recall Facility Notice dated 10.08.2018. The Information Utility record reflected 01.03.2018 as the date of default. The Financial Creditor also relied on acknowledgments in the Corporate Debtor’s audited financial statements, including the financial statement approved on 12.08.2020, and on the Supreme Court’s orders concerning exclusion of the period from 15.03.2020 to 28.02.2022 for limitation purposes. The Corporate Debtor opposed the petition, principally contending that it was barred by limitation and that the Financial Creditor had failed to properly realise pledged securities. It asserted that 2,52,17,391 shares of Adhunik Metaliks Limited had been pledged, with an approximate value of Rs. 50 crore at the time of pledge, and that the Financial Creditor had realised Rs. 8,30,61,278/- from invocation of pledged shares while continuing to hold 78,86,958 shares. It alleged that the recoveries had been appropriated substantially towards interest rather than principal and that the Financial Creditor’s conduct amounted to misconduct and abuse of the insolvency process. The Financial Creditor maintained that recoveries from pledgers/guarantors did not affect the Corporate Debtor’s liability, that the amounts realised had been duly accounted for in the Section 7 claim, and that the remaining default substantially exceeded the statutory threshold. It also relied on the Supreme Court’s judgment dated 30.07.2025, which had set aside the earlier NCLT and NCLAT orders on limitation and remitted the matter for decision on merits treating the Section 7 application as filed within limitation. On the first issue, the Tribunal held that the loan transaction satisfied the ingredients of a “financial debt” under Section 5(8) of the Code because money had been disbursed against consideration for the time value of money. On default, it found that the Corporate Debtor had failed to repay the instalments and that the NPA classification, recall notices and Information Utility record established the occurrence of default. On limitation, the Tribunal held that the issue no longer survived for determination. It noted that its earlier order dated 16.05.2024 dismissing the application on limitation had been affirmed by the NCLAT on 25.03.2025, but both orders were subsequently set aside by the Supreme Court on 30.07.2025. The Supreme Court had held that, reckoning the acknowledgment dated 12.08.2020 and excluding the period from 15.03.2020 to 28.02.2022, the application filed on 15.01.2024 was within time. The NCLT therefore treated the limitation objection as concluded and rejected it. On the pledged securities, the Tribunal examined Clause 6.2(b) of the Pledge Agreement. It found that the clause conferred upon the Financial Creditor a contractual right, but not an obligation, to sell or otherwise enforce the pledged securities after an Event of Default, subject to the stipulated notice requirements. The expression “shall be entitled (but not bound)” was treated as making enforcement permissive rather than mandatory. The Tribunal therefore held that the timing, manner and extent of enforcement fell within the Financial Creditor’s commercial discretion and did not affect the existence of the financial debt or occurrence of default. The Tribunal further found that notices had been issued before enforcement and that the Corporate Debtor had not disputed the disbursement of Rs. 24,44,44,456/-, the NPA classification on 01.03.2018, the recall notices or the occurrence of default. Even after taking the Corporate Debtor’s asserted recoveries of Rs. 8,30,61,278/- into account, the amount cl
rows.summary: NCLT Guwahati admitted IL&FS Financial Services’ insolvency petition against Adhunik Meghalaya Steels over an alleged Rs.55.45-crore loan default.

rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12333 Case Name Suresh Chand Goyal Vs ACIT (ITAT Delhi) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2023-2024 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Delhi Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Suresh Chand Goyal Vs ACIT (ITAT Delhi) Summary: The Delhi Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal allowed the appeals of Suresh Chand Goyal and Meera Goyal for Assessment Year 2023-24, deleting additions made under Section 69A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 in respect of cash found during a search conducted in the Goyal Group. The search was conducted on 10.01.2023. Cash of Rs.1,10,00,000/- was found in Locker No. 542 maintained with South Delhi Vaults & Credits Ltd., while cash of Rs.14,50,000/- was found at B-45, Maharani Bagh, New Delhi. Additions of Rs.1,10,00,000/- were made in the hands of Meera Goyal and Rs.10,00,000/- in the hands of Suresh Chand Goyal. Cash was also found at various other entities of the Goyal Group. In aggregate, cash of Rs.3,74,65,604/- was found, out of which Rs.3,59,99,000/- was seized. The assessees explained that the cash found and seized formed part of duly recorded cash balances maintained by various entities of the Goyal Group, particularly M/s Goyal Capital MG Gases Pvt. Ltd. They relied upon cash books, audited financial statements, ledgers, reconciliation and other supporting documentary evidence. According to the assessees, aggregate cash-in-hand available with the Goyal Group as on the date of search was Rs.4,10,60,052/-, which was sufficient to explain the entire seized cash of Rs.3,59,99,000/-. The Assessing Officer did not accept this explanation and relied upon Tally data available during the search, which reflected cash-in-hand of only Rs.54,20,908/- in the books of certain group entities. The AO consequently restricted the cash attributable to M/s Goyal MG Gases Pvt. Ltd. to Rs.8,54,320/- instead of Rs.3,69,02,334/- and denied credit for the balance while making additions under Section 69A in the hands of the appellants and other group concerns. Before the Tribunal, the assessees contended that the approach was inconsistent because M/s Goyal MG Gases Pvt. Ltd. had itself been assessed pursuant to the same search and the very same AO had accepted cash-in-hand of Rs.3,69,02,334/- as on the date of search. It was submitted that the Tally data relied upon during the search did not contain complete financial records of all group concerns because some premises could not be searched and the corresponding records were therefore unavailable during the search. The Tribunal noted that the same issue had already arisen in the case of another Goyal Group entity, Faridabad Implements Pvt. Ltd., in ITA No. 4591/Del/2025. The co-ordinate bench had considered cash of Rs.69,99,000/- found in a locker, out of which Rs.24,58,590/- was seized, and had held that the availability of cash-in-hand of Rs.3,69,02,334/- in the books of M/s Goyal MG Gases Pvt. Ltd. had never been disputed by the Department. Accordingly, credit for such recorded cash was required to be granted while explaining the cash found during search. The co-ordinate bench had consequently deleted the addition of Rs.25,58,590/- under Section 69A. Following that reasoning, the Tribunal accepted the assessees’ explanation that the cash-in-hand of Rs.3,69,02,334/- in M/s Goyal MG Gases Pvt. Ltd. had been accepted as duly recorded in its books and was therefore explained. Since the issue was also covered by the decision in the case of the group entity, the Tribunal held that the additions made in the hands of Suresh Chand Goyal and Meera Goyal were liable to be deleted. Accordingly, both appeals were allowed. Cases Discussed Faridabad Implements Pvt. Ltd. — ITA No. 4591/Del/2025, co-ordinate bench decision concerning cash found during the same search action and credit for recorded cash-in-hand of M/s Goyal MG Gases Pvt. Ltd. FULL TEXT OF THE ORDER OF ITAT DELHI These appeals preferred by the Assessee against the order of the Ld. Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals)-30, New Delhi (hereinafter referred to as the First Appellate Authority or ‘the ld. FAA’ for short) in appeals filed before him against the orders of the ld. Assessing Officer (hereinafter referred to as the Ld. AO, for short) passed u/s 143(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (hereafter referred to as ‘the Act’). Further details of the orders of the lower authorities are as under: – ITA No. & AY Ld. FAA who passed the appellate order Appeal No. & Date of order of the Ld. FAA AO who passed the assessment order & Date of order 5716/D/25 2023-24 CIT(A)30 New Delhi DIN No : ITBA/APL/M/250/2025-26/1080185221(1) Dated: 30.08.2025 ACIT, CC-31 New Delhi Dated 27.03.2025 5732/D/25 2023-24 CIT(A)-30 New Delhi DIN No : ITBA/APL/M/250/2025-26/1080514009(1) Dated: 10.09.2025 ACIT, CC-
rows.summary: Delhi ITAT held recorded cash balances can’t be taxed as unexplained income when supported by books, deleting Section 69A additions.

rows.title: Custom Duty | CESTAT Sets Aside Chapter 78 Classification for Imported Lead-Bearing Material
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12332 Case Name Mittal Pigments Pvt. Ltd. Vs C.C. Mundra (CESTAT Ahmedabad) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Ahmedabad Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Mittal Pigments Pvt. Ltd. Vs C.C. Mundra (CESTAT Ahmedabad) Summary: The Customs, Excise & Service Tax Appellate Tribunal, West Zonal Bench at Ahmedabad, considered the second round of litigation concerning the classification of imported lead-bearing material declared as “Lead Concentrate” under CTH 26070000. The Revenue contended that the goods were Lead Waste/Scrap classifiable under CTH 7802, more particularly CTI 78020090, and that powdered lead scrap/waste was restricted for import under the applicable Foreign Trade Policy. The matter had earlier been decided by the Tribunal in favour of the party, but the Supreme Court, in Commissioner of Customs, Mundra vs Mittal Pigments Private Limited, reported at 2022 (380) ELT 243 (SC), set aside the earlier Tribunal order because the rival submissions had not been considered and the order contained virtually no reasons. The appeal was restored for fresh disposal, with all rights and contentions on merits kept open. The record contained conflicting laboratory reports. Customs Laboratory, Kandla reported material having characteristics consistent with lead concentrate, whereas Customs Laboratory, CH Nhava Sheva reported that the goods were other than Lead Concentrate and had characteristics of used lead battery scrap. CRCL, New Delhi issued reports concerning the powder and also separately examined metallic/plastic pieces. Other reports concerning factory samples and remnant samples were not uniform. The Tribunal ultimately examined the reports and the composition of the samples in determining whether the Revenue could sustain classification under heading 7802. The Department relied upon the statement of Shri Ramesh Kumar Agarwal; load-port customs export documents; Pre-Shipment Inspection Certificates; Country of Origin Certificates; Form 9 under the Hazardous Wastes (Management, Handling and Transboundary Movement) Rules, 2008; the nature of the importers’ secondary metallurgical plants; their use of rotary furnaces; the absence of silver production; correspondence from the Central Pollution Control Board; and technical literature concerning primary and secondary lead production. The Department also relied upon judicial precedents concerning classification, redemption fine and confiscation. The appellants relied upon the chemical composition shown in the laboratory reports, common parlance, tariff provisions, HSN material, the conflicting reports and the decision in Gravitas India Ltd. v. Commissioner of Customs, Mundra. While analysing the conflicting reports, the Tribunal referred to the principle that, where scientific reports conflict, the basis of scientific investigation is to be preferred over an opinion without basis. It considered precedents including Jenson Enterprises vs Collector of Customs, Cochin and Another, Gastrade International vs CC Kandla, Hewlett Pack and India Sales Pvt. Ltd. vs Comm. Of Cus. (Import) Nhava Sheva, C.C., Mumbai vs Dilip Kumar and Co. and CC Mundra vs Sunrise Traders. The Tribunal also considered the earlier decision in Gravitas India Ltd. v. Commissioner of Customs, Mundra, which arose from the same investigation and concerned materially similar classification and evidentiary issues. The Tribunal examined the tariff headings and noted that “concentrate” was not defined in the tariff. It contrasted heading 2607, covering lead ores and concentrates, with heading 7802, covering lead waste and scrap. On the reports before it, the Tribunal found that the material was primarily composed of lead oxide and lead sulphate, with lead in metallic form present only in very small or minuscule quantities. It observed that lead oxide was specifically covered under heading 2824 and sulphates under heading 2833, whereas Chapter 78 applied to lead in metallic/primary form. On this reasoning, the Tribunal held that the Revenue’s proposed classification under heading 78020090 could not be sustained. It further recorded that, since the Revenue’s classification was not applicable to the goods, it was unnecessary to pronounce upon various grounds concerning the sample-drawing process, the conflicting reports, the benefit of doubt and whether the Department could independently seek retesting on the ground that a particular laboratory was not competent. The Tribunal accordingly set aside the impugned order classifying the goods under Chapter 78 and allowed the appeals. It concluded that the case of the Department could not be sustained and that the classification indicated by the party deserved to be undisturbed. Cases Discussed Commissioner of Customs, Mundra
rows.summary: CESTAT ruled the imported lead-bearing material was not lead scrap under restricted customs code 7802, affecting import classification and duty treatment.
