rows.title: Custom Duty | CESTAT Bangalore Upholds Customs Duty & Interest, Reduces Redemption Fine on Smuggled Bike
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12331 Case Name Anuj John Vs Commissioner of Customs (CESTAT Bangalore) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Bangalore Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Anuj John Vs Commissioner of Customs (CESTAT Bangalore) Summary: The appellant, Shri Anuj John, had purchased a Yamaha R-1 motorbike bearing registration No. MH 06 AR 8899 from Shri Mohammad on 10.04.2013. Acting on specific intelligence, the bike was recovered from a workshop. Verification from the RTO authorities showed that the address of the recorded owner was fake, while verification of the Bill of Entry disclosed that Bill of Entry No. 110190 dated 29.05.2008 was fake/fabricated and no customs duty had been paid. The original authority therefore ordered confiscation and imposed redemption fine of Rs. 50,000/- and penalty of Rs. 20,000/- under Section 112 of the Customs Act, 1962. The Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the order but dropped the penalty under Section 112. The appellant challenged the order before the Bench. The appellant contended that the bike had been imported through Indira Gandhi International Airport and that he had possessed the Bill of Entry, insurance policy documents, challan No.99975892 dated 30.05.2008 and a sale letter signed by M/s. Galaxy Trading. He stated that he purchased the bike from Mr. Mohammad in Bangalore for Rs. 5,00,000/- in 2013 under bona fide belief that the documents were genuine. He therefore argued that duty could not be collected from him and redemption fine could not be imposed. He relied on Commissioner of Customs (Import), Bombay vs. VXL India Ltd., Shanoob M.S. vs. Commissioner of Customs, Cochin and HCL HP Ltd. Vs. Commissioner of Customs on limitation. The Revenue submitted that the documents were fake and the import was fraudulent, so limitation did not arise. Reliance was placed on Commissioner of Customs (Preventive) vs. AAFLOAT Textiles (I) Pvt. Ltd. and Mercedes Benz India Pvt. Ltd. Vs. Commissioner of Customs, Delhi. The Revenue also submitted that, since duty had not been paid at import, the appellant was liable to duty and redemption fine. The Tribunal found it admitted that the motorbike had been smuggled illegally without payment of duty, that the RTO owner was fictitious and that the Bill of Entry was fake/fabricated. It held that the goods were liable to confiscation under Section 123(5) of the Customs Act, 1962. The principal challenge was limitation and the appellant’s claimed bona fide belief. The Tribunal found that the Revenue came to know of the fraudulent illegal import only on 17.04.2013 and that the show-cause notice dated 19.08.2013 was therefore within time. In addressing limitation, the Tribunal relied on the Supreme Court’s discussion in Commissioner of Customs (Preventive) vs. AAFLOAT Textiles (I) Pvt. Ltd. concerning fraud, forged documents and caveat emptor. The Tribunal treated the forged/fake nature of the documents as sufficient to extend the limitation period and rejected the appellant’s time-bar objection. The Tribunal then considered the liability to pay duty and interest when confiscated goods are redeemed on payment of fine. It relied on the Supreme Court’s decision in Navayuga Engineering Co. Ltd. vs. Union of India, which explains the relationship between confiscation, redemption under Section 125, and the assessment and determination of duty and interest. The Tribunal noted the Supreme Court’s principles that customs duty liability arises in connection with redemption under Section 125(2), that the duty obligation is distinct from the confiscation fine, and that Section 28 operates for assessment and determination of the duty and other charges. The Tribunal also considered Union of India v. M/s Security and Finance (P.) Ltd., which distinguished the obligation to pay import duty from the separate liability arising from confiscation, penalty and fine. It noted that Parliament subsequently introduced Section 125(2) to clarify that, in addition to fine, the owner or person referred to in Section 125(1) is liable to duty and charges payable in respect of the goods. The Tribunal further considered Fortis Hospital Ltd. v. Commr. of Customs, Import, where the Supreme Court held that the Section 125(2) duty liability is triggered when the option to pay fine and redeem the goods is actually exercised. The Tribunal concluded that the liability to pay duty and other charges under Section 125(2) arises when the owner exercises the redemption option and the Department accepts it. It further held that the decision in Jagdish Cancer and Research Centre does not establish that calculation, determination or assessment of duty arising under Section 125 cannot be made under Section 28. On interest, the Tribunal relied on the Supreme Court’s reasoning
rows.summary: CESTAT Bangalore upheld customs duty and interest on a smuggled bike, but reduced the redemption fine for the owner.

rows.title: Income Tax | Delhi HC Allows TDS Credit to Employee Despite Kingfisher Airlines’ Non-Deposit
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12330 Case Name Yatish Saxena Vs ACIT (Delhi High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Delhi High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Yatish Saxena Vs ACIT (Delhi High Court) Summary: The Delhi High Court allowed the writ petition filed by Yatish Saxena and quashed demands raised for Assessment Years 2009-10, 2010-11, 2011-12 and 2012-13 to the extent they arose from non-grant of credit for Tax Deducted at Source (TDS) deducted by Kingfisher Airlines, the petitioner’s erstwhile employer. The petitioner contended that demands of Rs. 4,52,188/- for AY 2009-10, Rs. 2,04,369/- for AY 2010-11, Rs. 49,48,730/- for AY 2011-12 and Rs. 26,29,922/- for AY 2012-13, including interest, had been raised through intimations under Sections 143(1) and 154 of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The demands arose because credit for TDS deducted by Kingfisher Airlines from the petitioner’s salary was not granted. The TDS amounts involved were Rs. 1,08,367/- for AY 2009-10, Rs. 10,88,879/- for AY 2010-11, Rs. 13,57,302/- for AY 2011-12 and Rs. 7,14,967/- for AY 2012-13. The petitioner submitted that the issue was squarely covered by the Delhi High Court’s judgment dated 01.10.2024 in Satwant Singh Sanghera v. The Assistant Commissioner of Income Tax & Anr. The Revenue’s counsel was not in a position to dispute the legal position stated by the petitioner. On merits, the Court observed that the respondent could perhaps have been justified in disallowing the TDS collected by Kingfisher Airlines because the deductor had not deposited the amount. However, the petitioner could not be blamed for the deductor’s failure and could not consequently be deprived of his legitimate right, in accordance with the principle laid down in Satwant Singh Sanghera. The Court therefore allowed the writ petition and quashed and set aside the impugned demands for AYs 2009-10, 2010-11, 2011-12 and 2012-13 insofar as they related to non-grant of credit for TDS deducted by Kingfisher Airlines. The relief was expressly confined to the amounts deducted by Kingfisher Airlines. The Court clarified that any other demand raised by the Assessing Officer would remain unaffected. The writ petition, along with the pending applications, was accordingly disposed of. Cases Discussed Satwant Singh Sanghera v. The Assistant Commissioner of Income Tax & Anr., W.P.(C) 13765/2024, judgment dated 01.10.2024. FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF DELHI HIGH COURT 1. Learned counsel for the petitioner contended that for the Assessment Years 2009-10, 2010-11, 2011-12, and 2012-13 demands of Rs. 4,52,188/- (Ref No. 2010200910040512521T), Rs. 2,04,369/- (Ref No. 20172010101599218801), Rs. 49,48,730/- (Ref No. 2016201137049076722T) and Rs. 26,29,922/- (Ref No. 2013201237013914932T) including interest have been raised by way of intimations under Sections 143(1) and 154 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 (hereinafter referred to as ‘the Act of 1961’) against the petitioner because the credit of TDS which Kingfisher Airlines (erstwhile employer) had deducted from the salary of the petitioner amounting to Rs. 1,08,367/- for AY 2009-10, Rs. 10,88,879/- for AY 2010-11, Rs. 13,57,302/- for AY 2011-12, and Rs. 7,14,967/-for AY 2012-13 was not given. 2. It is contended that the issue involved in the present writ petition is squarely covered by a judgment dated 01.10.2024 of this Court rendered in W.P.(C) 13765/2024 Satwant Singh Sanghera v. The Assistant Commissioner of Income Tax & Anr. 3. Mr. Ruchir Bhatia, learned Senior Standing Counsel for the Respondent, was not in a position to dispute the legal position of law as stated by the learned counsel for the Petitioner. 4. Heard learned Counsel for the Parties. 5. Adverting to the merits of the case, we are of the view that the Respondent could perhaps have been justified in disallowing the amount of TDS which was collected by Kingfisher Airlines from the Petitioner’s salary, as the same was not deposited by said deductor but the Petitioner cannot be blamed for that and deprived of his legitimate right, as has been held by this Court in its judgement Satwant Singh Sanghera (supra). 6. We therefore allow the writ petition and quash and set aside the impugned demands for the AY’s 2009-10, 2010-11, 2011-12, and 2012-13 to the extent they relate to the non-grant of credit of Tax Deducted at Source by the Kingfisher Airlines. 7. Needless to observe that our order shall confine to the amounts which have been deducted by the Kingfisher Airlines and in case there is any other demand raised by the Assessing Officer, the same shall not be effected. 8. The instant petition, alongwith pending applications, stands disposed of in the aforesaid terms. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Filed under hig
rows.summary: Delhi High Court ruled employees can still claim TDS credit even if Kingfisher Airlines failed to deposit the deducted tax.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Jaipur Allows Section 87A Rebate on STCG under Section 111A for AY 2024-25
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12329 Case Name ITO Vs Madhu Agarwal (ITAT Jaipur) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2024-25 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Jaipur Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); ITO Vs Madhu Agarwal (ITAT Jaipur) Summary: The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Jaipur Bench, considered the Revenue’s appeal against the order of the CIT(A), which had allowed rebate under section 87A of the Income-tax Act, 1961 on tax payable on short-term capital gains. The appeal concerned A.Y. 2024-25 and the assessee had opted for the new tax regime under section 115BAC. The solitary issue before the Tribunal related to denial of rebate under section 87A on tax arising from short-term capital gain. The rebate had initially been denied by the CPC while processing the return under section 143(1), but the CIT(A) allowed the assessee’s claim. The assessee’s total income for the year was stated to be Rs.4,99,250/-, comprising income from business or profession, income from other sources, short-term capital gain of Rs.3,61,100/- and long-term capital gain of Rs.44,082/-. The CIT(A) order recorded a rebate claim of Rs.23,276/-. The CIT(A) examined the first proviso to section 87A inserted by the Finance Act, 2023 with effect from 1 April 2024. The provision provides a rebate where total income chargeable under section 115BAC(1A) does not exceed Rs.7,00,000/-. The CIT(A) observed that the statutory provision did not expressly exclude tax computed on short-term capital gains chargeable under section 111A. It accordingly held that the rebate could not be denied merely because part of the income consisted of special-rate income. The CIT(A) also relied on the fact that Parliament had specifically provided a restriction concerning long-term capital gains under section 112A, whereas no corresponding restriction had been provided in section 111A. The CIT(A) further held that the limited scope of processing under section 143(1) did not justify a mechanical or restrictive interpretation where the applicability of the rebate provision involved interpretation of the statutory scheme. Before the Tribunal, the assessee relied upon decisions of the ITAT in Pranay M Kothari Vs. DCIT, Manojbhai C. Kamdar Vs. ITO, Jayshreeben Jayantibhai Palsana Vs. ITO, and Basty Keshava Shenoy Vs. ITO. The Departmental Representative was unable to distinguish those decisions or point out any contrary decision of the jurisdictional High Court or Supreme Court. The Tribunal noted that the cited ITAT decisions had consistently held that section 87A provides rebate with reference to the tax liability computed on “total income”, without distinguishing between normal-rate income and income taxable at special rates. The Tribunal reproduced the reasoning in Venkatachalam Venkatraman Vs. ITO, which relied upon the absence of an express exclusion in section 87A and referred to the Bombay High Court decision in Rajiv G Shah. The Tribunal also reproduced the reasoning in Jayshreeben Jayantibhai Palsana, including the distinction between section 112A(6), where the legislature had expressly dealt with rebate in relation to specified long-term capital gains, and section 111A, where no similar exclusion existed. It further considered the interaction between section 115BAC(1A) and Chapter XII, holding in the reproduced reasoning that section 115BAC(1A) concerns computation of tax under the concessional regime and does not, by itself, modify the independent rebate provision under section 87A. The Tribunal considered the Explanatory Memorandum to the Finance Bill 2025 and the prospective amendment to section 87A. The reasoning reproduced in the order treated the proposed restriction as prospective and observed that the Explanatory Memorandum could not override the plain language of the statute applicable to A.Y. 2024-25. The Tribunal also referred to The Chamber of Tax Consultants Vs. Director General of Income Tax (Systems), concerning system-based denial of section 87A rebate. The order records the view that the CPC utility or system configuration could not override statutory rights and that the claim had to be considered by the competent quasi-judicial authority on merits. The Tribunal ultimately held that the decision of the ITAT in the cited cases squarely applied to the present facts. It found no infirmity in the CIT(A)’s order holding the assessee entitled to rebate under section 87A on taxes paid on short-term capital gain. The Tribunal directed that the rebate of Rs.25,000/- claimed by the assessee be allowed and the tax liability recomputed. The Revenue’s appeal was consequently dismissed. Cases Discussed Pranay M Kothari Vs. DCIT, ITA No. 3469/Chny/2025. Manojbhai C. Kamdar Vs. ITO, ITA No. 572/RJT/2025. Jayshreeben Jayantibhai Palsana Vs. ITO, ITA No. 1014/Ahd
rows.summary: ITAT Jaipur held that, for AY 2024-25 under the new tax regime, section 87A rebate can apply to tax on short-term capital gains under section 111A.

rows.title: Service Tax | Lease Premium and Ground Rent Received by DDA Liable to Service Tax: CESTAT Delhi
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12328 Case Name Delhi Development Authority Vs Commissioner of Service Tax (CESTAT Delhi) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All CESTAT, CESTAT Delhi Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Delhi Development Authority Vs Commissioner of Service Tax (CESTAT New Delhi) Summary: The CESTAT New Delhi disposed of two appeals filed by Delhi Development Authority (DDA) arising from orders concerning service tax liability on activities involving Renting of Immovable Property and Club Services. The first appeal was Service Tax Appeal No. 50278 of 2017, arising from Order-in-Original No. DLI-SVTAX-002/COM-020/2016-17 dated 30.09.2016. The second was Service Tax Appeal No. 50191 of 2021, arising from Order-in-Original No. 11-14/TPS/PC/CGST/DSC/2020-21 dated 16.09.2020. The periods and amounts involved in the two appeals included substantial demands relating to lease/premium receipts and other activities. DDA was registered with the Service Tax department for services including Mandap Keeper Service, Health and Fitness Service, Architect Service and Club or Association Service. Audit proceedings revealed that DDA was receiving amounts from Renting of Immovable Property for commercial use without registration under that service and without payment of service tax. Show cause notices were consequently issued proposing demand and recovery of service tax, and the proposals were confirmed through the respective orders-in-originals. At the hearing on 13.05.2026, none appeared for DDA. The Departmental Representative argued that DDA is a corporate body managed under Section 3(3) of the Delhi Development Authority Act, 1957, but that the statutory character of an authority does not by itself exclude its taxable commercial activities. Reliance was placed on a Chennai Bench decision concerning a municipality, as well as the Larger Bench decision in RIICO Ltd. The Revenue contended that lease premium/salami and ground-rent related receipts were liable to service tax even though DDA claimed to be merely a custodian of Nazul land belonging to the Government of India. The Tribunal considered the Supreme Court decision in Krishi Upaj Mandi Samiti, New Mandi Yard, Alwar Vs. Commissioner of Central Excise & Service Tax, Alwar, which dealt with the distinction between statutory/sovereign functions and activities undertaken for consideration. The Tribunal also considered Circular No. 89/7/2006 dated 18.12.2006, under which statutory functions performed by sovereign/public authorities for compulsory statutory levies deposited into the Government treasury were distinguished from services undertaken for consideration. For the relevant pre-negative-list period, the Tribunal examined Section 65(105)(zzzz) of the Finance Act, 1994, defining the taxable service of Renting of Immovable Property. For the post-01.07.2012 period, it examined Section 65B(44) of the Finance Act, 1994, defining “service”, and Section 66D, containing the negative list. The Tribunal observed that DDA was letting/giving the Nazul lands on rent or lease on behalf of the Central Government and receiving ground rent and one-time premium. Although the object of the DDA Act was development of Delhi, the Tribunal held that if DDA earned profits while discharging functions under the statute, such amounts could be liable to tax. The receipts were not established to be statutory levies or fees deposited into the Government treasury; rather, they were admitted to be amounts received against Renting of Immovable Property. The Tribunal further considered the Larger Bench decision concerning RIICO Ltd., under which lease premium or salami was held liable to service tax under Renting of Immovable Property for the relevant period. It also noted an earlier DDA appeal, Service Tax Appeal No. 58914 of 2013, in which the matter had been remanded for consideration of the commercial or non-commercial nature of the property and the taxability of vacant land prior to 01.07.2010 in light of the decision in Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority Vs. CCE & ST, Noida. Following remand, one of the orders under challenge had held that leasing or Renting of Immovable Property constituted a taxable service, while renting of vacant land prior to 01.07.2010 was excluded from the service tax demand. The activity of charging membership and subscription for DDA’s sports complex was also held not to constitute a sovereign activity and was treated as commercial and taxable. The Tribunal found no infirmity in the findings of the original adjudicating authorities. It also noted that DDA had not appeared to make submissions and had failed to produce documents supporting its claim that the leasing of Government lands against rent, lease or premium constituted a sovereign function. Consequently
rows.summary: CESTAT Delhi held DDA must pay service tax on lease premiums and ground rent received for renting immovable property.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | GST Applies to Highway Annuity as Works Contract: Rajasthan High Court
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12327 Case Name Nagaur Mukundgarh Highways Pvt. Ltd. Vs Central Board of Indirect Taxes And Customs (Rajasthan High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Rajasthan High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Nagaur Mukundgarh Highways Pvt. Ltd. Vs Central Board of Indirect Taxes And Customs (Rajasthan High Court) Summary: The Rajasthan High Court considered a bunch of writ petitions led by D.B. Civil Writ Petition No. 10055/2024 filed by M/s Nagaur Mukundgarh Highways Pvt. Ltd. challenging the validity and applicability of Circular No.150/06/2021-GST dated 17.06.2021, a show cause notice dated 09.12.2022 and recovery order dated 07.07.2023 relating to levy of GST on annuity payments received under highway concession agreements. The petitioner contended that Entry 23A of Notification No.12/2017-Central Tax (Rate) dated 28.06.2017, issued under Section 11 of the CGST Act, exempted “service by way of access to a road or a bridge on payment of annuity” under Heading 9967. It was further contended that an advance ruling dated 12.02.2019 had already held Entry 23A applicable and, having not been challenged by Revenue, continued to bind the applicant and departmental authorities under Section 103 of the CGST Act. The petitioner argued that CBIC could not, through an administrative circular issued under Section 168, override, modify, dilute or retrospectively withdraw a statutory exemption. Reliance was placed upon DPJ Bidar-Chincholi (Annuity) Road Project Private Limited & Anr. Vs. Union of India & Ors., 2022 SCC OnLine Kar 1829. Revenue, on the other hand, maintained that Circular No.150/06/2021-GST merely clarified the statutory distinction between services by way of access to roads falling under Heading 9967 and construction services falling under Heading 9954. Revenue also relied upon CG Tollway Ltd. Vs. Union of India & Ors., Jorabat Shillong Expressway Ltd. Vs. Union of India and GMR Pochanpalli Expreessways Limited Vs. Additional Director, Directorate General of GST Intelligence & Ors. Revenue further invoked Section 103(2), arguing that an advance ruling remains binding only so long as the relevant law, facts and circumstances remain unchanged. The High Court principally relied upon the Coordinate Bench ruling in CG Tollway Ltd. v. The Union of India & Others, decided on 22.05.2026. That decision had examined Sections 2(31), 2(119) and Section 7 of the CGST Act, Schedule II and Rules 27 and 28 of the CGST Rules, 2017, and held that construction and maintenance obligations performed in return for valuable contractual rights constituted taxable works-contract services. It had also held that road-construction services fall under Heading 9954 rather than Heading 9967 and referred to Commissioner of Customs v. Dilip Kumar & Co. and Commissioner (CGST) v. Safari Retreats (P) Ltd. concerning interpretation of exemption notifications. Examining the petitioner’s concession agreement with NHAI, the Court noted that 50% of the Project Cost was payable in five equal instalments during the construction period while the remaining 50% was payable in twenty biannual instalments commencing from the 180th day of COD. The agreement described these deferred payments, together with interest, as “Annuity Payments”. The Court observed that the arrangement was essentially a design, build, operate and transfer project. Unlike CG Tollway, where the concessionaire bore the entire investment risk under the BOT arrangement, the petitioner had invested approximately 50% of the required funds while the remaining 50% was payable by NHAI on an annuity basis. Nevertheless, the Court held that this distinction did not change the essential nature of the services. The Court held that the concession agreement constituted “works contract services” and was taxable. The petitioner’s services were not confined merely to providing access to a road or bridge on payment of annuity; the contractual obligations included construction, design and maintenance of roads. Entry 23A related to transport services and did not exempt works-contract construction services. The Bench followed CG Tollway and declined to adopt the different view taken by the Single Bench of the Telangana High Court in GMR Pochanpalli Expreessways Limited, noting that CG Tollway had expressly distinguished that decision. The Court also rejected the challenge that Circular No.150/06/2021-GST impermissibly amended the exemption notification. According to the Court, the circular clarified terminology and prevented misinterpretation by authorities implementing the CGST Act, which fell within the Board’s domain under Section 168. It further rejected the petitioner’s reliance upon the earlier advance ruling, observing that an erroneous interpretation
rows.summary: Rajasthan High Court held highway annuity payments under concession agreements are taxable as works contracts, rejecting the GST exemption claim.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Mumbai Allows KPMG Unbilled Revenue Write-off for AY 2015-16
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12326 Case Name KPMG India Pvt. Ltd. Vs DCIT (ITAT Mumbai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2015-16 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Mumbai Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Vs DCIT (ITAT Mumbai) Summary: The Mumbai Bench of the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal adjudicated cross appeals filed by KPMG India Pvt. Ltd. and the Revenue for Assessment Year 2015-16. The appeals arose from orders of the National Faceless Appeal Centre dated 09.01.2026 passed under section 250 of the Income-tax Act, 1961. The assessee’s appeal concerned disallowance relating to reversal of opening accrued/unbilled income and billing done in earlier years, while the Revenue challenged deletion of a disallowance under section 40(a)(i) concerning professional fees paid to non-resident KPMG member firms. The order was pronounced on 12.08.2026. On the assessee’s appeal, KPMG India Pvt. Ltd. had filed its return on 29.11.2015 declaring total income of Rs.42,25,370/-. The case was selected for scrutiny under CASS and notice under section 143(2) was issued on 25.07.2017. The assessee rendered management consultancy services in Finance, Environment Audit, Investment and Information Technology. The assessment under section 143(3) was completed on 28.12.2018 determining total income at Rs.30,73,92,848/- after various additions and disallowances. During assessment, the Assessing Officer noticed unbilled revenue of Rs.32,38,60,326/- as at 31.03.2015. The assessee explained that it followed a rational accounting method based on working hours and allocation of sales according to the total contract value, with billing being undertaken on achievement of milestones. It stated that unbilled revenue of Rs.2,22,16,683/- had been reversed without raising invoices on clients. The AO did not accept the explanation, observing that the assessee had not substantiated the basis for reversal or produced correspondence showing that clients would not pay the amounts. The AO accordingly added Rs.2,22,16,683/- to income. The CIT(A) sustained the disallowance. Before the Tribunal, the assessee relied on the coordinate Bench decision in KPMG Advisory Services Private Limited for AYs 2012-13, 2015-16 and 2018-19 in ITA Nos. 5392 to 5396/Mum/2024. The Revenue’s Senior Departmental Representative supported the lower authorities but admitted that the issue was covered by that decision. The Tribunal reproduced the relevant portion of the coordinate Bench’s decision concerning reversal of unbilled revenue. That decision recorded that revenue was recognised under the mercantile system on the basis of time spent and chargeable rates; unbilled revenue was offered as professional income in the year of accrual and shown as an asset until invoicing. It further recorded the assessee’s explanation that the written-off amount related to unbilled revenue already accounted for and offered to tax in an earlier year. The coordinate Bench found that the AO and CIT(A) had neither controverted the supporting material and detailed submissions nor demonstrated any deficiency or suppression of material facts. The disallowance was therefore held to be unjustified. Following that decision, the Tribunal found the facts of KPMG India Pvt. Ltd.’s case to be similar and observed that the Senior Departmental Representative could not distinguish the earlier decision either on facts or in law. Grounds Nos. 1 and 2 of the assessee were accordingly allowed. Ground No. 3, concerning denial of opportunity of hearing, was not pressed and was dismissed as not pressed. The assessee’s appeal was therefore allowed. The Revenue’s appeal concerned professional fees of Rs.4,03,12,726/- paid to non-residents without deduction of tax under section 195. The AO, after examining invoices, agreements and the nature of services, treated the payments as consideration for imparting technical, commercial or industrial knowledge and held them to constitute royalty under section 9(1)(vi) and Articles 12 and 13 of the applicable tax treaties. The assessee’s contention that the income was taxable as business profits in the absence of a permanent establishment was rejected by the AO. The entire amount was consequently disallowed under section 40(a)(i). The payments comprised amounts paid to KPMG Advisory, Indonesia; KPMG Advisory N.V., Netherlands; KPMG Auditors & Consultores S.A., Mozambique; KPMG Australia; KPMG Dublin; KPMG LLP, United Kingdom; KPMG LLP, USA; KPMG S.A., France; KPMG Services Pte Ltd, Singapore; and KPMG Tax Services Ltd., Mauritius, aggregating to Rs.4,03,12,726/-. The CIT(A), however, allowed the assessee’s appeal by following the ITAT’s orders in the assessee’s own case for AYs 1999-00, 2001-02 and 2007-08 dated 23.12.2015, holding that the nature of payments,
rows.summary: ITAT Mumbai allowed KPMG to write off unbilled revenue, while also dealing with a tax dispute over payments to non-resident affiliates.

rows.title: Income Tax | Actuarial Deficit Fund Contributions Fully Deductible: Calcutta High Court
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12325 Case Name PCIT Vs Syama Prasad Mookherjee Port Kolkata (Calcutta High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2018-19 Courts All High Courts, Calcutta High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); PCIT Vs Syama Prasad Mookherjee Port Kolkata (Calcutta High Court) Summary: The Calcutta High Court considered a Revenue appeal under Section 260A of the Income Tax Act, 1961 against the ITAT Kolkata order dated 18.11.2024 for AY 2018-19 in the case of Syama Prasad Mookherjee Port Kolkata, formerly known as Kolkata Port Trust. The assessee had filed its original return on 27.09.2018 and revised return on 28.03.2019. Assessment under Section 143(3) read with Section 144B was completed on 24.09.2021 at total income of Rs.876,16,93,450, including disallowances of Rs.710,68,55,297 towards Superannuation Fund contributions, Rs.33,11,01,366 towards approved Gratuity Fund contributions and Rs.8,38,35,219 towards alleged belated employees’ PF/ESI contributions under Section 36(1)(va). The CIT(A) deleted the additions and the ITAT confirmed that decision. On the Superannuation Fund issue, the Assessing Officer had applied the 27% ceiling under Rule 87 of the Income-tax Rules, 1962. Salary for the relevant computation was Rs.446,33,18,867 and the AO calculated the permissible contribution at Rs.120,50,96,094, whereas the assessee had debited Rs.831,20,51,391 to its Profit & Loss account. The assessee explained that the payment was necessitated by a severe actuarial deficit caused by funding constraints over preceding years and represented an extraordinary ad hoc interim contribution intended to bridge the gap between the fund’s assets and its actuarial liabilities. The CIT(A) and ITAT treated the payment as neither an ordinary annual contribution under Rule 87 nor an initial contribution under Rule 88 and relied upon PCIT-1 Vs Exide Industries Limited. The Revenue sought to distinguish Exide Industries on the ground that funding of deficits had occurred regularly over several years and therefore could not be treated as an exceptional one-time contribution. The High Court rejected this argument. It held that the legal nature of the contribution depended upon its purpose, namely remedying an actuarial deficit, and not upon the number of years required to eliminate that deficit. A persistent deficit arising from earlier funding constraints could not convert ad hoc gap-filling payments into ordinary annual contributions. The Court further observed that applying the Rule 87 ceiling to necessary actuarially-backed funding of an approved fund would compromise the fund’s solvency and run contrary to the scheme of Section 36(1)(iv). It therefore upheld deletion of the disallowance of Rs.710,68,55,297 and answered substantial questions (1) and (3) against the Revenue. On the Gratuity Fund contribution of Rs.33,11,01,366, the Revenue relied upon the 8.33% ceiling prescribed by Rule 103. The Court held that a fundamental distinction existed between ordinary annual contributions and payments specifically made to bridge an actuarial valuation deficit. The payment was intended to bridge the shortfall between actuarial liability and actual availability in the approved Gratuity Fund maintained with LIC and therefore did not fall within the restrictive category of an ordinary annual contribution under Rule 103. The Court also noted that Section 36(1)(v) itself did not impose an 8.33% ceiling and allowed contributions to an approved gratuity fund created under an irrevocable trust for the exclusive benefit of employees. Relying upon CIT v. Eastern Equipment & Sales Limited, the Court held that once the Commissioner had approved the fund, the Assessing Officer could not sit in judgment over that approval or use Rule 103 to disregard the approved status of the fund. The second substantial question was accordingly answered against the Revenue. On the Rs.8,38,35,219 disallowance of employees’ PF/ESI contributions under Section 36(1)(va), the Court noted that the assessee was governed by the Kolkata Port Trust (Non-contributory Provident Fund) Regulations, 1988, notified under the Major Port Trusts Act, 1963, and those regulations prescribed no due date for depositing employees’ contributions. The 15th of the following month shown in Serial No.20(b) of Form 3CD had been entered because the e-filing software compulsorily required a date. The Court held that the general deadline under Clause 38 of the Employees’ Provident Fund Scheme did not apply to the respondent. In the absence of a legally prescribed due date under the applicable regulatory framework, there could be no “delay” capable of triggering Section 36(1)(va). The Court therefore upheld deletion of this disallowance also. Finally, the Court reject
rows.summary: The Calcutta High Court upheld full deduction for actuarial deficit fund contributions, rejecting the tax department’s disallowance for the port trust.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Chennai Rejects Reopening of Concluded Goodwill Depreciation Issue in Subsequent Year
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12324 Case Name DCIT Vs Magick Woods Exports Pvt. Ltd. (ITAT Chennai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2018-19 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Chennai Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); DCIT Vs Magick Woods Exports Pvt. Ltd. (ITAT Chennai) Summary: The Chennai Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal dismissed the Revenue’s appeal for Assessment Year 2018-19 and upheld the relief granted by the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals), National Faceless Appeal Centre, on two issues: depreciation of Rs.85.13 Crores on goodwill forming part of the opening block of intangible assets, and deduction of Rs.9.32 Crores towards vendor compliance expenses. The appeal arose from the order of the Ld.CIT(A), NFAC, dated 01.09.2025 passed under section 250 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, against the assessment order passed under section 143(3) dated 24.02.2022. Depreciation on goodwill Under a Scheme of Amalgamation effective from 01.04.2016, erstwhile Magick Woods Exports Private Limited and Modularkitchen.com Private Limited merged with Indyca Solutions (India) Private Limited. The Scheme was approved by the National Company Law Tribunal, Chennai, on 25.09.2017, following which the transferee company was renamed Magick Woods Exports Private Limited. The assessee followed the Purchase Method under Accounting Standard-14 and recorded the assets and liabilities transferred at their respective fair values. The excess of consideration discharged through issue of Compulsorily Convertible Preference Shares over the net value of assets acquired was recorded as goodwill amounting to Rs.454.05 Crores in FY 2016-17, forming part of the block of intangible assets. Depreciation was claimed at 25%. For AY 2017-18, the Assessing Officer had disallowed depreciation on the goodwill by treating its actual cost as nil with reference to the sixth proviso to section 32(1) and Explanation 7 to section 43(1) of the Act. The Ld.CIT(A), however, allowed the assessee’s claim by order dated 20.10.2023. The Revenue did not challenge that order, and the AO subsequently passed an order dated 26.08.2024 giving effect to it. The allowance of depreciation in the year of amalgamation therefore attained finality. For AY 2018-19, the assessee claimed depreciation of Rs.85.13 Crores at 25% on the opening WDV of the block of intangible assets comprising the goodwill. The AO again disallowed the claim on the same basis. The Ld.CIT(A) deleted the disallowance, holding that the claim in AY 2018-19 was consequential depreciation on the opening WDV already forming part of the block and was not a fresh claim arising from the amalgamation. The Ld.CIT(A) also examined the issue on merits and found in favour of the assessee. The Tribunal held that the goodwill was first recorded in AY 2017-18, entered the block of intangible assets in that year and depreciation was first claimed and allowed in that year. The very objections regarding actual cost, the sixth proviso to section 32(1), Explanation 7 to section 43(1) and eligibility of goodwill for depreciation had already been raised and rejected in AY 2017-18, and the Revenue had not challenged that decision. The Tribunal observed that in AY 2018-19 there was no fresh amalgamation, valuation exercise or addition to the block. The assessee claimed depreciation only on the opening WDV of intangible assets already forming part of the block as on 01.04.2017. It held that depreciation on the opening WDV of a block of assets, once the conditions of section 32 are satisfied, is a mandatory allowance and does not depend upon a fresh claim or re-examination every year. The Tribunal referred to Explanation 5 to section 32(1) and CBDT Circular No.14/2001 dated 09.11.2001. The Tribunal relied upon the principle reflected in Bodal Chemicals Ltd. Vs ACIT, 180 ITD 313, as referred to in the judgment, and considered Suzlon Global Services Ltd. v. PCIT, ITA Nos.67-68/AHD/2021, Johnson Matthey Chemicals India Pvt. Ltd., ITA No.1507/PUN/2012, and Hindustan Coca-Cola Beverages Pvt. Ltd. Vs DCIT. The Tribunal further noted that the Ld.CIT(A) had independently examined the eligibility of the goodwill for depreciation on merits, including its character as an intangible asset under Explanation 3(b) to section 32(1), with reference to CIT v. Smifs Securities Ltd., (2012) 348 ITR 302 (SC), and the valuation undertaken in connection with the amalgamation. It also referred to Trivitron Healthcare (P.) Ltd. v. PCIT, [2022] 98 ITR(T) 105 (Chennai-Trib.), Mylan Laboratories Ltd. v. DCIT, 113 taxmann.com 6 (Hyd.), and Kontoor Brands India Pvt. Ltd. v. ACIT (ITAT Bangalore). Finding no material change in facts, law or the composition of the block between AY 2017-18 and AY 2018-19, the Tribunal held that the Revenue could not re-
rows.summary: ITAT Chennai said tax authorities cannot reopen a settled goodwill depreciation issue in a later year and upheld related deductions.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Delhi HC Declines GST Refund Where Coercion Claim Raises Disputed Facts
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12323 Case Name Nector Foods Private Limited Vs Union of India (Delhi High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Delhi High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Nector Foods Private Limited Vs Union of India (Delhi High Court) Summary: The Delhi High Court considered a writ petition filed by M/s Nector Foods Private Limited concerning payments made through Form GST DRC-03 during a search of the petitioner’s premises. The petitioner sought, among other reliefs, a declaration that two DRC-03 debits dated 30 July 2025 were coerced and involuntary and a direction for refund of Rs.28,34,294/- representing interest and penalty. The petitioner also sought interest on the amount and directions concerning CCTV and audio-video recording in interrogation areas, referring to Paramvir Singh Saini v. Baljit Singh, (2021) 1 SCC 184. The petitioner’s case, as recorded by the Court, was that payments amounting to Rs.28,34,294/- together with interest had been compelled during the search and were made in violation of Instruction No.01/2022-23 (GST-Investigation) dated 25.05.2022 issued by the Commissioner (GST-Inv.), CBIC. The Instruction concerns deposit of tax during the course of search, inspection or investigation; a verified TaxGuru publication discussing the same instruction is Instruction No.01/2022-23 (GST-Investigation). The writ petition disclosed three payments made during the search proceedings. The first payment, under ARN AD0707250242951 dated 29.07.2025 at 6:29 PM, involved Rs.67,20,000/- which was stated as “not claimed”, with no interest or penalty and no amount claimed under Section 73(5) of the CGST Act, 2017. The second payment, under ARN AD070725024398T dated 30.07.2025 at 4:19 AM, comprised interest of Rs.16,47,050/- and penalty of Rs.10,08,000/-, totalling Rs.26,55,050/-, under Section 74(5). The third payment, under ARN AD070725024402C dated 30.07.2025 at 4:29 AM, comprised Rs.4,53,628/- tax, Rs.1,11,200/- interest and Rs.68,044/- penalty, totalling Rs.1,79,244/-, also under Section 74(5). The petitioner’s counsel expressly admitted that the payments of Rs.67,20,000/- and Rs.4,53,628/- were not being claimed because those payments were made voluntarily. The petitioner, however, maintained that the payment of Rs.26,55,050/- was made involuntarily. The respondents disputed the allegation of coercion and submitted that all the payments were made voluntarily and that there was no coercion by members of the search team. It was further submitted that the investigation against the petitioner was pending and was likely to be concluded shortly. The Court held that the question whether the payment of Rs.26,55,050/- was made voluntarily or under coercion involved a disputed question of fact. The Court considered this particularly significant because the petitioner did not dispute the voluntary nature of the other two payments made during the very same search proceedings. On that basis, the Court declined to issue a writ directing refund of the amount claimed by the petitioner. Importantly, the Court did not conclusively determine whether the disputed payment was voluntary or coerced. Instead, it observed that the petitioner, if so advised, could avail such alternative remedy as may be available in law. The writ petition was accordingly disposed of with those observations, and all pending applications were also closed. FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF DELHI HIGH COURT 1. Through this Writ Petition, the Petitioner prays for the following reliefs: “(a) DECLARE that the two Form GST DRC-03 debits dated 30.07.2025 (ARN AD070725024398T and ARN AD070725024402C) were coerced and involuntary. Issue a Writ of Certiorari or any other appropriate writ, order or direction QUASHING the recovery and retention of the interest and penalty of Rs.28,34,294 effected thereby. (b) Issue a Writ of Mandamus or any other appropriate writ, order or direction DIRECTING Respondent Nos. 1 to 3 to refund Rs. 28,34,294 to the Petitioner’s bank account (HDFC Bank, Account No. 50200077563997, IFSC HDFC0000090), and not by re-credit to any electronic ledger. The refund to be independent of, and not conditioned upon, any pending or future investigation or proceeding. (c)DIRECT payment of interest on the said sum from 30.07.2025 till realisation, at not less than 6 percent per annum, rising to 12 percent per annum should payment not be made within the period this Hon’ble Court fixes. (d)DIRECT the installation of CCTV and audio-video recording in the interrogation areas of the Respondent Commissionerate, in terms of Paramvir Singh Saini v Baljit Singh, (2021) 1 SCC 184, with night vision and audio as well as video capability, and preservation of recordings as therein directed. DIRECT that copies of such
rows.summary: Delhi HC denied an immediate GST refund because the taxpayer’s coercion claim raised factual disputes that need evidence, not writ relief.

rows.title: Company Law | NCLAT Rejects Third-Party Objection to Disclosure of Mall Revenue Records
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12322 Case Name Mega Mall Management Services Pvt. Ltd Vs Ajay Kumar Agarwal (NCLAT Delhi) Summary: The National Company Law Appellate Tribunal, Principal Bench, New Delhi, dismissed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1236 of 2025 filed by Mega Mall Management Services Pvt. Ltd. against the order dated 18.06.2025 of the National Company Law Tribunal, Kolkata Bench-II. The NCLT had allowed I.A. (IBC) No. 910 of 2024 filed by Ajay Kumar Agarwal, Resolution Professional of Avani Projects & Infrastructures Ltd., and directed the Appellant to furnish complete details of rent and parking charges collected from Avani Riverside Mall for Financial Years 2021-22 and 2022-23 and thereafter. Avani Projects and Infrastructures Ltd. was admitted into Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process on 13.03.2019 pursuant to a petition under Section 7 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. The Corporate Debtor had developed Avani Riverside Mall, while Mega Mall Management Services Pvt. Ltd. was involved in its management and maintenance. During the CIRP, the Resolution Professional had earlier filed an application under Section 19(2) of the Code alleging non-cooperation by the Appellant and other entities. The Adjudicating Authority, by order dated 13.06.2022, directed the respondents to cooperate with the Resolution Professional. The Appellant thereafter furnished copies of agreements executed with the Corporate Debtor, including the original agreement dated 01.06.2011 and the subsequent agreement dated 31.01.2018. Section 19 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code Contempt proceedings were subsequently initiated against the Appellant. During those proceedings, the Adjudicating Authority directed the Resolution Professional to ascertain whether Avani Riverside Mall or any part thereof continued to constitute an asset of the Corporate Debtor. By order dated 04.09.2023, directions were issued for physical inspection of shops, examination of ownership documents and verification of ownership details through the Registrar of Assurances. The Appellant relied upon the original agreement dated 01.06.2011 and the Supplemental Agreement dated 31.01.2018. According to the Appellant, the 2018 agreement materially altered and superseded the earlier arrangement. Under the revised arrangement, the Appellant was responsible for collecting CAM charges, electricity charges, gas charges and other operational income and utilising those collections for maintenance and upkeep of the mall. Any surplus after maintenance expenses was stated to belong exclusively to the Appellant, while any deficit was also to be borne by it. A separate tripartite agreement dated 31.01.2018 assigned rights and responsibilities concerning management, operation and collection of parking charges to Aster Buildtech Private Limited. The Resolution Professional subsequently sought details of rent and parking charges allegedly collected from the mall. The Appellant rejected the request, asserting that it was an independent third party, that it was neither collecting rent nor parking charges, and that parking charges were being collected by Aster Buildtech Private Limited. The Resolution Professional thereafter filed I.A. (IBC) No. 910 of 2024 under Section 60(5) of the Code seeking directions for disclosure. Section 60(5) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code Before the Appellate Tribunal, the Appellant contended that the impugned order was based upon an erroneous interpretation of the contractual arrangements. It argued that the Corporate Debtor’s ownership of the mall had not been established, that the 2018 agreements superseded the 2011 agreement, and that the Resolution Professional could not introduce allegations concerning the Appellant’s alleged related-party or step-down-subsidiary status through a rejoinder. The Appellant also relied upon Banarsi & Ors. v. Ram Phal, (2003) 9 SCC 606, contending that in the absence of a cross-appeal or cross-objection the Resolution Professional could not enlarge the controversy in the appeal. The Resolution Professional, on the other hand, submitted that under the 2011 agreement the Appellant had collected mall revenues on behalf of the Corporate Debtor and was entitled only to a fixed monthly fee. Reliance was placed upon financial records showing substantial revenues from the mall, the agreements executed on 31.01.2018, the tripartite arrangement with Aster Buildtech Private Limited, the winding-up proceedings, the alleged diversion of revenue, the transaction audit and the pending proceedings under Sections 45, 49 and 66 of the Code. rows.title: Company Law | NCLT Chandigarh Rejects AKB Ventures Plan, Orders Paytail Commerce Liquidation
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12321 Case Name In re Manindra Kumar Tiwari (NCLT Chandigarh) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts NCLT Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); In re Manindra Kumar Tiwari (NCLT Chandigarh) Summary: The National Company Law Tribunal, Chandigarh Bench (Court-II), Chandigarh, considered an application filed by Mr. Manindra Kumar Tiwari, Resolution Professional of Paytail Commerce Private Limited, under Section 30(6) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016, seeking approval of the Resolution Plan submitted by M/s AKB Ventures Pvt. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Panasonic Life Solutions India Private Limited Vs Commissioner of CGST & and Central Excise (CESTAT Ahmedabad) Summary: The CESTAT Ahmedabad allowed the appeal filed by Panasonic Life Solutions India Private Limited, Kutch, concerning recovery of Rs. 54,00,034/- taken as suo moto credit in the account current under Notification No. 39/2001-CE dated 31.07.2001. The appellant manufactures Glass Shell, Wires & Cables, Ceiling Fan, Switch Gear and other goods at its Kutch unit and was availing the area-based exemption under the Notification No. 39/2001-CE, as amended. The audit noticed that the appellant had taken suo moto credit of Rs. 54,00,034/- in April 2010 by endorsing it as “Re-credit (08-09 annual)”. A show cause notice dated 29.02.2016 proposed recovery under Section 11A read with Notification No. 39/2001-CE, together with interest under Section 11AA and penalty under Section 11AC read with Rule 25 of the Central Excise Rules, 2002. The Joint Commissioner confirmed the recovery, interest and equal penalty on 25.01.2018. The Commissioner (Appeals) rejected the appellant’s appeal, resulting in the present proceedings. The appellant principally contended that the demand was barred by limitation because the credit was taken in April 2010 whereas the show cause notice was issued on 29.02.2016. It was also submitted that an application/statement for the annual differential refund for financial year 2008-09 had been filed with the Jurisdictional Assistant Commissioner on 11.05.2009, but no decision had been communicated. The appellant relied on various judicial decisions, including Parle Product Pvt. Ltd., Government of India Vs. Citedal Fine Pharmaceuticals, Valley Valvet P. Ltd., SAL Steels Limited, Sun Pharma Laboratories Ltd., Reckitt Benckiser, Saurashtra Cement Ltd. and Amrit Foods. The appellant further contended that Para 2.2 of the notification permitted annual differential refund and that the amount of Rs. 54,00,038/- represented the differential between the duty paid and the amount already sanctioned through re-credit orders. It was also argued that there was no suppression, wilful misstatement, collusion or fraud because the appellant had disclosed the matter to the jurisdictional Assistant Commissioner in May 2009. The Revenue submitted that suo moto credit without waiting for the Assistant Commissioner’s order violated the notification and amounted to suppression of facts, justifying the extended limitation period. Reliance was placed on Garden Silk Mills Ltd., BDH Industries Ltd. and Krishna Electrical Industries Ltd. The Revenue also informed the Bench that the status of the refund application could not be ascertained. The Tribunal examined the relevant provisions of Notification No. 39/2001-CE, including Paras 2, 2A, 2B, 2C, 2.1 and 2.2. Para 2C permitted the manufacturer, subject to prescribed conditions, to take credit of the amount calculated under Para 2 in its account current. Para 2C required submission of a statement to the Assistant Commissioner, who was to determine the amount correctly refundable. Para 2C(g) provided for recovery of irregular or excess credit as if it were recovery of duty of excise erroneously refunded. Para 2.2(1) provided for annual differential refund where the total refund paid or payable during the financial year was less than the total duty paid, subject to the prescribed ceiling, while Para 2.2(2) required the Assistant Commissioner or Deputy Commissioner to refund the differential amount not later than 15 May of the subsequent financial year. On limitation, the Tribunal held that the notification read with Section 11A of the Central Excise Act, 1944 permitted recovery proceedings for erroneous refund within the applicable limitation period. Since the appellant had taken the suo moto credit in April 2010 and the notice was issued on 29.02.2016, the Tribunal held that the proceedings emanated from a time-barred show cause notice and were therefore unsustainable. The Tribunal also examined the merits. It noted that the appellant had submitted its annual differential duty statement on 11.05.2009, but the application had not been decided. During the proceedings, the department was unable to categorically state whether the refund claim was pending or had been disposed of. The Tribunal criticised the functioning of the Division Office and directed the Jurisdictional Chief Commissioner to enquire into the reasons for the prolonged inaction. The Tribunal held that the appellant had acted in accordance with the notification afte
rows.summary: CESTAT Ahmedabad ruled excise recovery was time-barred, setting aside demand, interest and penalty on Panasonic for a 2010 credit re-entry.

rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12319 Case Name Bhati & Company Vs Union of India (Rajasthan High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Rajasthan High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Bhati & Company Vs Union of India (Rajasthan High Court) Summary: The Rajasthan High Court at Jodhpur allowed two connected writ petitions concerning recovery of excess duty drawback paid to exporters following misclassification of exported handicrafts and artistic wooden furniture. The principal petition was filed by M/s Bhati & Company in D.B. Civil Writ Petition No. 19673/2022, and the connected petition concerned Latiyal Handicrafts Pvt. Ltd. The common order was pronounced on 12.08.2026 by Hon’ble Mr. Justice Munnuri Laxman and Hon’ble Mrs. Justice Sangeeta Sharma. In the case of M/s Bhati & Company, six shipping bills covering exports between 13.05.2011 and 20.05.2011 were involved, while Latiyal Handicrafts Pvt. Ltd. had exported under seven shipping bills commencing from 13.10.2009 to 25.05.2011. The petitioners had self-assessed the exported goods under Drawback Schedule Nos. 9401 and 940399. The respondents subsequently took the view that the appropriate classification was Drawback Schedule No. 442101. The resulting classification difference led to excess drawback payments. The petitioners had carried out self-assessment under Section 17 of the Customs Act, 1962. Following an audit objection, show cause notices dated 25.03.2013 were issued seeking recovery of the alleged excess drawback by invoking Section 142(1) read with Section 75A of the Act and Rule 16 of the Customs and Central Excise Duties and Service Tax Drawback Rules, 1995. The original orders determining the excess drawback were challenged in appeal. The revisional authority subsequently set aside the original and appellate orders and remanded the matters for fresh consideration. The principal issue before the High Court was whether, after self-assessment of export goods, the authorities could directly invoke Section 75A for recovery of drawback without first undertaking reassessment under Section 17. The petitioners contended that where the proper officer disagrees with self-assessment, the statutory mechanism requires verification and reassessment, and recovery can follow only after the liability is crystallised through that process. 3The Court examined Sections 17, 18, 50 and 51 of the Customs Act. It observed that an exporter entering export goods under Section 50 is required to self-assess the duty, if any, leviable on such goods. Where the proper officer does not agree with the self-assessment, the officer is required to proceed with reassessment under Section 17(4). Where the reassessment is not accepted by the exporter, a speaking order is required. The Court also considered Section 18 concerning provisional assessment and Section 75A(2), which deals with recovery of drawback that has been paid erroneously or has otherwise become recoverable under the Act or rules. The Court held that the present proceedings had proceeded on the assumption that the drawback payments were erroneous, whereas the payments had been made pursuant to the petitioners’ self-assessments. According to the Court, even if the self-assessment subsequently turns out to involve misdeclaration or misclassification, the authorities cannot directly proceed under Section 75A(2) while the self-assessment remains in force and has not been reassessed. If the misclassification results in excess drawback, the authority may have recourse to Section 17(4) or Section 18 for further inquiry, as applicable. The High Court therefore held that Section 75A could be invoked in the facts of the case only after the amount had been crystallised as a consequence of reassessment. Since the authorities had not invoked Sections 17 and 18 and had proceeded directly under Section 75A(2), the proceedings were held to be a misapplication of law. The Court consequently set aside the impugned orders dated 05.01.2015 and 24.10.2021. It allowed the writ petitions while giving liberty to the respondents to have recourse to Sections 17 and 18 of the Customs Act, if law permits them. Pending applications, if any, were also disposed of. FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF RAJASTHAN HIGH COURT 1. The issue involved in these two writ petitions is common. Therefore, both the writ petitions are being taken up for disposal by this common order. 2. Ltd., the petitioner had exported handicrafts/artistic wooden furniture items under seven shipping bills commen
rows.summary: Rajasthan High Court ruled customs cannot recover excess duty drawback from exporters without first reassessing the export classification.

rows.title: Fema / RBI | Five FEMA Missteps That Can Cost NRIs Heavily in India
rows.desc: Most NRIs I meet in practice don’t get into trouble because they’re trying to cheat the system. They get into trouble because nobody told them their compliance obligations changed the day their residential status did. FEMA (Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999) is a civil law, not a criminal one, but that doesn’t make its penalties gentle. Under Section 13, a contravention can cost you up to three times the amount involved where the sum is quantifiable, or up to ₹2 lakh where it isn’t, plus ₹5,000 for every day the violation continues. In cases involving undisclosed foreign assets worth more than ₹1 crore, the exposure gets considerably more serious. Here are five FEMA missteps that come up again and again, and what they can actually cost you. Table of Contents▸ 1. Running a resident savings account after you've become an NRI 2. Buying agricultural land, plantation property, or a farmhouse 3. Holding an NRE account jointly with a resident Indian 4. Not disclosing foreign assets that cross ₹1 crore 5. Continuing to trade through a resident demat or trading account The good news: most of this is fixable Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); 1. Running a resident savings account after you’ve become an NRI This is the single most common violation, mostly because it’s the easiest to overlook. The moment your residential status changes, typically once you’ve been living and working outside India with the intention of staying abroad, FEMA requires you to redesignate your existing resident savings account into an NRO (Non-Resident Ordinary) account, or close it and open an NRE (Non-Resident External) or FCNR account instead. A regular resident account cannot legally continue to receive your salary credits, rent, or dividend income once you’re no longer resident for FEMA purposes. People let this slide for years, sometimes because switching accounts feels like paperwork they can deal with later, sometimes because they simply don’t know the rule exists. The problem is that every transaction routed through that account after your status changed is technically a contravention, and the penalty exposure is calculated as up to three times the value of those transactions. Banks have also gotten sharper about catching this during periodic KYC updates, which is often when people first discover they’ve been out of compliance for years without realising it. Fix: the day your status changes, inform your bank and get the account converted. It takes a form and a copy of your visa or work permit, not the ordeal people imagine. 2. Buying agricultural land, plantation property, or a farmhouse NRIs can buy residential and commercial property in India freely, under the general permission route, without needing RBI approval. What they cannot buy , under any route is agricultural land, plantation property, or a farmhouse. This restriction trips up a lot of people who assume that because they’re allowed to invest in Indian real estate generally, all categories of land are fair game. They’re not, and this is one of the few property restrictions that doesn’t bend for NRIs the way it sometimes does for other classes of investment. The one legitimate route around this is inheritance; an NRI can inherit agricultural land from a resident Indian relative, or hold on to land they owned before their status changed. But purchasing such property fresh, even indirectly through a family member as a nominee, invites the same quantifiable-contravention penalty structure: up to three times the transaction value. Fix: if a property deal even brushes against agricultural or plantation land use, get the land classification confirmed with the local revenue authority before you sign anything, not after. 3. Holding an NRE account jointly with a resident Indian This one catches people off guard because it seems like such a natural, family-oriented thing to do; adding a parent or spouse back home as a joint holder on your NRE account “just in case.” Under FEMA rules, an NRE account can be held jointly only with another NRI (or with a resident relative under the specific “former or survivor” mandate for limited purposes) not as an active joint account with a resident who is meant to operate it independently. Because an NRE account holds repatriable foreign-origin funds and is meant to reflect a non-resident’s foreign earnings, giving a resident operational control over it undermines the entire rationale for the account’s tax-free, freely repatriable status. This is a contravention that tends to surface quietly, usually when a bank’s compliance team reviews account mandates, or when the RBI’s periodic checks flag inconsistent resident/non-resident combinations. It’s treated the same way as any other quantifiable contravention under Section 13(1) up to three times the amount involved. Fix: if you want a family member to have access to funds for household expenses, route it through a separate resident account via a transfer, rather than
rows.summary: NRIs can face heavy FEMA penalties for common mistakes like keeping resident accounts, owning restricted property, or failing to disclose foreign assets.
