Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Asrec (India) Limited Vs Landmark Motels and Travels Private Limited (NCLT Mumbai) Summary: The National Company Law Tribunal, Mumbai Bench-VI, considered a Section 7 application filed by ASREC India Limited against Landmark Motels and Travels Pvt. Ltd., together with an interlocutory application under Section 60(5) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. The Tribunal identified six principal issues: existence of financial debt and default; the allegedly contradictory dates of default; the applicability of Section 10A; the effect of Section 95 proceedings and the interim moratorium under Section 96 against personal guarantors; alleged non-compliance with RBI/MSME revival guidelines; and the effect of pending DRT/SARFAESI proceedings. On the debt issue, the Tribunal found that the credit facilities originally granted by State Bank of India and DHFL were subsequently taken over by Indian Bank, secured by mortgage of the Corporate Debtor’s properties, and later assigned to ASREC India Limited under the Assignment Agreement dated 28.02.2025. The Corporate Debtor did not dispute availing the financial facilities, execution of security documents, creation of the mortgage, restructuring or the assignment. The Tribunal treated the OTS proposal dated 21.01.2022 as a clear acknowledgment of liability and noted the NeSL record of default produced by the Financial Creditor. On the date of default, the Corporate Debtor relied upon differing dates appearing in SARFAESI notices, Section 95 proceedings and the present Section 7 proceedings. The Tribunal rejected the objection, holding that different proceedings may refer to different trigger events for different obligors and that the relevant Section 7 inquiry is whether default occurred. It relied on Dena Bank (Now Bank of Baroda) v. C. Shivakumar Reddy for the relevance of acknowledgment, restructuring and OTS proposals. The Tribunal held that the account first became overdue on 30.11.2019 and that restructuring did not obliterate the original default. On Section 10A, the Tribunal held that the default preceded the protected Covid-19 period. It relied on Power Trust (Promoter of Hiranmaye Energy Ltd.) v. Bhuvan Madan, IRP of Hiranmaye Energy Ltd. & Ors., B. Prashanth Hegde v. State Bank of India & Anr. and Raghavendra Joshi v. Axis Bank Ltd. & Anr. in considering the effect of restructuring on the original default. The Tribunal found that subsequent restructuring and the later GECL Covid-19 facility did not erase the earlier default. The principal legal controversy concerned Section 96. The Corporate Debtor argued that proceedings under Section 95 against its personal guarantors triggered an interim moratorium in relation to the same debt and therefore stayed the Section 7 proceedings. The Tribunal rejected that contention. It held that Section 96 operates in relation to the debtor against whom the Part III proceeding is instituted, namely the personal guarantor, and does not create a statutory bar to Section 7 proceedings against a separate corporate debtor. The Tribunal also relied on the 2026 insertion of Section 96(4), and on IL & FS Financial Services Ltd. v/s Serveall Constructions Pvt. Ltd. and Ors., as well as the decision of the NCLT Kochi in Furnace Fabrica (India) Limited v. State Bank of India. The Tribunal distinguished Tata Capital Ltd. v. Geeta Passi because that matter concerned a proprietorship concern without a separate juristic personality. On the MSME/RBI objection, the Tribunal noted that restructuring had in fact been granted pursuant to the Corporate Debtor’s request and additional facilities, including GECL assistance, had been sanctioned. It held that questions concerning compliance with RBI guidelines, restructuring norms, NPA classification or recovery measures did not negate the existence of debt and default for Section 7 purposes. Relying on Section 238 of the Code, the Tribunal held that the Code has overriding effect over inconsistent laws or instruments. It distinguished Pro Knits on the facts. As to pending DRT and SARFAESI proceedings, the Tribunal held that remedies under the Code are independent and concurrent with remedies under the SARFAESI Act and the Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act. The NeSL Form-D record reflected “Deemed to be Authenticated”, an outstanding amount of Rs.31,77,21,282.13/- and a date of default of 30.11.2019. Taking account of the acknowledgment contained in the OTS/restructuring proposals dated 21.01.2022 and 06.01.2025, the Tribunal found the Section 7 application filed on 27.10.2025 to be within limitation. In anal
rows.summary: NCLT Mumbai admitted ASREC India’s insolvency petition against Landmark Motels, finding a financial debt and default despite pending recovery actions.

rows.title: Company Law | Form ADT-1 for First Auditor: Mandatory Compliance or a Matter of Prudence?
rows.desc: Summary: Section 139(6) of the Companies Act, 2013 separately governs appointment of the first auditor of a non-Government company and, unlike Section 139(1) read with Rule 4(2) of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014, does not expressly mandate filing Form ADT-1. Although the revised ADT-1 effective 14 July 2025 now includes an option for appointment of the first auditor and ICSI recommends such filing, the enabling electronic form does not by itself create an express statutory requirement under Section 139(6). ICSI has also sought MCA clarification on this ambiguity. Accordingly, filing ADT-1 for the first auditor is advisable as a prudent compliance practice until MCA clarifies or amends the Rules, while past non-filing should not automatically be treated as a statutory default without examining the law and filing requirements applicable at the relevant time. Table of Contents▸ Is Form ADT-1 Mandatory for Appointment of the First Auditor under Section 139(6)? 1. Statutory Framework – Section 139(1) 2. Rule 4(2) and Form ADT-1 3. First Auditor is Governed Separately by Section 139(6) 4. What Changed from 14 July 2025? 5. Can a Revised Electronic Form Create a New Statutory Obligation? 6. ICSI MCA-21 V3 FAQ – An Important Development 7. ICSI Representation to MCA – 16 April 2026 8. Legal Requirement vs. Practical Compliance Legal Position Practical Position 9. What Should Professionals and Companies Do? For new companies For past cases where ADT-1 was not filed 10. Conclusion Key Legal References Show all 16 sections Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Is Form ADT-1 Mandatory for Appointment of the First Auditor under Section 139(6)? A Legal and Practical Analysis after the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Amendment Rules, 2025 The appointment of the first auditor of a company has traditionally been considered distinct from the appointment of an auditor at the Annual General Meeting. For years, a commonly accepted view among professionals has been that filing Form ADT-1 is not mandatory for the appointment of the first auditor under Section 139(6) of the Companies Act, 2013. However, the revised Form ADT-1 introduced with effect from 14 July 2025 specifically includes an option for appointment of the “First auditor by Board of directors/members/C&AG”. This change has created an important practical and legal question: Does the inclusion of the First Auditor in the revised Form ADT-1 make filing of ADT-1 mandatory for an appointment under Section 139(6)? Let us examine the issue from the statutory as well as practical perspective. 1. Statutory Framework – Section 139(1) Section 139(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 primarily deals with the appointment of an auditor by the members at the Annual General Meeting. The fourth proviso to Section 139(1) specifically requires the company to: inform the auditor concerned of his or its appointment; and file a notice of such appointment with the Registrar within 15 days of the meeting in which the auditor is appointed. Therefore, Section 139(1) itself contains an express requirement for intimation of the appointment to the Registrar. 2. Rule 4(2) and Form ADT-1 Rule 4(2) of the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Rules, 2014 provides the mechanism for such intimation. Rule 4(2) provides that the notice to the Registrar about the appointment of an auditor under the fourth proviso to Section 139(1) shall be in Form ADT-1. Therefore, the statutory linkage is clear: Section 139(1) → Intimation to Registrar → Rule 4(2) → Form ADT-1 There is, therefore, no ambiguity regarding an appointment falling under Section 139(1): filing of Form ADT-1 is required. 3. First Auditor is Governed Separately by Section 139(6) The appointment of the first auditor of a non-Government company is specifically governed by Section 139(6). Section 139(6) starts with the words: “Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-section (1)…” It provides that the first auditor shall be appointed by the Board of Directors within 30 days from the date of registration of the company. If the Board fails to appoint the first auditor within the prescribed period, it is required to inform the members, who shall appoint the auditor within 90 days at an Extraordinary General Meeting. The first auditor so appointed holds office until the conclusion of the first Annual General Meeting. An important distinction arises here: Section 139(6) does not expressly prescribe a requirement to file notice of such appointment with the Registrar. Further, Rule 4(2) expressly refers to the fourth proviso to Section 139(1), but does not expressly refer to Section 139(6). This distinction forms the basis of the view that filing of ADT-1 for the first auditor is not expressly mandated by the substantive provisions of the Act and Rules. 4. What Changed from 14 July 2025? The Ministry of Corporate Affairs issued the Companies (Audit and Auditors) Amendment Rules, 2025 vide Notification G.S.R. 359(E) dated 30
rows.summary: Companies should file ADT-1 for the first auditor as a precaution, but the law does not yet clearly make it mandatory.

rows.title: Company Law | Drafting Company AGM & EGM Minutes & Resolutions Under Companies Act, 2013
rows.desc: Minutes and Resolutions Masterclass: A Practical Guide to Drafting Board, AGM and EGM Records Summary: The article explains the preparation, recording, signing, preservation and practical drafting of minutes and resolutions for Board meetings, AGMs, EGMs and committee meetings. It identifies Section 118, Section 119, Section 173, Section 174, Section 179(3), Section 180, Section 103, and Rule 25 and Secretarial Standards SS-1 and SS-2 as the principal framework. It provides practical requirements for meeting details, attendance, quorum, previous minutes, interest and recusal, agenda-wise decisions, voting, signatures and custody, followed by core principles and sample resolutions covering directors, borrowings, related party transactions, private placement/preferential allotment and registered-office changes. It also gives meeting-specific tips, common pitfalls and a pre-submission checklist. Table of Contents▸ Introduction Legal framework at a glance Analysis of a valid minute Heading and basic details Attendance Chairman and quorum Confirmation of previous minutes Declaration of interest / recusal Agenda-wise discussion and decisions Voting details (especially for AGM/EGM) Signatures and custody Drafting resolutions: Core Principles Sample resolution formats Appointment / Re-appointment of Director (Sections 152/161) Borrowings (Section 180(1)(c)) Related Party Transaction (Section 188) Share Allotment (Private Placement / Preferential) – Section 42, 62(1)(c) Change in Registered Office (Within City/Town/Village) – Section 12 Minutes for specific meeting types: Practical Tips Board Meetings Annual General Meeting (AGM) Extraordinary General Meeting (EGM) Common pitfalls and how to avoid them Quick drafting checklist for practitioners Conclusion Show all 25 sections Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Introduction Minutes and resolutions are the backbone of corporate governance. They are not just routine records; they are the primary evidence of how a company takes decisions, complies with the law and protects the interests of shareholders and stakeholders. Under the Companies Act, 2013, minutes serve as legal evidence of proceedings at board meetings, general meetings and committee meetings. In inspections, secretarial audits, due diligence and disputes, regulators and courts rely heavily on minutes and resolutions. Poorly drafted minutes or vague resolutions can lead to regulatory observations, challenges to corporate actions and even personal liability for directors. This article provides a practical guide to drafting minutes and resolutions for Board meetings, AGMs and EGMs, along with sample clauses and common pitfalls. The focus is on what a Company Secretary or compliance professional actually needs at the desk, not just theoretical provisions. Legal framework at a glance The preparation, entry, signing and preservation of minutes are principally governed by the following: Section 118 of the Companies Act, 2013– Minutes of proceedings of general meetings, meetings of the Board of Directors and other meetings, and resolutions passed by postal ballot. Section 119 of the Companies Act, 2013– Inspection of minute-books of general meetings. Section 173– Meetings of the Board. Section 174– Quorum for meetings of the Board. Section 179(3)– Matters that must be exercised by the Board through resolutions passed at Board meetings. Section 180– Restrictions on specified powers of the Board requiring members’ approval by special resolution. Section 103– Quorum for general meetings. Rule 25 of the Companies (Management and Administration) Rules, 2014– Requirements relating to minutes of general meetings. Secretarial Standard–1 (SS-1) on Meetings of the Board of Directors and Secretarial Standard–2 (SS-2) on General Meetings, issued by ICSI and made mandatory through Section 118(10), to the extent applicable. For listed companies, additional requirements apply for e-voting, remote participation and disclosures, but the core drafting principles remain similar. Analysis of a valid minute A well-drafted minute should follow a clear structure. The following checklist can be used for Board, Committee, AGM and EGM minutes. Heading and basic details Include: Company name, CIN and registered office. Type of meeting: “Meeting of the Board of Directors” / “Annual General Meeting” / “Extraordinary General Meeting” / “Committee Meeting”. Date, time and venue (or statement that the meeting was held through video conferencing/other audio-visual mode). Common mistake: Omitting CIN, incorrect date/time, or not mentioning that the meeting was held through VC when applicable. Attendance Record: Directors: names, whether present physically or through video conferencing, and whether the Chairman was present. rows.title: Corporate Law | MP HC Holds Benami Suit Not Barred for Father’s Purchase in Minor Sons’ Names
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12317 Case Name Lateef Qureshi And Others Vs Ajeem Qureshi And Others (Madhya Pradesh High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Madhya Pradesh HC Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Lateef Qureshi And Others Vs Ajeem Qureshi And Others (Madhya Pradesh High Court) Summary: The Madhya Pradesh High Court at Jabalpur, in Lateef Qureshi and Others Versus Ajeem Qureshi and Others, considered whether a civil suit concerning properties purchased by a father in the names of his minor sons in 1968 and 1972 was barred by Section 4 of the Prohibition of Benami Property Transactions Act, 1988. The revision petition under Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure challenged the Trial Court’s order dated 25 September 2025, by which the defendants’ application seeking rejection of the plaint had been dismissed. The Trial Court had held that the suit was not barred under the 1988 Act, taking into account the amended definition of “benami transaction” under Section 2(9). The plaintiffs and defendants were members of the same family. According to the plaint, the father of defendants Nos. 9 and 10 had purchased the suit property in their names through two sale deeds, first in 1968 and again in 1972. At that time, the plaintiffs and defendants Nos. 11 and 12 had not been born. The defendants sought rejection of the plaint under Order VII Rule 11 CPC on the ground that the suit was barred by Section 4 of the 1988 Act. Before the High Court, the applicants argued that the Trial Court had wrongly relied upon Section 2(9), since that provision was introduced by the 2016 amendment and could not have retrospective operation. It was submitted that the unamended provisions had to be considered because the transactions pre-dated the 1988 Act itself. The applicants further contended that the Hindu Undivided Family coparcenary exception under the unamended Section 4(3)(a) was unavailable because the parties were Muslims, while the purchases in the names of the sons did not constitute purchases by a trustee or person standing in a fiduciary capacity. The plaintiffs, on the other hand, argued that the amended provisions should apply because the transactions occurred in 1968–1972, before enactment of the 1988 Act, whereas the suit was instituted in 2025 after the 2016 amendment. They further contended that the father had purchased the properties in the names of his minor sons and that the relationship between guardian and ward constituted a fiduciary relationship, thereby bringing the transaction within the protection of unamended Section 4(3)(b) as well. The High Court considered the Supreme Court’s decision in Manjula And Others Vs D.A. Srinivas, (2026) 488 ITR 407. The Supreme Court, as quoted in the order, held that the 2016 amendments, insofar as they were declaratory, procedural, curative and machinery-oriented, operated retrospectively/retroactively, whereas penal provisions creating new offences or enhancing punishment could operate only prospectively. The High Court therefore held that the provisions relied upon in the present case, being declaratory, would apply retrospectively. The High Court then examined amended Section 2(9), under which an exception is carved out where an individual acquires property in the name of a spouse or child. Since the transaction in the present case was alleged to have been made by the father in the names of his minor sons, the Court held that it fell within the exception under Section 2(9) and was therefore not hit by the 1988 Act. The Court further held that even if the pre-amended provisions were considered, the transaction would still be protected by Section 4(3)(b). That provision excluded transactions where the person in whose name property was held was a trustee or another person standing in a fiduciary capacity and the property was held for the benefit of another person towards whom such fiduciary capacity existed. For this purpose, the High Court relied upon Pawan Kumar v. Babulal, (2019) 4 SCC 367, in which the Supreme Court considered fiduciary relationships in the context of father and children and discussed the earlier decision in Marcel Martins v. M. Printer, (2012) 5 SCC 342. The quoted discussion explains that “fiduciary capacity” is not precisely defined in the 1988 Act but carries a recognised legal significance and encompasses relationships founded upon trust, confidence, good faith and an obligation to act for another’s benefit. The Supreme Court had also referred to CBSE v. Aditya Bandopadhyay, (2011) 8 SCC 497, for the meaning of fiduciary relationship. Applying that principle, the High Court observed that the transaction in favour of minor children involved the relationship between guardian and ward, which was undisputedly fiduciary. It ther
rows.summary: Madhya Pradesh High Court allowed a family property suit to proceed, finding a father’s purchases in his minor sons’ names may not be barred as benami.

rows.title: Income Tax | Old Credit Balances Cannot Be Taxed Under Section 68: ITAT Chennai
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12316 Case Name Ravindra Arunachala Nadar Vs ACIT (ITAT Chennai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2014-15 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Chennai Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Ravindra Arunachala Nadar Vs ACIT (ITAT Chennai) Summary: The appeal was filed by the assessee against the order of the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals)-15, Chennai dated 27.09.2019 for assessment year 2014-15. The assessee, a partner of M/s. Om Serma Enterprises, had filed his return declaring total income of Rs.26,85,900/-. The assessment under section 143(3) was completed on 29.12.2016 determining total income at Rs.1,43,43,706/- after, inter alia, additions relating to sundry creditors under section 41(1) and unexplained credits under section 68, with tax charged under section 115BBE. Before the CIT(A), the assessee contended that the credits were not trade credits for which any deduction had been claimed in earlier years and that the credits were not received during the relevant assessment year. According to the assessee, several balances had been brought forward from financial years 2006-07 and 2007-08 and some arose from partition of family properties. The CIT(A), however, confirmed additions relating to several creditors, principally on the basis that the assessee had not satisfactorily explained why the balances remained outstanding for several years and that the Department had not scrutinised the credits in the corresponding assessment years. Partial relief was granted in respect of the credit of Rs.25 lakhs in the name of Shri Dhanabalan and the credit of Rs.25,14,500/- relating to M/s. Om Sarma Enterprises, after supporting financial evidence and contra entries were furnished. Before the Tribunal, the assessee submitted that section 41(1) could not apply because there had been no earlier allowance or deduction in respect of the relevant liabilities. It was also submitted that the credits were old balances and therefore could not be assessed under section 68 in assessment year 2014-15. The Revenue supported the CIT(A)’s order, contending that the assessee had failed to establish the identity, genuineness and creditworthiness of the creditors. The ITAT Chennai noted that there was no dispute that all the credits had been brought forward from earlier assessment years and that both the Assessing Officer and CIT(A) had categorically admitted that the credits were brought forward from financial years 2006-07 and 2007-08. The Tribunal examined the statutory requirements of section 41(1) and held that an allowance or deduction in respect of the relevant loss, expenditure or trading liability in an earlier assessment year, together with a subsequent benefit by remission or cessation, was a prerequisite for invoking the provision. On the facts, the Tribunal found that the liabilities shown as sundry creditors were not trade liabilities for which deductions had been claimed in earlier years. It further found that the assessee had furnished evidence showing that certain credits arose from family partition and had been classified as sundry creditors because full effect had not been given to the partition on account of differences among family members. The Tribunal therefore held that section 41(1) could not be invoked in respect of the amounts of Rs.52,78,707/- relating to S/Shri ARKA. KaruthaPandian, K.A. Sekar and K. Sivasundarapappa. The Tribunal also held that the other credits of Rs.28,79,600/- relating to Late ARK Arunachala Nadar, Smt. Swarnalatha and Shri Dhanabalan were loans or advances rather than trade credits for which an earlier deduction had been claimed. Similarly, the Rs.10,00,000/- standing in the name of Shri Kumar represented a land advance received in financial year 2005-06. Since such loan or advance had not been claimed as a deduction, the Tribunal held that section 41(1) could not be applied. The Tribunal supported this position by referring to the Supreme Court decision in CIT v. Mahindra and Mahindra Ltd., reported in [2018] 404 ITR 1 (SC), and the Madras High Court decisions in ACIT vs. Transworld Garnet India Pvt. Ltd., reported in [2017] 397 ITR 233, and Narayanan Chettiary Industries vs. ITO, reported in [2005] 277 ITR 426. These decisions were referred to for the requirement of an earlier allowance or deduction before section 41(1) could be applied. Regarding section 68, the Tribunal observed that the relevant credits had not arisen during the current financial year. It noted that the credits relating to S/Shri ARKA. KaruthaPandian, K.A. Sekar, K. Sivasundarapappa and Late ARK Arunachala Nadar were received in financial year 2007-08; the credit relating to Smt. Swarnalatha was received in financial year 2006-07; and the land advance from Shri Kumar was received in financ
rows.summary: ITAT Chennai held that old brought-forward credit balances cannot be taxed as unexplained income under Section 68.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Rajkot Restricts Freight Disallowance and Upholds Relief on Loans, Gift and TDS
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12315 Case Name Shri Krishnabhagwan R. Sharma Vs ACIT (ITAT Rajkot) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2009-10 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Rajkot Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Shri Krishnabhagwan R. Sharma Vs ACIT (ITAT Rajkot) Summary: The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Rajkot Bench, disposed of cross appeals filed by the assessee, Shri Krishnabhagwan R. Sharma, proprietor of M/s. Kandla Cargo Carriers, and the Revenue for Assessment Year 2009-10. The appeals arose from the order of the learned CIT(A), Jamnagar dated 23.12.2014. The assessee’s appeal was partly allowed, while the Revenue’s appeal was dismissed. The principal issue in the assessee’s appeal and Revenue’s Grounds Nos. 1 to 3 concerned transportation charges of Rs.1,22,57,102/- shown as payable to eight transporters. The Assessing Officer treated the entire amount as bogus after an Inspector’s inquiry found that some parties were unavailable at the stated addresses and some denied having undertaken transactions with the assessee. The assessee also failed to produce original bills and proof of subsequent payments. The Assessing Officer accordingly made an addition of Rs.1,22,57,102/-. The CIT(A) upheld the finding that the liabilities and corresponding expenses were unverifiable, but rejected the methodology of adding the entire outstanding liability. He held that the liabilities represented trading expenses and that the proper approach was to determine the true business income by rejecting the books and estimating profit under section 145. Since the assessee had declared a net profit ratio of 1.61% on gross receipts of Rs.22,82,64,234/-, the CIT(A) applied a 4% net profit rate and sustained an addition of Rs.54,53,224/-. The Tribunal agreed that the transportation liabilities of Rs.1,22,57,102/- were not genuine or verifiable and observed that the assessee had not rebutted the specific findings of the lower authorities. However, it accepted the assessee’s contention that the estimation should consider the assessee’s own history. The Tribunal compared the results for AYs 2008-09, 2010-11 and 2011-12. It considered AY 2008-09 unsuitable for comparison because turnover was substantially lower, while the freight expenses in AYs 2010-11 and 2011-12 were about 56% of turnover compared with 66% in AY 2009-10. The excess was therefore approximately 10% of turnover. The Tribunal considered it fair and reasonable to restrict the disallowance to Rs.23,00,000/- and modified the CIT(A)’s order accordingly. Revenue’s Ground No.4 concerned Rs.37,85,407/- relating to four creditors. The Assessing Officer treated the liabilities as bogus because notices under section 133(6) were returned unserved and the assessee failed to produce original bills and proof of payment. The CIT(A), however, found that the liabilities were subsequently settled through banking channels and that there was no material disproving the evidence. The Tribunal upheld this finding and dismissed Ground No.4. Ground No.5 concerned an addition of Rs.3,01,49,768/- treated by the Assessing Officer as an unexplained gift from the assessee’s son. The assessee explained that two cheques received as gift and two cheques issued to M/s. Shreeji Overseas (India) Pvt. Ltd. were recorded on 31.03.2009 but were not cleared until 26.09.2009. The CIT(A) accepted the accounting explanation, noting that the received cheques were simultaneously offset by cheques issued and that the donor was the assessee’s son, an income-tax assessee. The Tribunal found that the accounting effects had been properly explained and that the Revenue had not rebutted the CIT(A)’s findings. The deletion of the addition was therefore upheld. Ground No.6 concerned unsecured loans of Rs.22,56,838/- from Malpani Securities and Shree Ganesh Traders. The Assessing Officer invoked section 68 because confirmations, PAN, bank statements and ITRs were not initially furnished. The CIT(A) admitted additional evidence showing repayment through banking channels in the subsequent year and relied upon the Gujarat High Court decision in Chandrashekhar Ayachi. He also relied upon Megha Industries for the alternative submission concerning credit of the trading addition. The Tribunal found no infirmity in the CIT(A)’s decision and dismissed Ground No.6. Ground No.7 concerned disallowance of Rs.9,00,000/- under section 40(a)(ia) in respect of dumper hire charges. Additional evidence established that TDS had been deducted and that the balance TDS of Rs.61,800/- was paid on 23.07.2009, before the due date for filing the return under section 139(1). Following the decision in Virgin Creations concerning the retrospective operation of the Finance Act, 2010 amendment, the CIT(A) deleted the disallowance. The Tribunal found th
rows.summary: ITAT Rajkot limited freight disallowance and upheld tax relief on loans, gifts and TDS after partially accepting the taxpayer’s appeal.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Nagpur Quashes Search Assessments for Invalid Section 153D Approval
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12314 Case Name Maheshwari Coal Benefication & Infrastructure Private Limited Vs DCIT Circle–1(1) (ITAT Nagpur) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2014–15 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Nagpur Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Maheshwari Coal Benefication & Infrastructure Private Limited Vs DCIT Circle–1(1) (ITAT Nagpur) Summary: The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Nagpur Bench, adjudicated seven appeals filed by Maheshwari Coal Benefication & Infrastructure Private Limited for assessment years 2014-15 to 2020-21 against orders dated 18.01.2024 passed by the CIT(A)-3, Nagpur. A search and seizure action under section 132 was conducted at the assessee’s premises on 11.07.2019. Assessments for A.Ys. 2014-15 to 2019-20 were completed under section 143(3) read with section 153A, while A.Y. 2020-21 was assessed under section 143(3). The Tribunal initially considered additions made in the unabated years on account of unexplained cash credits and interest on unsecured loans. Relying upon the Supreme Court ruling in PCIT v. Abhisar Buildwell (P) Ltd., the Tribunal held that, in completed/unabated assessments, additions under section 153A cannot be made in the absence of incriminating material found during the search. It further held that a statement recorded during a search conducted against a third party could not be used as incriminating material against the assessee without following the statutory mechanism under section 153C. The Tribunal also considered the assessee’s grievance that it had not been afforded cross-examination of the person whose statement was relied upon by the Assessing Officer, referring to the settled principle in Andaman Timber Industries concerning denial of cross-examination. The Tribunal separately examined the validity of the statutory approval granted under section 153D by the Additional CIT. For A.Ys. 2014-15 to 2019-20, the Assessing Officer had sought approval on 29.09.2021 for seven assessment years. The Tribunal found that the approval documents described the assessments as having been framed under section 143(3) read with section 153C even though the assessee itself was the person searched and the assessments for the six preceding years were required to be dealt with under section 153A. The Tribunal further examined the circumstances in which approval was granted on the very same day on which the Assessing Officer forwarded the assessment records/draft orders. It considered whether the Additional CIT had undertaken the meaningful and statutory exercise contemplated by section 153D or had granted approval mechanically without application of mind. On examination of the material and the approval process, the Tribunal concluded that the statutory approval under section 153D was not a proper and valid approval. The Tribunal held that the failure to demonstrate proper application of mind and the discrepancies concerning the statutory provision under which the assessments were framed resulted in invalid assumption of jurisdiction. Consequently, the assessments for A.Ys. 2014-15 to 2019-20 were quashed for want of valid statutory approval under section 153D. The assessment for A.Y. 2020-21 was also quashed on the same jurisdictional ground. As the assessments themselves were quashed, several remaining grounds concerning individual additions became academic and were left unadjudicated. The Tribunal nevertheless dealt with the issues concerning the unabated assessments and unsecured loans to the extent necessary, including the legal position that an addition under section 68 cannot ordinarily be made in respect of a brought-forward credit where there is no fresh credit during the relevant year, and the effect of repayment of the loan in a subsequent year where such repayment was accepted by the Revenue. The Tribunal also considered the material relied upon by the Revenue concerning alleged accommodation entries and the absence of an opportunity to cross-examine the third-party witness. The Tribunal ultimately partly allowed all seven appeals: ITA Nos. 113/Nag./2024, 114/Nag./2024, 115/Nag./2024, 116/Nag./2024, 117/Nag./2024, 118/Nag./2024 and 119/Nag./2024 for A.Ys. 2014-15 to 2020-21 respectively. The decisive jurisdictional finding was that the assessments could not survive in the absence of proper and valid statutory approval under section 153D. Cases Discussed PCIT v. Abhisar Buildwell (P) Ltd., [2023] 149 taxmann.com 399 (SC) — applied on the requirement of incriminating material for additions in completed/unabated assessments under section 153A. :contentReference[oaicite:1]{index=1} PCIT v. JPM Tools Ltd., (2022) 154 taxmann.com 44 (Del HC)— considered on statements recorded under section 132(4), incriminating material and denial of cross-examination. PCIT v.
rows.summary: ITAT Nagpur quashed search assessments because the required Section 153D approval was invalid and no incriminating evidence supported additions in completed years.

rows.title: Income Tax | Karnataka HC Holds Section 153C Mandatory for Search-Based Material in Regular Assessment
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12313 Case Name PCIT Vs VSL Mining Company Pvt Ltd (Karnataka High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Karnataka High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); PCIT Vs VSL Mining Company Pvt Ltd (Karnataka High Court) Summary: The Karnataka High Court dismissed the Revenue’s appeal under Section 260A of the Income-tax Act, 1961, arising from the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Bengaluru order dated 28 June 2019 concerning Assessment Year 2008-09. The principal dispute concerned whether material found and seized during a search conducted in the case of a third party could be relied upon while completing a regular assessment under Section 143(3), without invoking Section 153C of the Income-tax Act. M/s VSL Mining Company Pvt Ltd, belonging to the Lad group of companies and engaged in extraction and trading of iron ore, had filed its return for AY 2008-09 declaring total income of ₹55,96,22,255/-. A search under Section 132 had been conducted in the Lad group on 26 October 2007. Following notices under Sections 143(2) and 142(1), the Assessing Officer completed the assessment on 31 December 2009, determining taxable income at ₹115,89,54,044/- and balance tax payable at ₹44,31,32,567/-. Separately, a survey under Section 133A was conducted on 25 March 2008 and a search under Section 132 was conducted on 1 April 2008 in the case of Shri Manoj Kumar Jain. According to the Revenue, various documents concerning transactions between Shri Manoj Kumar Jain and the assessee were recovered and impounded. While completing the assessee’s assessment, the Assessing Officer considered those documents and statements of Shri Manoj Kumar Jain and made an addition of ₹28 crore for AY 2008-09 in relation to alleged unaccounted transactions. The assessee challenged the assessment before the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals), Mysuru. The Commissioner partly allowed the appeal on 17 October 2013. Both sides thereafter approached the Tribunal. By order dated 28 June 2019, the Tribunal dismissed the Revenue’s appeal and partly allowed the assessee’s appeal. The Revenue then filed the present appeal before the High Court. The High Court had admitted the appeal on 30 September 2020 and framed two substantial questions of law. The first concerned the assessee’s entitlement to deduction under Section 10B. The second concerned whether the Assessing Officer could take cognizance of seized material in proceedings under Section 143(3) without invoking Section 153C. On the Section 10B issue, the High Court noted that the Tribunal had adjudicated the matter in accordance with the coordinate Bench decision in Tata Elxsi Ltd. v. ACIT. As the Revenue had not demonstrated how the Tribunal’s decision was erroneous, the Court answered substantial question of law No. 1 against the Revenue and in favour of the assessee. On the second question, the Court examined the Tribunal’s reasoning concerning material seized during the search of Shri Manoj Kumar Jain. The Tribunal had found that the Assessing Officer did not invoke Section 153C after receiving the seized material, but instead used that material during the pending assessment proceedings under Section 143(3). The Tribunal concluded that the jurisdictional conditions prescribed for proceedings under Section 153C were distinct from those governing a regular assessment. It further held that the pending assessment proceedings would abate upon receipt of the seized material and that, if the Assessing Officer intended to act upon that material, the statutory procedure under Section 153C had to be followed after recording the requisite satisfaction. The High Court referred to the statutory scheme under Sections 153A, 153B and 153C, noting that these provisions were introduced by the Finance Act, 2003 with effect from 1 June 2003 to specifically deal with assessments in search or requisition cases. The Court also considered Dinakar Suvarna v. DCIT, where a coordinate Bench had considered a situation involving reopening based on search material without following the Section 153C procedure. The Court further considered the Division Bench judgment in Shyam Sunder Khandelwal v. ACIT, which held that where material belonging or relating to a person other than the searched person is seized, the Assessing Officer is required to proceed under Section 153C after satisfaction of the prescribed conditions. That judgment also recognised the special nature of Sections 153A to 153D in relation to regular assessment or reassessment provisions. The Karnataka High Court ultimately held that, once material pursuant to a search is relied upon, the Assessing Officer is required to follow the procedure contemplated under Sections 153A, 153B and 153C, and it is impermissible to continue t
rows.summary: Karnataka HC held that search-seized third-party material cannot be used in a regular assessment unless Section 153C is followed.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Pune Quashes Section 147 Reassessment Where Section 153C Applied to Search Information
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12312 Case Name Vijaykumar Mangilalji Chordiya Vs NFAC (ITAT Pune) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2013-14 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Pune Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Vijaykumar Mangilalji Chordiya Vs NFAC (ITAT Pune) Summary: The Pune Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal allowed the assessee’s appeal and quashed the reassessment completed under section 147 read with section 143(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, holding that where the information forming the basis of reopening emerged from a search conducted at the premises of a third party, the proper course was to proceed under section 153C rather than section 147. The assessee, an individual, had filed his return of income on 19.07.2013 declaring total income of Rs.3,80,300/- after claiming deduction of Rs.51,831/- under Chapter VI-A of the Act. The Assessing Officer obtained information that the assessee had made cash deposits of Rs.6,09,74,438/- as a member of M/s. Shri Renuka Mata Multistate Credit Society Ltd. The Assessing Officer considered the source of the deposits to remain unverified and reopened the assessment. The recorded reasons, however, referred to information concerning cash deposits of Rs.3,16,38,294/- during F.Y. 2011-12 and referred to A.Y. 2012-13. Notice under section 148 was issued. In response, the assessee filed a return on 14.03.2022 admitting income of Rs.10,00,300/-. Notices under sections 143(2) and 142(1) were thereafter issued. The Assessing Officer determined profit at 8% of the turnover of Rs.6,09,74,438/-, arriving at net profit of Rs.48,77,987/-. After giving credit for business income of Rs.8,19,119/- already offered by the assessee, an addition of Rs.40,58,868/- was made. Before the Assessing Officer, the assessee stated that his main sources of income were advisory and brokerage charges and that he also lent temporary advances or loans to businessmen or friends by obtaining money from other parties and earned commission or charges on such transactions. The assessee also submitted that the deposits included cash deposits as well as other deposits/transfers. The Assessing Officer, after noting regular deposits and withdrawals throughout the year, treated the entire deposits as turnover and estimated net profit at 8%, observing that the assessee was engaged in money-lending and other activities. The CIT(A)/NFAC upheld the addition. The appellate authority recorded that the assessee had admitted that he was engaged in money lending and had not maintained proper books of account. It held that the assessee had failed to explain the nature and source of the entire deposits and that his claim that the activity was entirely on commission basis at approximately 2% was unsupported by evidence. The 8% profit estimation was accordingly confirmed. Before the Tribunal, the assessee challenged the validity of reopening, the assessment procedure and the addition. An additional ground was also raised contending that the notice under section 148 was bad in law because the information had been received in the course of a search on a third party and therefore the Assessing Officer ought to have proceeded under section 153C. The assessee relied on National Thermal Power Co. Ltd. Vs. CIT, (1998) 229 ITR 383 (SC) and Jute Corporation of India Ltd. Vs. CIT, (1991) 187 ITR 688 (SC), submitting that the additional ground was purely legal and required no investigation of new facts. The Tribunal admitted the additional ground, holding that all necessary facts were already on record. On the jurisdictional issue, the assessee referred to section 153C and submitted that the recorded reasons themselves showed that the relevant information concerning the cash deposits had emerged during the search at M/s. Shri Renuka Mata Multistate Credit Society Ltd. Reliance was placed on the Pune Tribunal’s decision in ITO Vs. Narendra Sampatlal Bafna, ITA No.688/PUN/2024, order dated 19.08.2024, where the Tribunal had held in the circumstances considered therein that the proper course was initiation of proceedings under section 153C rather than section 147. The Revenue opposed the additional ground and submitted that the Assessing Officer had adopted the proper procedure. On merits, it contended that the profit rate adopted in an earlier assessment year could not bind the Assessing Officer because the principle of res judicata does not apply to income-tax proceedings. The Tribunal found force in the assessee’s jurisdictional contention. It considered the decision in ITO Vs. Narendra Sampatlal Bafna, ITA No.688/PUN/2024, in which, after considering section 153C and various decisions, the Pune Bench had held that where information concerning an assessee emerged from seized material found during a third-party search, proce
rows.summary: ITAT Pune held that tax reopening based on third-party search material must use section 153C, not section 147, and quashed the reassessment.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Supreme Court Upholds Arbitration Despite Full and Final Discharge Voucher
rows.desc: 1 REPORTABLE IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION CIVIL APPEAL No. 8550 OF 2019 (ARISING OUT OF SLP (C) NO. 34186 OF 2015) THE ORIENTAL INSURANCE CO. LTD. & ANR. ...APPELLANTS VERSUS DICITEX FURNISHING LTD. ...RESPONDENT J U D G M E N T S. RAVINDRA BHAT, J. 1.Leave granted. With the consent of counsel, the appeal was heard finally. The Oriental Insurance Co. Ltd (hereafter “the insurer” or “the appellant”) appeals the decision of a single judge of the Bombay High Court, who allowed the respondent’s application under Section 11(6) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 (hereafter “the Act”) and appointed an 2 arbitrator. The insurer’s objection about maintainability of the application on the ground that the respondent (hereafter “Dicitex”) had signed the discharge voucher and accepted the amount offered, thus, signifying accord and satisfaction, which in turn meant that there was no arbitrable dispute, was rejected. 2.The relevant facts in this appeal are that on 17.09.2011, Dicitex obtained a Standard Fire and Special Peril Policy; it was issued by the appellant to cover the stocks of goods lying in its three separate godowns located at Thane, Maharashtra, by three separate endorsements. The total sum insured was @ 13 crores.₹ Clause 13 of the terms and conditions of the said policy contained an arbitration clause. On 25.05.2012, a fire broke out at night on the ground floor of the building occupied by RFCL, which fire spread to the first floor of the building and completely engulfed all of the appellant’s three godowns which had stored its goods. All the stocks in all the three godowns were completely destroyed. Dicitex informed the appellant on 26.05.2012, about the fire and the consequential loss. The appellant appointed M/s. C.P. Mehta & Co. as Surveyors and Assessors to survey the loss suffered by Dicitex and to report on the claim to be lodged upon 3 the insurer­appellant, by the said company. Dicitex lodged a total and final claim upon the appellant for a sum of 14,88,14,327/­₹ comprising 13,52,85,752/­ towards cost of the materials₹ destroyed and 1,35,28,575/­ as overheads. Dicitex claims also₹ to have submitted comprehensive documentary evidence and detailed work sheets in support of the claim made to the insurer. On 14.08.2012, after visiting Dicitex’s factory and the godowns, and after scrutinizing the materials submitted by it in support of its claim, the Surveyor appointed by the insurer filed a Final Survey Report recommending that the claim be settled for an amount of 12,93,26,704.98/­ and that after deducting an₹ amount of 5% towards compulsory deduction for excess, a net amount of 12,28,60,369/­ be paid over to Dicitex. The latter₹ alleged that a copy of this survey report was not supplied to it, by the insurer, or the surveyor. 3.On 20.09.2012, Dicitex addressed a letter to the appellant’s chairman, informing him of the financial distress that it was facing, requesting for settlement of the claim on priority basis. Dicitex also informed him about a temporary loan obtained ­to the tune of 10 crores­ from Union Bank of India for 3 months at₹ 4 a high rate of interest which was due for repayment in September 2012 and requested him that it would be a great financial help if its claim could be settled on priority basis which would mitigate their hardship. Again, on 25.10.2012, Dicitex informed the insurer that the sale value of the goods destroyed was above 19₹ crores and that it had not only lost its goods but also its profits. Dicitex informed that it had already submitted all the documentary evidence supporting the claim to the Surveyor, M/s. C.P. Mehta & Co., yet another letter was addressed to the appellant’s chairman on 31.10.2012 placing on record that it had understood from the surveyor M/s. C.P. Mehta & Co. that the Head Office of the appellant asked for some more information in connection with the claim. Dicitex stated that compiling, organizing and sending various documents totalling around 35,000 in number, entailed voluminous work. It was stated that the surveyor had already gone through those documents and had picked up at random, sample of various concerned records. Dicitex stated that it was arranging to compile the documents and agreed to send them to the surveyor as soon as possible. In other letters (dated 10.01.2012, 28.01.2013), again requests were 5 made to the insurer to release the amounts. Apparently, the appellant appointed a Chartered Accountant (M/s Naveen Jhand & Associates) to carry out a resurvey of the claim made by it (Dicitex). The latter had already furnished 37,700 documents physically, which showed the exact quantity of furnishing fabrics in meters. Dicitex brought to the notice of the Chairman­cum­ Managing Director that the new surveyors had asked for large number of documents again and such documents could not be supplied. rows.title: Corporate Law | SC Bars Courts from Excluding Claims at Section 11 Arbitration Stage
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12309 Case Name Office for Alternative Architecture Vs Ircon Infrastructure and Services Ltd. (Supreme Court of India) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts Supreme Court of India Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Office for Alternative Architecture Vs Ircon Infrastructure and Services Ltd. (Supreme Court of India) Summary: The Supreme Court considered whether a court exercising jurisdiction under Section 11 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 can exclude particular claims from arbitration by holding them to be non-arbitrable or to fall within an excepted category, after finding that an arbitration agreement exists. The appeal arose from the judgment and order dated September 6, 2023 of the High Court of Delhi at New Delhi. While appointing an arbitral tribunal under Section 11 of the 1996 Act, the High Court had excluded certain claims referred to in paragraphs 48(ii), (iii) and (iv) of the claim petition, treating them as non-arbitrable/excepted matters in view of Clauses 50 and 50.2 of the agreement. The appellant, Office for Alternative Architecture, contended that once the Court found an arbitration agreement to exist, its enquiry under Section 11 had to remain confined to that question. According to the appellant, whether particular claims fell within an excepted category was a matter for the arbitral tribunal. The appellant therefore sought setting aside of the impugned order to the extent it excluded the specified claims, leaving all such pleas open before the arbitral tribunal. The respondent relied upon the Supreme Court’s decision in Emaar India Limited vs. Tarun Aggarwal Projects LLP and Anr., (2023) 13 SCC 661, to contend that the High Court was empowered to exclude non-arbitrable claims at the stage of appointment. The Supreme Court examined Section 11(6A) of the 1996 Act, which was inserted by Act 3 of 2016 with effect from October 23, 2015. The provision requires the Supreme Court or High Court, while considering an application under Section 11(4), (5) or (6), to confine its examination to the existence of an arbitration agreement. The Court noted that although Act 33 of 2019 omitted Section 11(6A), that amendment had not been notified and consequently Section 11(6A) continued to remain in the statute book. The Court also considered the statement of objects and reasons accompanying the 2015 amendment, which stated that while considering an application for appointment of an arbitrator, the Court should examine the existence of a prima facie arbitration agreement and “not other issues”. The significance of those words had been considered by the seven-Judge Bench in In Re: Interplay Between Arbitration Agreements under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996 and the Indian Stamp Act, 1899, 2023 INSC 1066. The Supreme Court in that decision observed that the issues beyond the existence of a prima facie arbitration agreement included matters arising from unnecessary judicial interference in arbitration proceedings. The Court further relied upon the three-Judge Bench decision in SBI General Insurance Co. Ltd. vs. Krish Spinning, 2024 INSC 532, which had considered the seven-Judge Bench decision in In Re: Interplay and held that the enquiry at the stage of appointment of an arbitrator is limited to scrutiny of the prima facie existence of the arbitration agreement. The Court also noted that the observations in Vidya Drolia vs. Durga Trading Corporation, (2021) 2 SCC 1, and NTPC vs. SPML Infra Limited, (2023) 9 SCC 385, concerning the extent of enquiry at the referral stage could not continue to apply in a manner inconsistent with the subsequent decision in In Re: Interplay. On that basis, the Supreme Court held that the High Court had erred in bisecting the appellant’s claims into arbitrable and non-arbitrable portions after finding that an arbitration agreement existed. The proper course was to leave the question of non-arbitrability of particular claims to the arbitral tribunal. The Court therefore allowed the appeal and set aside the High Court’s order insofar as it excluded the claims mentioned in paragraph 48(ii), (iii) and (iv), as referred to in paragraph 8 of the impugned order. The parties were left at liberty to raise the plea of non-arbitrability of particular claims before the arbitral tribunal, which was directed to decide that issue without being prejudiced by the observations contained in the High Court’s order. There was no order as to costs. Cases Discussed Emaar India Limited Vs. Tarun Aggarwal Projects LLP and Anr., (2023) 13 SCC 661 — referred to on the respondent’s contention that the High Court was empowered to exclude non-arbitrable claims while exercising jurisdiction under Section 11. In Re: Interplay Between Arbitration Agreements under the Arbi
rows.summary: The Supreme Court said courts appointing arbitrators cannot screen out specific claims as non-arbitrable once an arbitration agreement is found.

Clause 28 of the agreement provided that any dispute or difference between the parties, including regarding the validity or interpretation of the agreement, would be referred to the sole arbitration of the District Magistrate, Murshidabad. A dispute arose following a letter dated January 11, 2022 issued by Murshidabad Zilla Parishad alleging neglect and failure to pay rent. The respondent also raised suspicion regarding the actual amount collected by the petitioner in running the hospital and the figures disclosed to it. The petitioner challenged the termination notice by filing a suit before the Civil Judge (Senior Division), First Court, Murshidabad at Berhampore. In that suit, the respondent invoked Section 8 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, contending that the dispute arising from the termination letter was required to be decided through arbitration. The Trial Court rejected the Section 8 application and granted an injunction until disposal of the suit. The orders were challenged before the High Court in FMA 816 of 2025. By judgment dated July 15, 2025, the Division Bench allowed the appeal and held that the dispute ought to have been referred to arbitration under Section 8. The Division Bench also held that the injunction granted by the Trial Court was without jurisdiction because the Trial Court was required to refer the entire dispute to arbitration instead of entertaining the suit and deciding the prayer for injunction. According to the petitioner, the Division Bench had already held that the disputes raised in the suit were governed by the arbitration clause. Following disposal of the appeal, the petitioner issued a notice under Section 21 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, enumerating disputes including termination, arrear rent, audit discrepancies, eviction proceedings, denial of rents and extension. The petitioner also alleged that it had invested more than Rs.20 crores in running the hospital and claimed that such amount was recoverable from the respondent. The petitioner relied upon the Supreme Court decision in Central Warehousing Corporation and Another vs. Sidhartha Tiles & Sanitary Pvt. Ltd., reported at 2024 SCC OnLine SC 2983. The reliance was placed on the distinction between contractual disputes falling within an arbitration agreement and proceedings under a special statute governing eviction. The petitioner contended that even if the special statute governed eviction proceedings, the area of operation of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act and the West Bengal Public Land (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1962 were different and arbitration could not be refused merely because proceedings under the 1962 Act had been initiated. The respondent contended that the issues of eviction and termination were included in the notice invoking arbitration. It argued that its right to proceed against the petitioner under the 1962 Act was not an arbitrable issue and that the referral court should therefore resist referring the dispute concerning eviction and termination to arbitration. It was further submitted that the lease had expired by efflux of time on July 9, 2025 and that the petitioner had thereafter become an authorised occupant. According to the respondent, nothing prevented it from evicting the petitioner under the 1962 Act. The notice under that Act had been issued on July 22, 2025, before the notice invoking arbitration. The High Court noted that the respondent had accepted the existence of the arbitration clause. It further noted that, on the respondent’s own appeal, the dispute arising in the suit had already been referred to arbitration and that the principal dispute in the suit concerned termination of the tenancy prior to expiry of the lease. The Court also found from the notice invoking arbitration that there were claims and allegations apart from eviction. While considering the issue, the Court reproduced paragraphs 13 and 14 of the Supreme Court judgment in Central Warehousing Corporation. rows.summary: Calcutta HC held pending eviction proceedings under the 1962 Act do not bar arbitration of disputes under the parties’ agreement.

rows.title: Corporate Law | SC Upholds Arbitration for Contractual Disputes Despite Public Premises Act
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12307 Case Name Central Warehousing Corporation & Anr. Vs Sidhartha Tiles & Sanitary Pvt. Ltd. (Supreme Court of India) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts Supreme Court of India Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Central Warehousing Corporation & Anr. Vs Sidhartha Tiles & Sanitary Pvt. Ltd. (Supreme Court of India) Summary: The Supreme Court considered whether the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971 overrides the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, and whether the High Court erred in appointing an arbitrator under Section 11 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. Central Warehousing Corporation, a statutory body under the Warehousing Corporations Act, 1962 and under the administrative control of the Ministry of Consumer Affairs, Government of India, had provided 1295 sq. mtrs. of storage space to M/s Sidhartha Tiles & Sanitary Pvt. Ltd. Possession was handed over on 12.09.2012. A lease agreement dated 26.09.2012 provided for a three-year period commencing from 12.09.2012 and expiring on 11.09.2015, with renewal by mutual consent. The storage rate was fixed at Rs. 131 per square metre per month. Clause 16 contained an arbitration clause. During the subsistence of the agreement, the Corporation communicated revisions to the storage charges. A demand for enhanced payment with effect from 01.11.2012 was raised, followed by further communications dated 10.05.2013 and 31.12.2014. The storage charges were subsequently revised with effect from 01.04.2015, and the respondent was informed that the tariff would be Rs.177 per sq. mtr. per month. The respondent indicated its interest in continuing the facility and sought renewal of the agreement, while undertaking to clear arrears due under the original agreement. On 16.09.2015, the appellant rejected the request for renewal and raised a demand of Rs.16,10,004/-. Since the respondent had not vacated the premises after expiry of the lease on 11.09.2015, the appellant invoked the Public Premises (Eviction of Unauthorised Occupants) Act, 1971. The respondent subsequently vacated the premises on 13.11.2015 before an order of the Estate Officer could be passed. The Estate Officer nevertheless passed an order on 31.12.2015 holding that the respondent was in unauthorised possession from 11.09.2015 to 13.11.2015 and directing payment of certain dues. The respondent invoked arbitration by filing an application under Section 11(6) of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996, relying upon the subsisting arbitration clause. The disputes concerned the right of renewal of the contract and the legality and propriety of the revision of storage rates during the subsistence of the agreement. The High Court concluded that the claims raised in the notice and Section 11 application were covered by Clause 16 of the agreement and referred the disputes to arbitration. The appellant challenged that decision before the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court held that the submission concerning the overriding effect of the Public Premises Act had to fail. It observed that the disputes raised in the Section 11 application related to promises and reciprocal promises arising from the agreement dated 26.09.2012. The right of renewal and the legality and propriety of the enhanced demand arose during the subsistence of that agreement and depended upon its interpretation, construction and contractual obligations. The Court distinguished these contractual disputes from proceedings under the Public Premises Act, which authorises ejectment of a tenant in unauthorised occupation of public premises and consequential directions. Since the original lease validly subsisted until 11.09.2015, the Public Premises Act did not affect the contractual dispute relating to the period from 12.09.2012 to 11.09.2015. The Court further held that the Public Premises Act neither barred nor overlapped with the arbitration proceedings initiated under the Arbitration and Conciliation Act. On the appointment of the arbitrator, the Supreme Court held that the revision of storage charges occurred during the subsistence of the contract and that its legality and propriety would depend upon the terms of the agreement. The right of renewal likewise depended upon the construction of that agreement. Both disputes therefore arose out of the agreement and were covered by Clause 16. In considering the scope of Section 11(6), the Court relied upon its decision in SBI General Insurance Co. Ltd. vs. Krish Spinning, 2024 SCC OnLine SC 1754, and reproduced paragraphs 110, 111 and 114 concerning the limited enquiry at the referral stage. The Court stated that the referral court was required to examine the existence of an arbitration agreement and that the enquiry was confined to a prima facie scr
rows.summary: The Supreme Court said arbitration can still resolve contractual disputes even when the Public Premises Act also applies.

rows.title: Income Tax | TPO Reference Mandatory for Arm’s Length Price Determination: ITAT Delhi
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12306 Case Name DCIT Vs Meneta Automotive Components Pvt. Ltd. (ITAT Delhi) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2008-09 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Delhi Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); DCIT Vs Meneta Automotive Components Pvt. Ltd. (ITAT Delhi) Summary: The Revenue appealed against the order of the CIT(A)-44, New Delhi dated 30.11.2017 in the case of Meneta Automotive Components Pvt. Ltd. for Assessment Year 2008-09. The dispute concerned a transfer pricing adjustment of Rs.4,96,95,925/- made by the Assessing Officer (AO) himself without making a reference to the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO). The Revenue questioned whether the CIT(A) was justified in allowing the assessee’s appeal on the ground that the AO had not made a reference to the TPO and in deleting the transfer pricing adjustment by relying upon the judgment in M/s Ranbaxy Lab Ltd. Vs. CIT, 345 ITR 193 (Del.), despite the Revenue’s contention concerning the subsequent decision of the Bombay High Court in Vodafone India Services Pvt. Ltd. Vs. UOI, 361 ITR 531 (Bom.). The Tribunal recorded that the fact that the AO himself had determined the Arm’s Length Price (ALP) was not disputed by either party. The short question before the Tribunal was whether the AO could himself determine the ALP without referring the issue to the TPO. In deciding this issue, the Tribunal considered CBDT Instruction No. 3/2003 dated 20.05.2003, Instruction No. 15/2015 dated 16.10.2015 and the judgment of the Hon’ble Supreme Court dated 13.08.2019 in PCIT Vs M/s. S.G. Asia Holdings (India) Pvt. Ltd., Civil Appeal No. 6144 of 2019. Instruction No. 15/2015, reproduced in the Tribunal’s order, explains the respective functions of the AO and TPO under the transfer pricing provisions. It states that the power to determine the ALP is contained in Section 92C(3), while Section 92CA provides for reference by the AO to the TPO. Upon reference, the TPO determines the ALP by an order in writing and the AO thereafter computes the total income in conformity with the ALP determined by the TPO. The Instruction further provides that the AO must first satisfy himself that the taxpayer has entered into an international transaction with an associated enterprise. It identifies circumstances in which the AO must, as a jurisdictional requirement, record his satisfaction that income or potential income arises from or is affected by determination of the ALP before determining the ALP himself under Section 92C(3) or referring the matter to the TPO under Section 92CA(1). It also provides for an opportunity of being heard in the specified circumstances. The Instruction explains that, where a reference is made, the TPO’s role begins upon receipt of the reference from the AO and is limited to determination of the ALP of the international transactions referred to him, subject to the statutory provisions concerning other international transactions coming to his notice. It also requires the TPO to determine the transfer price using one of the methods specified under Section 92C and the most appropriate method under Section 92C(2), after considering the relevant facts and data and passing a speaking order. The Instruction further states that the AO is required to compute the total income having regard to the ALP determined by him under Section 92C(3), while, where the ALP is determined by the TPO under Section 92CA(3), the AO has to compute the total income in conformity with the ALP so determined. The Tribunal then considered the Supreme Court judgment in PCIT Vs M/s. S.G. Asia Holdings (India) Pvt. Ltd.. In that case, the Supreme Court considered CBDT Instruction No. 3/2003. The Supreme Court recorded that the Tribunal had held the transfer pricing adjustment made by the AO to be contrary to the mandatory CBDT instructions because the AO had not made a reference to the TPO. The Supreme Court agreed that, by not making the reference, the AO had breached the mandatory instructions issued by the CBDT. The Supreme Court, however, also held that the matter ought to have been restored to the AO so that an appropriate reference could be made to the TPO, leaving it to the authorities and the concerned Commissioner to consider the matter in terms of Section 92CA(1). The Supreme Court therefore allowed the appeal to that extent and directed the AO to take appropriate steps in terms of Instruction No. 3/2003. Following the CBDT instructions and the Supreme Court judgment, the Delhi Bench held that it was mandatory for the AO to refer the matter for determination of ALP to the TPO. According to the Tribunal, failure to do so resulted in breach of the mandatory instructions and an order passed without satisfying the requisite procedure would lead to nullity of such order. On that basis,
rows.summary: ITAT Delhi held that an income-tax officer cannot make a transfer-pricing adjustment without first referring the arm’s-length price issue to the TPO.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Bangalore Upholds Section 36(1)(iii) Disallowance on Interest-Free Subsidiary Loan
rows.desc: IN THE INCOME TAX APPELLATE TRIBUNAL RAJKOT BENCH, RAJKOT Before Shri A.L. Gehlot (AM) and Shri D.T. Garasia (JM) I.T.A. No. 552/Rjt/2008 (Assessment year 2005-06) M/s Woodman Trading Co Pvt Ltd vs the ITO (OSD) Plot No.573, Galpadar Road Gandhidham Gandhidham PAN : AAACW3815G (Appellant) (Respondent) Appellant by : Shri MP Sarda Respondent by: Shri Avinash Kumar O R D E R A.L. Gehlot : This is an appeal filed by the assessee and is directed against the order of the CIT(A)-II, Rajkot dated 29-09-2008 for the assessment year 2005-06. The ground raised in the appeal is that the CIT(A) erred in sustaining disallowance of Rs.3,99,452 out of the interest expenses. 2. During the assessment proceedings, the assessing officer noticed that the assessee has given advance free loans of Rs. 3,84,000 to different parties for which he did not charge any interest whereas the assessee has claimed interest expenses u/s 36(1)(iii) of the Act. The assessing officer was of the view that interest to the extent of those parties from whom interest has not been charged is disallowable. He accordingly calculated by applying 12% of the interest rate at Rs.3,99,452 and the same was added to the total income. 3. The CIT(A) confirmed the order of the assessing officer as under: “3.2 I have considered the arguments of the A.O. as well as A.R. carefully. With due respect, I wish to differ from the decision of Ahmedabad ITAT in the case of Torrent Financers. In the appellant’s case, ther A.O. tried to create direct link between interest-borne loans and interest-free advances. But, as per the www.taxguru.in ITA No.552/Rjt/2008 2 appellant, it had sufficient interest-free funds, including adequate reserves to cover interest-free advances. Here, it is pertinent to draw the support from the Apex Court’s decision in the case of S.A. Builders Ltd Vs. CIT(A)_(2007) 288 ITR 1. The Supreme Court clearly said that in order to decide whether interest on funds borrowed by the assessee given as an interest-free loan to be allowed as a deduction u/s 36(1)(iii) of the Act, one has to inquire whether the loan was given by the assessee as a measure of commercial expediency and also for the purpose of business. It further said that the authorities and courts should examine the purpose for which the assessee advanced the money and what the recipient did with the money. In this instant case, the appellant advanced interest-free loans to its relatives and friends and the appellant failed to prove that the advancement involved any logical grounds of commercial expediency. The A.R. also failed to elaborate how these friends and relatives utilized the said loan amounts purposefully. As the appellant failed to provide nexus between the expenditure and the purpose of business, I have no other go, except upholding the proportionate disallowance of interest is to be upheld.” 4. The ld.AR submitted that it was contended before the assessing officer and CIT(A) by the assessee that the assessee was having sufficient own fund out of which the assessee has given the interest free advances. He submitted that the assessee before the CIT(A) assessee cited decision of ITAT, Ahmedabad Bench in the case of Torrent Financers 73 TTJ (Ahd) 624 and M/s Choice Impex vs ITO (unreported) and SA Builders vs CIT 288 ITR 1 (SC) which were not found favour with the CIT(A). The learned AR also relied upon order of the ITAT in the case of Dy.CIT vs. HP Shah & Co ITA No.3694/Mum/2006 order dated 15-01-2009. The ld.DR, on the other hand relied upon the order of the CIT(A). 5. We have heard the learned representatives of the parties, record perused. The CIT(A) while upholding the order of the assessing officer observed that he want to differ from the decision of Ahmedabad ITAT in the case of Torrent Financers (supra). At the cost of repetition the relevant observations of the CIT(A) reproduced below: www.taxguru.in ITA No.552/Rjt/2008 3 “With due respect, I wish to differ from the decision of Ahmedabad ITAT in the case of Torrent Financers.” The above observations made by the CIT (A) are not warranted in judicial discipline. Here we would like to mention that the principles of judicial discipline require that the orders of higher appellate authorities should be followed by the subordinate authorities otherwise; entire judicial system would lead to chaos. In this regard we would like to refer following observations of Hon’ble Delhi High Court in the case of Nokai Corporation V.
