rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Delhi Quashes Income Tax Reassessment Notice Issued 3 Days Beyond Six-Year Limit
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12304 Case Name Ravindra Vs ITO (ITAT Delhi) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2015-16 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Delhi Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Ravindra Vs ITO (ITAT Delhi) Summary: These appeals were filed by the assessee against separate orders of the National Faceless Appeal Centre, Delhi, relating to Assessment Year 2015-16. ITA No. 161/DEL/2026 concerned the quantum proceedings, while ITA No. 162/DEL/2026 concerned the penalty proceedings. The assessment had been reopened under Section 148 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 and the assessment order was ultimately passed on 27.02.2024. A penalty order dated 05.08.2024 was also passed. The assessee sought admission of additional grounds challenging the jurisdictional validity of the reassessment. The Tribunal admitted the additional grounds, relying upon the principle laid down in National Thermal Power Corporation v. CIT, (1998) 229 ITR 383 (SC), that a legal ground going to the root of the matter could be raised before the Tribunal. The assessee principally contended that the notice under Section 148 dated 03.04.2022 was barred by limitation for AY 2015-16. The assessee relied upon the substituted reassessment provisions introduced by the Finance Act, 2021, particularly the first proviso to Section 149(1). The assessee argued that no notice under Section 148 for AY 2015-16 could be issued on or after 01.04.2022 and that the impugned notice dated 03.04.2022 was therefore beyond limitation. It was also submitted that the information regarding cash deposits in the Punjab National Bank account had been wrongly taken as Rs.90,00,000/- instead of Rs.45,00,000/- and that the amount was below the Rs.50 lakh monetary threshold. The reassessment had originated from information that the assessee had not filed a return for AY 2015-16 despite financial transactions involving cash deposits of Rs.90,00,000/-. The Assessing Officer issued notice under Section 148 on 03.04.2022. As no reply was filed to the statutory notices, the assessment was completed by making an addition of Rs.90,00,000/- under Section 69A. Penalty proceedings were also initiated and penalty of Rs.27,81,000/- was subsequently levied under Section 271(1)(c). The NFAC dismissed the assessee’s appeals without condoning the delays. Before the Tribunal, the assessee submitted that the notice under Section 148 was time-barred and that sufficient cause existed for the delay before the NFAC. Reliance was placed, inter alia, on Union of India & others v. Rajeev Bansal, (2024) 469 ITR 46 (SC), and the decision referred to as Himanshu Sharma v. Income Tax Officer, ITA No. 820/Del/2026. The Tribunal considered the Supreme Court’s decision in Rajeev Bansal and the material reproduced from the decision in Himanshu Sharma. The reproduced submissions in Himanshu Sharma recorded the Revenue’s concession that, for AY 2015-16, reassessment notices issued on or after 01.04.2021 would have to be dropped because they would not fall for completion within the period prescribed under the Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation and Amendment of Certain Provisions) Act, 2020 (TOLA). The Tribunal also considered the decision in The Gharthoon Agriculture Services Society v. The ITO, ITA Nos. 925 to 928/CHD/2025 dated 13.11.2025, concerning the consequence of time-barred jurisdiction. After considering the material, the Tribunal first took up the quantum appeal. It found that the notice under Section 148 dated 03.04.2022 was issued without jurisdiction. The Tribunal held that the NFAC ought to have appreciated this jurisdictional defect and should have condoned the delay of 543 days in filing the appeal before it, where the delay had occurred due to the assessee’s bona fide error. The Tribunal observed that remanding the matter to the NFAC merely for adjudication on merits after condonation of delay would unnecessarily multiply litigation. Once the Assessing Officer had wrongly assumed jurisdiction and the action was time-barred, there was no need to send the matter back to the NFAC. Following the Supreme Court’s judgment referred to in the order, the Tribunal held that the notice dated 03.04.2022 was without jurisdiction and that no assessment proceedings could have taken place on the time-barred notice. The assessment order was therefore quashed and the quantum appeal was allowed. The Tribunal thereafter considered ITA No. 162/DEL/2026 relating to penalty. Since the delay of 381 days before the NFAC was consequential to the quantum appeal, the Tribunal condoned the delay in the penalty appeal as well. The Assessing Officer had levied penalty of Rs.27,81,000/- under Section 271(1)(c) on account of concealment of income. As the assessment order itself had been quashed in the quantum appeal, the Tr
rows.summary: ITAT Delhi ruled a reassessment notice issued three days late was time-barred, quashing the tax reopening and related penalty proceedings.

rows.title: Corporate Law | Breach of Contract Not Cheating Without Initial Fraudulent Intent: SC
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12303 Case Name Sarabjit Kaur Vs State of Punjab & Anr. (Supreme Court of India) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts Supreme Court of India Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Sarabjit Kaur Vs State of Punjab & Anr. (Supreme Court of India) The appellant approached the Supreme Court after the High Court dismissed her petition seeking quashing of F.I.R. No. 430 dated 16.10.2017 registered under Sections 420, 120-B and 506 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860. The dispute arose from an Agreement to Sell concerning a one-kanal plot. The appellant had entered into an agreement to purchase the property from Malkit Kaur on 27.05.2013 and thereafter entered into an Agreement to Sell the same property to Sarabjit Kaur, wife of respondent No. 2, on 18.11.2013. The agreement specifically stated that the appellant was not then the owner of the property and was entitled to the property on the basis of the earlier agreement in her favour. An amount of ₹5,00,000/- was received as earnest money and the date for execution of the sale deed was initially fixed as 25.06.2014. The date was subsequently extended to 24.12.2014 upon receipt of an additional ₹75,000/-. Respondent No. 2, Darshan Singh, had earlier lodged a complaint on 30.09.2015 concerning the same alleged transaction, but the complaint was directed against property dealers Manmohan Singh and Ranjit Singh alias Billa. The complaint referred to two other transactions and sought recovery of ₹29,39,500/- from the property dealers. Following investigation by the Economic Offences Wing, a report was submitted and the District Attorney opined that no criminal offence was made out and that the complainant was at liberty to approach the civil court. The opinion was accepted by the Senior Superintendent of Police on 18.05.2016. A further complaint was made by Darshan Singh on 05.10.2016 with substantially the same allegations. That complaint was also enquired into and, having regard to the earlier complaint and finding that no criminal offence was made out, was consigned to record. The Supreme Court noted that the second complaint did not disclose the fate of the earlier complaint. Thereafter, further complaints were made and ultimately the F.I.R. in question was registered on the basis of the complaint dated 15.06.2017 against the appellant, Manmohan Singh and Ranjit Singh. The appellant contended that the dispute was purely civil in nature and that, if the sale deed had not been executed by the last date of 24.12.2014, the appropriate remedy was to seek specific performance of the Agreement to Sell or return of the earnest money. It was also submitted that no civil proceedings had been instituted and that the criminal complaint was filed nearly three years after the last date fixed for execution of the sale deed. The State opposed the appeal on the ground that the chargesheet had already been filed and that the appellant could raise her pleas before the trial court. Respondent No. 2 did not appear despite service of notice. On examining the material, the Supreme Court found that the Agreement to Sell itself specifically recorded the appellant’s position regarding title to the property. The Court also noted that neither the complainant nor the vendee had initiated civil proceedings seeking execution of the sale deed or, in the alternative, return of the earnest money. There was also no material showing that notice had been issued to the appellant either immediately before expiry of the extended date or thereafter demanding execution of the sale deed. The Supreme Court held that a breach of contract does not give rise to criminal prosecution for cheating unless fraudulent or dishonest intention is shown right at the beginning of the transaction. Mere failure to keep a promise is insufficient to initiate criminal proceedings. On the facts before it, the Court found that the case had progressively been improved in subsequent complaints: the first complaint did not allege cheating against the appellant and was directed only against the property dealers, whereas the appellant was subsequently implicated. The Court concluded that the apparent object of the criminal proceedings was to convert a civil dispute into a criminal case and exert pressure upon the appellant for return of the money allegedly paid. It emphasised that criminal courts are not meant to be used for settling scores or pressurising parties to settle civil disputes. Since continuation of the proceedings would amount to an abuse of the process of the Court, interference under Section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 was warranted. Accordingly, the Supreme Court set aside the impugned order of the High Court and allowed the appellant’s petition for quashing. F.I.R. No. 430 dated 16.10.2017 and
rows.summary: The Supreme Court said a contract dispute is not cheating unless there was fraudulent intent from the start, limiting criminal liability.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Delhi Directs Refund of Excess Dividend Distribution Tax Paid by Vedanta
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12301 Case Name Vedanta Ltd. Vs ACIT (ITAT Delhi) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2012-13 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Delhi Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Vedanta Ltd. Vs ACIT (ITAT Delhi) The Delhi Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal considered the assessee’s appeal against the order dated 12.04.2019 passed by the Commissioner of Income Tax-IX, New Delhi, for Assessment Year 2012-13. The dispute concerned the assessee’s claim of credit for dividends received from subsidiaries, which resulted in excess Dividend Distribution Tax (DDT) being paid by the assessee. The Tribunal clarified that the issue was not one concerning refund of DDT per se. Rather, it concerned refund of the excess credit of dividend tax paid over and above the actual amount payable. The Tribunal also distinguished the claim from a situation where the assessee sought to claim dividend tax itself as an expenditure. According to the Tribunal, the assessee was seeking refund of the excess dividend tax actually paid after taking into account the dividend received from subsidiaries. On this basis, the Tribunal directed that the matter be sent to the file of the Assessing Officer to issue the refund in accordance with the provisions of law at the earliest. The appeal was consequently allowed for statistical purposes. The Tribunal’s order therefore resulted in restoration of the matter to the Assessing Officer for giving effect to the refund direction rather than the Tribunal itself quantifying or directly issuing the refund. The supplied order does not discuss any judicial precedent. Accordingly, no separate Cases Discussed section is included. FULL TEXT OF THE ORDER OF ITAT DELHI The aforesaid appeal has been filed by the assessee against the impugned order dated 12.04.2019, passed by Ld. Commissioner of Income Tax-IX, New Delhi for the Assessment Year 2012-13. 2. The issue before us pertains to claim of credit of dividend received from subsidiaries which resulted in refund of excess Divident Distribution Tax (DTT) which was paid by the assessee. We find that this issue is not pertaining to refund of DTT perse but refund of excess credit of dividend tax which is in excess of the actual amount payable. Nor this is not a case of the assessee in claiming the dividend tax as expense but claiming the excess dividend tax paid as refund. Hence, the matter is being sent to the file of the Assessing Officer to issue the refund as per the provision of law at the earliest. 3. In the result, the appeal of the assessee is allowed for statistical purposes. rows.title: Income Tax | ESOP Discount Is Deductible Revenue Expenditure Under Section 37(1): Delhi HC
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12300 Case Name PVR LTD Vs CIT (Delhi High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Delhi High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); PVR LTD Vs CIT (Delhi High Court) The Delhi High Court considered whether the difference between the price at which stock options were offered to employees under the Employee Stock Option Plan (ESOP) and Employee Stock Purchase Scheme (ESPS), and the prevailing market price of the stock on the date of grant, was allowable as revenue expenditure under Section 37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961. The appeal had been admitted by the Court on 30 April 2013 on this question of law. During the pendency of the appeal, the Karnataka High Court in Commissioner of Income Tax vs. Biocon Ltd., [2020] 121 taxmann.com 351 (Karnataka) upheld the Special Bench decision of the Tribunal on the issue in favour of the assessee. The Delhi High Court reproduced the relevant reasoning from that judgment. The reasoning in Biocon Ltd., as reproduced by the Delhi High Court, was that Section 37(1) permits deduction for expenditure laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for business purposes and does not require an actual cash pay-out. In an ESOP, employees receive an option to acquire shares at a predetermined price lower than the prevailing market price. The discount represents the difference between the market price at the time of grant and the offer price. Employees are required to render services during the vesting period, and upon completion of the vesting period the options vest with them. The Karnataka High Court held that where an ESOP vests over a period of four years at 25% per year, the employee obtains a definite right to the relevant portion at the end of each year and the assessee becomes bound to allow such vesting. Relying on the principles stated in Bharat Movers and Rotork Controls India P. Ltd., the Court held that a business liability arising during the accounting year remains deductible even though its exact quantification and discharge may take place at a future date. The eventual determination of the actual benefit upon exercise of the option was treated as quantification of an existing liability rather than a contingent liability. The Karnataka High Court further held that the expression “expenditure” in Section 37(1) includes a loss. Therefore, where shares are issued at a discount and the assessee absorbs the difference between the issue price and the market value, the difference constitutes expenditure for the purposes of Section 37(1). The object of the arrangement was considered to be securing consistent employee services and earning profits, rather than wasting or diminishing capital. The Delhi High Court also noted that it had previously followed the Special Bench decision in Principal Commissioner of Income-tax vs. New Delhi Television Ltd., [2018] 99 taxmann.com 401 (Delhi). The Court further recorded that subsequent appeals, ITA 107/2015 and ITA 214/2019, filed by the Commissioner of Income Tax on similar issues, had been dismissed by it following the Karnataka High Court’s decision in Biocon Ltd.. Consequently, following the Karnataka High Court’s judgment in Biocon Ltd., the Delhi High Court decided the question of law in favour of the assessee. It held that the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal had erred in law in holding that the difference between the price at which stock options were offered to employees under ESOP and ESPS and the prevailing market price on the date of grant was not allowable revenue expenditure under Section 37(1). The impugned Tribunal judgment was set aside and the appeal was disposed of. Cases Discussed Commissioner of Income Tax vs. Biocon Ltd., [2020] 121 taxmann.com 351 (Karnataka) — followed; the Delhi High Court adopted the Karnataka High Court’s ruling that ESOP discount is allowable under Section 37(1) and is not merely a contingent liability. Principal Commissioner of Income-tax vs. New Delhi Television Ltd., [2018] 99 taxmann.com 401 (Delhi) — referred to because this Court had followed the Special Bench decision in Biocon Ltd. on the ESOP expenditure issue. FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF DELHI HIGH COURT 1. Present appeal had been admitted by this Court on 30th April, 2013 on the following question of law:- “Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal erred in law in holding that the difference between the price at which stock options were offered to employees of the appellant company under ESOP and ESPS and the prevailing market price of the stock on the date of grant of such options was not allowable revenue expenditure underSection 37(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1961.?” 2.During the pendency of the present appeal, the Karnataka High Court inC
rows.summary: Delhi High Court ruled ESOP discount can be deducted as business expenditure under Section 37(1), supporting employer tax claims.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Partly Allows Vodafone India Appeals on 80IA, Interest and Roaming Costs
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12299 Case Name Vodafone India Ltd. Vs ACIT (ITAT Mumbai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2006-07 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Mumbai Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Vodafone India Ltd. Vs ACIT (ITAT Mumbai) The Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Mumbai Bench, considered two appeals filed by Vodafone India Ltd. for Assessment Years 2006-07 and 2007-08. ITA No.216/Chandi/2011 concerned the assessment order dated 05/02/2011 for AY 2006-07, while ITA No.1173/Chandi/2011 concerned the order of the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals), Chandigarh dated 17/11/2011 for AY 2007-08. Since the grounds in both appeals arose from the same set of facts, the Tribunal adjudicated them together and dealt with the issues year-wise. For AY 2006-07, the assessee challenged, among other matters, denial of deduction under Section 80IA of the Income Tax Act, 1961, treatment of “Other Incomes” for Section 80IA purposes, depreciation on Asset Retirement Cost (ARC), disallowance under Section 14A, interest on loans advanced to subsidiaries, interest on capital work-in-progress and External Commercial Borrowings (ECB), expenditure incurred for raising loans, roaming charges under Section 40(a)(ia), book-profit computation under Section 115JB, initiation of penalty under Section 271(1)(c), and interest under Sections 234B, 234C and 234D. On the Section 80IA issue, the assessee relied upon the Tribunal’s decision in its own case for AY 2005-06. The Tribunal noted that the earlier order had held that the assessee commenced telecommunication services after 01/04/1995 and was consequently eligible for deduction under Section 80IA(4). The earlier Tribunal had also held that formation of the undertaking after merger/reconstruction did not prevent the deduction in view of CBDT Circular No.5 of 2005. Following its own earlier decision, the Tribunal allowed Ground No.1. The Tribunal also allowed the assessee’s claim for deduction under Section 80IA in respect of “Other Incomes”, including interest income and miscellaneous income. It followed the reasoning adopted in the assessee’s appeal for AY 2005-06, where reliance had been placed on Bharat Sanchar Nigam Limited, 156 ITD 847 (Del-Trib). On ARC, the assessee had capitalised the provision and claimed depreciation of Rs.63.60 lakh. The assessee alternatively sought deduction of the provision as revenue expenditure under Section 37(1), and further alternatively sought proportionate amortisation over the lease period. The Tribunal rejected the primary claim for depreciation because the Delhi Bench in the assessee’s group concern, DCIT vs. Vodafone Essar Digilink Ltd., 170 ITD 430 (Del-Trib), had rejected depreciation on the capitalised amount. Although an appeal against that order had been admitted by the Delhi High Court, there was no operative stay. The Tribunal, however, found that the assessee’s alternative claim under Section 37(1) required examination. Clause 11 of the licence agreement created an obligation to restore areas affected by installation work. The Tribunal observed that the liability was ascertained, although it would crystallise when the leased premises were vacated. Referring to the principles discussed in Rotork Control India Pvt. Ltd. vs. CIT and Vedanta Ltd. vs. JCIT, the Tribunal held that a provision could be allowable where it was for business purposes, related to a present obligation and was based on reliable estimates. Since the Assessing Officer had not examined the basis on which the assessee had purportedly computed the provision, the issue was restored to the Assessing Officer for examination in accordance with law. Ground No.3 was therefore partly allowed for statistical purposes. On Section 14A, the Tribunal recorded that the assessee had not earned any exempt income during the relevant year. It further noted that Rule 8D was applicable only from AY 2008-09. Following the principle stated in Godrej & Boyce Mfg. Co. Ltd. vs. DCIT, 328 ITR 81 (Bom), the Tribunal allowed Ground No.4 and deleted the disallowance. The Tribunal also deleted the disallowance of interest on interest-free loans advanced to subsidiaries. The assessee had advanced loans to group concerns operating in the same cellular telecommunications business and explained that the advances were made on account of commercial expediency, particularly because the subsidiaries were in their initial years and required substantial funds. Relying on S.A. Builders Ltd. vs. CIT, 288 ITR 1 (SC), the Tribunal held that once commercial expediency was established, the Assessing Officer could not substitute his judgment for that of the assessee concerning the commercial decision to advance funds to group concerns. The Tribunal also noted that the assessee had sufficient own funds to cov
rows.summary: Vodafone partly won its tax appeal, with the tribunal allowing some deductions and costs while disputing others, including interest and roaming charges.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Mumbai Excludes Wipro and Infosys from Capgemini Comparables
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12298 Case Name Capgemini India Pvt. Ltd Vs DCIT (ITAT Mumbai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2011-12 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Mumbai Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Capgemini India Pvt. Ltd Vs DCIT (ITAT Mumbai) The Mumbai Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal disposed of cross appeals filed by Capgemini India Pvt. Ltd. and the Revenue concerning Assessment Year 2011-12. The appeals arose from the final assessment order passed under section 143(3) read with section 144C(13) of the Income-tax Act, 1961, pursuant to directions of the Dispute Resolution Panel. The assessee had originally returned total income of Rs.129,87,11,835/-, while the final assessment determined total income at Rs.453,58,45,730/-, principally after a transfer pricing adjustment of Rs.323,60,70,374/-. The assessee challenged several aspects of the transfer pricing exercise. Grounds relating to reference to the TPO, use of single-year data, financial-year filtering, certain comparables, additional comparables and risk adjustment were either stated to be general in nature or not pressed. The Tribunal specifically adjudicated the inclusion of Wipro Technology Services Ltd. and Infosys Ltd., the working-capital adjustment and the markup applied to recovery of out-of-pocket expenses. On Wipro Technology Services Ltd., the assessee argued that the comparable operated in peculiar circumstances following its acquisition of Citigroup’s technology-services business and that a Master Service Agreement with Citigroup involved a prior controlled relationship. The assessee also pointed to the comparable’s unusually high margin of 54.42% on cost. The Revenue opposed exclusion merely because the comparable earned high profits. The Tribunal noted that the assessee had relied on the coordinate bench decision in Agilent Technologies (International) Pvt. Ltd. vs. ITO, ITA Nos. 1620/Del/2015, 477 & 6420/Del/2016, order dated 12.02.2018, where Wipro Technology Services Ltd. was excluded because the prior agreement meant that the transaction did not constitute an uncontrolled transaction. Following that proposition on identical facts, the Tribunal directed that Wipro Technology Services Ltd. be excluded from the comparable set. The Tribunal also excluded Infosys Ltd. The assessee had contended that Infosys possessed substantial brand value, intangibles and proprietary products, incurred substantial research and development expenditure and had a substantially different functional and risk profile, whereas Capgemini India was a risk-mitigated captive service provider without intangible assets. The Tribunal noted the substantial differences in the financials and business profile of the two companies and relied upon the coordinate bench decision in Fiserv India Pvt. Ltd. vs. ACIT, ITA No.700/Del/2016 for AY 2011-12, order dated 31.08.2020. That decision had followed the principle concerning the exclusion of Infosys from the comparable set of a captive software-development service provider. The Tribunal also referred to the assessee’s own case for AY 2008-09, where Wipro Technology Services Ltd. and Infosys Technologies Ltd. had been rejected as comparables because of their brand value, intangibles and R&D activities. Accordingly, both Wipro Technology Services Ltd. and Infosys Technologies Ltd. were directed to be excluded. On working-capital adjustment, the assessee submitted that such adjustment had been allowed in its earlier and subsequent years, including AY 2008-09 and AY 2009-10. The Tribunal observed that its own earlier decision had recognised that working-capital adjustments have a bearing on profitability. Since the lower authorities had not specifically substantiated why the adjustment could not be granted and the assessee had received the benefit in other years, the Tribunal found no justification to depart from its earlier approach. Ground No.15 was therefore allowed. The assessee also challenged the 12% markup imposed on recovery of out-of-pocket expenses amounting to Rs.24,41,84,621/-. According to the assessee, the expenses represented third-party costs such as travel, accommodation, visa, per diem, leased-line charges and other expenses recovered from associated enterprises on a cost-to-cost basis, without any service element or value addition. The Tribunal noted that the TPO had relied on the Master Service Agreement and applied a 12% markup but had not determined the arm’s length price by applying any method prescribed under the Act. The assessee relied on CIT vs. Kodak India (P) Ltd. and Barclays Bank PLC vs. ADIT (Intl. Taxn). Following the principle that the statutory transfer-pricing methods are mandatory and not directory, and that failure to apply a prescribed method affects the TPO’s jurisdicti
rows.summary: Mumbai ITAT ruled Wipro Technology Services and Infosys should be excluded as transfer-pricing comparables in Capgemini’s tax dispute.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Delhi Deletes Section 68 Addition on Demonetisation Cash Sales Without Rejecting Books
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12295 Case Name Fine Gujaranwala Jewellers Vs ITO (ITAT Delhi) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2017-18 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Delhi Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Fine Gujaranwala Jewellers Vs ITO (ITAT Delhi) The Delhi Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal allowed the assessee’s appeal against the order dated 21.06.2022 passed by the CIT(A)/National Faceless Appeal Centre for Assessment Year 2017-18. The dispute concerned an addition of Rs.1,37,95,042/- made by the Assessing Officer under Section 68 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 in respect of cash deposits attributed by the assessee to cash sales of jewellery, with tax sought to be charged under Section 115BBE. The assessee had filed its return declaring NIL income for AY 2017-18. The assessment was completed on 29.12.2019 by treating Rs.1,37,95,042/- as unexplained cash credit. The CIT(A), by order dated 21.06.2022, sustained the addition. The CIT(A) considered, among other matters, the fact that most cash-sale invoices for diamond items between 01.10.2016 and 31.12.2016 were below Rs.2 lakh and observed that cash sales during 01.10.2016 to 08.11.2016 constituted 90.59% of the cash sales for the relevant period. The CIT(A) also considered the average daily sales during the 39-day period and concluded that the cash-sales claim was an afterthought intended to explain the bank deposits during the demonetisation period. Before the Tribunal, the assessee submitted that the cash deposited in the bank represented sale proceeds of jewellery and that the transactions were supported by books of account, purchase vouchers, sales invoices, stock register, VAT records and bank statements. The assessee also pointed out that its books had not been rejected and that the relevant sales had been disclosed to and accepted by the VAT authorities. The assessee relied upon the principle that cash sales recorded in regular books and supported by available stock could not be treated again as unexplained cash credits merely because the cash was subsequently deposited in the bank. The Tribunal recorded that, in response to several notices issued under Section 142(1) and related proceedings, the assessee had furnished extensive material, including the audit report under Section 44AB, cash account, sales account, income-tax return and computation, audited financial statements, bank statements, GST registration certificate, VAT registration and returns, stock register, labour records, month-wise sales and purchases, month-wise cash sales and cash deposits, sale and purchase ledgers and invoices, month-wise ornament stock, and other supporting documents. The Tribunal noted that the assessee’s specific case was that the sale proceeds of jewellery constituted the source of the cash deposited in the bank. It further noted that the regular books of account had not been rejected and that no flaw, fallacy or deficiency in those books had been pointed out by the Assessing Officer. The Tribunal considered the decision of the Visakhapatnam Bench in ACIT Vs Hirapanna Jewellers, where the Tribunal had considered cash receipts accounted for as sales, availability of stock and the absence of defects in the books. The Tribunal also considered the other authorities cited by the parties. In distinguishing the Revenue’s reliance on Champalal S. Shah, Ravinder Kumar and Rajiv Jain, the Tribunal found material factual differences. According to the Tribunal, those cases involved circumstances such as absence of evidence supporting the alleged sales, undisclosed purchasers, lack of proof of delivery or other evidentiary deficiencies, whereas in the present case the assessee had maintained books and the cash deposits were claimed to arise from recorded sales supported by the available stock. The Tribunal rejected the reasoning that the fact that individual sales invoices were below Rs.2 lakh was by itself sufficient to establish that the sales were bogus or that they had been structured merely to avoid the reporting requirements under Section 285BA read with Rule 114E. It observed that there was no prohibition in law against making sale transactions below Rs.2 lakh and held that the Assessing Officer could not infer that the sales were bogus merely from the value of the individual invoices. The Tribunal further held that the evidence relied upon by the Assessing Officer was insufficient to establish that the sales were not genuine. It emphasised that the assessee’s books had not been rejected and that the sales had also been accepted under VAT. The Tribunal held that the lower authorities could not sustain the addition on the basis of conjectures and surmises without bringing corroborative material on record. The Tribunal also stressed that when an assessee furnis
rows.summary: ITAT Delhi deleted a ₹1.38 crore unexplained cash-credit addition on demonetisation-period jewellery cash sales, finding books weren’t rejected.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Nagpur Upholds Section 263 Revision for Lack of Inquiry into Unrecorded Sales
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12296 Case Name Abhishek Nagarmal Jangid Vs PCIT (Central) (ITAT Nagpur) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2018-19 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Nagpur Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Abhishek Nagarmal Jangid Vs PCIT (Central) (ITAT Nagpur) Summary: The appeal was filed by the assessee against the order of the PCIT (Central), Nagpur passed under Section 263 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 for Assessment Year 2018-19. The assessee had originally declared income of Rs.5,82,720/- in the return filed on 23.10.2018. The assessment was subsequently reopened under Sections 147 and 148, pursuant to which the assessee filed a return declaring income of Rs.9,13,980/-. A search and seizure action under Section 132 was conducted in the case of Dr. Rahul Mahajan on 20.02.2019. Documents seized during the search revealed cash payments exceeding one crore allegedly made by Dr. Rahul Mahajan to the assessee for construction of Chinmay Hospital and a residential building. Thereafter, a survey under Section 133A was conducted and the assessee’s statement was recorded under Section 131 on 03.04.2019. The assessee voluntarily offered additional income of Rs.13,00,000/- comprising Rs.8,00,000/- towards unrecorded sales and Rs.5,00,000/- towards initial investment. The Assessing Officer completed assessment under Section 143(3) read with Section 147, making an addition of Rs.5,00,000/- and assessing total income at Rs.14,13,980/-. Subsequently, the AO proposed revision under Section 263 on the ground that the assessment was erroneous and prejudicial to the interests of Revenue. The PCIT issued notice under Section 263 identifying, inter alia, failure to make inquiries or verification which should have been made and failure to inquire into the claim. The assessee submitted that it was engaged in furniture trading and that the sales made to Dr. Mahajan had been disclosed in the return filed in response to Section 148 proceedings. The assessee stated that purchases corresponding to the sales were supported by invoices and that it had offered profit at 8% of the sales during survey proceedings. It also explained that the business was generally conducted on an order basis, with advances received from customers and credit periods allowed by suppliers. The assessee therefore requested that the Section 263 proceedings be dropped. The PCIT, however, observed that the assessee had claimed purchases which were not recorded in the books and that the assessment records did not show any third-party inquiry regarding those purchases. The PCIT further noted that the purchase bills were allegedly in the range of Rs.20,000/- and above, potentially attracting Section 40A(3). According to the PCIT, the AO had failed to ascertain the correct facts instead of taxing the entire unrecorded sales of Rs.41,40,666/-. The assessment was therefore set aside for fresh assessment. Before the Tribunal, the assessee contended that the AO had examined the issue during reassessment proceedings and that complete details, including purchase invoices, supplier declarations, business-model explanation, gross profit rate and source of investment, had been furnished. It was argued that merely because the PCIT considered further inquiry desirable, the assessment could not be revised under Section 263. The assessee also submitted that the PCIT’s observations regarding possible cash payments and Section 40A(3) were based on presumptions and amounted to fishing and roving inquiries. The Department relied upon judicial precedents concerning the scope of inquiry by the Assessing Officer, including Malabar Industrial Co. Ltd. Vs CIT and Gee Vee Enterprises Vs Addl. CIT. Reliance was also placed on Nagesh Knitwears Pvt. Ltd. and NIIT Vs CIT (Central-II), among other authorities. The Tribunal examined the assessment records and found that the AO had accepted additional income of Rs.3,31,254/-, representing 8% of unrecorded sales of Rs.41,40,666/-. The Tribunal noted that the assessee had disclosed total turnover of Rs.2,21,88,785/- in Form No.3CD and that the unrecorded sales were over and above the turnover disclosed in the books. It found no finding in the assessment records establishing that corresponding unrecorded purchases had been made. The Tribunal further observed that regular business expenditure had already been debited to the profit and loss account and that no contemporaneous documentary evidence regarding corresponding expenditure had been produced during assessment proceedings. The Tribunal held that the AO was not justified in accepting only 8% profit on the unrecorded sales without proper verification. It further found that the AO had failed to examine the applicability of Section 69A in respect of the unrecorded receipts and the conse
rows.summary: ITAT Nagpur upheld revision of the assessment because the tax officer failed to properly investigate alleged unrecorded sales and related cash receipts.

rows.title: Company Law | Delhi HC Dismisses SFIO Investigation Writ for Lack of Territorial Jurisdiction
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12294 Case Name Anil Laxminarayan Biyani Vs Union of India and Anr. (Delhi High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Delhi High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Anil Laxminarayan Biyani Vs Union of India and Anr. (Delhi High Court) Summary: The Delhi High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by Anil Laxminarayan Biyani challenging the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) order dated 31.10.2025 directing the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) to investigate the affairs of Future Retail Limited (FRL) and Future Consumer Retail Private Limited (FCRPL). The petition was dismissed on the ground of territorial jurisdiction, with the Court holding that the High Court of Bombay was the appropriate and convenient forum. The Court expressly clarified that it had not examined the merits of the challenge or any other issue relating to the investigation. FRL and FCRPL were incorporated in 2007. The judgment records the restructuring discussions concerning the Future Group’s HomeTown and FabFurnish businesses during 2016–2017 and the proposed demerger into Praxis Home Retail Private Limited. Amazon acquired a 49% stake in Future Coupons Private Limited in 2019. SEBI subsequently initiated proceedings concerning alleged insider trading in FRL shares during the period from 10.03.2017 to 20.04.2017. The SEBI order dated 03.02.2021 was challenged before the Securities Appellate Tribunal, which on 20.12.2023 quashed the SEBI order and exonerated the appellants, holding, inter alia, that the trading was not based on UPSI. FRL was admitted into CIRP before the NCLT, Mumbai, and was subsequently ordered to be liquidated on 29.07.2024 after expiry of the maximum CIRP period without approval of a resolution plan. Insolvency proceedings against FCRPL were initiated on 24.09.2024. The judgment notes that, unlike FRL, no application under Section 66 of the IBC was filed against FCRPL and no transaction audit report was furnished in its insolvency proceedings. On 20.11.2024, IBBI made a reference to MCA concerning alleged avoidance transactions involving approximately ₹15,856.68 crore in relation to FRL and FCRPL. On 31.10.2025, MCA passed the impugned order under Section 212(1)(c) of the Companies Act, 2013, directing SFIO to investigate FRL and FCRPL. The petitioner challenged the order before the Delhi High Court on 19.01.2026. The respondents raised a preliminary objection that Delhi lacked territorial jurisdiction. They submitted that the companies under investigation had their registered offices in Mumbai; their statutory, financial and compliance records were maintained there; ROC Mumbai was the concerned Registrar; insolvency and avoidance proceedings were pending before the NCLT, Mumbai Bench; and any consequential prosecution would be before the competent Special Court having jurisdiction in Mumbai under Section 436 of the Companies Act, 2013. Reliance was placed upon Oil and Natural Gas Commission v. Utpal Kumar Basu, (1994) 4 SCC 711, and Kusum Ingots & Alloys Ltd. v. Union of India, (2004) 6 SCC 254. The respondents contended that the mere situs of the authority passing an order could not, by itself, establish territorial jurisdiction and that the doctrine of forum conveniens required the Court to consider the forum having the closest connection with the dispute. The petitioner, on the other hand, argued that the impugned order had been issued by MCA from New Delhi and that SFIO’s investigation machinery was operating from Delhi. It was submitted that SFIO’s Delhi office had issued notices to the petitioner and that the investigation was being controlled from Delhi. The petitioner also contended that Article 226(2) of the Constitution governed the territorial jurisdiction of the writ proceedings and that Section 2(29) of the Companies Act had no bearing on such constitutional jurisdiction. The Court rejected the petitioner’s contention. It held that merely because MCA was situated in New Delhi and had passed the investigation order there, territorial jurisdiction could not automatically be conferred upon the Delhi High Court. The Court observed that the expression “may” in Article 226(2), as opposed to “shall”, indicates that even where part of the cause of action arises within a High Court’s territorial jurisdiction, the Court is required to consider whether it is the appropriate and convenient forum. The Court also rejected the contention that the posting of an SFIO officer at its Delhi headquarters established that the investigation itself had its principal nexus with Delhi. Merely because an officer stationed at headquarters filed an affidavit on behalf of SFIO could not constitute a substantial part of the cause of action. On the contrary, the Court found consid
rows.summary: Delhi High Court dismissed the challenge to MCA’s SFIO probe order on jurisdiction grounds, leaving the investigation itself unreviewed.

rows.title: Custom Duty | CBIC Rationalizes EMI Scheme Documentation Requirements for Eligible Manufacturer Importers
rows.desc: Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Summary: Central Board of Indirect Taxes & Customs (CBIC), Ministry of Finance, Department of Revenue, has issued Circular No. 39/2026-Customs dated 3 September 2026 to amend Circular No. 08/2026-Customs dated 28.02.2026 concerning documentation requirements under the Eligible Manufacturer Importer (EMI) Scheme. The earlier circular was issued pursuant to Notification No. 12/2026-Customs (N.T.) dated 01.02.2026, which extended the facility of deferred payment of Customs import duty under the proviso to sub-section (1) of section 47 of the Customs Act, 1962 to Eligible Manufacturer Importers. The deferred-payment framework is governed by the Deferred Payment of Import Duty Rules, 2016. The principal change made by Circular No. 39/2026-Customs is a substantial rationalisation of the data and documentary requirements for prospective EMI applicants. Under revised Appendix-I, several data elements previously required under Circular No. 08/2026-Customs are no longer required, including details relating to EXIM documents filed during the previous financial year, GSTIN status, manufacturing activity declared in FORM GST REG-01, filing status of GSTR-3B, aggregate turnover and GST payment, commencement of business/GST registration, ITC-04 filing particulars, manufacturing premises, property rights, plant and machinery, major raw materials and finished goods with HSN details, and job-worker particulars. The Circular also dispenses with uploading copies of IEC, PAN, GST Registration Certificates, GSTR ITC-04 returns, GSTR-9C, audited financial statements for the preceding two financial years, and documents concerning ownership, lease or rental of premises. The Circular expressly retains three categories of supporting documents: the UDYAM Registration Certificate where MSME status is claimed; a Chartered Accountant’s Certificate bearing UDIN in the prescribed format; and an authorization letter for the authorised signatory. Consequently, the number of documents required to be uploaded is reduced from ten to three in the revised application format, with “Others” shown as optional in revised Appendix-II. Appendix-III has also been revised so that the Chartered Accountant must furnish reasons where the applicant has negative net worth or negative net current assets. The Circular states that these changes are intended to simplify the application process and reduce compliance burden while permitting verification of relevant particulars through backend IT systems. The revised requirements amend Appendices I, II and III to Circular No. 08/2026-Customs dated 28.02.2026. The Circular specifically provides that eligible importers will be able to apply for enrolment under the EMI Scheme from 15.09.2026 using the modified documentation requirements. The accompanying revised Appendix-I retains eligibility-related declarations, including whether the applicant is a manufacturer as defined under section 2(72) of the CGST Act, 2017, and provisions concerning job work under section 143 of the CGST Act, while simplifying the information and document burden. Madam/Sir, Attention is invited to Circular No. 08/2026-Customs dated 28.02.2026 (hereinafter referred to as the “said Circular”), issued in pursuance of Notification No. 12/2026-Customs (N.T.) dated 01.02.2026, extending the facility of deferred payment of Customs import duty under the proviso to sub-section (1) of section 47 of the Customs Act, 1962 to “Eligible Manufacturer Importers” (EMI). 2. These include non-submission of details pertaining to EXIM documents filed during the previous financial year, GSTIN status, declaration of manufacturing activity in FORM GST REG-01, GSTR-3B filing status, aggregate turnover and GST payment, date of commencement of business/GST
rows.summary: CBIC has eased EMI Scheme application paperwork by removing several mandatory data and document requirements for eligible manufacturer importers.

rows.title: Corporate Law | IBBI Suspends Insolvency Professional for Two Years Over Private Sale Contraventions
rows.desc: Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Summary: The Disciplinary Committee (DC) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI), vide Order No. IBBI/DC/343/2026 dated 03 September 2026, suspended the registration of Insolvency Professional Shri Kannan Tiruvengadam for two years. The proceedings arose from his role as Resolution Professional and subsequently Liquidator of BRG Iron & Steel Co. Private Limited. The Board had initiated an investigation under Section 218 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC) read with Regulation 7 of the IBBI (Inspection and Investigation) Regulations, 2017. The principal allegation concerned the private sale of the corporate debtor as a going concern to Rimjhim Ispat Limited for Rs. 507.20 crore. The DC examined whether the sale had been conducted without the requisite prior consultation with the Stakeholders Consultation Committee (SCC) and whether the liquidator’s independence in the sale process had been compromised. The IP contended, inter alia, that six public auctions had failed, the private-sale consideration exceeded the reserve price of the last failed auction, and the requirement of prior SCC consultation under Regulation 33(2) of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 was introduced only with effect from 12.02.2024. He also relied upon the SCC meetings and subsequent proceedings before the Adjudicating Authority to contend that the sale process had been transparent. The DC, however, held that Regulation 31A(1)(b), as applicable at the relevant time, imposed an obligation concerning consultation on matters relating to sale, including the manner of sale. It found that the specific binding offer, its price, related legal opinions and the decision to accept the offer had not been placed before the SCC before completion of the sale. The DC held that Shri Kannan Tiruvengadam conducted the private sale without prior SCC consultation and contravened Section 208(2)(a) to (e) of the Code read with Regulation 31A(1)(b) of the Liquidation Regulations and Clauses 1, 2, 12 and 14 of the Code of Conduct under the IBBI (Insolvency Professionals) Regulations, 2016. The DC separately noted his repeated failure to personally attend disciplinary hearings despite three opportunities and considered this conduct relevant to his continuing “fit and proper person” status under Regulation 4(1)(g) of the IP Regulations. Exercising powers under Section 220 of the Code read with Regulation 13 of the Inspection and Investigation Regulations, the DC suspended his registration for two years. In terms of Section 206 of the Code, he was also held ineligible to continue his existing assignments, requiring the respective CoC/SCC to replace him with another Resolution Professional/Liquidator. The order will come into force after 30 days from its date of issuance. INSOLVENCY AND BANKRUPTCY BOARD OF INDIA (Disciplinary Committee) Order No. IBBI/DC/343/2026 Dated: 03 September 2026 This Order disposes of the Show Cause Notice (SCN) No. COMP-11012/3/2026-IBBI/1966/804 dated 09.07.2026, issued to Shri Kannan Tiruvengadam, who is an Insolvency Professional (IP) registered with the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI/Board) with Registration No. IBBI/IPA-001/IP-P00253/2017-2018/10482 and a Professional Member of the The Indian Institute of Insolvency Professional of ICAI (IIIPI). 1. Background 1.1. The corporate insolvency resolution process (CIRP) of BRG Iron & Steel Co. Private Limited (CD) commenced vide order of the NCLT, Kolkata Bench (AA) dated 05.03.2019. Shri Kannan Tiruvengadam was appointed as Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) vide the said order and later confirmed as the Resolution Professional (RP) in the matter. The liquidation process of CD commenced vide order dated 03.02.2020, and Kannan Tiruvengadam was appointed as Liquidator in the said matter. 1.2. The Board, having reasons to believe that the matter needs investigation, in exercise of its powers conferred under Section 218 of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (Code) read with Regulation 7 of the IBBI (Inspection and Investigation) Regulations, 2017 (Inspection and Investigation Regulations), appointed the Investigating Authority (IA) to conduct investigation in the matter. The IA served a notice of investigation as per Regulation 8(1) of the Inspection and Investigation Regulations on 19.02.2026. After considering response of Shri Kannan Tiruvengadam to the notice of investigation and material available on record, the IA submitted the Investigation Report. 1.3. On the basis of the findings in the investigation report, the Board formed a prima facie view that Shri Kannan Tiruvengadam has contravened provisions of the Code and Regulations made thereunder and accordingly issued the SCN to Shri Kannan Tiruvengadam on 09.07.2026. The reply of Shri Kannan Tiruvengadam to the SCN was received by the Board on 24.07.2026. 1.4. The SCN, reply of Shri Kannan Tiruvengadam to

rows.title: SEBI | SEBI Proposes Net Settlement of Funds for Mutual Fund Cash Market Transactions
rows.desc: Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Summary: The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) issued a consultation paper on September 03, 2026 seeking comments, views and suggestions on a proposal to permit net settlement of funds for transactions undertaken by mutual fund schemes in the cash market, while continuing settlement of securities on a gross basis. The proposal is intended to facilitate ease of doing business, improve settlement efficiency and reduce temporary liquidity requirements without disturbing delivery-backed settlement, scheme-wise accounting, valuation and investor-protection safeguards. The paper notes that the SEBI Master Circular for Stock Exchanges and Clearing Corporations dated December 30, 2024 requires institutional trades to be delivery-backed and obligations to be fulfilled on a gross basis. It also refers to SEBI’s April 24, 2026 circular permitting net settlement of funds for outright transactions undertaken by Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs). SEBI proposes a similarly tailored framework for mutual fund schemes, subject to safeguards. The consultation defines an “outright transaction” as either a purchase transaction or a sale transaction, but not both, in a security in a settlement cycle undertaken by a mutual fund scheme. Securities with only outright purchases or only outright sales may be considered for determining the scheme’s net fund obligation. Where a scheme has both purchase and sale transactions in the same security in the same settlement cycle, that security would be treated as non-outright and excluded from netting. Such transactions would continue to be settled on a gross basis. The proposal is expressly limited to net settlement of funds and would not permit trade or delivery netting. Securities settlement would continue on a gross basis, and STT and stamp duty would continue to be levied on delivery basis, as applicable. Netting would be available only at the individual scheme level. No netting or adjustment would be permitted across different schemes of the same mutual fund or AMC, or between schemes or portfolios. SEBI explains that the existing gross-funding model can create temporary liquidity pressures and operational inefficiencies because purchase obligations must be funded independently of sale proceeds receivable in the same settlement cycle. The issue may be particularly relevant during index rebalancing and periods of large investor subscriptions or redemptions. The proposed framework is intended to reduce avoidable temporary funding requirements and may also reduce intraday borrowing used by mutual fund schemes for settlement purposes. Operational safeguards proposed in the draft framework include scheme-wise identification of outright purchase transactions, outright sale transactions, non-outright transactions, gross and net fund obligations, and securities pay-in and pay-out obligations. Custodians would maintain a clear audit trail. AMCs and custodians would have to prevent cross-scheme adjustment or inter-scheme funding, while trustees would review implementation in the interest of unit-holders. Recognised Clearing Corporations and Stock Exchanges would make necessary system and reporting changes. The consultation further proposes that implementation standards be formulated by the Association of Mutual Funds in India (AMFI), in consultation with custodians, recognised Clearing Corporations, recognised Stock Exchanges and other relevant stakeholders. These standards may address file formats and reporting, confirmation and settlement timelines, reconciliation, audit trails, rejected or unconfirmed trades and exception handling. The draft also proposes system-readiness measures for mutual funds, AMCs, custodians, stock brokers, recognised Stock Exchanges and recognised Clearing Corporations. SEBI has invited comments on four issues: whether net settlement of funds should be permitted for outright transactions undertaken by mutual fund schemes in the cash market; whether transactions involving both purchase and sale in the same security in the same settlement cycle should continue to be excluded from netting; whether the framework should initially be limited to mutual fund cash-market transactions; and any other suggestions with rationale. Comments are invited latest by September 24, 2026 through the online web-based form. The draft circular is placed at Annexure A. Objective 1. The objective of this consultation paper is to seek comments, views and suggestions from the public and stakeholders on the proposal to permit net settlement of funds for transactions undertaken by mutual fund schemes in cash market, while continuing settlement of securities o
rows.summary: SEBI is seeking comments on allowing mutual funds to net cash-market fund settlements while keeping securities settlement gross, to improve efficiency and reduce liquidity needs.

rows.title: CA, CS, CMA | ICSI Council Approves Revised Auditing Standards, CSEET Eligibility and Student Fund
rows.desc: Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Summary: The Council of the Institute of Company Secretaries of India (ICSI), at its meeting dated 28 August 2026, approved 12 important proposals covering professional standards and guidance, student eligibility and support, Chapter administration, infrastructure and recognition of examination achievers. Among the professional measures, the Council approved the Guidance Note on Securities and Exchange Board of India (Prohibition of Insider Trading) Regulations, 2015 (Revised Edition, 2026) and the ICSI Auditing Standards (CSAS-1 to CSAS-4), Revised Edition 2026. The latter covers the four ICSI Auditing Standards relating to Audit Engagement, Audit Process and Documentation, Forming of Opinion and Secretarial Audit. The Council also approved amendments to the ICSI Chapter Management Guidelines, 2024 and Standard Operating Procedures subsequent to the constitution of a New Evolving Chapter. On the education front, approval was given to the Exposure Draft of New Syllabus 2027, comprising the scheme of papers, Mode of Examination and Assessment Pattern, for stakeholder consultation. A significant decision concerns the Company Secretary Executive Entrance Test (CSEET): the eligibility criteria for registration are to be revised to permit provisional registration of students who have passed Class X/Matriculation. The Council also approved free ICSI Online Doubt Clearing Classes for Executive and Professional Programme students and constitution of the ICSI Students’ Benevolent Fund to provide financial assistance to registered students facing unforeseen emergencies.
