rows.title: Income Tax | Allahabad HC Allows Reassessment to Proceed Despite Identity Theft Defence
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12278 Case Name Vyome Mehta Vs ITO (Allahabad High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Allahabad High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Vyome Mehta Vs ITO (Allahabad High Court) Summary: The Allahabad High Court considered a challenge to reassessment proceedings for A.Y. 2022-23 initiated against the petitioner, who described himself as a salaried employee of a private Corporation and denied having carried on any business activity. He had filed his return declaring annual income of Rs.4,15,630/- and stated that he had no other income. A show cause notice dated 30.3.2026 under Section 148-A(1) referred to information derived through the Income Tax Portal under the risk management strategy. The information linked transactions to the petitioner’s PAN, including a purchase transaction by a dummy entity of Rs.11,16,10,199, total sales reported under GSTR-1 of Rs.24,03,22,375, total sales reported under GSTR-3B of Rs.29,46,36,781, and a TDS statement for professional services or royalty of Rs.5,83,597. The notice also recorded that the return of income filed on 17.07.2022 declaring Rs.4,15,630/- did not commensurate with those transactions. The petitioner denied the business transactions, denied knowledge of Hari Om Traders, described as his proprietary concern, and denied association with its stated business address. He stated that his identity may have been stolen while submitting online loan applications. He also relied on an e-mail dated 29.4.2026 from the GST Authorities, which stated that registration of M/s Hari Om Traders had been obtained using PAN and Aadhaar documents pertaining to Sh. Vyome Mehta, that the firm was not found at the stated principal place of business during field inspection, and that its registration was subsequently cancelled. The GST communication also stated that the firm had operated for three months, October 2021 to December 2021, before the registration was suo moto cancelled from its date of registration. The Income Tax Officer rejected the objections and passed an order dated 16.6.2026 under Section 148-A(3), treating the prima facie material as relevant and drawing reassessment proceedings. The petitioner submitted that his objections had not been dealt with point-wise and that preliminary enquiries should first ascertain whether he was the real person behind the business transactions attributed to Hari Om Traders. For the revenue, it was contended that after amendment of the law the strict test of “reason to believe” no longer applied in the earlier form and that the revenue was required to establish the existence of relevant material. Reliance was also placed on GKN Driveshafts (India) Ltd. Vs. Income Tax Officer and others, (2003) 1 SCC 72, with the submission that dealing with objections did not necessarily require detailed reasoning on each individual objection at the preliminary stage. The High Court held that, although the rule of recording detailed “reasons to believe” to initiate assessment proceedings no longer exists in the same form, under Section 148-A(1) the assessing authority is required to determine whether or not it is a fit case to issue notice under Section 148. The Court observed that no detailed “reasons to believe” are required, but the time-tested requirements of relevancy of material and application of mind to the objection raised may still survive. On the facts, the Court noted that the petitioner did not dispute that financial transactions had been linked to his PAN, but disowned involvement and claimed identity theft. He had lodged a complaint under Delhi jurisdiction and made enquiries with the GST Authorities. The Court found that the GST communication was not conclusive because no enquiry had yet been conducted by the GST Authorities to return a positive finding that the petitioner was not the person who performed the transactions. The Court also noted that the GST registration had been granted on the petitioner’s identity, while the firm was not found at the stated principal place of business, the notice remained unresponded, the registration was cancelled, and no bank account was found attached to the GST account. The Court therefore held that the petitioner’s defence could remain alive during reassessment proceedings, but the preliminary stage was not the stage to accept that defence and drop the proceedings. Evidence would have to be led, documents examined and an enquiry made before a firm conclusion on identity theft could be drawn. At the preliminary stage, no further enquiry was required to determine that the case was fit for reassessment proceedings to arise. At the same time, the Court expressly held that the revenue was not absolved of its responsibility to lead positive evidence establish
rows.summary: Allahabad High Court allowed income-tax reassessment to continue despite the taxpayer’s claim that PAN-linked transactions arose from identity theft.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Delhi HC Relegates GST Writ Petition to Statutory Appeal Under Section 107
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12277 Case Name Marginmart Ifosystems Private Limited Vs Assistant Commissioncr CGST (Delhi High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Delhi High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Marginmart Ifosystems Private Limited Vs Assistant Commissioncr CGST (Delhi High Court) Summary: The Delhi High Court considered W.P.(C) 9013/2026 filed by MarginMart IFOSYSTEMS Private Limited, along with CM APPL. 42192/2026 and CM APPL. 42193/2026, challenging a Show Cause Notice dated 27.09.2025 and the consequential order dated 24.03.2026 passed pursuant thereto. The impugned order recorded that proceedings under Section 122(1)(ii) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 were initiated against the Petitioner on the allegation that invoices had been issued without actual supply of goods and inadmissible Input Tax Credit had been passed on to M/s Enriche Retail Private Limited. The order further recorded that, during the investigation, M/s Enriche Retail Private Limited was found to be non-existent at its registered place of business, following which the proceedings culminated in the impugned order. The judgment therefore concerned a challenge to GST proceedings arising from allegations of invoices issued without actual supply and passing on of inadmissible ITC. The Petitioner contended that the Show Cause Notice and consequential order had been issued and passed mechanically and in a predetermined manner, without independent examination qua the Petitioner. It was further submitted that the proceedings were without jurisdiction and violative of the principles of natural justice. On these grounds, the Petitioner urged the High Court to exercise its extraordinary writ jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. The Court noted that the Petitioner admittedly had an efficacious statutory remedy of appeal under Section 107 of the CGST Act. The Court held that the contentions raised by the Petitioner, including the challenges concerning the manner in which the proceedings were initiated and decided, could appropriately be examined by the Appellate Authority in proceedings under Section 107. Accordingly, the Delhi High Court declined to entertain the writ petition in view of the availability of the statutory appellate remedy. The Court expressly stated that it was not expressing any opinion on the merits of the contentions raised by the Petitioner. The Petitioner was relegated to avail the remedy of appeal before the competent Appellate Authority, if so advised. The Writ Petition was consequently disposed of with liberty to the Petitioner to avail the statutory remedy in accordance with law. The Court further clarified that it had not expressed any opinion on the merits of the controversy and that all questions were left open for consideration by the Appellate Authority. The order therefore does not finally adjudicate the allegations concerning invoices, actual supply, inadmissible ITC, jurisdiction or natural justice. Those issues were expressly left open for consideration by the statutory Appellate Authority. The Court’s disposition was confined to declining writ intervention because an efficacious statutory appeal under Section 107 was available. FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF DELHI HIGH COURT 1. Through the present Petition, the Petitioner seeks issuance of a writ in the nature of certiorari for quashing the Impugned Show Cause Notice dated 27.09.2025, and the consequential Impugned Order dated 24.03.2026 passed pursuant thereto. 2. The Impugned Order records that proceedings under Section 122(1)(ii) of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017 [„the Act‟] were initiated against the Petitioner on the allegation that invoices were issued without actual supply of goods and that inadmissible Input Tax Credit was passed on to M/s Enriche Retail Private Limited. It further records that, during the course of investigation, M/s Enriche Retail Private Limited was found to be non-existent at its registered place of business, and on that basis the proceedings culminated in the passing of the Impugned Order. 3. Admittedly, the Petitioner has an efficacious statutory remedy of appeal under Section 107 of the Act. 4. Learned counsel representing the Petitioner submits that the Impugned Show Cause Notice as well as the consequential Impugned Order have been issued and passed in a mechanical and pre-determined manner, without any independent examination qua the Petitioner. It is further submitted that the proceedings are without jurisdiction and are also violative of the principles of natural justice. On these grounds, it is urged that this Court ought to exercise its extraordinary writ jurisdiction under Article 226 of the Constitution of India. 5. The aforesaid content
rows.summary:
The Delhi High Court declined to entertain MarginMart IFOSYSTEMS Private Limited’s writ petition challenging a GST show cause notice dated 27.09.2025 and the consequential order dated 24.03.2026. The impugned order stated that proceedings had been initiated under Section 122(1)(ii) of the CGST Act, 2017 on the allegation that the company issued invoices without actual supply of goods and passed on inadmissible input tax credit to M/s Enriche Retail Private Limited; the order also noted that Enriche Retail Private Limited was found to be non-existent at its registered place of business during investigation. The petitioner argued that the notice and order were passed mechanically and in a predetermined manner, without independent examination, and contended that the proceedings were without jurisdiction and violated natural justice, asking the High Court to intervene under Article 226.

The Court held that the petitioner had an adequate statutory appellate remedy under Section 107 of the CGST Act and that the petitioner’s objections, including those going to the initiation and manner of the proceedings, could be examined by the appellate authority in that forum. On that basis, the Court refused writ relief and relegated the petitioner to file an appeal before the competent Appellate Authority if so advised. The Court expressly stated that it was not expressing any opinion on the merits of the allegations or defenses, and that all questions relating to the alleged fake invoicing, inadmissible ITC, jurisdiction, and natural justice were left open for consideration in the Section 107 appeal. This order therefore does not decide the substantive GST liability or validity of the proceedings; it only confirms that the proper immediate compliance step is to pursue the statutory appeal rather than seek High Court writ intervention.

rows.title: Income Tax | ITAT Mumbai Restores Transfer Pricing and MAT Issues for Fresh Adjudication
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12276 Case Name Markel Capital Limited Vs DCIT (ITAT Mumbai) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Related Assessment Year 2022-23 Courts All ITAT, ITAT Mumbai Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Markel Capital Limited Vs DCIT (ITAT Mumbai) Summary: Markel Capital Limited, a company incorporated in and tax resident of the United Kingdom and engaged in insurance/reinsurance business, filed an appeal before the Mumbai Bench of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal against the final assessment order dated 29.12.2025 passed by the Deputy Commissioner of Income Tax (International Taxation), Circle 3(2)(1), Mumbai under section 143(3) read with section 144C(13) of the Income-tax Act, 1961. The assessment followed directions dated 08.12.2025 issued by Dispute Resolution Panel-3, Mumbai under section 144C(5). The assessee had filed its return of income on 28.11.2022 declaring total income of Rs.29,28,390/- under the normal provisions of the Act and book profit of Rs.2,76,79,197/- under section 115JB. During the year, it entered into international transactions with its Associated Enterprises. The Transfer Pricing Officer, by order dated 28.01.2025 under section 92CA(3), determined the arm’s length price of payments for support services at NIL and proposed aggregate transfer-pricing adjustment of Rs.13,35,91,039/-. This comprised Rs.7,87,99,410/- paid to Markel Services India Private Limited and Rs.5,47,91,629/- paid to Markel International Services Limited. The draft assessment order dated 13.03.2025 also proposed an addition of Rs.7,71,90,607/- to book profit concerning the Reserve for Unexpired Risks. The DRP rejected the objections and the Assessing Officer subsequently passed the final assessment order assessing total income at Rs.13,65,19,430/- under the normal provisions and computing book profit at Rs.10,48,69,804/-. Before the Tribunal, the assessee filed an application under Rule 29 of the Income-tax (Appellate Tribunal) Rules, 1963 seeking admission of additional evidence. The evidence included contemporaneous e-mails concerning regular business operations, business contracts and invoices intended to substantiate the nature, actual rendition and receipt of services and the benefit derived therefrom. The assessee explained that the Transfer Pricing Officer had issued a show-cause notice on 13.01.2025 requiring a response by 16.01.2025, leaving only three days to identify and collate extensive supporting records. It submitted that during the transfer-pricing proceedings its focus had primarily been on regulatory requirements flowing from the IRDAI (Lloyd’s India) Regulations, 2016, and that only while preparing the appeal, upon legal advice, was the necessity of placing the contemporaneous documentary record in its present form appreciated. According to the assessee, the earlier non-production of evidence was neither deliberate nor attributable to lack of bona fides. The assessee sought admission of the additional evidence and restoration of Grounds 3 to 6 concerning the transfer-pricing adjustment to the Assessing Officer/Transfer Pricing Officer for fresh examination. On the MAT issue under section 115JB, it contended that the Reserve for Unexpired Risks had not been debited to the statement of profit and loss and therefore could not be added while computing book profit. It also submitted that an identical issue had been decided in its own case for assessment year 2021-22 and requested that the Assessing Officer be directed to decide the issue in conformity with that decision. The Departmental Representative opposed admission of the additional evidence. Without prejudice, it submitted that if the evidence was admitted, it required verification by the Assessing Officer/Transfer Pricing Officer and that no finding on its merits should be recorded at the appellate stage. Regarding section 115JB, the Department submitted that the issue could be examined by the Assessing Officer in accordance with law. The Tribunal admitted the additional evidence under Rule 29. It found that the documents were contemporaneous primary documents directly bearing upon whether the services were actually rendered and received, whether the assessee derived benefit from them and whether the payments satisfied the arm’s length standard. The Tribunal noted that the transfer-pricing adjustment had principally been made for want of complete and sufficient evidence concerning the need, rendition and benefit of the services and the underlying costs. The Tribunal also considered the short interval of three days between the show-cause notice and the date fixed for reply, together with the assessee’s explanation that it had concentrated upon the regulatory framework during the proceedings. It held that this constituted a reasonable explanat
rows.summary:
The Mumbai ITAT restored both the transfer-pricing dispute and the MAT/book-profit issue in Markel Capital Limited’s case for fresh examination, rather than finally deciding them on the existing record. Markel Capital Limited, a UK tax resident engaged in insurance/reinsurance business, had filed its return for AY 2022-23 on 28.11.2022 declaring total income of Rs.29,28,390 under the normal provisions and book profit of Rs.2,76,79,197 under section 115JB; the assessment ultimately became a final order dated 29.12.2025 under section 143(3) read with section 144C(13), following DRP directions dated 08.12.2025. The transfer-pricing officer had earlier, by order dated 28.01.2025 under section 92CA(3), determined the arm’s-length price of support-service payments at NIL and made an aggregate adjustment of Rs.13,35,91,039, comprising Rs.7,87,99,410 paid to Markel Services India Private Limited and Rs.5,47,91,629 paid to Markel International Services Limited; the draft assessment also proposed a section 115JB addition of Rs.7,71,90,607 relating to the Reserve for Unexpired Risks, and the final assessment increased normal-income tax exposure to Rs.13,65,19,430 and book profit to Rs.10,48,69,804. Before the Tribunal, the assessee was allowed under Rule 29 of the ITAT Rules to file additional evidence—contemporaneous emails, contracts, invoices, and other primary records—to show that the services were actually rendered, received, and beneficial, and the Tribunal accepted the explanation that the evidence had not been produced earlier because the TPO’s show-cause notice on 13.01.2025 allowed only three days to respond by 16.01.2025 and the assessee had been focused on regulatory requirements under the IRDAI (Lloyd’s India) Regulations, 2016 during the earlier proceedings. Because the added material went directly to the core transfer-pricing questions, the Tribunal restored Grounds 3 to 6 to the Assessing Officer/TPO for fresh adjudication after verification, rather than recording findings on merits at the appellate stage.

On the MAT side, the assessee argued that the Reserve for Unexpired Risks could not be added back under section 115JB because it had not been debited to the profit and loss account, and it also pointed out that an identical issue had already been decided in its own favor for AY 2021-22. The Department opposed merits findings but agreed that, if needed, the Assessing Officer could examine the issue in accordance with law. The Tribunal therefore left the section 115JB question open for reconsideration by the Assessing Officer in light of the earlier year’s decision and applicable law. In practical compliance terms, the ruling emphasizes the need for taxpayers to maintain and be ready to produce contemporaneous, transaction-level support for intra-group service charges and to expect that short response windows in transfer-pricing proceedings may still be scrutinized if evidence was omitted; it also confirms that book-profit adjustments for reserves must be tested against the actual accounting treatment and prior-year consistency, not assumed automatically addable.

rows.title: Income Tax | Gujarat HC Quashes Reopening as Change of Opinion on Section 80P(2)(d) Deduction
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12275 Case Name Gujarat State Co. Op. Agricultural And Rural Development Bank Ltd. Vs ITO (Gujarat High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Gujarat High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Gujarat State Co. Op. Agricultural And Rural Development Bank Ltd. Vs ITO (Gujarat High Court) Summary: The Gujarat High Court allowed the writ petition filed by The Gujarat State Co. Op. Agricultural and Rural Development Bank Ltd. and quashed the notice dated 16/12/2019 issued under Section 148 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 for Assessment Year 2014-15. The Court held that the reopening was nothing but a change of opinion. The judgment also records that the reopening was required to be quashed and set aside on merits in light of Diamond Jubilee Co Operative Bank Limited Vs Union of India & Ors.. The petitioner, a co-operative Bank, filed its return for A.Y. 2014-15 on 17/11/2014 declaring total income at Rs.NIL after claiming exemption of Rs.28,91,29,255/- under Section 80P. The return was selected for scrutiny. During the scrutiny proceedings, the Assessing Officer issued a show cause notice dated 21/11/2016 concerning, among other matters, “interest income” claimed exempt under Section 80P(2)(d) and “other income” claimed exempt under Section 80P(2)(c). The petitioner supplied details concerning interest from co-operative banks and nationalized banks and furnished justification for its exemption claims. After considering the material furnished, the Assessing Officer framed the scrutiny assessment under Section 143(3) on 02/12/2016. The assessment made two additions: Rs.11,28,91,418/- under Section 80P(2)(d) in respect of interest income from nationalized banks and Rs.32,61,000/- under Section 80P(2)(c) in respect of miscellaneous income and rental income. The assessed income was determined at Rs.11,61,52,425/-. The petitioner challenged the assessment before the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals), which dismissed the appeal on 17/02/2018. No further appeal was preferred against that appellate order. Thereafter, the respondent issued the impugned Section 148 notice dated 16/12/2019 seeking to reopen the assessment. The petitioner filed a return in response on 23/01/2020 and requested the reasons for reopening and the sanction obtained from the Pr.CCIT. The reasons supplied on 07/02/2020 stated, broadly, that Rs.5,93,32,466/- representing interest earned from various co-operative banks had been exempted under Section 80P(2)(d), whereas, according to the respondent, such interest did not arise from the business operations of the petitioner and was therefore not eligible for exemption. The respondent accordingly recorded that income of Rs.5,93,32,466/- chargeable to tax had escaped assessment. The petitioner objected to the reopening on 18/02/2020, raising factual and legal submissions. The respondent disposed of those objections by order dated 04/03/2020 and held that the reopening was justified. Before the High Court, the petitioner relied upon the Gujarat High Court decision in Diamond Jubilee Cooperative Bank Limited vs. Union of India, reported in [2025] 181 taxmann.com 177 (Gujarat), and submitted that deduction under Section 80P(2)(d) was available to co-operative societies on income earned as interest or investment made with a co-operative Bank, which in turn was a co-operative society itself. The petitioner also contended that the reopening amounted to a change of opinion because all relevant material had been supplied during the scrutiny assessment and no fresh or tangible material had come into the possession of the Assessing Officer. The Revenue opposed interference at the reopening stage and submitted that the action was undertaken in view of Section 147. According to the Revenue, the petitioner had claimed deduction of Rs.5,93,32,466/- in respect of interest income earned from various co-operative Banks and such income could not be regarded as arising from the business operation of the assessee for purposes of Section 80P(2)(d). The High Court accepted the petitioner’s challenge on the ground of change of opinion. The Court noted that the return had been subjected to scrutiny and that the Assessing Officer had found the petitioner’s explanation concerning exempt interest income under Section 80P(2)(d) satisfactory while passing the scrutiny assessment under Section 143(3) on 02/12/2016. The Court further noted that the Assessing Officer had already made an addition under Section 80P(2)(d) concerning interest from nationalized Banks. According to the Court, the reopening through the Section 148 notice was premised on the same material and the same issue that had already been examined by the Assessing Officer during the scrutiny assessment. rows.summary:
The Gujarat High Court quashed the Section 148 reassessment notice dated 16/12/2019 issued to The Gujarat State Co. Op. Agricultural And Rural Development Bank Ltd. for Assessment Year 2014-15, holding that the reopening was barred as a mere “change of opinion.” The assessee, a co-operative bank, had filed its return on 17/11/2014 declaring NIL income after claiming exemption of Rs. 28,91,29,255 under Section 80P; the return was scrutinized, and during assessment the AO issued a show-cause notice on 21/11/2016 specifically asking about interest income claimed exempt under Section 80P(2)(d) and other income under Section 80P(2)(c). After the assessee furnished details of interest from co-operative banks and nationalized banks and explained its exemption claim, the AO completed assessment under Section 143(3) on 02/12/2016, making additions of Rs. 11,28,91,418 under Section 80P(2)(d) (interest from nationalized banks) and Rs. 32,61,000 under Section 80P(2)(c) (miscellaneous and rental income), determining assessed income at Rs. 11,61,52,425.

The assessment was appealed to the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals), but the appeal was dismissed on 17/02/2018, and no further appeal was filed. Nearly two years later, the department reopened the case by issuing the Section 148 notice on 16/12/2019; when the assessee sought reasons and sanction details, the reasons furnished on 07/02/2020 stated that Rs. 5,93,32,466 of interest earned from various co-operative banks had been wrongly exempted under Section 80P(2)(d) because, according to the department, that income did not arise from the assessee’s business operations and was therefore taxable. The assessee objected on 18/02/2020, but the objections were rejected by order dated 04/03/2020.

The High Court held that reopening was impermissible because the same issue and the same material had already been examined in the original scrutiny assessment; there was no fresh tangible material, and the AO had already called for and considered the assessee’s explanation about exempt interest income before completing the 143(3) assessment. The Court also noted that the reopening was liable to fail on the merits in light of its decision in Diamond Jubilee Co-operative Bank Limited v. Union of India & Ors. ([2025] 181 taxmann.com 177, Gujarat), which recognized Section 80P(2)(d) deduction for interest/investment income earned from a co-operative bank treated as a co-operative society. For compliance purposes, the key point is that the judgment reinforces that once an issue has been specifically examined in scrutiny and decided, a later Section 148 reopening on the same facts will be vulnerable as a change-of-opinion challenge unless the department can point to new material; here, the reopening was struck down and the notice stood quashed.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Rajni Dua Vs ITO (ITAT Delhi) Summary: The appeal was preferred by Rajni Dua against the order dated 21.11.2025 passed by the Commissioner of Income Tax (Appeals), Delhi under section 250 of the Income-tax Act, 1961, whereby the appeal of the appellant was dismissed. The appeal concerned Assessment Year 2005-06. The return of income was filed on 31.10.2005 declaring total income of Rs.10,25,309/-. Subsequently, the Assessing Officer noticed differences between the amounts of trade discount and cash discount debited in the Profit & Loss account and the amounts appearing in the respective ledger accounts. The Assessing Officer also noticed that bonus of Rs.1,66,397/- debited in the Profit & Loss account had not actually been paid till the date of filing of the return. On this basis, the Assessing Officer formed the view that income of Rs.1,51,11,690/- had escaped assessment and initiated reassessment proceedings under section 147 by issuing notice under section 148 dated 22.03.2012. The reassessment was completed on 25.03.2013 under sections 147/143(3), assessing total income at Rs.1,62,27,150/- after making an addition of Rs.1,51,11,690/- on account of the differences in trade discount, cash discount and bonus allegedly not paid before filing of the return. Before the Tribunal, the learned Authorised Representative submitted that the reassessment deserved to be quashed because it had been initiated solely on the basis of an objection raised by the Revenue audit party and represented a review or re-appraisal of the same assessment records, without any fresh tangible material coming into the possession of the Assessing Officer after the original assessment. It was submitted that the original assessment had been completed on 16.08.2011 under sections 143(3)/154, assessing income at Rs.11,15,455/-. The Departmental Representative relied upon the orders passed by the lower authorities. The Tribunal examined the assessment order and found that the case had been reopened only on the basis of the audit objection raised by the Revenue audit party. In considering the legal position, the Tribunal referred to the Delhi High Court decision in FIS Global Business Solutions India (P.) Ltd. v. Asst CIT, [2019] 102 taxmann.com 471 (Delhi-HC). The Tribunal reproduced the relevant observations concerning the earlier decision in Carlton Overseas (P.) Ltd. v. ITO, [2010] 188 Taxman 11 (Delhi), under which a subsequent audit report was held not to constitute tangible material where it merely expressed an opinion regarding the availability of a deduction. The Tribunal also considered the principle stated in CIT v. Kelvinator of India Limited, [2010] 320 ITR 561 (SC), as referred to in the extracted portion of the Delhi High Court decision. The principle considered was that reassessment cannot be founded upon a mere change of opinion and that reopening must be based upon tangible material. The Tribunal found substance in the appellant’s contention that the Assessing Officer had reopened the assessment solely on the basis of the audit party objection and that there was no fresh tangible material. It observed that, where reassessment was initiated solely on an audit objection without new facts and on issues already examined in the original assessment, the initiation constituted a mere change of opinion and was invalid. The Tribunal accordingly held that the Assessing Officer had erred in making the addition of Rs.1,51,11,690/- in the reassessment order under sections 147/143(3) dated 25.03.2013. The addition was directed to be deleted. The appeal of the assessee was consequently allowed. The order was pronounced in the Open Court on 20.08.2026. Cases Discussed FIS Global Business Solutions India (P.) Ltd. v. Asst CIT, [2019] 102 taxmann.com 471 (Delhi-HC) — relied upon for the proposition that an audit objection merely constitutes information and that reassessment based solely on such objection is not sustainable. Carlton Overseas (P.) Ltd. v. ITO, [2010] 188 Taxman 11 (Delhi) — considered through the extract reproduced from the FIS Global decision, concerning the absence of fresh or tangible material where the Assessing Officer relied only upon the Revenue audit party’s opinion. CIT v. Kelvinator of India Limited, [2010] 320 ITR 561 (SC) — referred to in the reproduced Delhi High Court extract for the principle that reassessment cannot be based upon a mere change of opinion and requires tangible material. rows.summary:
The ITAT Delhi held that the reassessment against Rajni Dua for Assessment Year 2005–06 could not be sustained because it had been reopened solely on the basis of a Revenue audit objection, with no fresh tangible material coming to the Assessing Officer after the original assessment. The assessee had originally filed its return on 31.10.2005 declaring income of Rs. 10,25,309, and an earlier assessment had already been completed on 16.08.2011 under sections 143(3)/154 at Rs. 11,15,455. The Assessing Officer later claimed that differences in trade discount and cash discount entries, plus bonus of Rs. 1,66,397 shown as a deduction though allegedly not paid by the return-filing date, caused income of Rs. 1,51,11,690 to escape assessment; on that basis, notice under section 148 was issued on 22.03.2012 and reassessment under sections 147/143(3) was completed on 25.03.2013, resulting in total income of Rs. 1,62,27,150.

On appeal, the Tribunal found that the reopening was triggered only by the Revenue audit party’s objection and amounted to a review/re-appraisal of material already on record rather than the discovery of new facts. Relying on Delhi High Court and Supreme Court principles, including FIS Global Business Solutions India (P.) Ltd., Carlton Overseas (P.) Ltd., and CIT v. Kelvinator of India Ltd., the Tribunal reiterated that reassessment cannot rest on a mere change of opinion and must be supported by tangible new material. Because the same issues had already been examined in the original assessment and no new evidence had emerged, the Tribunal held the reassessment invalid, deleted the addition of Rs. 1,51,11,690, and allowed the assessee’s appeal. The order was pronounced in open court on 20.08.2026.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that reopening an assessment merely because an audit party disagrees with the original treatment is vulnerable to challenge unless the department can point to fresh, objective material discovered after the original assessment; otherwise, the reassessment may be struck down as an impermissible change of opinion.

(Bombay High Court) Summary: The Bombay High Court considered a writ petition filed by Green Woods, a firm registered under the Goods and Services Tax Act, 2017, challenging the Order-in-Appeal dated 4 August 2025 passed by the Commissioner, CGST and CX Appeals-II, Mumbai. The Petitioner had been issued summons on 27 December 2021, following which an investigation was initiated. During the investigation, the Petitioner made deposits on four different occasions totalling Rs. 2,60,24,954/-. Upon completion of the investigation, a Show Cause Notice in GST DRC-01 under Section 74 read with Section 122 of the CGST Act was issued, alleging contravention of the Act and proposing recovery of tax along with interest and penalty. The Petitioner contested the Show Cause Notice by filing a Reply. Thereafter, the Joint Commissioner passed an Order-in-Original dated 26 December 2024 confirming the demand of ITC and imposing penalty upon the Petitioner. Aggrieved by the Order-in-Original, the Petitioner preferred an appeal before the Appellate Authority. There was, however, a shortfall of Rs. 33,18,000/- towards the statutory 10% pre-deposit required for the appeal. On 1 April 2025, the Petitioner deposited the additional Rs. 33,18,000/-, thereby completing the statutory pre-deposit of 10%. Despite this, the appeal was dismissed by the Order-in-Appeal dated 4 August 2025 on the ground that the Petitioner had failed to pay the statutory pre-deposit as required under Section 107(6)(b) of the GST Act, 2017. Before the High Court, the Petitioner submitted that the delay in depositing the shortfall occurred due to a genuine financial constraint. It was argued that the amount was deposited within the grace period of one month, during which the Appellate Authority had the power to condone the delay after considering the explanation furnished by the Petitioner. The Petitioner contended that the appeal had nevertheless been dismissed mechanically and without providing an adequate opportunity to explain its position. The Petitioner relied upon JEM Exporter Vs. Union of India, 2023 (76) G.S.T.L. 4 (Bom.), Delphi World Money Ltd. Vs. Union of India, 1 (92) G.S.T.L. 226 (Bom.), G. Khanna & Company Vs. Union of India, 2025 (95) G.S.T.L. 429 (Bom.), and DN Polymers Vs. Union of India, 2023 (92) G.S.T.L. 226 (Bom.). The Respondents submitted that the appeal was liable to be dismissed because the statutory 10% pre-deposit had not been made at the time of filing the appeal. However, the departmental counsel did not dispute that the Petitioner had completed the statutory pre-deposit within the one-month grace period provided by the statute and before the impugned Order-in-Appeal dated 4 August 2025 was passed. The High Court considered the earlier decision in JEM Exporter Vs. Union of India. In that case, the Appellate Authority had dismissed an appeal on the grounds that the appellant had failed to make the statutory pre-deposit and had also failed to file the certified copy of the order. The High Court had interfered with the appellate order and remanded the matter to the Appellate Authority with directions to issue a defect memo pointing out the procedural defects and provide adequate opportunity to rectify them. The Court reproduced paragraph 11 of JEM Exporter, wherein it was observed that requirements relating to proof of pre-deposit, filing of a certified copy of the order and authentication of the appeal memo were procedural requirements, and that justice could not be denied for failure to comply with such procedure without giving the appellant an opportunity to rectify the procedural defects. The Commissioner (Appeals) was required to issue a defect memo calling upon the petitioner to produce proof of pre-deposit, file the certified copy and authenticate the appeal memo. Having regard to the peculiar facts and circumstances and the explanation offered by the Petitioner for failure to make the pre-deposit in time, the High Court held that the ratio of the aforementioned decisions was applicable to the present case. rows.summary:
The Bombay High Court restored Green Woods’ GST appeal after holding that the dismissal for alleged non-payment of the mandatory pre-deposit was not sustainable once the shortfall had been cured. Green Woods, a GST-registered firm, had been issued summons on 27 December 2021 and was investigated; during that investigation it made four deposits totaling Rs. 2,60,24,954. After the department issued a GST DRC-01 show cause notice under Section 74 read with Section 122 of the CGST Act alleging contraventions and proposing tax, interest, and penalty, the Joint Commissioner passed an Order-in-Original on 26 December 2024 confirming the ITC demand and imposing penalty. Green Woods then filed an appeal, but initially fell short by Rs. 33,18,000 toward the statutory 10% pre-deposit required under Section 107(6)(b); it made up that deficiency on 1 April 2025, completing the 10% deposit.

Despite the shortfall being cured, the Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed the appeal by Order-in-Appeal dated 4 August 2025 on the ground that the statutory pre-deposit had not been paid. Before the High Court, Green Woods argued that the delay was due to genuine financial hardship and that the additional amount was paid within the one-month grace period, during which the appellate authority could have condoned the delay after considering an explanation; the petitioners also argued that the dismissal was mechanical and violated natural justice. The department maintained that the appeal was liable to be rejected because the 10% deposit had not been made when the appeal was filed, but did not dispute that the full pre-deposit had in fact been completed within the one-month grace period and before the impugned order was passed.

Relying on its earlier decisions in JEM Exporter, Delphi World Money, G. Khanna & Company, and DN Polymers, the Court reiterated that requirements such as proof of pre-deposit, filing a certified copy of the order, and authentication of the appeal memo are procedural in nature and cannot justify denial of a hearing without giving the appellant a chance to cure defects. The Court noted that the Commissioner (Appeals) should issue a defect memo and allow rectification where procedural deficiencies exist, and that failure to do so is contrary to natural justice. Applying that reasoning to this case, the Court held that the appeal should not have been dismissed once the pre-deposit deficiency was cured within the permissible period, and the appellate proceedings were restored for consideration on merits.

rows.title: Goods and Services Tax | Rajasthan HC Condones 645-Day GST Appeal Delay Over Portal-Only Order Service
rows.desc: Case Law Details TaxGuru Citation 2026 taxguru.in 12272 Case Name Kalu Ram Vs State of Rajasthan & Ors. (Rajasthan High Court) Appeal Number Only available for paid members Date of Judgement/Order Only available for paid members Courts All High Courts, Rajasthan High Court Upgrade to Basic or Premium to download. Already Upgraded? Log in. Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Kalu Ram Vs State of Rajasthan & Ors. (Rajasthan High Court) Summary: The Rajasthan High Court considered a writ petition filed by M/s Kalu Ram seeking quashing and setting aside of the Order-in-Original dated 05.12.2023 passed by the Assistant Commissioner, Circle-B, Jaipur-III, and a direction to condone the delay in filing the appeal against that order. The petitioner’s appeal had been filed on 08.01.2026, resulting in a delay of 645 days. The proceedings under Section 74 of the RGST Act had arisen on account of alleged non-payment of GST on royalty and District Mineral Foundation Trust (DMFT) contributions. The Appellate Authority, by order dated 20.04.2026, dismissed the appeal on the ground of limitation, holding that it did not have the power to condone the delay. The petitioner submitted that the delay occurred due to bona fide circumstances beyond his control and was attributable to genuine and sufficient cause rather than negligence or lack of diligence. It was submitted that an amount of Rs. 1,64,221/- remained outstanding and that the Order-in-Original dated 05.12.2023 came to the petitioner’s knowledge only when the GST Department proceeded to attach and freeze his bank account. The petitioner specifically contended that the Order-in-Original had never been served upon him and that limitation could not commence merely from the date on which the order was passed in the absence of valid communication. The petitioner also challenged the demand on merits, including the levy of GST on royalty and DMFT contributions, and sought waiver of interest and penalty on the ground of non-communication of the order, which, according to the petitioner, had merely been uploaded on the GST portal. The petitioner relied upon several Division Bench judgments of the Rajasthan High Court, namely M/s M R Traders v. UOI, M/s Molana Construction Company v. Central Goods and Service Tax Department & Ors., Man Singh Tanwar v. Commissioner, Central goods and Services Tax Department & Ors., and the two decisions in RPC PSIPL JV Vs. State of Rajasthan & Ors.. It was argued that sufficient cause had been demonstrated and that the appeal should be considered on merits after condonation of delay. The respondents opposed the petition and contended that the impugned order had rightly been passed and that the appeal was barred by limitation. The High Court observed that the Appellate Authority was indeed bound by the statutory limitation provisions contained in Section 107 of the RGST/CGST Act, 2017. However, considering the reasons for which the petitioner could not submit the appeal within the stipulated period, and particularly the circumstances being beyond his control, the Court held that non-adjudication of the appeal on merits would cause grave injury and prejudice to the petitioner. The Court noted that in the judgments relied upon by the petitioner, it had directed that delayed GST appeals be entertained and considered on merits. The Court also considered the Division Bench judgment of the Punjab and Haryana High Court in Luxmi Traders versus Union Territory of Chandigarh and Ors. In that case, the Punjab and Haryana High Court had held, inter alia, that service of a Show Cause Notice could not be deemed sufficient merely because it had been uploaded on the Common Portal unless its receipt was acknowledged or a reply was filed. It had further held that where an order-in-original passed after contest was served only by uploading it on the Common Portal, the period of limitation for filing an appeal would not be triggered. Where an appeal had been dismissed on limitation because the order had been served only by portal upload, the appellate order was liable to be set aside and the appeal restored for decision on merits. The Rajasthan High Court expressly recorded that, after giving thoughtful consideration to the view expressed by the Punjab and Haryana High Court, it was in respectful agreement with that view and saw no reason why its benefit should not be accorded to the petitioner. Accordingly, following the consistent view already taken by the Rajasthan High Court and the principle concerning portal-only service, the Court allowed the writ petition to the extent of condoning the delay in filing the appeal. However, the relief was made subject to a condition. The appeal was directed to be decided as expeditiously as possible subject to the petitioner depositing 50% of the total outstanding tax amount. If any part of the amount had already been deposited, it was directed to be adjusted while calculating the balance 50%. Sub
rows.summary:
The Rajasthan High Court granted relief to M/s Kalu Ram in a GST dispute arising from proceedings under Section 74 of the RGST Act concerning alleged non-payment of GST on royalty and District Mineral Foundation Trust (DMFT) contributions. The petitioner’s appeal against the Order-in-Original dated 05.12.2023 had been filed only on 08.01.2026, creating a delay of 645 days, and the Appellate Authority had rejected the appeal on 20.04.2026 solely as time-barred because it believed it had no power to condone the delay. The High Court held that, while the limitation scheme under Section 107 of the RGST/CGST Act remains binding, the delay could be condoned because the petitioner showed sufficient cause: the order had allegedly never been validly served and was only uploaded on the GST portal, and the petitioner learned of it only when the department attached/froze his bank account. The Court relied on its own earlier Division Bench decisions and agreed with the Punjab & Haryana High Court’s view in Luxmi Traders that portal-only upload of an order is not enough to start limitation where there is no acknowledged receipt or other valid service, so an appeal dismissed on that basis can be restored and heard on merits.

As a compliance consequence, the Court directed that the delayed appeal be entertained and decided on merits, but only after the petitioner deposits 50% of the total outstanding tax amount; any amount already paid must be adjusted toward that 50% threshold. The document states that an outstanding amount of Rs. 1,64,221 remained, so the deposit condition and any credit for prior payments would apply against that figure. For compliance teams, the key operational point is that, at least in this line of authority, mere GST portal upload of an order-in-original may be insufficient for valid service and for starting the appeal limitation clock; actual communication/acknowledged service matters, and limitation defenses based only on portal publication may fail. The decision also reinforces that GST appellate authorities may be directed to hear delayed appeals on merits where non-service or other circumstances beyond the taxpayer’s control prevented timely filing.

Advertisement (adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({}); Dibyajyoti Mishra Vs State of Odisha (Orissa High Court) Summary: The petitioner, Dibyajyoti Mishra, approached the High Court of Orissa at Cuttack apprehending arrest in connection with alleged violation of provisions of the GST Act. The petitioner submitted that he was working as a priest in a temple at Rourkela and had been falsely implicated. He had received summons and, on that basis, apprehended that he might be taken into custody. He therefore sought protection by way of pre-arrest bail. The matter was heard by Justice V. Narasingh on 21.08.2026. Learned counsel for the petitioner reiterated the apprehension of arrest. On behalf of the State, learned counsel appeared before the Court. Mr. A. Kedia, learned Junior Standing Counsel, Central GST and Central Excise, on instruction, submitted that in the case at hand assessment had been made raising a demand of Rs.33,05,562/- on account of Financial Year 2018-19. It was further submitted on instruction that the apprehension of the petitioner being taken into custody was misconceived. Upon considering the rival submissions, the High Court did not find force in the petitioner’s submission that there was even any perceptible threat of arrest. The Court accordingly did not grant the requested pre-arrest protection and disposed of the ABLAPL. The Court, however, granted liberty to the petitioner to renew his prayer if there was any fresh cause of action. FULL TEXT OF THE JUDGMENT/ORDER OF HIGH COURT OF ORISSA AT CUTTACK 1. Heard learned counsel for the Petitioner and learned counsel for the State. 2. It is submitted that the Petitioner, who is working as a priest in a temple at Rourkela, has been falsely implicated for violation of provisions of GST Act. He has received summons. Therefore, he apprehends arrest and, hence, may be protected by pre-arrest bail. 3. Mr. Kedia, learned Junior Standing Counsel, Central GST and Central Excise, on instruction, submits that in the case at hand assessment has been made raising a demand of Rs.33,05,562/- on account of Financial Year 2018-19. It is further submitted by the learned Junior Standing Counsel, Central GST and Central Excise, on instruction, that the apprehension of the Petitioner being taken into custody is misconceived. 4. On considering the rival submissions, this Court does not find force in the submissions made by the learned for the Petitioner that there is even any perceptible threat of arrest. 5. Accordingly, the ABLAPL stands disposed of. 6. Liberty is given to the Petitioner to renew his prayer if there is any fresh cause of action. rows.summary:
The Orissa High Court in **Dibyajyoti Mishra v. State of Odisha** refused to grant **pre-arrest bail (ABLAPL)** to the petitioner, who said he was working as a **temple priest in Rourkela** and feared arrest after receiving GST summons. The petitioner argued that he had been falsely implicated for alleged violation of the **GST Act** and sought protection on the basis of his apprehension of custody, but the Court found **no perceptible or credible threat of arrest** on the record.  

A key fact noted by the State, through counsel for the **Central GST and Central Excise**, was that an assessment had already been completed for **FY 2018–19**, raising a **demand of Rs. 33,05,562**. On that basis, the State submitted that the petitioner’s fear of being taken into custody was misconceived. After hearing both sides on **21.08.2026**, the Court agreed with the State’s position and held that the petitioner had not shown any real basis for pre-arrest protection.  

As a result, the Court **disposed of the ABLAPL without granting bail/protection**, but expressly gave the petitioner **liberty to renew his prayer if a fresh cause of action arises**. For compliance purposes, the decision is significant mainly as a confirmation that **mere receipt of GST summons and an assessed tax demand, without more, did not persuade the Court that arrest was imminent** in this case; no new procedural rule or GST compliance deadline was laid down in the judgment itself.

rows.desc: Buzzing :Stock Market LiveStock to Watch TodayNifty OutlookNepal FloodsNitin Gadkari Retrofit DeviceNatural Disaster InsuranceESDS Software sharesAbhinandan Varthaman Quits IAFDelhi weather forecast .trendSlideBox .slide-arrow { position: absolute; width: 25px; height: 25px; padding: 0; background-size: 100%; } .trendSlideBox .slide-arrow.slide-arrow-prev { left: 0; bottom: 0; } .trendSlideBox .slide-arrow.slide-arrownext { right: 0; bottom: 0; } @media (max-width:767px) { .header-active .headerabt .logo-div .bpdAll { max-width: 60px !important; } .header-active .headerabt .logo-div .bpdialogue { max-width: 55px !important; } .header-active .headerabt .logo-div .bpdround { max-width: 60px !important; } .header-active .headerabt .logo-div .bpdlogolens { max-width: 40px !important; } } @media (min-width:768px) and (max-width:1024px) { .header-active .headerabt .logo-div .bpdAll { max-width: 100px !important; } .header-active .headerabt .logo-div .bpdialogue { max-width: 90px !important; } .header-active .headerabt .logo-div .bpdround { max-width: 110px !important; } .header-active .headerabt .logo-div .bpdlogolens { max-width: 68px !important; } } Home / India News / Isro launches EOS-05, India's 1st imaging satellite in geosynchronous orbitIsro launches EOS-05, India's 1st imaging satellite in geosynchronous orbitThe 2,367-kg EOS-05, India's heaviest Earth observation satellite so far, was placed in its intended sub-geosynchronous transfer orbit about 18 minutes after lift-offGSLV-F17 is the 19th flight of India’s Geosynchronous Satellite Launch Vehicle (GSLV) | Source: ISRO X PlatformShine Jacob Chennai 3 min read Last Updated : Sep 04 2026 | 10:26 AM IST @media (min-width:1100px) and (max-width:1280px) { .storymeta .meta-info { flex: 0 0 45%; } } Listen to This ArticleThe Indian Space Research Organisation (Isro) on Friday successfully launched India’s first dedicated imaging satellite in geosynchronous orbit from the spaceport in Sriharikota. The EOS-05 satellite, dubbed the “eye in the sky”, was launched aboard a GSLV-F17 rocket at 2.55 am on Friday from the second launch pad at the Satish Dhawan Space Centre, after a 27-hour countdown that began on Wednesday evening. The rocket's payload mass was 2,367 kilograms, making EOS-05 India’s heaviest Earth observation satellite so far. Isro said the satellite was successfully placed in the intended sub-geosynchronous transfer orbit (sub-GTO) about 18 minutes after lift-off. “Yet another outstanding achievement by Isro and a proud moment for our nation. The successful launch of GSLV-F17 carrying EOS-05, India’s first-ever imaging satellite from geosynchronous orbit is a reflection of the excellence, innovation and growing capabilities that define India’s space sector,” Prime Minister Narendra Modi said in a post on X. The RBI’s special swap measures mobilised a higher-than-expected $136.4 billion in foreign currency inflows till August 31. The rupee on Thursday settled at 94.49 per dollar, its strongest close since June 25. The rupee had closed at 94.98 on Wednesday. During the session, it touched an intraday high of 94.27 per dollar. The rupee has gained more than 1 per cent in the last week, making it one of Asia’s best-performing currencies. Market participants said dollar inflows have strengthened the RBI’s hand in managing pressure on the rupee at a time when elevated crude oil prices and rising global bond yields have weighed on emerging-market currencies. In the early stages of the FCNR(B) scheme, the rupee’s appreciation remained muted due to a stronger influence of global factors on the local currency. However, dealers said the RBI has since stepped up direct intervention in the spot market to contain volatility in the exchange rate. } } Listen to This ArticleThe Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI’s) recent proposal to ban revolving credit offered by non-banking financial companies (NBFCs) would impact a larger section of players and products, as compared to what was estimated earlier, the Finance Industry Development Council (FIDC) told the regulator on Thursday. FIDC is a self-regulatory organisation for shadow banks. The FIDC and representatives of NBFCs met RBI Deputy Governor S C Murmu and shared their feedback. The Council urged the regulator to rethink the decision on such a blanket ban, sources told Business Standard. “Initially, the impact was seen to be limited to three or four NBFCs. But the feedback has shown that a much larger section of the industry could be impacted. The RBI may, therefore, look at a partial restriction rather than a blanket ban,” an NBFC chief executive said. Around 30-40 lenders have submitted their responses to FIDC. All suggestions discussed by the industry will be consolidated and sent to the RBI through the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII), sources said. “The RBI is still receiving a lot of views. The purpose of putting out a draft is to take the public view, absorb the feedback, and then convert it into regulation,” another NBFC chief executive said. A key concern for lenders is the treatment of products that allow limited redraw or replenishment within an existing sanctioned facility. NBFCs have argued that such facilities do not necessarily constitute the kind of revolving lending that the RBI seeks to restrict. “The issue is that there is something in between a conventional term loan and what the RBI may be defining as revolving credit. There are products that technically may not fit neatly into the definition, and that is where the industry has sought greater clarity,” an industry executive said. Supply chain finance is another area where NBFCs have sought an exemption or specific clarification. Lenders said such financing is closely monitored through goods and services tax (GST) data, and that loans are disbursed directly to suppliers rather than borrowers. The RBI's proposal is aimed at ensuring repayment discipline and addressing concerns around borrower creditworthiness and loan evergreening. NBFCs, however, have said a broad definition could capture legitimate lending products. “The industry is not opposed to the objective of preventing evergreening or ensuring borrower credibility. The concern is over a blanket definition that could capture products which are not being used for that purpose,” an another NBFC chief executive said. The final guidelines on revolving credit could take another two months as the RBI assesses the feedback before deciding on the scope of restrictions. Separately, NBFCs have sought clarity on whether recovery calls can be made through the 1600-number series mandated for service and transactional calls by regulated financial entities. “Sales calls should be outside the 1600 series. We fully agree with that. But whether recovery calls fall under service calls is still a question. That needs to be clarified,” a source said. The Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (Trai) has mandated regulated financial entities to use the 1600 series for service and transactional voice calls. NBFCs said the framework could create difficulties
rows.summary: NBFCs warned RBI that a revolving credit ban could affect more products and asked for clarity on redraw, supply-chain finance, and recovery calls.

The moderation in revolving credit is partly structural, as consumers have become more conscious of making timely repayments, while digital platforms and payment reminders have reduced instances of customers inadvertently carrying balances, the bank said. Speaking after the launch of the Axis Bank-Scapia co-branded credit card, Dixit said, “Revolvers have been coming down for roughly five years.” She said the trend was a combination of industry evolution and the credit cycle, with greater consumer awareness and multiple platforms and mechanisms reminding customers to pay their dues on time, reducing instances of accidental revolving. The moderation in revolvers, however, does not necessarily mean weaker growth in the overall credit card book. Point-of-sale transactions converted into equated monthly instalments (EMIs) can continue to generate revenue-accretive spending and support growth in card receivables. “Newly acquired customers also take time to contribute meaningfully to the book. Typically, it takes six to 12 months for a new cardholder to build meaningful spending on the card, providing banks with a pipeline for future receivables growth,” she said.Also Read Axis Bank's safety tool: Set UPI limit, declare overseas travel before tripJuly per-credit card spending slips 2.4% Y-o-Y, issuances outpace transactionpremiumAxis Bank sees 'Death Cross' formation on chart; analyst flags key levels

rows.title: RBI may use FCNR inflows to shrink its $136.8 billion forward book
rows.desc: Articles 2 min read RBI may use FCNR inflows to shrink its $136.8 billion forward book More than $45 billion of the RBI’s total short forward book of $136.8 billion as of end-July 2026 is set to mature between July 2026 and July 2027, creating an opportunity for the central bank to use incoming forex flows to retire some of these positions. ETBFSI Research ETBFSI Published On Sep 4, 2026 at 08:40 AM IST var news_msid = 133750633; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook The Reserve Bank of India could use incoming FCNR flows to retire some of its soon-to-mature dollar forward positions, potentially helping the central bank absorb part of the rupee liquidity being generated by the surge in foreign currency deposits while reducing the size of its large forward book.More than $45 billion of the RBI’s total short forward book of $136.8 billion as of end-July 2026 is set to mature between July 2026 and July 2027, creating an opportunity for the central bank to use incoming forex flows to retire some of these positions, according to Barclays India.Alternative to OMO sales Advt The potential move comes as the RBI weighs how to manage the liquidity impact of the FCNR dollar inflows without inadvertently tightening financial conditions further. Indian government bond yields are largely back to June 5 levels, and announcing open market sales could weigh on yields further and distort the supply-demand balance in the G-sec market.Using incoming forex flows to retire soon-to-mature forwards would incidentally also absorb liquidity from the banking system. It could therefore provide the RBI with a way to manage excess rupee liquidity without adding further government securities supply through OMO sales.The strategy would, however, come at a cost. Using the incoming forex flows to retire forwards would take away from the replenished foreign exchange reserves war-chest and would be akin to a sell-buy swap.Reducing the longer-term burdenWhile this may not be the RBI’s preferred tool, retiring some of the soon-to-mature forwards could reduce the size of the problem the central bank would have to deal with over a longer tenor of three to five years.The existing swaps have added to an already large forward book, creating future obligations for the central bank. Using incoming dollar flows to retire some of the positions as they mature would reduce that burden over time, even as it draws down part of the replenished FX reserves war-chest. Advt The RBI therefore faces a cost-benefit trade-off. It can preserve the replenished FX reserves war-chest while retaining a large forward book, or use part of the incoming forex flows to reduce forward liabilities while also absorbing some of the liquidity entering the banking system.For banks, the choice of liquidity-management tool will determine how much of the FCNR dollar inflow translates into persistent domestic liquidity. A strategy of retiring maturing forwards could simultaneously reduce excess rupee liquidity and shrink the RBI’s outstanding forward positions. rows.title: Corporate credit drives bank loan growth as retail demand remains subdued
rows.desc: Articles 2 min read Corporate credit drives bank loan growth as retail demand remains subdued Public sector banks are growing loans at around 17% year-on-year and private banks at around 15%, with the recovery broad-based across ticket sizes, sectors and regions. ETBFSI Research ETBFSI Published On Sep 4, 2026 at 08:42 AM IST var news_msid = 133750673; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook Bank loan growth remains strong at around 15% year-on-year, but the incremental momentum is increasingly coming from non-retail lending, particularly corporate credit, even as retail and household loan growth remains below 15%.Public sector banks are growing loans at around 17% year-on-year and private banks at around 15%, with the recovery broad-based across ticket sizes, sectors and regions. Lenders' confidence to grow is supported by a benign asset quality environment, according to Kotak Institutional Equities.Higher-ticket loans are showing the fastest recovery in growth. Loans above Rs1 billion, which account for 28% of outstanding loans, are growing around 20% year-on-year. Loans in the Rs1 million-Rs10 million segment, representing 27% of outstanding loans, are growing 15%, while mid-ticket segments between Rs10 million and Rs1 billion are also showing strong growth of around 20%. Advt Public sector banks continue to be aggressive in pursuing loan growth, while recovery is visible across regions. Private banks have a higher concentration in metro regions, which account for around 65% of their loan mix, where they continue to compete aggressively with public sector banks.Corporate lending gains momentumLoan growth by sector shows a broad-based recovery, but the acceleration is more pronounced in private corporate lending, which is growing around 20% year-on-year. Retail and household lending remains below 15%.Recovery is also visible across products, including short-term products such as overdrafts and demand loans, as well as medium-term lending. Long-term loans to financial companies are growing at more than 20%, while the industry segment is expanding around 15%.The sharp recovery in corporate lending could partly reflect a substitution of funding sources. The second half of FY26 saw a sharp increase in bond yields, which probably led corporates to substitute bank funding for bond funding. Short-term demand also emerged following tensions in the Middle East.Lenders have been comfortable with borrowers' balance sheets, particularly with support coming through ECLGS, resulting in higher-than-normalised demand. Retail loan growth, however, is yet to show clear signs of acceleration, with borrower confidence remaining somewhat subdued compared with prior years even as lenders appear increasingly willing to extend credit. Advt NIM outlook could improve in FY27Net interest margins remain a key area of focus, as the benefits of stronger loan growth have largely been offset by margin compression. The underlying trajectory is expected to improve as loan growth moderates, particularly in the corporate segment, supporting a healthier asset mix and loan yields.Lower reliance on wholesale deposits, aided by strong FCNR deposit mobilisation, is also expected to support margins. At the same time, a more rational competitive environment could help as funding franchises across private and public sector banks normalise.Loan growth is therefore expected to moderate from current levels, while stronger deposit growth and a healthier asset mix could provide banks with a better NIM outlook in FY27. rows.title: RBI DG Murmu meets FIDC, NBFC CEOs; industry hopeful of partial ban on revolving credit
rows.desc: Articles 4 min read RBI DG Murmu meets FIDC, NBFC CEOs; industry hopeful of partial ban on revolving credit RBI DG S C Murmu recently held a meeting with NBFCs and the Finance Industry Development Council (FIDC), having already received 350 feedbacks from the industry on central bank's draft proposal of banning revolving credit. Exemption to Supply chain financing has garnered repeated attention during the discussion, with one of the senior industry participant saying final guidelines may come in another two months. Shrishti Sharma ETBFSI Updated On Sep 4, 2026 at 11:27 AM IST Read by 100 Professionals var news_msid = 133737739; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook The Reserve Bank of India may reconsider its proposed blanket ban on revolving credit facilities by non bank lenders after receiving feedback that the draft could affect a much wider section of the NBFC industry than initially envisaged, sources said.RBI Deputy Governor Shirish Chandra Murmu recently held a meeting with NBFCs and the Finance Industry Development Council (FIDC) to discuss the proposed restrictions on revolving credit, with the central bank listening to concerns raised by lenders, according to people aware of the discussions.The RBI had initially envisaged the impact of the proposed ban to be limited to around three to four NBFCs. However, feedback received during the consultation has indicated that a significantly larger section of the industry could be affected, prompting the central bank to consider whether a blanket prohibition is appropriate, sources said. Advt “Initially, the impact was seen as being limited to three or four NBFCs. But the feedback has shown that a much larger section of the industry could be impacted. RBI may therefore look at a partial restriction rather than a blanket ban,” an NBFC CEO said.The contours of any changes are yet to be finalised, the person added and all the suggestions discussed will be sent to RBI by Confederation of Indian Industry (CII).The development comes after substantial industry feedback on the draft. Around 30-40 lenders have submitted their responses to FIDC, while the RBI has received around 350 responses on the proposed revolving credit restrictions, according to sources.“RBI is still receiving a lot of views. The purpose of putting out a draft is to take the public view, absorb the feedback and then convert it into regulation,” another NBFC CEO said.The RBI's proposal had raised concerns across the NBFC industry over the scope of its definition of revolving credit and its potential impact on products and lending structures that are not necessarily intended to perpetually roll over credit.The central bank's concern behind the proposal is linked to the credibility and creditworthiness of borrowers, sources said. The proposed framework seeks to ensure greater discipline around the repayment and continuation of credit facilities rather than allowing credit limits to remain available on a revolving basis. Advt However, NBFCs have argued that there are several products where limited redraw or replenishment within an existing sanctioned facility does not necessarily amount to the kind of revolving lending that RBI is seeking to restrict.“The issue is that there is something in between a conventional term loan and what RBI may be defining as revolving credit. There are products that technically may not fit neatly into the definition, and that is where the industry has sought greater clarity,” an industry professional said.The industry has also pointed to the potential impact on working-capital and other lending products if the definition is applied too broadly. Advt “RBI has been quite positive in the discussions and is listening to the points being raised by the industry. That gives us confidence that the feedback will be considered before the final regulation,” an NBFC CEO said.The issue is not new, with NBFCs having raised concerns around the treatment of revolving credit with the RBI in earlier discussions as well. However, the latest draft has brought the issue into sharper focus by putting the proposed restrictions in writing.“There were discussions on the same issue even earlier, but there were no guidelines in writing. The moment something is put into a regulation, the grey areas become much more important because businesses have to comply with the exact wording,” an industry professional said. Advt The consultation process is therefore expected to play a key role in determining whether RBI retains the blanket restriction or introduces exemptions or a more targeted prohibition.Sources said the final guidelines could take another two months to be issued, giving the central bank time to assess the responses received from lenders and industry bodies.“The industry is not opposed to the objective of preventing evergreening or ensuring borrower credibility. The c

rows.title: Loan recovery calls: NBFCs seek RBI clarity on TRAI’s 1600 series rules
rows.desc: Articles 2 min read Loan recovery calls: NBFCs seek RBI clarity on TRAI’s 1600 series rules Non-banking finance companies have sought clarity from the Reserve Bank of India on whether recovery calls fall under the service-call category permitted through the 1600 numbering series, amid concerns that customers increasingly block calls originating from the series, sources part of the discussion told ETBFSI. Shrishti Sharma ETBFSI Updated On Sep 4, 2026 at 11:31 AM IST var news_msid = 133737944; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook The issue was raised by NBFC CEOs and industry representatives during a meeting with RBI Deputy Governor S C Murmu on Thursday, where the industry flagged concerns around the implementation of the Telecom Regulatory Authority of India’s (TRAI) mandatory 1600-series framework for regulated financial entities.“Sales calls should be outside the 1600 series. We fully agree with that. But whether recovery calls fall under service calls is still a question. That needs to be clarified,” a source told ETBFSI.The 1600 series was allocated by the Department of Telecommunications (DoT) for service and transactional voice calls by Government and BFSI entities. TRAI, in November 2025, subsequently mandated a phase-wise migration of RBI-, SEBI- and PFRDA-regulated entities to the series, with the objective of allowing consumers to distinguish legitimate calls from regulated financial institutions from spam, promotional and potentially fraudulent calls. Advt For RBI-regulated entities, commercial banks were required to adopt the 1600 series by January 1, 2026, while large NBFCs with asset size above Rs 5,000 crore, payments banks and small finance banks were given a February 1, 2026 deadline. Remaining NBFCs, co-operative banks, regional rural banks and other entities were required to migrate by March 1, 2026.RBI regulated entities covered by the mandate are not permitted to initiate service or transactional voice calls from numbers other than those allocated under the 1600 series, even where they have explicit or inferred customer consent.TRAI's stated objective is to prevent promotional calls from being made under the guise of service or transactional calls and to give BFSI entities a distinct identity that allows consumers to make informed decisions about whether to answer a call.However, NBFCs said the framework does not clearly address recovery communications. Lenders typically make large volumes of calls to borrowers regarding overdue payments, repayment schedules and other recovery-related matters, and the industry wants to know whether such calls qualify as service calls under the 1600 framework.“The distinction between a sales call, a service call and a recovery call is important. I agree that a sales call should not be made through 1600. But whether a recovery call is considered a service call is not clear,” the NBFC CEO said.The concern is compounded by the possibility of customers blocking calls originating from the 1600 series. Industry participants said that while the dedicated series is intended to help consumers identify genuine financial-sector calls, borrowers may still block such numbers as unwanted or spam, particularly when they receive repeated recovery calls. Advt “If you are doing mass recovery calls and people are blocking those numbers, the whole purpose is lost,” the source said.According to the industry, the problem becomes particularly acute when a borrower does not respond to repeated calls from a lender’s 1600 number.“Imagine a 1600 call. If the customer does not pick up, how will a banker communicate? If we try once or twice and the number is blocked, can we then call from our normal number? That is the question,” the CEO said. By Shrishti Sharma , ETBFSI Published On Sep 3, 2026 at 07:06 PM IST Telegram Facebook Copy Link Comments What are your thoughts?
