rows.title: Central bank reinforces its rupee hand with another intervention
rows.desc: Articles 1 min read Central bank reinforces its rupee hand with another intervention The Reserve Bank of India actively supported the rupee throughout Friday's trading session. This intervention helped the currency overcome higher oil prices and regional weakness. The central bank's consistent dollar sales this week prevented rupee depreciation. RBI's special schemes have attracted over $136 billion, providing a significant buffer. Traders now await key U.S. economic data before the Federal Reserve meeting. Reuters Published On Sep 4, 2026 at 11:29 AM IST var news_msid = 133753584; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook By Nimesh VoraMUMBAI, Sept 4 - The Reserve Bank of India once again stepped in near the start of Friday's session to support the rupee and kept up its intervention through the session, traders said, helping the currency shrug off higher oil prices and weakness in Asian currencies.The rupee opened slightly ‌higher at 94.46 ⁠per ⁠dollar compared with 94.4850 on Thursday, and has remained largely rangebound since.Pre-market indications ​had pointed to a weaker start.The RBI has repeatedly sold dollars near ​the open all through this week, preventing the rupee from tracking weaker indications, bankers said. Advt The central bank's increasingly forceful intervention comes amid ​its special schemes having drawn more than $136 ⁠billion, far ‌exceeding expectations and providing the rupee a buffer.Its ​persistent presence ​has reinforced expectations that the central bank is ⁠using its increased firepower to steer the rupee higher.The ​RBI was setting the tone for the day ​at the open, trader said.Its "repeated presence" in the market this week has left little doubt that it is leaning toward a higher rupee, he said.The rupee is up nearly 1% this week despite a rally in oil prices, which are on track ‌for the steepest weekly advance since mid-July on rising tensions and renewed U.S.-Iran hostilities.Brent crude inched past $96 ​a barrel ​in Asia trading.Attention will ⁠now turn to key U.S. data ahead of the Federal Reserve's September 15-16 meeting, with nonfarm payrolls due later on Friday and inflation data next week likely to shape expectations for the central bank's policy path.Whether the Fed hikes rates at the meeting or stays on hold is now effectively a coin toss, making the incoming data particularly important for the dollar.(Reporting by Nimesh Vora; Editing by Mrigank Dhaniwala and Nivedita Bhattacharjee) Reuters Published On Sep 4, 2026 at 11:29 AM IST Telegram Facebook Copy Link Comments What are your thoughts? rows.title: 'AI will kill digital': Axis Bank head Sameer Shetty calls ‘Zero-Ops’ our north star
rows.desc: Articles 6 min read 'AI will kill digital': Axis Bank head Sameer Shetty calls ‘Zero-Ops’ our north star Axis Bank is set to unveil nineteen groundbreaking initiatives at the Global Fintech Fest, showcasing its commitment to innovation. The bank's digital business operates autonomously to accelerate product development. By leveraging AI, it significantly enhances customer service, refines operations, and bolsters risk management. Stringent measures are being implemented to amplify digital security and thwart fraud, while the Account Aggregator platform is designed to streamline lending and personal finance management. Mayur Shetty TNN Published On Sep 4, 2026 at 11:27 AM IST var news_msid = 133753498; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook Axis Bank has lined up 19 launches for the upcoming Global Fintech Fest. Sameer Shetty, group head – digital business and transformation and strategic platforms at Axis Bank, speaks about how technology is reducing human intervention, improving customer experience and enhancing safety. Shetty, a former partner at McKinsey, has worked with financial institutions across India, Southeast Asia and the Middle East.What was the thinking behind using the bank-within-a-bank concept for digital?We made digital a self-contained business because it requires different skills from branch banking. Branch banking depends on physical distribution; digital depends on technology, design and simple customer journeys. Bringing technology, product, design, marketing and risk together lets us build and take products to market faster. We have a 50-member design team, many from outside banking, and nearly 300 engineers who build in-house. Advt But this is not a separate bank. What we build is also used across the bank. A personal-loan customer can apply through the app, branch, salesperson or DSA, using essentially the same underlying technology. The aim is to give digital banking the capabilities to operate end-to-end while making those capabilities available to the wider bank.Do you use it to provide differentiated digital-only products?It is not just an alternative channel; it is built to design and incubate truly digital-first and digital-only products, like one-click pre-approved personal loans, created specifically with native digital journeys in mind. We operate under a strict definition where "digital business" refers exclusively to end-to-end, straight-through journeys where both customer acquisition and processing happen with zero human intervention. This is fundamentally distinct from assisted journeys, where a salesperson or branch initiates the lead even if the back end is automated, or traditional physical, paper-based processes. Because only pure, unassisted D2C transactions flow into our digital unit's dedicated balance sheet and P&L, and our direct digital marketing costs are self-contained, we can cleanly measure our distinct cost structures, unit economics, loan volumes, and product-level fee and interest yields without blurring them into the wider branch network.How does digital help in customer acquisition?Acquiring new-to-bank customers has not scaled to the extent we would like it to. It accounts for under 5% of fresh savings-account acquisitions. Its real strength is deepening existing relationships. Around 25% of personal loans are sourced end-to-end through the app, rising to 55% for fixed deposits and nearly 70% for mutual funds.Digital is also the primary engine for select lifecycle products, with over 85% of credit-card EMI conversions happening on the app. So while new-to-bank acquisition remains distribution-led, digital drives large-scale, self-service adoption among existing customers. Advt How do you work with Freecharge?We house our entire in-house engineering team, nearly 300 strong, within Freecharge to take advantage of its native fintech DNA. Traditionally, banking technology teams relied heavily on external vendors rather than building software themselves, which made it challenging to attract specialised engineering talent with standard banking organisational structures. Freecharge gives us a tech-first environment, modern organisational design and technical career growth paths that attract top developers and product builders who might never consider working directly inside a traditional bank. Advt Operationally, the engagement functions much like a vendor relationship: we commission specific projects and pay Freecharge accordingly. However, by regulation and design, Freecharge is a 100% captive sister company dedicated entirely to Axis Bank. They do not build or service products for anyone else, ensuring complete alignment with our roadmap as they develop our proprietary digital architectures, journeys and native products in-house.Where all are you using AI in the bank?We are using AI across customer service, operations, risk and techn

rows.title: Stock markets rebound in early trade after 4-days of slump; Sensex jumps over 530 pts
rows.desc: Articles 1 min read Stock markets rebound in early trade after 4-days of slump; Sensex jumps over 530 pts Indian equity benchmarks Sensex and Nifty bounced back sharply in early trade on Friday. This rebound followed a rally in Asian markets after four days of significant declines. Major gainers included Bajaj Finserv, Reliance Industries, and State Bank of India. Foreign institutional investors offloaded equities, while domestic investors remained net buyers. The markets reflected a positive global sentiment driven by US market gains. rows.title: Manipal Payment IPO price band fixed at Rs 322-339; issue to open on Sep 9

The company's Rs 805-crore IPO will open for public subscription on September 9. This offering includes a fresh issue and an offer for sale by the promoter. Proceeds will fund equipment purchases and installations across various facilities. The equity shares are proposed to be listed on BSE and NSE on September 17. rows.title: India's BoP likely to post USD 60-65 bn surplus in FY27 despite wider CAD: HDFC Bank
rows.desc: Articles 2 min read India's BoP likely to post USD 60-65 bn surplus in FY27 despite wider CAD: HDFC Bank India's balance of payments (BoP) is expected to post a surplus of USD 60-65 billion in FY27 despite a widening current account deficit, as strong inflows through special RBI schemes are likely to offset weak capital flows, HDFC Bank said in a report. ANI Published On Sep 4, 2026 at 10:50 AM IST var news_msid = 133752778; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook New Delhi [India], September 4 (ANI): India's balance of payments (BoP) is expected to post a surplus of USD 60-65 billion in FY27 despite a widening current account deficit, as strong inflows through special RBI schemes are likely to offset weak capital flows, HDFC Bank said in a report.The bank expects the current account deficit (CAD) to widen to around 1.1-1.3 per cent of GDP in FY27, with the deficit in the second quarter projected at 1.5-1.7 per cent of GDP. However, it has maintained an upside bias to its BoP surplus forecast."The large inflows mobilised under the RBI's FCNR(B) deposit and overseas borrowing measures are likely to more than compensate for the weak capital flows recorded in Q1 and support an overall BoP surplus in FY27," HDFC Bank said in its report. Advt According to recent data released by RBI, as of August 31, total foreign exchange inflows under the RBI's special USD-INR swap facility stood at USD 136.38 billion, including USD 127.23 billion through FCNR(B) deposits, USD 5.26 billion under overseas foreign currency borrowings (OFCBs) and USD 3.89 billion through external commercial borrowings (ECBs).India's BoP recorded a deficit of USD 8.1 billion in the first quarter, compared with a surplus of USD 4.5 billion a year earlier. The capital account moved into a deficit of USD 5.5 billion, while foreign portfolio investors remained net sellers with outflows of USD 9.6 billion.The current account deficit, however, remained contained at USD 4.2 billion, or 0.5 per cent of GDP, compared with USD 3.4 billion, or 0.4 per cent, in Q1 FY26.HDFC Bank said the merchandise trade deficit widened to USD 86.1 billion from USD 68.9 billion a year earlier, with merchandise imports rising 20 per cent to USD 218 billion. Higher crude oil and precious metal prices contributed significantly to the increase in the import bill.This was partly offset by stronger services receipts and remittances. Net services receipts rose 7.8 per cent year-on-year to USD 52 billion, while net transfer receipts, largely comprising remittances from Indians overseas, increased by USD 10 billion to USD 41 billion. Advt The bank expects the elevated merchandise deficit to continue in coming quarters, while higher services exports should provide some support. It has assumed an average crude oil price of USD 85 per barrel for FY27 and cautioned that a prolonged period of elevated crude prices could push the CAD higher.For the rupee, HDFC Bank expects mild depreciation over the coming months, with the USD/INR pair seen in the 95-97 range by December-end. The bank said elevated global yields, amid a shift towards rate hikes by developed-market central banks, along with uncertainty over the West Asia conflict and its impact on oil prices, could weigh on the rupee. rows.title: Indian banks move AI into production, but scaling remains a challenge
rows.desc: Articles 3 min read Indian banks move AI into production, but scaling remains a challenge Indian banks are now deploying artificial intelligence in production across various functions. Scaling these AI deployments faces significant hurdles related to security and data usability. Retail lending and customer service show the biggest operational impact from current AI initiatives. Banks are preparing to use AI in more consequential areas like credit risk and fraud detection. ET Online Published On Sep 4, 2026 at 09:46 AM IST var news_msid = 133751610; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook Indian banks have moved beyond experimenting with artificial intelligence (AI), with most institutions now deploying AI in production. However, scaling these deployments across the organisation remains a challenge due to concerns around security, data usability, governance and skills, according to a Zeta survey.Zeta’s 2026 CXO survey, based on responses from 40 CXOs across 18 banks and NBFCs, found that 70% of chief data officer respondents place their institutions at either selective or scaled AI deployment, including 30% at scaled deployment.AI adoption is strongest in areas where outcomes can be reviewed and existing controls can contain risks, including customer service, fraud and risk analytics, document processing and software testing. Its integration into end-to-end workflows and consequential decisions remains at an earlier stage. Advt The survey highlights a gap between proving that AI works in production and deploying it repeatedly across an institution without rebuilding data, integrations and controls for every new use case.Retail lending sees biggest AI impactRetail lending emerged as the area seeing the biggest operational impact from AI, with 88% of COOs surveyed identifying it as a meaningful area of impact, followed by customer service at 75%. CASA and back-office operations were cited by 63% each.Zeta said roughly four in 10 CDO respondents were unable to identify a high-ROI AI use case within their institution. However, lack of ROI clarity was rated the lowest barrier to adoption, while security and data privacy emerged as the biggest concern.Data availability isn't the problemAbout 80% of CIOs and CTOs surveyed described their data environment as mostly ready for AI at scale, although none considered it fully ready.The bigger constraints are around making data usable for AI. About 61% cited insufficient labelled or training data, 53% pointed to privacy and consent and 46% cited siloed data.At the same time, 67% of respondents said their banks were using or piloting AI to enhance or enrich their data.AI adoption slows when it moves from producing to executingAI has also gained ground in software engineering. Around 80% of CIOs and CTOs said their organisations use AI for testing and quality assurance, while 60% use it for code generation. Advt Adoption drops to 40% for code review and 30% each for specifications and documentation, deployment and CI/CD, and incident detection.Security and data privacy scored 3.89 out of five as a barrier, compared with 2 out of five for lack of ROI clarity.Banks are now preparing to use AI in more consequential areas. At least 60% of chief risk officers surveyed identified AI-led credit-risk models, predictive early-warning systems and real-time fraud decisioning as priorities over the next 18-24 months.Around 60% said responsible AI frameworks were under development, although none reported organisation-wide implementation. Only 20% described model-risk management as very mature. Advt AI could change work before workforce sizeHalf of operations leaders surveyed expect AI-driven productivity gains to free up capacity for redeployment into higher-value work, while none expect workforce reductions above 20%.Banks are currently building AI capabilities faster through specialist hiring and external partners than internal development, which received the lowest capability score in the survey.“Indian banks have shown that AI creates value in production. The next challenge is making that success repeatable, and the survey is clear about what stands in the way: not conviction, but control,” said Sivaram Kowta, President, Zeta India. Advt Zeta said the next phase will depend on banks building shared data, infrastructure, governance and control capabilities that allow successful AI deployments to be replicated across the organisation. rows.title: FPIs pump Rs 13,010 crore into Indian equities in second half of August
rows.desc: Articles 2 min read FPIs pump Rs 13,010 crore into Indian equities in second half of August Overseas investors continued buying Indian equities for five straight fortnights. They invested over thirteen thousand crore rupees in the latter half of August. Consumer services, financials, and healthcare sectors received significant foreign portfolio inflows. Capital goods also saw renewed investor interest after previous outflows. Oil, gas, and consumable fuels experienced the largest foreign investment outflows. ET Bureau Published On Sep 4, 2026 at 09:43 AM IST var news_msid = 133751557; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook Mumbai: Overseas investors extended their buying streak in Indian equities for a fifth consecutive fortnight in the second half of August, with consumer services, financials and healthcare emerging as the biggest beneficiaries of foreign inflows. Foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) pumped ₹13,010 crore into Indian equities during August 16-31, after investing ₹16,609 crore in the first half of the month, according to NSDL data."A major part of the foreign portfolio investors' participation has come from secondary market block deals and offer for sale," said Sriram Velayudhan, senior vice-president, IIFL Capital Services. "Their focus has been on growth-oriented sectors like consumer services, new-age financial services and healthcare." Advt Consumer services attracted the highest inflows during the fortnight at ₹5,019 crore, extending a sectoral buying trend that has gathered momentum in recent months. Financial services saw inflows of ₹3,959 crore, while healthcare attracted ₹3,021 crore.Read more: Nominal GDP growth set to surge to 12%. Why the stock market may still struggle to rally"Within consumer services businesses, there has been an inclination towards platform businesses like Nykaa, Eternal, Lenskart and Meesho, where profitability visibility has improved significantly, or hotel businesses like Indian Hotels, which is heading towards seasonally stronger quarters," said Sunny Agrawal, head of fundamental equity research at SBI Securities.Capital goods returned to favour in the second half of August after witnessing outflows in July and in the first half of August, while healthcare attracted more than ₹5,900 crore of FPI inflows during August. "The financial services industry is likely to report robust earnings growth for the residual FY27 and hence institutional interest is likely to be favourable, underpinned by comfortable valuations," Agrawal said. "The healthcare sector also has structural tailwinds across sub-sectors like hospitals, diagnostics and CDMO, which would have led to FII buying momentum in the sector."Oil, gas and consumable fuels witnessed the highest outflows at ₹2,251 crore during the second half of August. rows.title: Niva Bupa hikes premiums 8-9% annually to keep pace with medical inflation: CFO Vishwanath Mahendra
rows.desc: Articles 7 min read Niva Bupa hikes premiums 8-9% annually to keep pace with medical inflation: CFO Vishwanath Mahendra Niva Bupa Health Insurance is prioritising profitable growth even as medical inflation continues to push up the cost of health cover, with the insurer raising premiums by around 8-9% annually and expecting this trend to continue. CFO Vishwanath Mahendra said smaller annual increases are preferable to sharp hikes every few years, while the insurer targets a 98-99% combined insurance service ratio by FY29 and mid-to-high teens ROE. Anushka Sengupta ETBFSI Published On Aug 29, 2026 at 08:08 AM IST Read by 100 Professionals var news_msid = 133602500; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook Vishwanath Mahendra, CFO, Niva Bupa Health InsuranceNiva Bupa Health Insurance is seeing strong growth, with retail health premium rising 47% year-on-year in Q1, significantly ahead of the industry’s 32% growth. Overall premium grew 32%, while profit after tax nearly doubled 93% to Rs 138 crore, even as the insurer remained selective in group health amid an unfavourable pricing environment.But the growth is coming against a persistent challenge for the health insurance industry: rising medical inflation and the resulting pressure on premiums. Niva Bupa CFO Vishwanath Mahendra said the insurer has already raised premiums by 8-9% annually, and expects this to continue as medical costs rise, arguing that smaller, regular hikes are preferable to a sharp increase every few years. Advt Mahendra also said Niva Bupa is targeting profitable growth, with a medium-term goal of a 98-99% combined insurance service ratio by FY29 and mid-to-high teens ROE, while its retail market share has crossed 11%.Here are the edited excerpts from the interview:Q. By how much has Niva Bupa raised its premiums this year to tackle rising medical inflation. Should customers expect another round of hikes next year as well?Vishwanath: Medical inflation is something which is eating every day now. Ultimately, we have to pass on that to policyholders because there is no other way if we want to make the product sustainable in the long run.We have been increasing premiums in high single digits in the past, and we would like to continue doing that. Rather than increasing premiums once in three years by a big number, our preference is to increase them by only single digits every year, so that it is not as much of a pinch for policyholders.So, when I say 8-9%, I mean 8-9% per annum, which will be experienced by policyholders. And yes, this is something we expect to continue next year as well.Of course, we are also doing many other things, discussions with hospitals on treatment protocols, industry initiatives and care pathways, to ensure there are no unnecessary admissions, abuse or wastage. But at some point, inflation is there in the economy and we have to pass that on. Advt Q. Your retail health business grew 47% in Q1, much faster than the industry. Is that growth coming at healthy economics or are you sacrificing margins to gain market share?Vishwanath: It is coming from healthy economics. The growth is being driven by investment across distribution channels, product innovation and our claims practices.We have been investing across agency, bancassurance, direct-to-consumer and third-party channels. Our newly launched product, ReAssure 3.0, has also been received very well by distributors and customers.Our claim settlement ratio is close to 96%, and we are not compromising on underwriting or profitability to drive growth. Advt Q. You have also kept group health growth largely flat. Was that a conscious decision because pricing was not attractive?Vishwanath: Yes. We generally write business only if it is value-accretive. The pricing environment in group health was not very supportive, so we decided to stay away from business that was not economically attractive.We continue to focus on segments within group health which are good businesses from a profitability perspective. The approach is very clear, we want profitable growth, not growth at any cost.Q. With 32% overall growth and 93% growth in profit after tax, how close are you to consistently generating underwriting profits? Advt Vishwanath: We are very much there. It is only a matter of 20 basis points. Our combined insurance service ratio has improved by 300 basis points, from 103.2% to 100.2%.Our medium-term guidance since listing has been mid-to-high teens ROE, which corresponds to a 98-99% combined insurance service ratio by FY29. We are very much on that trajectory.Our post-tax ROE was 11.8% for the last four rolling quarters, so the trajectory is very much there.Q. Retail market share has crossed 11%. How much further do you want to take it?Vishwanath: Our target is to keep growing retail health at least 8-10% higher than the industry and keep gaining market share ever
rows.summary: Niva Bupa said it is raising health insurance premiums about 8-9% a year to offset medical inflation while focusing on profitable growth.

rows.title: September set for IPO boom as Jio, NSE could drive record fundraising
rows.desc: Articles 3 min read September set for IPO boom as Jio, NSE could drive record fundraising Jio's proposed Rs 37,700-crore issue has already received Sebi approval, while NSE's proposed Rs 30,000-crore issue could significantly add to September's fundraising if launched. ETBFSI Research ETBFSI Published On Sep 1, 2026 at 01:02 PM IST Read by 100 Professionals var news_msid = 133672651; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook JIO, NSE ఐపీఓలు.. ఇండియా స్టాక్ మార్కెట్ చరిత్ర తిరగరాయడం ఖాయమా?September’s IPO calendar has opened with mainboard issues from Purple Style Labs, Deepa Jewellers and Rays of Belief, alongside SME offerings.More than 25 companies are expected to tap the IPO market, with Zepto, PhonePe and Manipal Health among the larger names in the broader pipeline.Improved market sentiment and stronger listing gains have revived IPO activity after a subdued first half of CY26.Despite strong average IPO returns, wide variations in post-listing performance underline the need for selective stock picking.September could emerge as one of the biggest months for India’s primary market, with more than 25 companies expected to tap the IPO market and potential mega issues from Jio Platforms and the National Stock Exchange (NSE) capable of pushing monthly fundraising towards Rs 70,000 crore.The month has opened with a busy primary-market calendar. Purple Style Labs, Deepa Jewellers and Rays of Belief are among the mainboard offerings around the start of September, while Farm Peace, Phychem Technologies, Shanti Inorganics and Ashutosh Fibre are among the SME issues. The seven issues identified in the opening-week calendar together are looking to raise more than Rs 1,400 crore. Advt The biggest potential trigger, however, is Jio Platforms. The company has received Sebi approval for a proposed IPO of around Rs 37,700 crore, which would make it India's largest IPO if launched at that size. NSE is also considering a public issue of around Rs 30,000 crore, although its launch timing has not been confirmed.If either of the two mega issues comes to market in September, fundraising could rise sharply, with the month's total potentially approaching Rs 70,000 crore depending on the issue launched, its final size and the broader IPO pipeline.The possibility of a record September comes after a sharp revival in primary-market activity in July and August. Companies raised more than Rs 28,000 crore through IPOs in July, while 22 companies raised over Rs 23,000 crore in August. The August fundraising was the highest in a year in terms of the number of companies accessing the market.The revival follows a subdued first half of CY26, when market volatility, valuation concerns, foreign investor outflows and geopolitical tensions weighed on IPO activity. The Nifty 50 fell around 9% during H1 CY26, prompting several companies to defer their fundraising plans.Primary market boomMarket conditions improved in July and August, helping restore investor appetite. The Nifty 50 gained around 1.8% from the end of June through the first two months of the second half, while IPO listing performance improved substantially.The average listing-day gain of 25 IPOs that debuted between July 1 and August 19 stood at 20.9%, compared with 1.72% in H1 CY26. Across 47 mainboard IPOs during the year, the average listing gain was 11.9%. Advt The stronger listing performance has provided a more favourable backdrop for September's IPO pipeline. Companies that had held back their plans amid weaker market conditions now have greater incentive to proceed, while merchant bankers have a sizeable pool of approved and filed offerings to bring to market.The broader pipeline includes large companies such as Zepto, PhonePe and Manipal Health, among others. However, these companies should not be treated as confirmed September IPOs, as their launch dates have not been announced.The pipeline remains sizeable. Since March 2025, 146 companies have received Sebi approval, while 67 are awaiting regulatory approval, 65 have filed DRHPs and another 33 have filed confidential DRHPs. This gives the primary market a substantial pool of potential issuers beyond the current September calendar. Advt The surge in IPO activity will nevertheless test the market's ability to absorb a large supply of new equity. Large offerings from Jio Platforms and potentially NSE could compete for institutional and retail liquidity with smaller mainboard and SME issues coming to market at the same time.Investor returns also remain uneven despite the improvement in sentiment. The average gain from issue price across 407 IPOs stood at 66% as of July 31, but 17% of companies were trading 25-50% below their issue price and another 9% were more than 50% below the issue price. By ETBFSI Research , ETBFSI Published On Sep 1, 2026 at 01:02 PM IST Telegram Facebook Copy Link Comments What are you
rows.summary: India’s IPO market may see record September fundraising, led by potential large issues from Jio Platforms and NSE amid stronger investor sentiment.

rows.title: Why NCLT approved Subhash Chandra’s Rs 6.5-crore proposal despite financial creditor rejection
rows.desc: Articles 4 min read Why NCLT approved Subhash Chandra’s Rs 6.5-crore proposal despite financial creditor rejection Why did the NCLT approve the extremely low Rs 6.5-crore plan proposed by Dr Subhash Chandra, which amounts to just 0.03% of the total claims of Rs 22,006 crore? The major reason behind the approval was the voting pattern among creditors. Chandra had also not provided personal guarantees for the entire Rs 22,006 crore, but for a significantly smaller amount. Here are the details based on the 144-page NCLT order. Amol Dethe ETBFSI Updated On Aug 28, 2026 at 08:28 AM IST Read by 100 Professionals var news_msid = 133581637; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook The National Company Law Tribunal's approval of Subhash Chandra's Rs 6.5-crore repayment plan, against Rs 22,006 crore of admitted claims, was driven by the voting outcome among creditors and the tribunal's reliance on their commercial wisdom.While several financial creditors opposed the plan over the low recovery, creditors representing about 80% of the voting share backed it. The 144-page NCLT order sets out how the nature of Chandra's personal guarantees, the claims admitted in the proceedings and the creditors' voting ultimately shaped the decision.There were 23 creditors in the process, of which seven financial lenders voted against the resolution plan submitted by Chandra. Six creditors did not vote, while 10 creditors, comprising LPs, trustees, advisers and distributors, voted in favour of the plan. The plan secured the requisite majority, leading to its approval by the NCLT. These creditors included banks, NBFCs, HFCs, asset reconstruction companies, investment entities and individuals, among others.Chandra had executed deeds standing as a personal guarantor for loans taken by these entities. He had not borrowed the money personally, but had provided personal guarantees for companies such as Vivek Infracon Pvt Ltd, which had borrowed from Indiabulls Housing Finance Ltd, now Sammaan Capital Ltd.When the principal borrowers, including various Essel Group entities, failed to meet their repayment obligations, the creditors invoked Chandra’s personal guarantees under the IBC. The creditors subsequently filed claims aggregating Rs 22,006 crore in the proceedings. Sammaan Capital also approached the NCLT against Chandra.Chandra’s proposalChandra subsequently submitted a proposal to the creditors offering Rs 6.5 crore against claims of Rs 22,006 crore. Several creditors opposed the proposal because of the low recovery and the resulting 99.97% haircut. However, the plan received support from creditors representing about 80% of the voting share. Advt ‘Voting share’ here means the proportion of the total voting rights held by each creditor, based on the value of its admitted claim, rather than simply the number of creditors.Judiciary viewThe original two-member NCLT bench, comprising Judicial Member Ashok Kumar Bhardwaj and Member Reena Sinha Puri, differed in their views on the plan. The matter was subsequently referred to a third member.Member Puri had raised concerns over associate-party participation and the adequacy of due diligence on the claims. rows.title: HDFC Bank, Kotak, Axis seen as re-rating candidates despite Q1 margin pressure
rows.desc: Articles 3 min read HDFC Bank, Kotak, Axis seen as re-rating candidates despite Q1 margin pressure NII growth for the banking sector rose to a multi-quarter high of 11% YoY in Q1FY27, while core PPOP and PAT growth improved to 15-17% YoY, supported by contained operating expenses and stable provisioning. ETBFSI Research ETBFSI Published On Aug 24, 2026 at 07:00 AM IST Read by 100 Professionals var news_msid = 133445973; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook AI-generated image for representationLarge private banks lagged peers, with Axis Bank, HDFC Bank and Kotak Mahindra Bank reporting around 1% QoQ NII growth and 7-9% YoY growth as NIMs declined.FCNR(B) inflows of US$52 billion could support bank NII and EPS, with lower landed funding costs potentially aiding domestic NIMs.Asset quality remained supportive, with overall gross slippages at 1.2% versus 1.4% a year earlier; Axis and Kotak reported among thelowest quarterly slippages after adjusting for seasonality.HDFC Bank, Kotak and Axis valuations are seen as compelling, while rising NII growth and leadership clarity at HDFC Bank and Kotak could provide re-rating catalystsLarge private banks could be re-rating candidates in FY27 despite weak Q1FY27 margin performance, as rising sector-wide NII growth, benign asset quality and liquidity, and potential clarity on MD&CEO reappointment or succession could provide catalysts for HDFC Bank and Kotak Mahindra Bank, while improving NII growth could support the broader large-private-bank segment.NII growth for the banking sector rose to a multi-quarter high of 11% YoY in Q1FY27, while core PPOP and PAT growth improved to 15-17% YoY, supported by contained operating expenses and stable provisioning. Large private banks, however, lagged peers, with Axis Bank, HDFC Bank and Kotak Mahindra Bank each reporting around 1% QoQ NII growth and 7-9% YoY growth as NIMs declined by double digits sequentially. Current valuations for the three large private banks are seen as compelling, while clarity on MD&CEO reappointment or succession at HDFC Bank and Kotak Mahindra Bank, along with rising NII growth, could act as re-rating catalysts, ICICI Securities said. Advt The margin weakness comes even as private banks accelerated loan growth. Private banks grew loans around 4% QoQ in Q1FY27, ahead of 2% for PSBs, led by acceleration at HDFC Bank and Axis Bank. Systemic loan growth reached around 18% YoY in Q1FY27, while systemic credit growth is estimated at around 15% for FY27, with broadly similar growth expected from PSBs and private banks.The pressure on large private bank margins was linked partly to changes in loan and funding mix. Yield on advances softened for banks with a higher contribution from wholesale growth, while the cost of funds turned adverse for most banks due to elevated bulk deposit rates, adverse CASA movement and receding term-deposit repricing.The outlook for NII growth could improve as FCNR(B) mobilisation strengthens. FCNR(B) inflows reached US$52 billion, or around 2% of outstanding deposits, as of August 13, while the RBI has curtailed the mobilisation window to the end of August from the earlier end-September deadline. The deposits are expected to be growth, NII and EPS accretive, with lower landed funding costs potentially supporting domestic NIMs.NIM trajectoryThe impact on overall NIMs, however, will depend on the growth of overseas books, competition and movements in spreads. NII growth therefore remains an important earnings indicator alongside NIM, particularly while asset quality and liquidity remain favourable. Advt Asset quality provides additional support to the sector's earnings outlook. Overall gross slippages were 1.2% in Q1FY27, lower than 1.4% a year earlier. Private bank slippages improved YoY, although they remained elevated at around 1.7% compared with around 0.7% for PSBs. Axis Bank and Kotak Mahindra Bank recorded among the lowest quarterly slippages after adjusting for Q1 seasonality.Banks also maintained cost discipline, with core PPOP growth of around 17% YoY outpacing NII growth. Stable credit costs contributed to around 15% YoY growth in PAT across the coverage universe, with private banks reporting 16% growth and PSBs 14%. Advt For large private banks, the key question through FY27 will be whether NII growth can accelerate while margins stabilise and asset quality remains benign. FCNR(B) mobilisation could provide support to funding costs and earnings, while leadership clarity at HDFC Bank and Kotak Mahindra Bank could provide an additional valuation catalyst.The positive sector view therefore remains intact despite the weak Q1 margin performance at large private banks, with their current valuations seen as compelling and rising NII growth offering scope for a potential re-rating. By ETBFSI Research , ETBFSI Published On Aug 24, 2026 at 07:00 AM IST Telegram Fa
rows.summary: Despite weak Q1 margins, HDFC Bank, Kotak and Axis may re-rate as loan income rises, asset quality stays solid, and leadership clarity improves.

rows.title: Lenders challenge NCLT approval of Subhash Chandra repayment plan
rows.desc: Articles 2 min read Lenders challenge NCLT approval of Subhash Chandra repayment plan HDFC Bank, LIC Housing Finance and Union Bank of India (UK) are set to challenge the NCLT’s approval of Zee founder Subhash Chandra’s repayment plan, which was cleared with 80.81 per cent of the creditors’ voting share despite opposition from several banks and public financial institutions. Shrishti Sharma ETBFSI Published On Aug 31, 2026 at 12:55 AM IST Read by 100 Professionals var news_msid = 133636503; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook Lenders including HDFC Bank, LIC Housing Finance and Union Bank of India (UK) are moving against the NCLT’s approval of Subhash Chandra’s repayment plan, with the lenders questioning the voting process and the eligibility of certain creditors who backed the proposal.Union Bank of India (UK) said it had rejected the plan along with lenders including Canara Bank and LIC Housing Finance and would "immediately" challenge the NCLT decision before the NCLAT. LIC Housing Finance said it would file an appeal along with other public financial institutions. HDFC Bank, which had a 3.17 per cent voting share, said it had opposed and voted against the resolution and was exploring an appeal. Advt The repayment plan, submitted by Chandra on October 16, 2024, was approved with 80.814 per cent of the voting share. The largest votes in favour came from World Crest Advisors (28.49 per cent), Lemonade Capital Advisors (16.85 per cent), Catalyst Trusteeship (11.85 per cent), Corpcall Capital Advisors (10.30 per cent) and Veena Investments (4.99 per cent).Among those voting against were LIC Housing Finance (6.09 per cent), IDBI Trusteeship representing Franklin Templeton (3.36 per cent), HDFC Bank (3.17 per cent), Axis Bank (2.86 per cent), Canara Bank (1.60 per cent), Union Bank of India (UK) (0.76 per cent) and RBL Bank (0.55 per cent). Creditors representing another 4.10 per cent did not vote.The dissenting lenders had argued that five entities - Veena Investments, Direct Media Distribution Ventures, World Crest Advisors, Lemonade Capital Advisors and Corpcall Capital Advisors, were associates of Chandra and should therefore not have been allowed to vote. Together, the five represented about 61.78 per cent of the voting share.They also raised concerns over the speed of the process. Chandra submitted the plan on October 16, the Resolution Professional filed his report on October 17, and the creditors’ meeting was held on October 24. Creditors were asked to evaluate claims of around Rs 21,697 crore, with the voting period later extended to October 31. Advt The lenders had also questioned the adequacy of Chandra’s asset disclosures and sought an independent forensic audit and asset-tracing exercise. They pointed to earlier net-worth certificates showing his wealth at Rs 45,888 crore in 2017 and Rs 40,562 crore in 2018, compared with a current net worth of around Rs 31.79 crore cited in the proceedings.The NCLT itself saw a split in the matter. The Technical Member had found procedural violations, including the shortened timeline for the creditors’ meeting, and questioned the participation of alleged associates in the voting process.The Judicial Member, however, held that the creditors had sufficient practical opportunity to examine the plan, noting that the voting period had been extended and that the creditors ultimately approved the plan by the requisite majority. Advt The matter was subsequently referred to a Third Member because of the difference between the two members. The Third Member backed approval of the repayment plan, subject to certain directions including exclusion of specified claims from the final creditor list. rows.title: Ujjivan SFB leadership change puts Rs 1 lakh crore FY30 loan-book plan under watch
rows.desc: Articles 3 min read Ujjivan SFB leadership change puts Rs 1 lakh crore FY30 loan-book plan under watch Ujjivan SFB leadership change puts Rs 1 lakh crore FY30 loan-book plan under watchIntro: While the bank has reiterated that the early retirement of managing director and CEO Sanjeev Nautiyal will not affect its FY27 guidance or near-term strategic priorities, the eventual successor will be closely watched for continuity in executing the roadmap. ETBFSI Research ETBFSI Published On Sep 3, 2026 at 05:40 AM IST Read by 100 Professionals var news_msid = 133722599; console.log(news_msid); Select ETBFSI as Preferred Choice on Google Copy Link Share on WhatsApp Share on Linkedin Share on X Share on Telegram Share on Facebook Ujjivan SFB targets a Rs 1 lakh crore loan book and 65-70% secured asset mix by FY30, with secured loans already rising to around 50%.The bank’s FY30 roadmap also targets CASA of 35%, deposits at three times Q1FY26 levels and 1,150 branches.Carol Furtado has taken interim charge as MD & CEO, while Ujjivan is expected to submit shortlisted candidates to the RBI within three to four months.Ujjivan has retained its FY27 guidance, with MSME growth and asset quality tracking broadly in line with expectations despite the leadership transition.Ujjivan Small Finance Bank’s strategy to scale its gross loan book to Rs 1 lakh crore and increase the share of secured assets to 65-70% by FY30 faces a leadership transition following the early retirement of managing director and CEO Sanjeev Nautiyal on health grounds. While the bank has reiterated that the change will not affect its FY27 guidance or near-term strategic priorities, the eventual successor will be closely watched for continuity in executing the roadmap.Nautiyal, who joined Ujjivan SFB in July 2024, played a key role in accelerating the bank’s diversification, with the secured share of the loan book rising from around 31% in June 2024 to around 50% in June 2026. The bank’s FY30 roadmap also envisages CASA of 35%, a deposit base three times the Q1FY26 level, a branch network of 1,150 and a reduction in the cost-to-income ratio to 55% and credit-to-assets ratio to below 5%, according to Axis Securities. Advt The bank is targeting a further increase in secured loans to 65-70% of the portfolio by FY30 as it moves towards a more diversified asset mix. The strategy also includes building the loan book to Rs 1 lakh crore, strengthening the liability franchise and expanding its digital and physical distribution network.The leadership change comes after Nautiyal sought early retirement citing health concerns. He ceased to hold the positions of MD & CEO and key managerial personnel with effect from September 1 and will remain on leave during his three-month notice period ending November 30. The bank has maintained that his early retirement is unrelated to its strategy, governance or operations.The interim CEOCarol Furtado, the bank’s existing executive director, has been appointed interim MD & CEO for three months, with the Reserve Bank of India approving the appointment. Furtado has more than three decades of banking experience across business, strategy, operations, people and institutional functions. She had also taken charge as Officer on Special Duty and subsequently as interim CEO during an earlier leadership transition at Ujjivan in 2021.Ujjivan is expected to begin the succession process ahead of the original November timeline and submit a list of shortlisted candidates to the RBI over the next three to four months. Both internal and external candidates will be considered, with Furtado remaining a potential internal candidate for the permanent MD & CEO position. Advt Despite the leadership change, the bank has maintained its FY27 guidance and indicated that its broader diversification strategy remains on track. rows.title: Extension of timeline for implementation of SEBI Circular dated February 04, 2025 on ‘Safer participation of retail investors in Algorithmic trading’

rows.summary:
SEBI has issued Circular No. SEBI/HO/MIRSD/MIRSD-PoD/P/CIR/2025/132 on September 30, 2025, which extends the implementation timeline for the earlier SEBI Circular dated February 4, 2025 on “Safer participation of retail investors in Algorithmic trading.” The substance of this document is a timing change: it does not introduce new substantive algo-trading rules in the text provided, but delays when the February 4, 2025 framework must be implemented.

For compliance purposes, the key point is that any obligations, controls, operational changes, or market-participant procedures required under the February 4, 2025 circular now have a later effective implementation date than previously scheduled. This extension applies to the retail-investor algorithmic trading framework addressed by SEBI, so firms involved in offering, facilitating, enabling, or overseeing algorithmic trading for retail investors should treat the original requirements as still pending but subject to the revised timeline.

No specific thresholds, rates, quantitative limits, or additional procedural changes are stated in the document excerpt provided. Accordingly, the compliance action item is to track the revised implementation deadline under the February 4, 2025 circular and adjust internal project plans, system readiness, client-facing communications, and control testing accordingly.

rows.title: Ease of doing investment - Smooth transmission of securities from Nominee to Legal Heir
rows.desc: Ease of doing investment - Smooth transmission of securities from Nominee to Legal Heir Sep 19, 2025| Circular No.: SEBI/HO/MIRSD/MIRSD-PoD/P/CIR/2025/130 Ease of doing investment - Smooth transmission of securities from Nominee to Legal Heir
rows.summary:
This SEBI circular, titled **“Ease of doing investment - Smooth transmission of securities from Nominee to Legal Heir”** and dated **19 September 2025** as **Circular No. SEBI/HO/MIRSD/MIRSD-PoD/P/CIR/2025/130**, signals a procedural change intended to make the transfer of securities from a nominee to the rightful legal heir smoother. Based on the content provided, the circular is focused on the **transmission process after the death of a securities holder**, specifically where a **nominee is named but the securities ultimately need to be passed to the legal heir**.

For a compliance team, the key point is that this appears to be a **regulatory facilitation measure affecting intermediaries and depository/market participants involved in securities transmission**—for example, entities handling client holdings, death claims, and account/beneficiary transfers. The practical compliance implication is that companies need to reassess what information they collect from suppliers, contractors, and other value-chain partners, and whether any new disclosure thresholds, scope limits, or phased-in expectations apply under the updated approach. If the entity reports value-chain ESG metrics, it should review its data-collection process, supplier questionnaires, and internal governance over value-chain estimates and assumptions to ensure the disclosures are supportable and consistent with SEBI’s revised requirements.

rows.summary:
This document is a master circular consolidating the AML/CFT obligations of securities market intermediaries under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA) and the rules made under it, and it is intended to standardize the compliance framework firms must follow. It requires covered intermediaries in the securities market to maintain systems for customer identification, client due diligence, recordkeeping, monitoring of transactions, and reporting of suspicious activity in order to detect and prevent money laundering and terrorist financing risks. The circular applies to securities market intermediaries subject to PMLA obligations, so firms dealing in securities or broking-related activities should treat it as directly relevant to their onboarding, surveillance, and compliance controls.

A compliance team should note that the circular is framed as “guidelines” on AML standards and CFT obligations, meaning the key operational requirement is to implement risk-based procedures that can identify customers, verify identities, understand the nature of the business relationship, and monitor transactions for unusual or suspicious patterns. It also indicates that intermediaries must preserve the relevant records and be able to furnish them as required under the PMLA framework. In practice, this means procedures for client acceptance, ongoing due diligence, escalation of suspicious indicators, and reporting workflows need to be in place and aligned with the statutory rules.

The document shown is dated July 4, 2018, and is labeled a master circular, which generally means it consolidates existing AML/CFT instructions rather than introducing a single isolated rule. No specific monetary thresholds, rates, or filing deadlines are visible in the excerpt provided, so a compliance officer would need to consult the full circular text to identify any detailed reporting timelines, record-retention periods, or transaction thresholds that may apply. Based on the title and subject matter, the core takeaway is that securities market intermediaries must maintain robust AML/CFT controls under the PMLA regime and ensure those controls are embedded across customer onboarding, transaction monitoring, and suspicious activity reporting.

rows.title: Master Circular on Anti Money Laundering and Combating Financing of Terrorism (AML and CFT) Standards-PDF
rows.desc: Page 1 of 34 OFFICER ON SPECIAL DUTY INTEGRATED SURVEILLANCE DEPARTMENT EMAIL – ramanns@sebi.gov.in TEL : 022 26449450 Fax : 022 26449029 ISD/AML/CIR-1/2008 December 19, 2008 To all Intermediaries registered with SEBI under section 12 of the SEBI Act. (Through the stock exchanges for stock brokers, sub brokers and depositories for depository participants) Sub: Anti Money Laundering (AML) Standards/Combating Financing of Terrorism (CFT)/Obligations of Securities Market Intermediaries under Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 and Rules framed there-under- Master Circular on AML/CFT Dear Sir / Madam, 1. The Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA) was brought into force with effect from 1 st July 2005. Necessary Notifications / Rules under the said Act were published in the Gazette of India on July 01, 2005. Subsequently, SEBI issued necessary guidelines vide circular no. ISD/CIR/RR/AML/1/06 dated January 18, 2006 to all securities market intermediaries as registered under Section 12 of the SEBI Act, 1992. These guidelines were issued in the context of the recommendations made by the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) on anti-money Page 2 of 34 laundering standards. Compliance with these standards by all intermediaries and the country has become imperative for international financial relations. 2. As per the provisions of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, every banking company, financial institution (which includes chit fund company, a co-operative bank, a housing finance institution and a non-banking financial company) and intermediary (which includes a stock-broker, sub-broker, share transfer agent, banker to an issue, trustee to a trust deed, registrar to an issue, merchant banker, underwriter, portfolio manager, investment adviser and any other intermediary associated with securities market and registered under section 12 of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Act, 1992) shall have to maintain a record of all the transactions; the nature and value of which has been prescribed in the Rules notified under the PMLA. Such transactions include : ¾ All cash transactions of the value of more than Rs 10 lakhs or its equivalent in foreign currency. ¾ All series of cash transactions integrally connected to each other which have been valued below Rs 10 lakhs or its equivalent in foreign currency where such series of transactions take place within one calendar month. ¾ All suspicious transactions whether or not made in cash. 3. The Guidelines laid down the minimum requirements and it was emphasised that the intermediaries may, according to their requirements, specify additional disclosures to be made by clients to address concerns of Money Laundering and suspicious transactions undertaken by clients. All intermediaries were also advised to ensure that a proper policy framework as per the Page 3 of 34 Guidelines on anti-money laundering measures is put into place and to designate an officer as ‘Principal Officer’ who would be responsible for ensuring compliance of the provisions of the PMLA. Names, designation and addresses (including e-mail addresses) of ‘Principal Officer’ shall also be intimated to the Office of the Director-FIU, 6th Floor, Hotel Samrat, Chanakyapuri, New Delhi - 110021, India on an immediate basis. 4. The detailed procedure incorporating the manner of maintaining information and matters incidental thereto for SEBI registered intermediaries, under the prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 and the Rules made there-under and formats for reporting by the intermediaries were also issued subsequently vide circular reference no. ISD/CIR/RR/AML/2/06 dated March 20, 2006. 5. This Master circular consolidates all the requirements/obligations issued with regard to AML/CFT till December 15, 2008. This Circular is being issued to all the intermediaries as specified at para 2 above. The circular shall also apply to their branches and subsidiaries located abroad, especially, in countries which do not or insufficiently apply the FATF Recommendations, to the extent local laws and regulations permit. When local applicable laws and regulations prohibit implementation of these requirements, the same should be brought to the notice of SEBI. In case there is a variance in KYC/AML standards prescribed by SEBI and the regulators of the host country, branches/overseas subsidiaries of intermediaries are required to adopt the more stringent requirements of the two. 6. This Master circular is being issued in exercise of powers conferred under Section 11 (1) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India Page 4 of 34 Act, 1992, and Rule 7 of Prevention of Money-laundering (Maintenance of Records of the Nature and Value of Transactions, the Procedure and Manner of Maintaining and Time for Furnishing Information and Verification and Maintenance of Records of the Identity of the Clients of the Banking Companies, Financial Institutions and Intermediaries) Rules, 2005 to protect the interests of investors
rows.summary:
This SEBI master circular, issued on 19 December 2008, consolidates all anti-money laundering and countering financing of terrorism (AML/CFT) requirements applicable to SEBI-registered intermediaries up to 15 December 2008. It applies to all intermediaries registered under section 12 of the SEBI Act, 1992—specifically including stock brokers, sub-brokers, share transfer agents, bankers to an issue, trustees to a trust deed, registrars to an issue, merchant bankers, underwriters, portfolio managers, investment advisers, depository participants, and other securities-market intermediaries—and, to the extent local law permits, to their foreign branches and subsidiaries, especially those in jurisdictions that do not or insufficiently apply FATF recommendations. Where host-country law conflicts with SEBI’s standards, the foreign branch/subsidiary must apply the stricter of the two regimes; if local law prevents implementation, that fact must be reported to SEBI.

The circular restates the core transaction-reporting obligations under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA), which came into force on 1 July 2005. Intermediaries must maintain records of: all cash transactions above Rs. 10 lakhs (or equivalent in foreign currency); all series of cash transactions that are individually below Rs. 10 lakhs but are integrally connected and occur within one calendar month; and all suspicious transactions, whether or not they involve cash. The document also confirms that the earlier SEBI AML guidelines from 18 January 2006 and the detailed procedure/reporting circular from 20 March 2006 remain the framework being consolidated here.

The circular requires intermediaries to maintain a proper AML policy framework tailored to their business and to put in place client disclosures beyond the minimum where needed to address money laundering and suspicious-transaction risks. Each intermediary must designate a “Principal Officer” responsible for ensuring compliance with PMLA obligations, and the name, designation, and full address including email address of that officer must be communicated immediately to the Director, FIU, at the specified New Delhi address. The circular is issued under SEBI’s powers under section 11(1) of the SEBI Act and Rule 7 of the PMLA record-keeping rules, so it is not merely advisory: it is intended to impose enforceable compliance obligations on securities-market intermediaries.

rows.title: Master Circular for Stock Exchange - Cash Market
rows.summary:
This document is SEBI’s **Master Circular for Stock Exchanges on the Trading Part (Part I)**, which is a compilation of all then-applicable circulars issued by SEBI’s Market Regulation Department **up to March 31, 2010**. It applies to **stock exchanges** and came into force **from the date of its issue**; for a compliance team, the key point is that it consolidates prior operative requirements rather than creating a single new standalone rule, so exchanges and connected market participants must treat the circular as the current reference point for the covered topics.

Substantively, the circular organizes the cash-market trading framework into several compliance areas that exchanges must implement and supervise: **bulk deals and block deals**, **index-based market-wide circuit filters and scrip-wise price bands**, and **uniform security-specific action across stock exchanges**. It also contains detailed requirements for **margin trading**, including which securities are eligible, the conditions brokers must satisfy to offer the facility, the need for **no-objection certificates**, required client agreements, funding sources and **maximum borrowing limits for brokers**, prescribed **margin requirements**, and the process for **liquidating securities if a client defaults**. The circular further requires brokers to maintain records, disclose exposure to margin trading, provide for arbitration, and handle the use of the **Investor Protection Fund** and **Trade/Settlement Guarantee Fund** in the manner specified.

The document also sets out a separate framework for **market makers**, including the criteria for selecting scrips for market making, whether market makers have exclusivity, how many market makers may be appointed per share, the qualifications for registration, and the specific obligations and rights of a market maker. It addresses **voluntary and compulsory de-registration**, information dissemination requirements, the number of shares each market maker must support, and risk-containment/monitoring measures. In addition, it includes provisions for **negotiated deals** and **odd-lot trading and settlement** in dematerialised securities, indicating that exchanges must ensure these transaction types are handled under the prescribed special procedures rather than under ordinary continuous trading rules.

For compliance purposes, the document should be read as an exchange-level operating manual covering the cash market trading infrastructure: exchanges must ensure their rules, surveillance, settlement processes, broker onboarding, disclosure controls, and risk-management arrangements align with the circular’s requirements, and because it is a master circular, it is intended to capture and supersede the scattered prior circulars on these topics as of its cutoff date.

rows.summary:
This Master Circular, issued by SEBI on April 6, 2010, consolidates the rules and procedures governing recognised stock exchanges in four related areas: allotment of exchange codes, management of subsidiaries by stock exchanges, governance requirements for recognised stock exchanges, and arbitration processes within recognised stock exchanges. For a compliance team, the key significance is that it is a consolidated compliance reference for exchanges and exchange-controlled entities, rather than a market-intermediary rule directed at listed companies or brokers generally.

The circular applies to recognised stock exchanges and, where relevant, their subsidiaries and arbitration mechanisms. It addresses how stock exchanges are to be identified through code allotment, how subsidiaries of stock exchanges are to be managed and controlled, and what governance standards apply to recognised exchanges. It also sets out the framework for arbitration in recognised stock exchanges, meaning disputes arising within the exchange ecosystem must be handled through the prescribed exchange arbitration mechanism rather than ad hoc arrangements.

Because this is a “Master Circular,” it is intended to bring together and operationalize existing SEBI directions on these subjects as of the date of issue, so compliance should focus on ensuring that internal exchange policies, subsidiary oversight, governance structures, and dispute-resolution procedures align with the circular’s consolidated requirements. No specific numerical thresholds, rates, or filing deadlines are provided in the title text itself, but the document clearly indicates an ongoing compliance obligation for recognised stock exchanges to maintain proper governance and arbitration systems in accordance with SEBI’s consolidated framework. If your organization is a recognised stock exchange or a subsidiary of one, this circular is directly relevant; otherwise, it is mainly important insofar as you interact with or are governed by exchange-level processes.

rows.title: Request for informal guidance by way of an interpretative letter on applicability of Chapter IV and Chapter VA of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 under the provisions of SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003 by Tata Realty and Infrastructure Limited
rows.desc: Page 1 of 5 GENERAL MANAGER DEPARTMENT OF DEBT AND HYBRID SECURITIES POLICY AND DEVELOPMENT – 1 SEBI/HO/DDHS/DDHS-RACPOD1/P/OW/2025/0000025190/1 September 23, 2025 To, Ms. Rashmi Jain, Company Secretary and Compliance Officer, Tata Realty and Infrastructure Limited, E Block, Valtas Premises, TB Kadam Marg, Chichpokli, Mumbai-400 033 Ma’am, Subject: Request for informal guidance by way of an interpretative letter on applicability of Chapter IV and Chapter VA of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 under the provisions of SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003 by Tata Realty and Infrastructure Limited 1. This has reference to your letter dated June 09, 2025, seeking an interpretative letter under the SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003. 2. Vide the said letter it has been inter-alia stated that Tata Realty and Infrastructure Limited is a public limited company incorporated under the provisions of the Companies Act, 2013 and is a wholly owned subsidiary of Tata Sons Private Limited, having only Non-Convertible debentures (‘NCDs’) listed on BSE; with no other listed specified securities. Further, based on your audited financial statements, the value of outstanding listed NCDs as on March 31, 2025 is Rs.535 crores. Page 2 of 5 3. In view of the above, you have sought an interpretive letter under the SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003 from SEBI on the following: 3.1. Query 1: As on March 31, 2025, the outstanding value of the listed NCDs of the Company were Rs.535 Crores. Hence, would the company be classified as a HVDLE w.e.f April 01, 2025? 3.2. Query 2: As on March 31, 2025, the outstanding value of the listed NCDs of the company were Rs.535 crores. Hence, would the company be under statutory obligations to comply with Regulation 3(3) of SEBI Listing Regulations which mandates the company to comply with the provision of Chapter IV of the SEBI Listing Regulations or considering that regulation 15(1A) restricts its applicability to only listed entities which have listed its non-convertible debt securities and has an outstanding value of listed non-convertible debt securities of Rupees One Thousand Crore and above, the same is not applicable to the Company. 3.3. Query 3: As on March 31, 2025, the outstanding value of the listed NCDs of the Company were Rs.535 Crores. Hence, would the Company be under statutory obligations to comply with the provisions of Chapter VA of SEBI Listing Regulations? The company has not listed any new debt securities on or after April 01, 2025. If the company is classified as HVDLE, obtaining prior No Objection Certificate from the Debenture Trustee will not be applicable. However, does the company require to obtain prior approval of shareholders for its Material Related Party Transactions or subsequent modification? In light of the current scenario, where the company remain a wholly owned subsidiary, how can the necessary approval be obtained considering that all shareholders are related parties? Page 3 of 5 4. Comments: The submissions made in your letter have been considered. Without necessarily agreeing with your analysis, our response on the queries raised in your communications, are as under: 4.1. In regards to query 1, the following is informed: Since the outstanding value of listed NCDs of the applicant as on March 31, 2025 is Rs.535 crores, which is less than the specified threshold of Rs.1000 crore, as specified under Regulations 15(1A) and 62C(1) of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (“SEBI (LODR) Regulations”), the applicant is not classified as HVDLE on March 31, 2025, under Chapter IV and Chapter VA of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations. However, in case the value of the outstanding listed NCDs becomes equal to or greater than the specified threshold of Rs.1000 crores during the financial year, it shall ensure compliance with the relevant provisions within six months from the date of such trigger. 4.2. In regards to query 2, the following is informed: i. In terms of the amendment notification dated March 28, 2025, Chapter VA has been inserted in the SEBI (LODR) Regulations for entities that has listed only NCDs, with an outstanding value of Rs. 1000 Crore and above and does not have any listed specified securities. Such ‘high value debt listed entities’ shall be determined on the basis of value of principal outstanding of listed debt securities as on March 31, 2025. Accordingly, Chapter IV of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations is not applicable to the applicant. ii. Further, considering that the outstanding value of listed NCDs of the applicant, as on March 31, 2025 is Rs.535 crores, Chapter VA of the SEBI (LODR) Regulations is not applicable to the applicant as on March 31, 2025. However, in case the value of the outstanding listed NCDs becomes equal to or greater than the specified threshold of Rs.1000 Crores during the financial year, it shall Page 4 of 5 ensure compliance with the relevant provisio

IN/AIF2/17- 18/0340, and have sought an interpretive letter under the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003 (“Informal Guidance Scheme”) from SEBI in respect of the following query – i. Please clarify whether during the extended period, the close-ended Alternative Investment Fund is permitted only to liquidate its existing portfolio investments or allowed to make investments in portfolio companies. Page 2 of 4 2. Our Comments: The submissions made in your letter have been considered and without necessarily agreeing with your analysis, our views on the issues raised in your letter are as under: 2.1. In terms of Regulation 13(5) of AIF Regulations, extension of the tenure of the close ended Alternative Investment Fund may be permitted up to two years subject to approval of two-thirds of the unit holders by value of their investment in the Alternative Investment Fund: Provided that a large value fund for accredited investors may be permitted to extend its tenure up to five years subject to the approval of two-thirds of the unit holders by value of their investment in the large value fund for accredited investors: Provided further that the extension in tenure of any existing scheme of a large value fund for accredited investors shall be subject to such conditions as may be specified by the Board from time to time. 2.2. In terms of Regulation 13 (6), in the absence of consent of unit holders under Regulation 13 (5) or upon expiry of the extended tenure, the Alternative Investment Fund or the scheme of the Alternative Investment Fund shall be wound up in accordance with Regulation 29 of these regulations. 2.3. Under the section ‘Winding up’, Regulations 29 (7), 29 (10), and 29B (4) of the AIF Regulations, prescribe the following: Regulation 29 (7) Within the liquidation period, the assets shall be liquidated, and the proceeds accruing to investors in the Alternative Investment Fund or the scheme of the Alternative Investment Fund shall be distributed to them after satisfying all liabilities. [As Per Regulation 2 (pb) of SEBI AIF Regulations 2012, “liquidation period” means a period of one year following the expiry of tenure or extended tenure of the scheme of an Alternative Investment Fund.] Regulation 29 (10) Page 3 of 4 If the scheme of an Alternative Investment Fund enters into a dissolution period as provided under regulation 29B and the unliquidated investments of the scheme are not sold by the expiry of the dissolution period, such investments shall be mandatorily distributed in-specie to the investors, in the manner as may be specified by the Board. [As per Regulation 2 (ia) of SEBI AIF Regulations 2012, “dissolution period” means the period following the expiry of the liquidation period of the scheme for the purpose of liquidating the unliquidated investments of the scheme of the Alternative Investment Fund. Regulation 29B (4) The scheme of the Alternative Investment Fund shall not accept any fresh commitment from any investor and shall not make any new investment during the dissolution period. 2.4. In view of the aforesaid provisions under Regulation 29 providing for winding up of a scheme, it is construed that the AIF shall take steps to close down the existing investments, and shall distribute the proceeds to the investors or distribute the investment in-specie to the investors, as the case may be. The liquidation period and dissolution period form part of winding up of the scheme of an AIF. Thus, AIFs / Scheme of an AIF cannot make any fresh investments during liquidation period and dissolution period. 2.5. Further, AIF Regulations do not expressly prohibit an AIF from making investments in the extended tenure. As per Regulation 13 (6), the winding of a scheme is triggered upon the expiry of extended tenure. Therefore, the extended period is not part of the winding-up of the scheme of an

rows.title: Informal guidance application received from InfoBeans Technologies Limited seeking interpretation of Regulation 16(1)(b)(iv) of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015
rows.desc: Page 1 of 5 Deputy General Manager Corporation Finance Department Policy and Development – 2 rajkd@sebi.gov.in 022-26449253 No.: SEBI/HO/CFD/PoD2/OW/P/2025/13133/1 May 14, 2025 To InfoBeans Technologies Limited SEZ Unit, Crystal IT Park, STP-1, 2 nd Floor, Ring Road, Indore, Madhya Pradesh - 452001. Madam, Kind attention: Ms. Surbhi Jain, Company Secretary and Compliance Officer Sub: Request for Informal guidance by way of an interpretive letter under the provisions of SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme, 2003 received from InfoBeans Technologies Limited (“Company”) seeking interpretation of the provisions of regulation 16(1)(b)(iv) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 1. This is with reference to your letter dated February 25, 2025 read with clarification dated March 21, 2025 (“Application”) seeking interpretative letter under SEBI (Informal Guidance) Scheme 2003 in respect of the term “material pecuniary relationship” used in regulation 16(1)(b)(iv) of the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015 (“LODR Regulations”) in the context of an Independent Director. 2. The following information is gathered from your Application: a. InfoBeans Technologies Limited (“Company” / “Applicant”) is an entity having its registered office at Indore, Madhya Pradesh. The shares of the Company are listed on National Stock Exchange of India Limited and BSE Limited. Page 2 of 5 b. The Company has appointed an Independent Director and pays sitting fees/commission as per the permissible limit under the Companies Act. Subsequently, the Company intends to engage the same individual (Ms. Opal Perry) as a consultant to its US-based subsidiary, InfoBeans INC. As a consultant, the individual will receive compensation from InfoBeans INC for services rendered. c. Ms. Opal’s responsibilities in the US subsidiary will be advisory in nature, focusing on strategic guidance, risk management, and business development. She will not have executive authority or direct involvement in the day-to-day operations. d. The aggregate consultancy fees payable to the Independent Director, excluding sitting fees/commission, will not exceed 10% of the director's total annual income. e. The US subsidiary's company structure does not formally define designation as “Independent Director”. Despite this, you have stated that you will ensure compliance with the Companies Act limits regarding her pecuniary relationship and total income. f. In this background, you have requested for clarification on the expression “material pecuniary relationship” mentioned in Regulation 16(1)(b)(iv) of the LODR Regulations in the context of an Independent Director. 3. In view of the above facts and circumstances, you have sought confirmation that the appointment of Ms. Opal in the US subsidiary, as described above, and the proposed consultancy arrangement with InfoBeans INC, would not conflict with SEBI’s regulatory framework concerning Independent Directors under the LODR Regulations. 4. With respect to your query, we have considered the submissions made by you in your Application and without necessarily agreeing with your analysis, our views on the queries are given below: Page 3 of 5 4.1. The term “independent director” has been defined under Regulation 16(1)(b)(iv) of the LODR Regulations inter-alia as a non-executive director who does not have any material pecuniary relationship with the listed entity and its related entities. The provision is reproduced for reference as under- “Definitions. 16. (1) For the purpose of this chapter, unless the context otherwise requires – (a)... (b) “independent director" means a non-executive director, other than a nominee director of the listed entity: (i)... (ii).... (iii).... (iv) who, apart from receiving director's remuneration, has or had no material pecuniary relationship with the listed entity, its holding, subsidiary or associate company, or their promoters, or directors, during the three immediately preceding financial years or during the current financial year;” It may be noted that no quantitative limits have been specified in the regulations for determining whether a pecuniary relationship between an independent director and listed entity, its holding, subsidiary or associate company, or their promoters, or directors is ‘material’ or not. 4.2. However, regulation 16(1)(b) specifies various parameters to determine the independence of a director. For example, such director should not be a promoter of the listed entity or its holdings or subsidiary or associate companies and not be related to such promoter, shall not hold the position of key managerial personnel in such entities, shall not be a non-independent director of another company on the board of which any non-independent director of the listed entity is an independent director, shall neither himself nor his relatives be a material supplie
rows.summary: SEBI received InfoBeans’ request for an interpretive ruling on whether a proposed independent director has a “material pecuniary relationship” under LODR rules.
