rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Urban Co-operative Banks (Voluntary Amalgamation) Directions, 2025** apply **with immediate effect** to **all Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs)**, meaning **Primary Co-operative Banks** as defined under section 5(ccv) read with section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949. The directions govern **voluntary amalgamation of two or more UCBs** and define the key parties: the **“amalgamated entity”** is the bank transferring its business, and the **“amalgamating entity”** is the bank acquiring that business under the scheme. RBI states it will consider only proposals where the acquiring UCB commits to **protecting all depositors of the amalgamated UCB**, regardless of whether the amalgamated bank has a **positive or negative net worth**; if the net worth is negative, this protection must be provided either by the amalgamating UCB itself or **with upfront financial support from the State Government** as part of the amalgamation process. RBI will also only consider proposals where the **post-amalgamation CRAR** of the amalgamating UCB meets the **minimum regulatory requirement prescribed by RBI**.

At the governance stage, the decision to amalgamate must be approved by a **two-thirds majority of the total number of board members** of **both** the amalgamating and amalgamated UCBs; this is explicitly **not** limited to two-thirds of those present and voting. When boards consider the proposal, they must especially assess matters such as whether a due diligence exercise has been carried out and other prudential, financial, and operational considerations relevant to the merger. The directions then require **shareholder approval** and subsequent **RBI approval** before the amalgamation can proceed, and the RBI may sanction the scheme only after reviewing the proposal against the conditions set out in the directions.

The document also establishes a framework for the **sanction of the scheme of amalgamation** and for the **entitlement of dissenting shareholders**, meaning there is a formal process for handling shareholders who do not agree with the merger and determining their rights/consideration under the scheme. It further states that the directions **repeal and supersede earlier RBI directions on the subject to the extent of inconsistency**, while preserving actions already taken under the earlier framework. The directions also clarify that they do **not bar the application of other laws** where relevant, and that undefined terms will be interpreted using the RBI Act, the Banking Regulation Act, RBI’s Glossary of Terms, or ordinary commercial usage as appropriate.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Licensing, Scheduling and Regulatory Classification) Guidelines, 2025
rows.desc: DOR/2025-26/269 December 04, 2025 Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks – Licensing, Scheduling and Regulatory Classification) Guidelines, 2025 A. Licensing of Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) 1. No fresh proposals for organization of new UCBs or for conversion of co- operative credit societies into UCBs are being considered by Reserve Bank of India. In this context, Urban Co-operative Banks shall mean Primary Co-operative Banks as defined under section 5(ccv) read with Section 56 of Banking Regulation Act, 1949. B. Categorization of UCBs for Regulatory Purposes 2. Given the heterogeneity in the urban cooperative sector, a four-tiered regulatory framework has been adopted to balance the spirit of mutuality and cooperation more prevalent in banks of smaller sizes and those with limited area of operation vis-à-vis the growth ambitions of the large-sized UCBs to spread their area of operation and undertake more complex business activities. Accordingly, the UCBs are categorized into the following four tiers for regulatory purposes: (1) Tier 1 - All unit UCBs and salary earners' UCBs (irrespective of deposit size), and all other UCBs having deposits up to ₹100 crore; (2) Tier 2 - UCBs with deposits of more than ₹100 crore and up to ₹1000 crore; (3) Tier 3 - UCBs with deposits of more than ₹1000 crore and up to ₹10,000 crore; (4) Tier 4 - UCBs with deposits of more than ₹10,000 crore. 3. The deposits referred to above shall be reckoned as per the audited balance sheet as of 31 st March of the immediately preceding financial year. 2 4. If a UCB transits to a higher Tier on account of an increase in deposits in any year, it can use a glide path of up to a maximum of two years (financial year in which the threshold was crossed and the succeeding financial year) to comply with higher regulatory requirements, if any, of the transited higher Tier. C. Second Schedule to the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 - Norms for inclusion 5. In terms of clause (a) of sub-section (6) of section 42 of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 and the Government of India notification F.No.3/16/2023-AC dated September 04, 2023 (published in Gazette of India on September 23, 2023), the licensed UCBs (except Salary Earners’ Banks), which are in compliance with Eligibility Criteria for Business Authorisation (as defined in Reserve Bank of India (Urban Cooperative Banks – Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025) and the following additional norms, may apply to the Regional Office concerned of the Reserve Bank for inclusion in the Second Schedule to the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934: (1) Maintenance of minimum deposits required for categorisation as a Tier 3 UCB for two consecutive years by a UCB; (2) CRAR of at least three per cent more than the minimum CRAR requirement applicable to the bank; and (3) No major regulatory and supervisory concerns. 6. The above information shall be based on the assessed financials and findings of the RBI inspection report or audited financial statements, whichever is the latest. An eligible UCB shall submit its application with the following documents: (1) Copy of the resolution passed by the Annual General Body / Board of Directors to make an application to RBI for inclusion in the Second Schedule to the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 and containing the name(s) of bank official(s) authorized to correspond with RBI in this regard; and (2) Major financial details of the bank together with copies of the published balance sheet for the last three years.
rows.summary:
The RBI’s 2025 guidelines state that it is **not considering any fresh proposals** to organize new Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) or to convert co-operative credit societies into UCBs. For these purposes, “Urban Co-operative Banks” are defined as **Primary Co-operative Banks** under section 5(ccv) read with section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949.

The guidelines replace a one-size-fits-all approach with a **four-tier regulatory framework** based on deposit size and bank type. **Tier 1** covers all unit UCBs and salary earners’ UCBs regardless of size, plus all other UCBs with deposits of **up to ₹100 crore**. **Tier 2** covers UCBs with deposits of **more than ₹100 crore and up to ₹1,000 crore**. **Tier 3** covers deposits of **more than ₹1,000 crore and up to ₹10,000 crore**, and **Tier 4** covers UCBs with deposits of **more than ₹10,000 crore**. Deposits are to be measured using the **audited balance sheet as of 31 March of the immediately preceding financial year**. If a bank crosses into a higher tier because deposits increase, it is allowed a **glide path of up to two years**—the financial year in which the threshold is crossed and the following financial year—to meet any higher regulatory requirements of the new tier.

For inclusion in the **Second Schedule to the RBI Act, 1934**, licensed UCBs (other than **Salary Earners’ Banks**) may apply to the RBI’s Regional Office if they satisfy the RBI’s business authorisation eligibility criteria and three additional conditions. First, the bank must have maintained the **minimum deposits required for Tier 3 status for two consecutive years**. Second, its **CRAR** must be at least **3 percentage points higher than the minimum CRAR requirement applicable to that bank**. Third, the bank must have **no major regulatory or supervisory concerns**. The assessment must be based on the **latest** of the RBI inspection findings or the audited financial statements, and the application must include a **board/AGM resolution** authorizing the application and naming the officer(s) who may correspond with RBI, as well as **major financial details** and copies of the **published balance sheets for the last three years**.

From a compliance perspective, the document affects existing UCBs’ classification, capital planning, and schedule-inclusion readiness, but it does **not** open the door to new bank licensing or credit-society conversions. Firms operating or advising UCBs should verify current tier placement using the prior year’s audited 31 March balance sheet, monitor for threshold crossings, and, if applicable, track the two-year transition period for meeting more stringent requirements. They should also assess whether a bank is positioning for Second Schedule inclusion, particularly ensuring the Tier 3 deposit history, CRAR buffer, and supervisory-clean status are documented before any application is submitted.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Urban Co-operative Banks - Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s 2025 Directions on Urban Co-operative Banks (UCBs) branch authorisation consolidate and replace the RBI’s existing branch-opening framework for UCBs, with effect from **December 04, 2025** (the date of the directions). They apply to **urban co-operative banks** and govern when and how they may open, shift, close, or operationalise places of business, including branches, extension counters, ATMs/CDMs/CRMs, as well as how they may use **Business Facilitators (BFs)** and **Business Correspondents (BCs)** and provide doorstep banking. The directions also establish reporting obligations through RBI’s **Central Information System for Banking Infrastructure (CISBI)** and expressly repeal the earlier branch-authorisation directions, while preserving actions already taken under the old framework and making clear that other applicable laws are not displaced.

A key governance requirement is that each UCB’s **Board of Directors must approve and periodically review** policies governing branch authorisation and related operational matters; the board is responsible for ensuring the bank complies with the RBI’s eligibility and procedural conditions before opening or relocating offices. The directions structure branch expansion around RBI-defined **Eligibility Criteria for Business Authorization (ECBA)** and the bank’s **area of operation**, meaning a bank cannot simply open a branch wherever it wants without first satisfying the relevant geographic and business parameters. UCBs must also follow specific RBI procedures for opening a **new place of business**, for selecting the route for opening a branch either under the **automatic route** or the **prior approval route**, and for opening an **extension counter** or operationalising an **ATM/CDM/CRM**. Likewise, there are separate compliance steps for **shifting a place of business**, **closing a place of business**, and dealing with **leased premises** where the bank does not comply with **section 11(1) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (as applicable to co-operative societies/AACS)**.

The directions also permit UCBs to engage third parties under two distinct outsourcing-style models: the **BF model** and the **BC model**. Only entities that meet the RBI’s eligibility requirements may be appointed, and the scope of activities is limited to the activities specifically permitted by the directions and the bank’s approved arrangements. The BC/BF framework includes detailed conditions on appointment, oversight, responsibility allocation, and operational controls, so a bank using these models must ensure written contractual arrangements, internal monitoring, and compliance with the RBI’s prescribed activity boundaries and risk-management expectations. Separate provisions also govern **doorstep banking**, indicating that UCBs offering such services must do so only within the operational framework set out by the RBI, rather than on ad hoc terms.

Finally, the directions require UCBs to submit **bank/branch information in the prescribed proforma through CISBI**, which creates an ongoing regulatory reporting obligation tied to branch authorisation status and infrastructure details. Because the document is a comprehensive replacement framework, compliance officers should treat it as controlling for all branch expansion, relocation, closure, outsourced banking-channel engagement, and infrastructure reporting decisions made **from December 04, 2025 onward**, while also verifying whether any existing branch-related arrangements need to be brought into conformity with the new procedures, board approvals, and reporting templates.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks - Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Rural Co-operative Banks (Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025** were issued under **Section 23 read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949** and take **immediate effect on December 04, 2025**. They apply to **Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs)**, meaning **State Co-operative Banks (StCBs)** and **Central Co-operative Banks (CCBs)** as defined under the **NABARD Act, 1981**. Although the excerpt provided ends in the definitions section, the table of contents shows that the directions comprehensively regulate **branch authorisation, extension counters, ATMs/CDMs/CRMs, shifting or closure of business locations, doorstep banking, and reporting through the Central Information System for Banking Infrastructure (CISBI)**, replacing prior instructions through a repeal-and-savings framework.

From the structure of the document, the new framework is organized around **eligibility criteria for business authorization (ECBA)** and the **area of operation of District Central Co-operative Banks (DCCBs)**, followed by detailed rules for opening new places of business. It distinguishes between a **branch opened under the automatic route** and one opened under a **prior approval route**, which indicates that some branch openings may proceed without case-by-case RBI approval if the bank satisfies the prescribed conditions, while others require RBI permission in advance. The directions also impose **additional conditions on StCBs** for opening branches, and separately regulate the opening and operation of **extension counters**, **ATMs/CDMs/CRMs**, and the **shifting of a place of business**, which suggests compliance obligations not only at branch-inception but also for subsequent changes to the network. The inclusion of a dedicated provision on **closure of a place of business** and **doorstep banking services** indicates that the RBI is also controlling service continuity and customer access, not just physical branch count.

A notable compliance point is the separate chapter on **reporting**, which requires banks to use a **proforma** and submit branch and bank details under **CISBI**, meaning branch authorization decisions and branch network changes are expected to be captured in the RBI’s central infrastructure reporting system. The document also anticipates situations where a co-operative bank **does not comply with Section 11(1) of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 (as applicable to co-operative societies)**, and contains special rules for **shifting, acquisition, surrender of leased premises, etc.** in those cases, implying enhanced restrictions or procedural safeguards for banks with capitalization/regulatory deficiencies. Finally, the directions preserve the application of other laws and include an interpretation clause, so compliance teams should treat these directions as operating alongside, not instead of, other banking and co-operative law requirements.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Rural Co-operative Banks – Miscellaneous Directions, 2025** (dated **December 4, 2025**, circular reference **DOR/2025-26/319 / DOR.SOG(SPE).REC.No.332/13-04-001/2025-26**) consolidates and updates compliance requirements for **rural co-operative banks**, covering **State Co-operative Banks (StCBs), District Central Co-operative Banks (DCCBs), and related rural co-operative banking entities** to the extent made applicable in the text. The directions take effect from the date specified in the operative provisions of the instrument and reorganize obligations across board governance, depositor education fund compliance, KYC outreach, legal/name-change matters, prohibited activities, staff leave, and business continuity planning.

A major compliance area is the **Depositor Education and Awareness Fund (DEAF)**. Banks must transfer eligible unclaimed amounts to the Fund in accordance with the prescribed procedure, maintain records, and comply with refund and interest rules when a depositor later makes a valid claim. The directions set out detailed **registration, transfer, claim, reporting, disclosure, audit, record-retention, and information-furnishing requirements**, including specific **returns to RBI**, **notes-to-accounts disclosure**, and preservation of supporting records. Banks must also maintain contact details for claim handling and follow RBI’s interpretation of the scheme where clarification is needed.

The directions require **board-level governance controls**, including **board-approved policies** and periodic **board reviews** of specified compliance areas. They also mandate **camps and awareness campaigns for periodic updation of KYC**, meaning banks must actively conduct outreach to keep customer KYC information current rather than relying only on routine branch-level updates. In addition, banks must comply with the detailed rules on **change of name**, **display of the bank’s name**, and, where relevant, the **norms for inclusion of an StCB in the Second Schedule to the RBI Act, 1934**, as well as obey any **court directives** affecting operations.

The directions also reinforce prohibitions on certain **financial conduct and ancillary activities**. Rural co-operative banks are restricted from **holding shares in other co-operative societies**, must follow RBI’s rules on **payment of bonus**, and are prohibited from **accepting deposits at the instance of private financiers or unincorporated bodies**. They are also barred from **associating with prize chit schemes** or **selling lottery tickets**, which should be treated as prohibited business lines and compliance risks requiring internal monitoring and staff instruction.

On the operational side, the directions impose requirements for **mandatory leave** and a formal **business continuity planning (BCP)** framework, indicating banks must have workable continuity arrangements for disruptions and ensure leave practices are managed in accordance with the RBI’s prescribed norms. The final chapter contains **repeal and saving provisions**, meaning prior inconsistent instructions are superseded to the extent provided, while actions already taken or rights/obligations accrued under the earlier framework may be preserved where the savings clause applies.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025** on **28 November 2025**, and they take **immediate effect**. They apply to **all Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs)**, meaning **State Co-operative Banks and Central Co-operative Banks** as defined in the **NABARD Act, 1981**, and they cover **any outsourcing arrangement with a service provider located in India or abroad**. For compliance purposes, the key point is that the RBI is imposing a formal risk-management framework for outsourcing by RCBs, with board-level accountability, management oversight, due diligence, contractual controls, ongoing monitoring, grievance handling, and specific restrictions on what can and cannot be outsourced.

The directions require each RCB’s **Board** to approve a **written outsourcing policy** and remain ultimately responsible for all outsourced activities; outsourcing does **not** transfer the bank’s regulatory responsibility or accountability. The policy must set out the bank’s risk appetite, the kinds of activities that may be outsourced, approval processes, due diligence standards, confidentiality and data-security expectations, business continuity requirements, and exit/termination planning. Senior management must implement the policy, maintain records, conduct risk assessments, and ensure that outsourced services remain subject to effective internal controls, auditability, and ongoing supervision.

A central requirement is that certain **core banking, decision-making, and fiduciary functions cannot be outsourced**. While the document must be read for the exact prohibited activities, the substance is that RCBs may not outsource functions that would undermine managerial control, regulatory compliance, or the bank’s ability to supervise and answer for the activity. Where outsourcing is permitted, the RCB must do prior evaluation of the vendor’s capability, financial soundness, reputation, internal controls, information security, ability to meet service levels, and ability to maintain business continuity and disaster recovery. The outsourcing agreement must be in writing and must clearly define scope, performance standards, access rights, confidentiality obligations, audit/inspection rights for the RCB and regulators, sub-contracting limits, incident reporting, data-handling rules, termination rights, and continuity/transition support.

The directions also require **continuous monitoring** of outsourced functions and formal procedures for handling service failures, breaches, and customer complaints arising from outsourced activity. RCBs must ensure that customers are not denied service or grievance redress merely because a function was outsourced; the RCB remains responsible for complaint handling and regulatory compliance. Special rules apply to **offshore outsourcing**, which is treated as a higher-risk arrangement and is subject to additional due diligence and control expectations, including ensuring that RBI access, audit, and supervisory needs are not impaired. The directions conclude by repealing prior inconsistent outsourcing guidance for RCBs while preserving actions already taken, and they clarify that other applicable laws continue to apply and that RBI’s interpretations govern any ambiguity.

rows.summary:
This RBI Direction, issued on **November 28, 2025** and titled **“Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Responsible Business Conduct) Directions, 2025”** (updated as of **July 1, 2026**), applies to **all Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs) operating in India**, meaning **State Co-operative Banks and Central Co-operative Banks** as defined under the NABARD Act, 1981. The Directions take effect **from the date of issue unless a specific provision states otherwise**, and they are issued under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and related enabling powers. For compliance teams, this is a comprehensive conduct framework covering **customer service, customer protection, accessibility, payments/remittances, deposit accounts and liabilities, responsible lending, and miscellaneous operational obligations**, with detailed annexures containing prescribed forms and standards.

At a high level, the Directions require RCBs to implement a **formal institutional framework** for responsible business conduct, including governance arrangements, accountability, and internal processes to ensure that customer-facing activities are handled fairly and transparently. They also impose requirements on **branch customer service**, including clear customer guidance, disclosure practices, complaint-handling support, and service standards at the branch level. The customer-protection chapter expands these obligations by requiring banks to provide customers with understandable information about products and services, protect customers from unfair practices, and maintain procedures that reduce the risk of mis-selling or misunderstanding. The document further adds obligations related to **financial inclusion and accessibility**, indicating that RCBs must make services accessible to underserved or vulnerable customers and ensure that branch/service delivery arrangements do not exclude eligible customers.

The Directions also specifically regulate **payment and remittance services**, meaning RCBs must handle such services in a manner consistent with RBI’s conduct expectations, likely including proper disclosure, service reliability, and customer support for transaction issues. In the section on **deposit accounts and other liabilities**, the framework addresses account operations, claims, and liability-handling procedures; the annexes show that RBI has standardized several forms for **settlement of claims**, including cases involving **nomination or joint accounts with survivorship clauses** and cases where neither exists. The document defines “**accounts with survivorship clause**” as joint accounts styled as **“either or survivor,” “anyone or survivor,” “former or survivor,” “latter or survivor,” or similar wording**, which is important because those account types trigger specific claim-settlement procedures. The annexes also include prescribed formats for **inventory of locker contents**, **inventory of articles kept in safe custody**, and **indemnity/surety/disclaimer/affidavit forms**, showing that banks must follow standardized documentation when settling claims for deceased customers or releasing locker/safe-custody contents.

The most substantial operational change for lending is the chapter on **responsible lending conduct**, which indicates that RCBs must apply conduct controls throughout the lending lifecycle, from sourcing and disclosure to sanction, servicing, and recovery. The inclusion of a **Key Facts Statement** in the annexes indicates a requirement for standardized pre-disbursal disclosure of loan terms, likely to improve customer understanding of interest, fees, repayment obligations, and other material conditions. The “Rates at a quick glance” annex suggests RBI expects prominent disclosure of applicable rates/charges in a simplified form, while the “Comprehensive Notice Board” format indicates specific branch display requirements for customer-facing information. For compliance, this means product documentation, sanction letters, disclosures, and branch notice boards must be aligned to the prescribed RBI formats rather than left to bank discretion.

The document is organized into ten chapters, with **Chapter X – Repeal and Other Provisions** indicating that prior instructions on the subject are being superseded or consolidated, so compliance teams should verify which earlier circulars/instructions remain operative and which are replaced. The annexures are not merely illustrative; they include **mandatory formats** for notices, claim forms, affidavits, indemnities, and inventory records, all of which should be built into bank operating procedures. Because the Directions are updated as of **July 1, 2026**, compliance staff should treat the text as a living consolidation and confirm whether any provisions in the updated version carry later effective dates, transitional rules, or revised forms. Overall, the document establishes a detailed RBI conduct regime for RCBs that requires formal governance, transparent customer communication, standardized claim and locker procedures, accessibility measures, and more disciplined loan and deposit practices.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Rural Co-operative Banks – Know Your Customer Directions, 2025** are a consolidated KYC/AML/CFT framework for **rural co-operative banks**, issued under the RBI’s master-direction style rulemaking and updated as of **December 29, 2025**. The document is intended to prevent these institutions from being used for **money laundering (ML)** or **terrorist financing (TF)** and aligns bank procedures with India’s **Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA)** and **Prevention of Money-Laundering (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005**, as well as FATF standards. For compliance teams, the key point is that the directions cover the full customer lifecycle: acceptance policies, customer identification, due diligence, beneficial ownership, ongoing monitoring, record retention, reporting to FIU-India, and handling of international-agency communications.

The directions apply specifically to **rural co-operative banks** and require them to maintain a formal **board-approved governance framework** for KYC/AML controls. Banks must have documented policies and procedures for customer acceptance, risk management, customer identification procedures (CIP), and customer due diligence (CDD), with higher scrutiny for riskier customers and simplified steps only where the rules expressly permit. The document also organizes obligations by customer type, including **individuals, sole proprietorships, legal entities, and beneficial owners**, indicating that compliance officers must ensure the institution has distinct onboarding and verification workflows for each category rather than a single generic KYC process.

A major operational requirement is **ongoing due diligence** after account opening, not just at onboarding. Rural co-operative banks must monitor transactions and customer behavior for consistency with the expected profile, refresh KYC information as needed, and escalate unusual or suspicious activity through internal controls and reporting channels. The directions also require maintenance of KYC records and reporting obligations to **Financial Intelligence Unit–India (FIU-IND)**, so institutions must be able to preserve identification, transaction, and due-diligence records in a way that supports regulatory inspection and suspicious activity analysis.

The document also addresses special handling for customers and situations subject to **international-agency communications** and other legal obligations, meaning banks must have a process to act on sanctions-style or cross-border regulatory inputs where applicable. Chapter XI indicates **repeal and saving** provisions, confirms that application of other laws is **not barred**, and provides interpretive guidance, so compliance teams should treat this as the controlling RBI KYC framework for rural co-operative banks while still continuing to apply other relevant statutory requirements. Because the excerpt provided is the table of contents and introduction, it does not show specific numeric thresholds, documentary standards, or exact deadlines for individual procedures, but it clearly signals a comprehensive, mandatory KYC/AML control regime that must be embedded across onboarding, monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting.

The Reserve Bank of India’s 2025 Directions on “Rural Co-operative Banks – Prudential Norms on Declaration of Dividends” apply immediately upon issuance, and they govern all Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs), meaning State Co-operative Banks and Central Co-operative Banks as defined under the NABARD Act, 1981. The directions replace and repeal the prior RBI directions, instructions, and guidelines on prudential norms for dividend declaration for RCBs, as referenced in the RBI circular dated November 28, 2025, subject to any saving provisions for actions taken before the new directions came into force.  

Under the new rules, an RCB may declare dividends only if it satisfies all of the following conditions for the financial year for which the dividend is proposed: it must meet the applicable regulatory capital requirement; its net non-performing asset (NNPA) ratio must be at or below 5%; it must have complied with Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) requirements throughout that financial year; and it must have made all required provisions for impaired assets, income tax, employee benefits, and similar items. In addition, the dividend can only be paid out of the net profit of that same financial year, after making all statutory provisions and fully adjusting any accumulated losses.  

The directions also make clear that any prudential treatment involving reversal of excess provisions, dividend payments arising from such reversals, and unrealized profits from transfer of loans and Security Receipts guaranteed by the Government of India must be handled in accordance with the RBI’s separate “Rural Co-operative Banks – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk” Directions, 2025. When deciding whether to declare equity dividends, the Board of Directors must specifically assess the bank’s current and projected capital position against applicable capital requirements, the adequacy of provisions, and broader factors such as the economic environment and the bank’s profitability outlook.  

For compliance purposes, the key operational change is that dividend declaration is now explicitly conditioned on a documented prudential review of capital adequacy, asset quality, reserve/CRR/SLR compliance, provisioning completeness, and profitability, with a hard NNPA threshold of 5% for the relevant financial year. The directions took effect immediately on November 28, 2025, so any dividend decision made after issuance must conform to these requirements.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025**, which apply specifically to **Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs)**—that is, **State Co-operative Banks and Central Co-operative Banks** as defined under the **National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development Act, 1981**. The Directions **take effect on the day they are placed on RBI’s official website**; the title also notes an **“Updated as on April 1, 2026”** status, which is relevant for ensuring the version in use reflects subsequent updates by that date.

For financial statement preparation, every RCB must prepare its **Balance Sheet and Profit and Loss Account** for all business transacted **as on the last working day of the year or period concerned**, using the **forms in the Third Schedule of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, as substituted under Section 56. In compiling those statements, the bank must follow the **ICAI’s pronouncements on Accounting Standards**, but only **subject to RBI’s directions and guidelines**; in other words, where RBI has specific requirements, those override general ICAI guidance to the extent of any inconsistency.

The document then establishes a detailed framework for **presentation and disclosure in notes to accounts** and later adds **other compliance instructions** affecting items such as **inter-branch account provisioning for net debit balances, reconciliation of Nostro accounts and treatment of outstanding entries, transfers to or appropriations from reserve funds, provisioning for fraud, unreconciled balances, deferred tax liability on special reserves created under Section 36(1)(viii) of the Income Tax Act, payment of fees and allowances to directors, and restrictions on window dressing**. It also contains a **repeal and saving** section, indicates that the application of other laws is **not barred**, and provides interpretive guidance, meaning compliance teams should read these Directions alongside the Banking Regulation Act and other applicable law rather than treating them as the sole rulebook.

The operative legal basis is important: RBI states it is acting under **Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, along with other enabling provisions, and frames the Directions as necessary in the public interest. For compliance purposes, the key action point is that affected RCBs must ensure their statutory financial statements and disclosures are formatted and compiled in line with the specified BR Act forms and RBI-prescribed disclosure rules, and must also implement the separate controls and accounting treatments required for the other specified items once the Directions are in force.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Rural Co-operative Banks – Treatment of Wilful Defaulters and Large Defaulters) Directions, 2025** take **immediate effect** and apply to **State Co-operative Banks and Central Co-operative Banks** (collectively, “RCBs”) as defined under the NABARD Act, 1981. The Directions are intended to create a system for disseminating credit information on wilful defaulters so lenders can prevent further institutional finance from being extended to them. Although issued for RCBs, the document states that the restrictions on further financial accommodation to wilful defaulters and the provisions on large defaulters apply to **all Reserve Bank-regulated entities**, even if they are not “lenders” within the Directions’ defined term.

For **wilful defaulters**, an RCB must not grant any additional credit facility to a person/entity classified as a wilful defaulter by any lender, and this prohibition also extends to any **associated entity**. The restriction remains in place for **one year after the wilful defaulter’s name is removed** from the List of Wilful Defaulters. RCBs are also barred from granting credit for the **floating of new ventures** to the wilful defaulter or any associated entity for **five years after removal** from the list. If an associated entity is no longer associated with the wilful defaulter, the penal restrictions cease to apply to that entity. Restructuring of wilful defaulters or their associated entities must follow the Reserve Bank’s **Rural Co-operative Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025**.

The Directions define when an entity is “associated” with a wilful defaulter. If the wilful defaulter is a **company**, association includes a **subsidiary**, a **joint venture**, or an **associate company** under the Companies Act, 2013. If the wilful defaulter is a **natural person**, then all entities where the person is a **promoter**, **director**, or otherwise **in charge of and responsible for management** are deemed associated. This means the credit restrictions can reach multiple related entities, not just the named defaulter.

The document also includes a reporting framework for **wilful defaulters and large defaulters**, indicating that RCBs will have specific reporting obligations, including submission of a **List of Large Defaulters** in the prescribed format set out in **Annex I**. However, the excerpt provided cuts off before the detailed reporting requirements, thresholds, or timelines in Chapter III are fully visible, so a compliance team should review the full text to confirm the exact reporting triggers, due dates, and submission mechanics. There is also a Chapter IV on **repeal and other provisions**, but the substantive content is not shown in the excerpt.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs) – Resolution of Stressed Assets Directions, 2025**, issued on **November 28, 2025** and updated as of **July 1, 2026**, set out a comprehensive framework for **early identification, reporting, and time-bound resolution of stressed assets** in rural co-operative banks. The directions also **rationalize and harmonize rules on compromise settlements and technical write-offs**, with the stated goal of improving resolution outcomes across the sector. RBI notes that some RCBs may be involved in state government **Debt Relief Schemes (DRS)** that waive or sacrifice debt obligations for targeted borrowers in exchange for fiscal support, and it highlights the prudential and credit-discipline risks if such schemes are frequent or poorly designed, including delayed recoveries, mismatches between amounts claimed and amounts admitted by government, and mandatory requirements to extend fresh credit.

For compliance purposes, the document applies to **Rural Co-operative Banks** and establishes a requirement for **board-approved policies** governing stress recognition and resolution, which means each bank must have formally approved internal policies rather than ad hoc case handling. It requires **early identification of stress** and **reporting**, so institutions must monitor accounts proactively and escalate signs of stress before default becomes severe. The directions also impose **disclosure obligations**, meaning banks must make the prescribed stress/resolution information available in the manner required by the RBI framework. Where an account is being restructured, the prudential norms in the document govern how restructuring may be done, implying that restructuring cannot be used informally to mask asset quality issues.

The directions contain specific treatment for **special cases**, including **compromise settlements and technical write-offs**, which are now brought within a harmonized RBI framework. They also create a dedicated chapter for **resolution of accounts impacted by calamities**, assigning roles to the **State Level Bankers’ Committee (SLBC)**, **Union Territory Level Bankers’ Committee (UTLBC)**, and **District Consultative Committee (DCC)** in coordinating responses. Banks must then **implement the resolution plan** in accordance with the directions, use the specified **ancillary measures**, and comply with **reporting requirements** for such calamity-affected accounts. The structure indicates that relief in disaster situations is not discretionary or informal; it must follow a documented committee-led process and bank implementation steps.

The document also addresses **Government Debt Relief Schemes (DRS)** and sets prudential treatment for those schemes, reflecting RBI’s concern that relief measures should not undermine credit discipline or create unrecognized exposure. In addition, it includes **special trade relief measures**, though the excerpt does not give the detailed mechanics in the text provided. Finally, the directions include standard legal clauses on **repeal and saving**, confirm that **other applicable laws are not barred unless expressly overridden**, and reserve RBI’s power of interpretation. For compliance teams, the key takeaway is that RCBs must align internal policies, monitoring, reporting, restructuring, write-off, compromise settlement, and government-relief handling processes to this RBI framework, and should ensure board approval, documentation, and timely reporting are in place across all stressed-asset workflows.

rows.summary:
This RBI circular issues the **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025**, and states that they **came into force immediately** on **28 November 2025**. They apply to **Rural Co-operative Banks**, meaning **State Co-operative Banks and Central Co-operative Banks** as defined under the **NABARD Act, 1981**. Banks must also comply with any **State Co-operative Societies Act/rules or other statutory law** where those local requirements are **more stringent** than the RBI directions.

The document’s purpose is to standardize how these banks must treat **income recognition, asset classification, and provisioning** for their advances portfolio, to improve consistency and transparency in reported accounts. It is issued under the RBI’s powers under **Sections 21, 35A, and 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**. The directions also include a definitions section that is operationally important for compliance; for example, it defines **“crop season”** as the period up to harvesting as determined by the **State Level Bankers’ Committee (SLBC)** in each State, and **“long duration crops”** as crops whose crop season exceeds **one year**.

From the material provided, the document is organized into chapters covering: general instructions, disclosure requirements, asset classification norms, special classification cases, categories of NPAs, treatment where security value has eroded, upgrade of NPA accounts, provisioning requirements, additional provisioning where a resolution plan is implemented under the related **RBI (Rural Co-operative Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025**, and income recognition. The inclusion of a separate chapter on **repeal and saving** indicates the new framework is intended to supersede prior norms while preserving any saved actions/rights, and there is also a provision confirming that application of other laws is **not barred**.

Because the excerpt stops partway through the definitions section, the specific prudential thresholds, overdue periods, provisioning percentages, and exact NPA-upgrade rules are not visible here; however, a compliance team should note that this is a **full prudential framework** for rural co-operative bank loan accounting, not just a disclosure update. The key action point from the visible text is that affected banks should ensure their internal policies, accounting systems, and branch-level loan monitoring procedures are aligned with the RBI’s immediate-effective-date prudential directions, while also checking whether any stricter state-law requirements apply in parallel.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Asset Liability Management) Directions, 2025
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Asset Liability Management) Directions, 2025** on **November 28, 2025** under **Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**. These Directions set out mandatory asset-liability management (“ALM”) and liquidity/interest-rate-risk governance requirements for **rural co-operative banks**, with specific treatment for **Scheduled State Co-operative Banks (StCBs)** where the text refers to access to the **Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF)** and **Marginal Standing Facility (MSF)**. The Directions replace the prior framework through a repeal-and-savings provision, so compliance teams should treat this as the governing ALM/liquidity standard going forward unless a specific saved item or other law applies.

At the governance level, the document places primary responsibility on the **board of the bank** to oversee ALM, approve relevant policies, set limits, and review risk positions periodically. The board is expected to ensure that the institution has an adequate **ALM information system**, an appropriate **ALM organization**, and a functioning ALM process capable of measuring and managing liquidity and interest rate risk. The Directions emphasize that ALM is not a purely treasury activity: it requires formal board-approved oversight, defined internal responsibilities, reporting lines, and regular monitoring.

The liquidity-risk chapter requires banks to measure and manage **maturity/cash flow mismatches** and to conduct **dynamic liquidity assessments**, not just static balance-sheet reviews. The annexed statements indicate that institutions must prepare formal liquidity reports, including a **Structural Liquidity Statement**, a **Short-term Dynamic Liquidity Statement**, and a **Maturity Profile – Liquidity** statement, which implies regular maturity-bucket reporting and cash-flow forecasting. The Directions also address **behavioural patterns** and **embedded options**, meaning the bank must make assumptions for products whose actual behavior differs from contractual maturity and must incorporate option risk into liquidity analysis. For **Scheduled StCBs**, the document specifically references use of RBI liquidity support tools through **LAF and MSF**, so those institutions need to understand any operational access conditions and how those facilities interact with their liquidity buffers.

On interest-rate risk, the Directions require banks to manage **IRR** through **traditional gap analysis** and by preparing an **Interest Rate Sensitivity Statement**. The annexes show that banks must maintain formal sensitivity reporting, including an **Interest Rate Sensitivity Statement** and a **Maturity Profile – Liquidity** template, so compliance officers should expect standardized reporting formats and disciplined measurement of repricing mismatches. The document also mentions a **transfer price mechanism**, which means banks are expected to allocate funding costs/credits internally in a way that supports ALM discipline and accurate business-line incentives. Financial reporting and the role of auditors are also addressed, indicating that ALM information and risk metrics are not only internal management tools but also part of the institution’s audited control environment.

Finally, the Directions establish **monitoring and reporting** obligations and contain a **repeal and saving clause**, plus a statement that other applicable laws are not barred and that RBI interpretations control where needed. Because the document is a comprehensive directions instrument rather than a narrow circular, compliance teams should confirm: the bank’s ALM policy is board-approved and current; reporting templates match the annexes; liquidity and IRR measurements are produced on the required schedule; assumptions for behavioural deposits, loan prepayments, and embedded options are documented; and any special arrangements for Scheduled StCB access to LAF/MSF are operationally ready.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on May 18, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Rural Co-operative Banks – Classification, Valuation and Operation of Investment Portfolio) Directions, 2025”** set out the RBI’s consolidated rules for how **rural co-operative banks** must organize, classify, value, and transact in their investment portfolios. The directions apply to the relevant rural co-operative banks covered by the instrument and are organized around board governance, investment-policy controls, portfolio classification into **permanent** and **current** investments, valuation and market-value recognition rules, and operational requirements for government securities and non-SLR instruments. The document is dated **November 28, 2025** and is noted as **updated as on May 18, 2026**, so a compliance team should treat the updated version as the operative text and check for any changes reflected by the 2026 update against prior internal policies and procedures.

A core compliance requirement is that each bank must have a formal **investment policy** approved and overseen by the board, with board-level responsibility for the bank’s overall investment framework and for ensuring systems and controls are in place. The directions then require banks to classify investments properly between **permanent** and **current** categories and to follow the prescribed rules for moving securities between categories when needed. This classification is not merely accounting presentation: it drives the valuation method and the recognition of gains or losses, so compliance teams need to confirm that treasury, finance, and board reporting are aligned with the regulatory categories and that any reclassification is done under the RBI’s rules rather than ad hoc management judgment.

The valuation chapter requires **permanent investments** and **current investments** to be valued in accordance with the RBI’s prescribed approach, with market-value treatment addressed separately for **quoted securities**, **unquoted SLR securities**, and **unquoted non-SLR securities**. In practice, this means the bank must maintain reliable market valuation processes and documentation, including how prices are sourced and how fair value is determined when securities are not quoted. Compliance officers should verify that the bank has controls for periodic valuation, impairment/mark-to-market recognition where required, and audit trails showing that the stated values are supportable under the RBI framework.

A substantial portion of the directions governs **government securities** operations. Banks are required to follow RBI-prescribed procedures for access to **NDS-OM**, use of **Subsidiary General Ledger (SGL) accounts**, maintenance and operation of **gilt accounts**, settlement of government securities transactions, participation in **primary auctions**, use of **repo/reverse repo** in government securities, **short sale** transactions, retailing of government securities, and trading on stock exchanges. For compliance purposes, this means treasury operations must be configured so that each activity is conducted only through the authorized RBI/market infrastructure and with the proper account structure, settlement mechanics, and internal approvals; any bank engaging in these activities needs documented procedures, account reconciliations, and transaction controls that match the prescribed operational model.

The directions also regulate **non-SLR securities** and related exposure controls. They set requirements for permissible non-SLR instruments, establish a **prudential limit**, and provide specific rules for transactions in **commercial papers (CPs)** and **certificates of deposit (CDs)**, as well as trading and settlement in **corporate bonds**. The board is assigned a specific role in approving and monitoring these investments, and the document includes “other requirements” and prudential systems/controls that would typically require robust internal limits, counterparty checks, broker controls, and ongoing monitoring of concentration and compliance with exposure caps. In practical terms, the compliance team should confirm that the bank’s investment policy, treasury limits, broker engagement process, settlement procedures, and reporting lines all reflect the RBI’s specified prudential limits and activity-level restrictions, and that staff are trained not to exceed them.

rows.summary:
The RBI’s **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Interest Rates on Advances) Directions, 2025** apply to **Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs)**, meaning **State Co-operative Banks and Central Co-operative Banks** as defined under the NABARD Act, 1981. The Directions are **effective immediately upon issuance** and replace the prior framework through a new consolidated set of requirements on how RCBs must determine, disclose, and apply lending rates on advances.  

RCBs must set lending rates based on **cost of funds, transaction costs, and other relevant factors**, but only under the **approval of the Board of Directors or a duly delegated Board committee**, and the bank must ensure the pricing is transparent and consistent with normal banking practice. Each bank must **publish its minimum and maximum interest rates** and **display them in every branch**, so customers can readily see the range of rates charged.  

A key operational rule is that **interest on all advances must be charged at monthly rests**, except for **agriculture and allied agricultural activities**, where the bank may continue its existing practice of charging or compounding interest according to **crop seasons** rather than monthly rests. For **small-value loans**, especially **personal loans and similar products**, banks are expected to have a documented prior-approval process that considers the borrower’s cash flows, to price in a **reasonable and justified risk premium** based on internal borrower rating and the presence or absence of security, and to ensure that the **total borrower cost** (interest plus all other charges) is justified by the bank’s own cost of extending the loan and expected return. The Directions also contemplate a **publicly communicated ceiling** on interest and ancillary charges for such loans.  

For **microfinance loans**, each bank must adopt a **Board-approved pricing policy** and maintain a **well-documented interest rate model/approach** for arriving at the **all-inclusive interest rate**. That policy must separately identify the components of pricing, such as **cost of funds, risk premium, and margin**, so the bank can show how the final rate is determined. The document continues beyond the excerpt provided, so any additional detailed microfinance pricing requirements or transitional/repeal provisions would need the full text to confirm.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India has issued the **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Transfer and Distribution of Credit Risk) Directions, 2025**, a consolidated framework governing when and how rural co-operative banks may transfer loan exposures and related credit risk. The directions **take effect immediately on the date they are placed on the RBI’s official website**. They apply to **Rural Co-operative Banks**, defined here as **State Co-operative Banks and Central Co-operative Banks** under the NABARD Act, 1981.

A key restriction is that **RCBs are permitted to act only as transferors of stressed loans under Chapter IV**; they **cannot otherwise act as transferors or transferees in any loan transfer transaction**. Separately, banks may acquire loans only from a transferor that qualifies as a **“lender” under paragraph 11(4)** unless a specific exception applies, and **no loan transfer or acquisition is permitted unless it is expressly allowed by these directions and carried out in the prescribed manner**. The scope expressly covers loan transfers done by **novation or assignment**, and where a transfer occurs, **legal ownership must be transferred to the transferee to the extent of the economic interest transferred**.

The directions also define the core concepts used in the framework. **“Credit enhancement”** means a contractual arrangement that gives other transaction parties added protection to reduce credit risk on acquired exposures. **“Default”** is defined as non-payment when a debt or instalment is due and unpaid, and for **revolving facilities such as cash credit**, default also includes an outstanding balance that remains **continuously above the sanctioned limit or drawing power, whichever is lower, for more than 30 days**. **“Economic interest”** refers to the risks and rewards associated with the loan exposure over the life of that exposure. The definition of **“lenders”** begins by listing eligible lender categories, including **Scheduled Commercial Banks, Regional Rural Banks, Local Area Banks, Primary (Urban) Co-operative Banks, State Co-operative Banks, and other specified entities**; the text provided is cut off before the full list is visible, so compliance teams should review the full Chapter II for the complete definition.

Finally, the document states that these rules are **self-contained** and are issued under the RBI’s powers under **sections 21 and 35A read with section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act, 1949**. It also makes clear that the new framework does **not override separate RBI regimes such as the Master Direction on External Commercial Borrowings, Trade Credits and Structured Obligations dated March 26, 2019, or other RBI-permitted guarantee/products frameworks**. For compliance purposes, the practical takeaway is that RCBs need to verify whether any planned loan transfer is expressly permitted under this Direction, confirm the counterparty status of any transferee or transferor, and ensure that any stressed-loan transfer activity stays within the narrow role allowed for RCBs.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s “Rural Co-operative Banks (Concentration Risk Management) Directions, 2025” apply immediately upon issuance, and they are mandatory for all Rural Co-operative Banks, meaning both State Co-operative Banks and Central Co-operative Banks as defined under the NABARD Act, 1981. The RBI states that any non-compliance may trigger supervisory and enforcement action, so these are enforceable prudential requirements rather than guidance. The directions are issued under the Banking Regulation Act, 1949 and related enabling powers.

The document begins by defining the key terms used to measure concentration exposure. “Capital fund” means paid-up capital plus free reserves, excluding revaluation reserves and similar unrealized asset revaluation balances. “Exposure” is defined broadly to include funded facilities such as working capital limits, short-term or temporary loans, term loans, interim/bridge loans, and non-funded facilities such as guarantees and letters of credit; for cash credit, the higher of the sanctioned limit or outstanding amount is counted, for term loans the outstanding amount is used, and for non-funded limits only 50% of the limit, or the outstanding amount if higher, is counted. “Lendable Resources” are calculated as share capital, reserves and provisions (excluding the balance in the Agricultural Credit Stabilisation Fund), deposits and borrowings, less optimum liquid assets equal to 35% of demand and time liabilities (DTL), fixed assets, accumulated losses, and any other commitments other than loans and advances.

Each RCB must put in place a comprehensive Board-approved policy covering its lending and concentration risk management framework. The policy must specifically address loan and advance sanctions to individuals and financing of commercial requirements, and the chapter indicates that further details in later paragraphs govern these policies. In other words, the compliance obligation is not just to have a policy in place, but to ensure the policy is formally approved by the board and covers the required lending categories and exposure controls.

The opening text also makes clear that the directions are aimed at managing concentration risk arising from exposures to counterparties and sectors of the economy, building on prior prudential norms issued under Credit Monitoring Arrangements and other RBI instructions. For compliance teams, the key action is to assess existing lending and exposure aggregation methodologies against these RBI definitions, confirm that board-approved policies are in place and current, and ensure internal systems calculate exposure in the prescribed way, especially for cash credit, term loans, guarantees, and letters of credit.

As credit exposures of RCBs encompass varied sectors, borrower types and products with their own idiosyncratic complexities as well as systemic implications due to interconnectedness among themselves, credit risk management of RCBs involve a range of prudential tools, including statutory and regulatory restrictions / prohibitions on certain activities. Recognising this, the Reserve Bank has, from time to time, issued guidelines to strengthen credit risk management practices. rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Risk Management) Directions, 2025”** apply to **all Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs)**, meaning **State Co-operative Banks (StCBs) and Central Co-operative Banks (CCBs)** as defined under the NABARD Act, 1981. The Directions were issued on **November 28, 2025** and state that they **come into effect immediately upon issuance**; the document you provided is marked **updated as on July 01, 2026**, so a compliance team should treat the text as the current consolidated version. The RBI has issued them under its powers in the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949** (including Sections **20, 21 and 35A read with Section 56**) to strengthen credit risk management because credit risk can affect other risk types and because RCB exposures span multiple sectors, borrower types, and products.

A key compliance point is that these Directions are not just general guidance; they create a structured framework of **prudential tools, statutory restrictions, and regulatory restrictions/prohibitions** for RCB lending and credit administration. The preliminary definitions section expands the regulated terminology used throughout the Directions, including **“cash credit (CC)”** as a running credit facility against hypothecation/pledge of goods, book debts, standing crops, etc., with **drawing power (DP)** periodically determined by eligible current assets and the outstanding amount repayable on demand. It also defines **“current account”** as a demand deposit account allowing withdrawals any number of times depending on balance or up to an agreed amount, and deems it to include deposit accounts that are neither savings nor term deposits. The updated definitions further clarify that **“director of a RCB”** includes a nominee and independent director, **“entity”** means a “person” other than an individual and a Hindu undivided family, and **KMP** means all employees one level below the Board plus anyone designated by the Board.

From the table of contents and chapter structure, the Directions impose requirements across several compliance areas: **Board-approved policies**, **credit risk evaluation**, **statutory restrictions**, **regulatory restrictions**, **property valuation and empanelment of valuers**, **CERSAI filing of security interests** for **immovable property (other than equitable mortgage), movable assets, and intangible assets**, and **maintenance of cash credit, current, and overdraft accounts by banks**. For a compliance officer, the important takeaway is that the RBI is tying credit risk management to both governance and operational controls: the Board must approve policies, banks must evaluate credit risk appropriately, property-backed lending requires proper valuation discipline, and security interests must be reported in CERSAI where required. The inclusion of a dedicated chapter on cash credit/current/overdraft accounts indicates the Directions also expect banks to maintain these accounts in a regulated manner, not merely at the point of sanction but throughout account operation.

The document also signals that these are **mandatory RBI Directions**, not optional best practices, and they apply specifically to **RCBs as a sector**, rather than to all banks generally. A compliance team should therefore ensure internal lending, collateral, documentation, valuation, filing, and account-maintenance procedures are aligned with the Directions as amended through **July 1, 2026**, and should monitor the later amendment references embedded in the text for any clause-specific effective dates. Because the excerpt provided cuts off in the middle of the definitions section, there may be additional detailed thresholds, prohibitions, or procedural rules in the full text that would need separate review, but based on the content shown, the core compliance burden is a comprehensive credit-risk governance and security-interest control framework for StCBs and CCBs.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Information Reporting) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on July 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Information Reporting) Directions, 2025** create a standardized mandatory framework for **how rural co-operative banks must report, update, use, and correct credit information** and for how they must support **customer access, service, and grievance redressal** related to that reporting. The directions apply to **all Rural Co-operative Banks**, which are treated collectively as **Credit Institutions (CIs)**, and they come into force **immediately** unless a specific provision states otherwise. The stated policy goals are to improve the **quality, consistency, confidentiality, and security** of credit data shared with Credit Information Companies (CICs), while also giving consumers a mechanism to access their credit information and pursue complaints about reporting errors or related issues.

A major operational requirement is that affected banks must participate in the credit information ecosystem through the relevant **CICs** and comply with the RBI’s rules on **data formats, reporting timelines, and periodic updation** of borrower data. The directions require banks to follow the RBI-prescribed reporting standards for credit accounts and related information, to promptly correct or re-submit **rejected data**, and to monitor and improve their **Data Quality Index (DQI)** as part of ongoing compliance. They also require procedures to **correct inaccuracies in Credit Information Reports**, and they address how credit information may be used in **credit appraisal**, including obligations around the display or communication of credit information where required.

The document also establishes a **Technical Working Group** to support the framework, reflecting that the RBI expects continued technical oversight of reporting processes and data quality. On the customer side, the directions require banks to strengthen **customer service and grievance redressal**, and they set out a **framework for compensation to customers** where reporting failures or related lapses cause harm. The directions also integrate the **Reserve Bank-Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021**, meaning complaints that fit that framework may be taken through the RBI’s ombudsman mechanism.

In addition, the directions include **best practices**, repeal-and-saving provisions, and rules clarifying how they interact with other laws and existing RBI instructions. The document is intended to replace or supersede inconsistent prior arrangements to the extent specified, while preserving lawful actions already taken and clarifying that other applicable legal requirements are not barred by these directions. For compliance purposes, the key point is that rural co-operative banks must treat credit information reporting as a regulated, ongoing operational obligation with requirements for **timely, accurate reporting; error rectification; data-quality controls; customer access and complaint handling; and compensation/ombudsman escalation where applicable**.

rows.summary:
The Reserve Bank of India’s **“Rural Co-operative Banks – Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025”** take **immediate effect** and apply to **all Rural Co-operative Banks (RCBs)**, meaning **State Co-operative Banks and Central Co-operative Banks** as defined under the NABARD Act, 1981. The directions govern the **general and conduct rules for debit cards**, including **co-branded debit cards**, and must be read together with any other RBI requirements on **prudential, payment, technology, and cyber-security matters** that apply to debit and co-branded debit cards.  

Each bank must put in place **Board-approved comprehensive policies and procedures** covering debit card issuance, co-branding arrangements where relevant, a **standard operating procedure for discretionary blocking, deactivation, or suspension of debit cards**, the **time period for completing formalities after a lost card is blocked**, and a **grievance redressal and compensation framework**. The document makes clear that these policy requirements are not standalone; they are to be implemented in line with the more detailed requirements set out in the later chapters of the Directions.  

On issuance, the bank must adopt a **Board-approved comprehensive debit card issuance policy** and issue cards only in accordance with it. The document also defines the key instruments and relationships: a **debit card** may be **physical or virtual**, must be linked to a **savings or current account**, and may be used for cash withdrawal, online payments, PoS/QR transactions, fund transfers, and similar transactions subject to prescribed terms; a **form factor** is any physical or virtual substitute used to carry out a payment or banking transaction; a **co-branded card** is issued jointly with a co-branding entity and bears both entities’ names; and a **card loyalty/reward programme** includes incentives such as digital coupons, points, discounts, cashbacks, or other monetary benefits that can be redeemed on the same or later transactions after accumulation.  

The Directions also specify that “convenience fee” means a **fixed or pro-rata charge** for using a debit card as an alternative payment method where that payment method is **not ordinarily accepted** compared with other forms of payment. Finally, any terms not specifically defined in the Directions are to take their meaning from the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, the **RBI Act, 1934**, or, where appropriate, their ordinary commercial meaning.  

Because the excerpt provided cuts off mid-provision in Chapter III, there may be additional operational or product-specific requirements later in the document that are not visible here. However, from the text provided, the compliance-critical immediate obligations are: **implement Board-approved debit card and co-branding policies, establish procedures for card blocking and lost-card follow-up, and ensure grievance/compensation handling is formally documented and aligned with RBI’s broader card-related requirements**.

rows.title: Reserve Bank of India (Rural Co-operative Banks – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025 (Updated as on April 01, 2026)
rows.summary:
This Reserve Bank of India directive, effective as updated through **April 1, 2026**, consolidates the RBI’s requirements for **rural co-operative banks** on credit facilities, with detailed rules spanning board-approved lending policies, digital lending, gold/silver-backed lending, microfinance, housing loans, and non-fund-based credit facilities. It applies to the banks covered by the “rural co-operative banks” framework and requires those institutions to align their lending practices, customer protections, underwriting, valuation, reporting, and technology controls to the specific standards set out in the directions.

A major compliance theme is **digital lending**: rural co-operative banks that lend through **lending service provider (LSP)** arrangements must meet RBI-prescribed governance, conduct, data, and technology requirements, including customer-protection controls, reporting of credit information and digital lending applications (DLAs), and rules for **loss-sharing arrangements in case of default**. The document also imposes general provisions for how these arrangements must be structured and supervised, meaning banks need documented policies, board oversight, and operational controls rather than ad hoc outsourcing. Compliance teams should treat this as a substantive regulatory regime for third-party digital loan sourcing, servicing, and customer interaction.

The directions also set out strict rules for **loans against gold and silver collateral**, including restrictions and ceilings, valuation and assaying standards, **loan-to-value (LTV)** requirements, and other operational conditions. This means banks must ensure collateral is properly tested and valued before disbursement, loans remain within permitted exposure limits, and procedures exist to manage pledge, safekeeping, and release of precious-metal collateral in line with RBI expectations. Any credit product secured by gold or silver will need controls around purity assessment, valuation documentation, and exposure monitoring.

For **microfinance lending**, the directions define the product and require banks to assess **household income**, then use that assessment to cap the **total loan repayment obligations of a household**. The compliance implication is that the bank cannot rely only on borrower self-declaration or single-loan underwriting; it must have a household-level affordability assessment process and ensure aggregate repayments stay within the RBI’s permitted threshold. The chapter also includes additional provisions that banks must follow when originating and servicing these loans.

The **housing loan** chapter sets out which housing schemes are eligible, who the permissible borrower categories are, the security requirements, loan tenor, and rules for **graduated instalments** and **additional/supplementary finance**. It also addresses lending to housing boards, defines borrower categories, sets **individual housing loan limits**, and permits certain **innovative housing loan products** including **upfront disbursal of housing loans** under specified conditions. Separate rules cover finance for housing and for **construction of buildings/ready-built houses**, so banks need product-specific underwriting and disbursal controls rather than a single generic housing policy.

Finally, the directions regulate **non-fund based (NFB) credit facilities**, including **guarantees** and **co-acceptances**, plus requirements for certain other specific guarantees and exclusions. Rural co-operative banks therefore need to verify that their contingent exposure practices comply with RBI’s conditions for issuing guarantees, handling co-acceptances, and identifying transactions that are not permitted or require special treatment. In practice, this document requires banks to maintain board-approved policies, product-level controls, customer-protection procedures, and reporting/technology systems across all of these lending activities, with the updated rules effective as of **April 1, 2026**.
