rows.title: Advancing its strategic planning process, the PCAOB has requested public input on draft goals and objectives for its 2026-2030 strategic plan.
rows.desc: 1666 K Street NW Washington, DC 20006 Office: 202-207-9100 Fax: 202-862-8430 www.pcaobus.org PCAOB Release No. 2026-006 July 20, 2026 Summary: In early 2026, the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (the “Board” or “PCAOB”) initiated a process to develop a new strategic plan. The PCAOB’s 2026-2030 strategic plan (“Plan”) will articulate the organization’s goals and objectives in support of its statutory mission to protect investors and further the public interest in the preparation of informative, accurate, and independent audit reports. In addition to serving as a five-year roadmap for the organization, the PCAOB’s strategic plan will be used to develop the PCAOB’s budget each year. As a new and initial step in the strategic planning process, on March 31, 2026, the Board requested public comment on the PCAOB’s strategic priorities. The stakeholder feedback received through that process helped to inform the development of the Draft 2026-2030 Strategic Plan Goals and Objectives. For the next phase of the strategic planning process, the Board is seeking input regarding PCAOB’s Draft 2026-2030 Strategic Plan Goals and Objectives. Additional input from our stakeholders will help the Board and staff further refine the strategic direction, goals and objectives before the final Plan is presented for Board consideration. The Board welcomes and will consider all comments received to inform the continued development of the Plan. All comments will be made public and posted on the PCAOB website. You are encouraged, but not required, to provide your name and professional affiliation. Public Comment: Interested persons may submit written comments to the Board. Comments should be sent by email to comments@pcaobus.org, or through the PCAOB website at www.pcaobus.org. Comments may also be sent to the Office of the Secretary, PCAOB, 1666 K Street NW, Washington, DC 20006-2803. All comments should reference the Request for Public Comment Draft 2026-2030 Strategic Plan Goals and Objectives Request for Public Comment Draft 2026-2030 Strategic Plan Goals and Objectives PCAOB Release No. 2026-006 July 20, 2026 2 Board release number, PCAOB Release No. 2026-006, in the subject or reference line, and should be received by the Board by September 4, 2026. Board Contact: Lorene Rosenberg, Chief Strategy Officer, Office of the Chief Operating Officer (202-372- 5926, rosenbergl@pcaobus.org) On the 20 th day of July, in the year 2026, the foregoing was, in accordance with the Bylaws of the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board, ADOPTED BY THE BOARD. /s/ Phoebe W. Brown ________________________ Phoebe W. Brown Secretary Request for Public Comment Draft 2026-2030 Strategic Plan Goals and Objectives PCAOB Release No. 2026-006 July 20, 2026 3 Draft 2026-2030 Strategic Plan Goals and Objectives Job Aid Introduction To guide the PCAOB’s work over the current and next four years in ways that best serve our mission, vision, and values, and to support the development of the annual budgets, we have organized our draft 2026-2030 Strategic Plan Goals and Objectives around three reinforcing priorities: Advance Audit Quality and Investor Protection We will advance audit quality and investor protection by directing our oversight to the areas that have the most significant effect on audit quality—promoting a high-quality standard-setting approach, modernizing inspections through a quality control-focused approach, and targeting enforcement toward conduct that creates meaningful risk to investors. Clarify Expectations and Our Bases for Decisions Leading to Understandable Outcomes Effective regulation depends on clarity and consistency. Transform How Oversight Is Delivered We will transform our operations through strategic investments in technology and data capabilities, strengthening internal coordination and governance, and investing in our people to ensure oversight remains effective, efficient, and fit for purpose. rows.title: The PCAOB has announced the members of the Inspections Modernization Council, a resource group composed of outside parties with a stake in the PCAOB’s inspection activities.
rows.desc: PCAOB Announces Members of the Inspections Modernization Council WASHINGTON, Jul. 9, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) today announced the members of the Inspections Modernization Council (IMC). A resource group composed of outside parties with a stake in the PCAOB’s inspection activities, the IMC will provide perspectives to inform the PCAOB’s efforts to modernize its inspection program and thereby improve audit quality. Potential changes that the IMC will consider include generating more meaningful outputs for consumers of inspection reports, leveraging technological innovations such as automation and artificial intelligence, and focusing inspections on firms’ systems of quality control. “I was pleased with the tremendous number of high-quality applicants we received for the Inspections Modernization Council. rows.title: The PCAOB announced the appointment of George Kostolampros as General Counsel.
rows.desc: George Kostolampros Named PCAOB General Counsel WASHINGTON, Jul. 1, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) today announced that George Kostolampros has been appointed the PCAOB’s General Counsel. As General Counsel, Mr. Kostolampros will provide legal advice and counsel on all PCAOB operations and will manage the Office of the General Counsel (OGC). “OGC’s work underpins the PCAOB’s ability to execute its mission to protect investors,” said PCAOB Chairman Demetrios (Jim) Logothetis. “We are grateful that George is joining us to fill this critical leadership role.” Mr. Kostolampros brings more than 25 years of experience advising organizations and senior leaders on complex legal, regulatory, governance, compliance, and risk-management matters. Prior to his appointment as General Counsel, Mr. Kostolampros was a partner at Venable LLP, where he advised public companies, boards of directors, audit committees, financial institutions, and senior executives on compliance, governance, and regulatory matters, and represented clients in internal investigations, government enforcement matters, regulatory proceedings, and complex litigation. Before returning to private practice, he served as Senior Counsel in the Division of Enforcement at the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. Mr. Kostolampros received his J.D., magna cum laude, from Widener University School of Law and his B.A. from Syracuse University. “I am honored to join the PCAOB, and I look forward to working with the talented OGC staff to advance the PCAOB’s priorities and mission,” said Mr. Kostolampros. Matt Goldin, who was named Acting General Counsel in January 2026, will resume his role as Deputy General Counsel, advising the Board on PCAOB programs and operations and assisting with OGC’s management. “Matt is a valued member of the OGC team, and we thank him for his distinguished service as Acting General Counsel,” said Chairman Logothetis.*****About the PCAOBThe PCAOB is a nonprofit corporation established by Congress to oversee the audits of public companies in order to protect investors and further the public interest in the preparation of informative, accurate, and independent audit reports. The PCAOB also oversees the audits of brokers and dealers registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission, including compliance reports filed pursuant to federal securities laws. rows.title: The PCAOB announced the appointment of Dr. Ying Li Compton as its Chief Economist and Director of the Office of Economic and Risk Analysis.
rows.desc: Dr. Ying Li Compton Named PCAOB Chief Economist and Director of Its Office of Economic and Risk Analysis WASHINGTON, Jun. 29, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) today announced the appointment of Dr. Ying Li Compton as the PCAOB's Chief Economist and Director of its Office of Economic and Risk Analysis (OERA). At the PCAOB, OERA conducts independent, evidence-based economic and risk analyses to inform the organization’s oversight activities, including inspections, investigations, rulemaking, standard setting, and post-implementation reviews. “Evidence-based economic and risk analyses are critical to strengthening the PCAOB’s oversight and, by extension, its ability to accomplish its investor-protection mission,” said PCAOB Chairman Demetrios (Jim) Logothetis. “Dr. Compton brings to the PCAOB a strong combination of analytical experience and accounting expertise.” Dr. Compton joins the PCAOB from PwC International Limited, where she served as a managing director advising the Global Assurance Leadership Team. Before that, she was chief of staff to the PwC US Assurance Leader. Prior to joining PwC, Dr. Compton served as Senior Accounting and Economic Advisor to the Chief Accountant in the SEC’s Office of the Chief Accountant, after beginning her time at the agency as a financial economist in the Division of Economic and Risk Analysis. Previously, Dr. Compton worked as an assistant professor of accounting at the George Washington University and Baruch College. She holds a Ph.D. in accounting from Massachusetts Institute of Technology. “It is an honor to join the PCAOB and my OERA colleagues, and I look forward to our work together to build on the PCAOB’s reputation for high-quality analysis,” said Dr. Compton. Dr. Erik Durbin, who was named the Acting Chief Economist and Acting OERA Director in December 2025, will resume his role as OERA’s Deputy Chief Economist, Economic Analysis, responsible for the process and teams that develop the economic analysis for standard-setting and rulemaking projects and for the post-implementation review of their effectiveness. “We thank Erik, both for stepping in as Acting Director during a transition period and for his continued contributions as an important member of the OERA team,” added Chairman Logothetis. *****About the PCAOBThe PCAOB is a nonprofit corporation established by Congress to oversee the audits of public companies in order to protect investors and further the public interest in the preparation of informative, accurate, and independent audit reports. The PCAOB also oversees the audits of brokers and dealers registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission, including compliance reports filed pursuant to federal securities laws. rows.title: Chief Auditor Barbara Vanich will leave the PCAOB after more than 17 years of service.
rows.desc: Chief Auditor Barbara Vanich to Depart the PCAOB WASHINGTON, Jun. 26, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) today announced that Chief Auditor Barbara Vanich will leave the PCAOB on July 15, 2026, after more than 17 years of service. “I have greatly valued Barb’s expert advice – her accomplishments at the PCAOB have been extraordinary,” said PCAOB Chairman Demetrios (Jim) Logothetis. “We thank her for her leadership and dedication, and we wish her well as she embarks on a new professional opportunity.” Ms. Vanich joined the PCAOB in February 2009. After serving in several roles at the PCAOB – including Associate Chief Auditor, Special Adviser to a Board Member, Deputy Chief Auditor, and Acting Chief Auditor – she was named Chief Auditor in October 2022. During her tenure as Chief Auditor, the PCAOB adopted several new standards that represented important milestones in the PCAOB’s work to improve audit quality and protect investors. Most notably, the PCAOB in May 2024 adopted QC 1000, A Firm’s System of Quality Control. The standard, which will become effective December 15, 2026, features a risk-based approach designed to drive continuous improvement in audit quality. Additionally, Ms. Vanich oversaw the development of other major standard-setting projects, the creation of resources to help audit firms with implementation of new standards, the launch of the PCAOB’s Audit Practitioner Fellowship Program, the PCAOB’s first-ever request for comment on potential future areas of focus for standard setting, and the creation of a Firm Consultation Process through which registered public accounting firms can submit standards-related questions directly to PCAOB staff and receive informal staff views. “It has been an honor to advance the PCAOB’s investor-protection mission, together with my talented colleagues in the Office of the Chief Auditor and so many others across the PCAOB,” said Ms. Vanich. The PCAOB is beginning a search to fill the Chief Auditor role and will solicit applications from qualified candidates soon. *****About the PCAOBThe PCAOB is a nonprofit corporation established by Congress to oversee the audits of public companies in order to protect investors and further the public interest in the preparation of informative, accurate, and independent audit reports. The PCAOB also oversees the audits of brokers and dealers registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission, including compliance reports filed pursuant to federal securities laws. rows.title: The PCAOB today announced the establishment of a Firm Consultation Process designed to provide timely and consistent guidance from PCAOB staff.
rows.desc: PCAOB Staff Launches Firm Consultation Process to Enhance Clarity and to Support Application and Implementation of PCAOB Standards WASHINGTON, Jun. 25, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) today announced the establishment of a Firm Consultation Process, led by its Office of the Chief Auditor (OCA), designed to provide more timely and consistent guidance from PCAOB staff. The new process will allow registered public accounting firms to submit questions directly to OCA staff and receive informal staff views regarding the implementation of new standards and application of existing standards. “Delivering clear guidance is essential to the PCAOB’s efforts to drive further improvement in audit quality,” said Chairman Demetrios (Jim) Logothetis. “This staff-led consultation process is designed to help firms implement new standards and apply our standards more consistently, which will ultimately fulfill the PCAOB’s mission to protect investors.” As part of the Firm Consultation Process, registered firms may request a consultation with OCA on the interpretation and application of PCAOB auditing, attestation, and quality control standards and related rules and forms, as well as PCAOB standards and rules on ethics and independence. If the firm decides to proceed with a consultation under this new process, a request for consultation should be submitted by completing the Consultation Intake Form. OCA does not plan to make consultation requests public but may publish public guidance for questions that are frequently asked or may be of use more generally.*****About the PCAOBThe PCAOB is a nonprofit corporation established by Congress to oversee the audits of public companies in order to protect investors and further the public interest in the preparation of informative, accurate, and independent audit reports. rows.title: The PCAOB announced the appointment of George G. Demos as Director of its Division of Enforcement and Investigations.
rows.desc: George G. Demos Named Director of the PCAOB’s Division of Enforcement and Investigations WASHINGTON, Jun. 15, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) today announced that George G. Demos has been named Director of the PCAOB’s Division of Enforcement and Investigations (DEI). In this role, he will oversee and direct the PCAOB’s investigations and enforcement of violations of its rules, professional standards, and other applicable securities regulations. “Detecting and deterring misconduct is an essential part of how the PCAOB works to improve audit quality and protect investors,” said PCAOB Chairman Demetrios (Jim) Logothetis. “George’s enforcement experience will help the PCAOB advance its goals and fulfill its mission.” Mr. Demos was formerly a litigation partner at DLA Piper LLP, where he represented companies under federal and state investigation and conducted internal corporate reviews. Previously, he served as Senior Counsel at the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission’s Division of Enforcement – leading investigations and prosecutions into accounting fraud, insider trading, and market manipulation – and has been an adjunct professor at UC Davis School of Law. Mr. Demos received a B.A. from Columbia University and a J.D. from Fordham University School of Law. “I am thankful for the opportunity to join the PCAOB, and I look forward to working with the exceptional attorneys, accountants, and other experts on the PCAOB’s enforcement staff,” said Mr. Demos. William Ryan, who was appointed Acting DEI Director in December 2025, will resume his role as DEI’s Chief Counsel, a position to which he was named in 2023. “I want to thank Bill Ryan for his distinguished service over the last six months as Acting Director,” said Chairman Logothetis. “We are fortunate to have Bill on the DEI team.” Learn more about the PCAOB’s enforcement program on the PCAOB website. *****About the PCAOBThe PCAOB is a nonprofit corporation established by Congress to oversee the audits of public companies in order to protect investors and further the public interest in the preparation of informative, accurate, and independent audit reports. The PCAOB also oversees the audits of brokers and dealers registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission, including compliance reports filed pursuant to federal securities laws. Related Topics About the PCAOB

rows.title: The PCAOB has published its annual report on broker-dealer audits.
rows.desc: Annual Report on the Interim Inspection Program Related to Audits of Brokers and Dealers PCAOB Release No. 2026-003 June 11, 2026 Annual Report on the Interim Inspection Program Related to Audits of Brokers and Dealers | 2 PCAOB Release No. 2026-003June 11, 2026 CONTENTS Introduction 3 Overview of 2025 Inspections Results 5 2025 Inspections Approach 9 Information About Selected Firms and Engagements 11 Observations From Inspections 14 PCAOB Standards and Rules Associated With Inspection Observations 34 Learn More 35 Annual Report on the Interim Inspection Program Related to Audits of Brokers and Dealers | 3 PCAOB Release No. 2026-003June 11, 2026 INTRODUCTION The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB or “Board”) has, among its areas of statutory jurisdiction, registration, inspection, standard-setting, and disciplinary authority over the auditors of brokers and dealers registered with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) that are obligated to file with the SEC financial statements subject to audit by a PCAOB-registered firm. Overseeing the audits of these SEC-registered broker-dealers 1 is a key component of our mission to protect investors and further the public interest in the preparation of informative, accurate, and independent audit reports. This Annual Report on the Interim Inspection Program Related to Audits of Brokers and Dealers (“Annual Report”) provides: yInformation about our 2025 inspections approach; and yA summary of our 2025 inspections observations. The information in this Annual Report is provided under the requirements of PCAOB Rule 4020T, Interim Inspection Program Related to Audits of Brokers and Dealers, which addresses, among other things, reporting under the interim inspection program. Under Rule 17a-5 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934 (“Exchange Act”), broker-dealers registered with the SEC are generally required to file the following documents annually with the SEC: 1. Financial Report: A financial report includes financial statements and supporting schedules (“supplemental information”); 2. Compliance or Exemption Report: yA compliance report is required if the broker-dealer did not claim it was exempt f rom Exchange Act Rule 15c3-3, Customer Protection – Reserves and Custody of Securities (“Customer Protection Rule”), or yAn exemption report is required if the broker-dealer did claim it was exempt f rom the Customer Protection Rule or was otherwise eligible under SEC rules to file an exemption report; 2 and 3. Independent Public Accountant Reports: An independent public accountant’s audit report and, based on the broker-dealer’s status, either: yAn examination report on the broker-dealer’s compliance report, performed pursuant to PCAOB attestation standard No. 1, or yA review report on the broker-dealer’s exemption report, performed pursuant to PCAOB attestation standard No. 2. Collectively, AT No. 1 examination engagements and AT No. 2 review engagements are referred to as “attestation engagements.” 1 The use of the term “broker-dealer” in this Annual Report refers to entities that are registered with the SEC as both a broker and a dealer and to entities that are registered as only one or the other. 2 Broker-dealers that carry customer accounts, maintain custody or control of customer cash and securities, or clear securities transactions on behalf of customers, typically do not qualify for an exemption under the Customer Protection Rule. As a result, these broker-dealers are required to file compliance reports. Conversely, most broker-dealers, including those that act solely as introducing broker-dealers, file exemption reports. rows.title: The PCAOB is seeking investors, audit committee members, auditors, financial executives, and other experts to serve on a new advisory body: the Inspections Modernization Council. Applications are due on June 15, 2026.
rows.desc: PCAOB Announces Inspections Modernization Council, Seeks Participation From Outside Experts Focused on modernizing PCAOB inspections, the new advisory body will leverage perspectives from a cross-section of capital markets experts; Deadline for applications is June 15, 2026 WASHINGTON, May 28, 2026 The Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) announced today that it is forming a new advisory body, the Inspections Modernization Council, and is seeking outside parties with a stake in the PCAOB’s inspection activities to participate in its work. Since its creation more than 20 years ago, the PCAOB inspection program has played a significant role in enhancing audit quality. Today, opportunities exist to modernize PCAOB inspections so they remain relevant and resilient. Consultation with outside experts can facilitate such modernization. For the Inspections Modernization Council, the Board seeks participants with capital markets expertise and knowledge of the PCAOB’s inspection program, including investors, audit committee members, financial executives at public companies, academics, technologists, other regulators, and practitioners from public accounting firms of varying sizes. Applicants should have a demonstrated commitment to the interests of investors and the public. “Modernization of PCAOB inspections has the potential to bring improved audit quality and other significant benefits to investors and other stakeholders,” said PCAOB Chairman Demetrios (Jim) Logothetis. “The Inspections Modernization Council will help us shape the future of PCAOB inspections, and we invite individuals of the highest integrity to join us in this effort.” Application and other information can be found on the Inspections Modernization Council page. The application period will close on June 15, 2026. *****About the PCAOBThe PCAOB is a nonprofit corporation established by Congress to oversee the audits of public companies in order to protect investors and further the public interest in the preparation of informative, accurate, and independent audit reports. The PCAOB also oversees the audits of brokers and dealers registered with the Securities and Exchange Commission, including compliance reports filed pursuant to federal securities laws. Related Topics About the PCAOB
rows.summary: The PCAOB is forming an advisory council to help modernize audit inspections and is seeking outside experts to apply by June 15, 2026.

rows.desc: 1666 K Street NW Washington, DC 20006 Office: 202-207-9100 Fax: 202-862-8430 www.pcaobus.org PCAOB Release No. 105-2025-026 July 8, 2025 By this Order Instituting Disciplinary Proceedings, Making Findings, and Imposing Sanctions (“Order”), the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (the “Board” or “PCAOB”) is: (1) censuring Michael Coglianese, CPA P.C. (“Respondent,” or the “Firm”), (2) imposing a civil money penalty in the amount of $50,000 upon the Firm, and (3) requiring the Firm to undertake certain remedial actions as described in Section IV of this Order. The Board is imposing these sanctions on the basis of its findings that the Firm repeatedly violated PCAOB rules and standards across seventeen “broker” and/or “dealer” audits by failing to obtain from a qualified engagement quality reviewer an engagement quality review. I. The Board deems it necessary and appropriate, for the protection of investors and to further the public interest in the preparation of informative, accurate, and independent audit reports, that disciplinary proceedings be, and hereby are, instituted pursuant to Section 105(c) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002, as amended (the “Act”), and PCAOB Rule 5200(a)(1) against Respondent. ORDER INSTITUTING DISCIPLINARY PROCEEDINGS, MAKING FINDINGS, AND IMPOSING SANCTIONS In the Matter of Michael Coglianese, CPA P.C., Respondent. Order PCAOB Release No. 105-2025-026 July 8, 2025 2 II. In anticipation of the institution of these proceedings, and pursuant to PCAOB Rule 5205, Respondent has submitted an Offer of Settlement (“Offer”) that the Board has determined to accept. Solely for purposes of these proceedings and any other proceedings brought by or on behalf of the Board, or to which the Board is a party, and without admitting or denying the findings herein, except as to the Board’s jurisdiction over Respondent and the subject matter of these proceedings, which is admitted, Respondent consents to entry of this Order. 1 III. On the basis of Respondent’s Offer, the Board finds that: A. Respondent 1. Michael Coglianese, CPA P.C. is a public accounting firm located in Bloomingdale, Illinois. Respondent is licensed to practice public accounting by the Illinois Department of Financial & Professional Regulation (license number 066005163). 2 The Firm has one owner and one partner (the “Partner”). At all relevant times, the Firm was registered with the Board pursuant to Section 102 of the Act and PCAOB rules. B. Summary 2. This matter concerns the Firm’s repeated violations of AS 1220, Engagement Quality Review, 3 by its failure to have an engagement quality review performed by a partner or partner equivalent on multiple broker-dealer audit and attestation engagements. It also involves the Firm’s violation of QC Section 20.01, System of Quality Control for a CPA Firm’s Accounting and Auditing Practice, through the Firm’s failure to establish a system of quality control that provided reasonable assurance that engagement quality reviews would be performed on all audits in accordance with PCAOB standards. 1 The findings herein are made pursuant to the Respondent’s Offer and are not binding on any other person or entity in this or any other proceeding. 2 Respondent is also licensed to practice public accounting in Connecticut (license number CPAP.0005552), New Jersey (license number 20CZ00007300), Georgia (license number ACF005935), and North Carolina (license number 32504). 3 All references to PCAOB rules and standards in this Order are to the versions of those rules and standards, and to their organization and numbering, in effect at the time of the audits discussed herein. Order PCAOB Release No. 105-2025-026 July 8, 2025 3 C. Respondent Violated PCAOB Rules and Standards 3. PCAOB rules require that registered public accounting firms and their associated persons comply with applicable auditing and related professional practice standards. 4 PCAOB rules further require registered firms and their associated persons to comply with PCAOB quality control standards. 5 As set forth below, the Firm repeatedly failed to comply with AS 1220 and failed to comply with PCAOB quality control standards. i. The Firm Repeatedly Violated PCAOB Rules and Standards by Failing to Use a Qualified Engagement Quality Reviewer to Provide Concurring Approvals of Issuance 4. PCAOB standards require that an engagement quality review be performed on all audits, as well as on all attestation engagements performed pursuant to Attestation Standard No. 1, Examination Engagements Regarding Compliance Reports of Brokers and Dealers, or Attestation Standard No. 2, Review Engagements Regarding Exemption Reports of Brokers and Dealers. 6 5. A firm may grant permission to a client to use an engagement report only after an engagement quality reviewer provides concurring approval of issuance of the report. 7 An engagement quality reviewer from the firm that issues the engagement report must be “a partner or another individual in an equiva
rows.summary: The PCAOB censured Michael Coglianese, CPA P.C., fined it $50,000, and ordered fixes after finding quality review failures on 17 audits.

rows.title: PCAOB imposes a total of $8.5 million in fines on three Dutch firms for quality control violations related to widespread training exam misconduct.

If we include a deficiency in Part I.A, Part I.B, or Part I.C of this report, it does not necessarily mean that the firm has not addressed the deficiency. The identified deficiencies primarily related to the firm’s testing of controls over and/or substantive testing of revenue and related accounts and long-lived assets. The most common Part I.A deficiencies in 2025 related to evaluating the appropriateness of the issuer’s accounting method or disclosure, testing the design or operating effectiveness of controls selected for testing, and testing an estimate. The Part I.B deficiencies in 2025 related to audit committee communications, management communications, critical audit matters, the firm’s audit report, and Form AP. The most common Part I.C deficiencies in 2025 related to audit committee pre-approval, unpaid fees, financial relationships, and non-audit services. A-1 KPMG Auditores Independentes Ltda., PCAOB Release No. 104-2026-062, June 11, 2026 | 2 2025 INSPECTION In the 2025 inspection of KPMG Auditores Independentes Ltda., the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) assessed the firm’s compliance with laws, rules, and professional standards applicable to the audits of issuers. We selected for review three audits of issuers with fiscal years ending in 2024. For each issuer audit selected, we reviewed a portion of the audit. We also evaluated elements of the firm’s system of quality control. 2025 Inspection Approach In selecting issuer audits for review, we use a risk-based method of selection. We make selections based on (1) our internal evaluation of audits we believe have a heightened risk of material misstatement, including those with challenging audit areas, and (2) other risk-based characteristics, including issuer and firm considerations. In certain situations, we may select all of the firm’s issuer audits for review. When we review an audit, we do not review every aspect of the audit. Rather, we generally focus our attention on audit areas we believe to be of greater complexity, areas of greater significance or with a heightened risk of material misstatement to the issuer’s financial statements, and areas of recurring deficiencies. We may also select some audit areas for review in a manner designed to incorporate unpredictability. Our selection of audits for review does not necessarily constitute a representative sample of the firm’s total population of issuer audits. Additionally, our inspection findings are specific to the particular portions of the issuer audits reviewed. They are not an assessment of all of the firm’s audit work or of all of the audit procedures performed for the audits reviewed. View the details on thescope of our inspections and our inspections procedures. We use a risk-based method to select audits for review and to identify areas on which we focus our review. rows.desc: May 21, 2026 2025 Inspection KPMG LLP (Headquartered in New York, New York) THIS IS A PUBLIC VERSION OF A PCAOB INSPECTION REPORT PORTIONS OF THE COMPLETE REPORT ARE OMITTED FROM THIS DOCUMENT IN ORDER TO COMPLY WITH SECTIONS 104(g)(2) AND 105(b)(5)(A) OF THE SARBANES-OXLEY ACT OF 2002 PCAOB RELEASE NO. 104-2026-087 KPMG LLP, PCAOB Release No. 104-2026-087, May 21, 2026 | 1 EXECUTIVE SUMMARY Our 2025 inspection report on KPMG LLP provides information on our inspection to assess the firm’s compliance with Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) standards and rules and other applicable regulatory and professional requirements. This executive summary offers a high-level overview of what is included in this report: Part I.A of the report discusses deficiencies (“Part I.A deficiencies”) in certain issuer audits that were of such significance that we believe the firm, at the time it issued its audit report(s), had not obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence to support its opinion(s) on the issuer’s financial statements and/or internal control over financial reporting (ICFR). Part I.B of the report discusses certain deficiencies (“Part I.B deficiencies”) that relate to instances of non-compliance with PCAOB standards or rules other than those where the firm had not obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence to support its opinion(s). This section does not discuss instances of apparent non-compliance with rules related to maintaining independence. Part I.C of the report discusses instances of apparent non-compliance with rules related to maintaining independence (“Part I.C deficiencies”). If we include a Part I.A or Part I.B deficiency in this report — other than those deficiencies for audits with incorrect opinions on the financial statements and/or ICFR — it does not necessarily mean that the issuer’s financial statements are materially misstated or that undisclosed material weaknesses in ICFR exist. If we include a Part I.C deficiency in this report, it does not necessarily mean that the Board has concluded the firm was not objective and impartial throughout the audit and professional engagement period. If we include a deficiency in Part I.A, Part I.B, or Part I.C of this report, it does not necessarily mean that the firm has not addressed the deficiency. KPMG LLP, PCAOB Release No. 104-2026-087, May 21, 2026 | 2 Overview of the 2025 Deficiencies Included in Part I Eight of the 64 audits we reviewed in 2025 are included in Part I.A of this report due to the significance of the deficiencies identified. The identified deficiencies primarily related to the firm’s testing of controls over and/or substantive testing of inventory and other assets. The most common Part I.A deficiencies in 2025 related to identifying controls related to a significant account or relevant assertion, testing the design or operating effectiveness of controls selected for testing, and performing substantive testing to address a risk of material misstatement. The Part I.B deficiencies in 2025 related to retention of audit documentation, audit committee communications, audit planning, risk assessment, critical audit matters, the firm’s audit report, and Form AP. The most common Part I.C deficiencies in 2025 related to audit committee pre-approval, financial relationships, and business relationships. A-1 Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu Auditores Independentes Ltda., PCAOB Release No. 104-2026-051, April 30, 2026 | 2 2024 INSPECTION In the 2024 inspection of Deloitte Touche Tohmatsu Auditores Independentes Ltda., the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) assessed the firm’s compliance with laws, rules, and professional standards applicable to the audits of public companies. We selected for review three audits of issuers with fiscal years ending in 2023. For each issuer audit selected, we reviewed a portion of the audit. We also evaluated elements of the firm’s system of quality control. 2024 Inspection Approach In selecting issuer audits for review, we use a risk-based method of selection. We make selections based on (1) our internal evaluation of audits we believe have a heightened risk of material misstatement, including those with challenging audit areas, and (2) other risk-based characteristics, including issuer and firm considerations. In certain situations, we may select all of the firm’s issuer audits for review. When we review an audit, we do not review every aspect of the audit. Rather, we generally focus our attention on audit areas we believe to be of greater complexity, areas of greater significance or with a heightened risk of material misstatement to the issuer’s financial statements, and areas of recurring deficiencies. We may also select some audit areas for review in a manner designed to incorporate unpredictability. Our selection of audits for review does not necessarily constitute a representative sample of the firm’s total population of issuer audits. Additionally, our inspection findings are specific to the particular portions of the issuer audits reviewed. They are not an assessment of all of the firm’s audit work or of all of the audit procedures performed for the audits reviewed. View the details on thescope of our inspections and our inspections procedures. We use a risk-based method to select audits for review and to identify areas on which we focus our review. Because our inspection process evolves over time, it can, and often does, focus on a different mix of audits and audit areas from inspection to inspection and firm to firm. A-1 Ernst & Young LLP, PCAOB Release No. 104-2026-044, March 26, 2026 | 2 2024 INSPECTION In the 2024 inspection of Ernst & Young LLP, the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) assessed the firm’s compliance with laws, rules, and professional standards applicable to the audits of public companies. Our inspection was conducted in cooperation with the Financial Reporting Council of the United Kingdom. We selected for review three audits of issuers with fiscal years ending in 2023. For each issuer audit selected, we reviewed a portion of the audit. We also evaluated elements of the firm’s system of quality control. 2024 Inspection Approach In selecting issuer audits for review, we use a risk-based method of selection. We make selections based on (1) our internal evaluation of audits we believe have a heightened risk of material misstatement, including those with challenging audit areas, and (2) other risk-based characteristics, including issuer and firm considerations. In certain situations, we may select all of the firm’s issuer audits for review. When we review an audit, we do not review every aspect of the audit. Rather, we generally focus our attention on audit areas we believe to be of greater complexity, areas of greater significance or with a heightened risk of material misstatement to the issuer’s financial statements, and areas of recurring deficiencies. We may also select some audit areas for review in a manner designed to incorporate unpredictability. Our selection of audits for review does not necessarily constitute a representative sample of the firm’s total population of issuer audits. Additionally, our inspection findings are specific to the particular portions of the issuer audits reviewed. They are not an assessment of all of the firm’s audit work or of all of the audit procedures performed for the audits reviewed. View the details on thescope of our inspections and our inspections procedures. Ernst & Young LLP, PCAOB Release No. 104-2026-044, March 26, 2026 | 3 OVERVIEW OF THE 2024 INSPECTION AND HISTORICAL DATA BY INSPECTION YEAR The following information provides an overview of our 2024 inspection as well as data from the previous inspection. We use a risk-based method to select audits for review and to identify areas on which we focus our review. Because our inspection process evolves over time, it can, and often does, focus on a different mix of audits and audit areas from inspection to inspection and firm to firm. Further, a firm’s business, the applicable auditing standards, or other factors can change from the time of one inspection to the next. As a result of these variations, we caution that our inspection results are not necessarily comparable over time or among firms. Our inspection was conducted in cooperation with the Belgian Audit Oversight Board. We selected for review three audits of issuers with fiscal years ending in 2024. For each issuer audit selected, we reviewed a portion of the audit. We also evaluated elements of the firm’s system of quality control. 2025 Inspection Approach In selecting issuer audits for review, we use a risk-based method of selection. We make selections based on (1) our internal evaluation of audits we believe have a heightened risk of material misstatement, including those with challenging audit areas, and (2) other risk-based characteristics, including issuer and firm considerations. In certain situations, we may select all of the firm’s issuer audits for review. When we review an audit, we do not review every aspect of the audit. Rather, we generally focus our attention on audit areas we believe to be of greater complexity, areas of greater significance or with a heightened risk of material misstatement to the issuer’s financial statements, and areas of recurring deficiencies. We may also select some audit areas for review in a manner designed to incorporate unpredictability. Our selection of audits for review does not necessarily constitute a representative sample of the firm’s total population of issuer audits. Additionally, our inspection findings are specific to the particular portions of the issuer audits reviewed. They are not an assessment of all of the firm’s audit work or of all of the audit procedures performed for the audits reviewed. View the details on thescope of our inspections and our inspections procedures. A-1 PricewaterhouseCoopers Statsautoriseret Revisionspartnerselskab, PCAOB Release No. 104-2026-036, January 29, 2026 | 2 2025 INSPECTION In the 2025 inspection of PricewaterhouseCoopers Statsautoriseret Revisionspartnerselskab, the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) assessed the firm’s compliance with laws, rules, and professional standards applicable to the audits of issuers. Our inspection was conducted in cooperation with the Danish Business Authority. We selected for review three audits of issuers with fiscal years generally ending in 2024. For each issuer audit selected, we reviewed a portion of the audit. We also evaluated elements of the firm’s system of quality control. 2025 Inspection Approach In selecting issuer audits for review, we use a risk-based method of selection. We make selections based on (1) our internal evaluation of audits we believe have a heightened risk of material misstatement, including those with challenging audit areas, and (2) other risk-based characteristics, including issuer and firm considerations. In certain situations, we may select all of the firm’s issuer audits for review. When we review an audit, we do not review every aspect of the audit. Rather, we generally focus our attention on audit areas we believe to be of greater complexity, areas of greater significance or with a heightened risk of material misstatement to the issuer’s financial statements, and areas of recurring deficiencies. We may also select some audit areas for review in a manner designed to incorporate unpredictability. Our selection of audits for review does not necessarily constitute a representative sample of the firm’s total population of issuer audits. Additionally, our inspection findings are specific to the particular portions of the issuer audits reviewed. They are not an assessment of all of the firm’s audit work or of all of the audit procedures performed for the audits reviewed. View the details on thescope of our inspections and our inspections procedures. A-1 KPMG AS, PCAOB Release No. 104-2026-004, November 10, 2025| 2 2024 INSPECTION In the 2024 inspection of KPMG AS, the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) assessed the firm’s compliance with laws, rules, and professional standards applicable to the audits of public companies. Our inspection was conducted in cooperation with the Financial Supervisory Authority of Norway. We selected for review three audits of issuers with fiscal years ending in 2023. For each issuer audit selected, we reviewed a portion of the audit. We also evaluated elements of the firm’s system of quality control. 2024 Inspection Approach In selecting issuer audits for review, we use a risk-based method of selection. We make selections based on (1) our internal evaluation of audits we believe have a heightened risk of material misstatement, including those with challenging audit areas, and (2) other risk-based characteristics, including issuer and firm considerations. In certain situations, we may select all of the firm’s issuer audits for review. When we review an audit, we do not review every aspect of the audit. Rather, we generally focus our attention on audit areas we believe to be of greater complexity, areas of greater significance or with a heightened risk of material misstatement to the issuer’s financial statements, and areas of recurring deficiencies. We may also select some audit areas for review in a manner designed to incorporate unpredictability. Our selection of audits for review does not necessarily constitute a representative sample of the firm’s total population of issuer audits. Additionally, our inspection findings are specific to the particular portions of the issuer audits reviewed. They are not an assessment of all of the firm’s audit work or of all of the audit procedures performed for the audits reviewed. View the details on thescope of our inspections and our inspections procedures. rows.summary:
This PCAOB public inspection report covers Rehmann Robson LLC, headquartered in Saginaw, Michigan, and is dated October 23, 2025. The Board’s 2025 inspection assessed the firm’s compliance with applicable laws, PCAOB rules, and professional standards in connection with issuer audits, and also evaluated selected elements of the firm’s quality control system. For the 2025 cycle, PCAOB reviewed portions of two issuer audits using a risk-based selection process; the report emphasizes that the selected audits and audit areas are not a representative sample of the firm’s full issuer-audit population, and findings relate only to the portions reviewed.

The historical data in the report shows the firm’s issuer-audit footprint increased from 3 total issuer audit clients in the prior inspection year shown (2022) to 7 in 2025, with 1 total engagement partner on issuer audit work in 2025. The report also notes that the firm was the lead auditor on both audits reviewed in 2025, and that there were no Part I.A deficiencies in the 2025 inspection sample shown in the table. The report cautions that if a Part I.A deficiency is identified, that does not necessarily mean the firm failed to remediate it; remedial actions can include additional audit work, informing management of needed financial statement or ICFR changes, or steps to prevent reliance on prior audit reports, and PCAOB may review the adequacy of those remedial actions on a sample basis.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that this document is an inspection report rather than a rulemaking or enforcement directive: it does not announce a new filing deadline, threshold, or rate, but it does signal how PCAOB is evaluating the firm’s audit quality and quality-control practices. Rehmann Robson’s obligations in this context are to ensure continued adherence to PCAOB auditing standards, maintain effective quality control over issuer audits, and respond appropriately if inspection findings identify deficiencies in future reports. The report is expressly a public version, with portions omitted to comply with Sections 104(g)(2) and 105(b)(5)(A) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act.

rows.summary:
This PCAOB public inspection report covers Nichols, Cauley & Associates, LLC, headquartered in Dublin, Georgia, and reflects the Board’s 2025 inspection dated October 23, 2025. The inspection reviewed one issuer audit for a fiscal year ending in 2024, selected using the PCAOB’s risk-based methodology; only a portion of that audit was reviewed, and the PCAOB also assessed elements of the firm’s system of quality control. The report emphasizes that the inspection findings apply only to the specific portions reviewed and are not a conclusion about all audit work performed by the firm or all procedures in the audit.

For 2025, the firm had one total issuer audit client for which it served as lead auditor and one total engagement partner on issuer audit work. The PCAOB reviewed one audit, which was a lead-auditor engagement and was not an integrated audit of financial statements and internal control over financial reporting (ICFR). The firm had a Part I.A deficiency in the audit reviewed, resulting in a 100% rate of audits with Part I.A deficiencies for both 2025 and the prior 2023 inspection data shown in the report. The report also notes that the existence of a Part I.A deficiency does not necessarily mean the firm failed to address it afterward, because remedial actions may include additional audit procedures, notifying management of needed financial statement or ICFR changes, or taking steps to prevent reliance on the affected work.

The document explains that the PCAOB’s audit selection process is risk-based and focuses on areas judged to have a heightened risk of material misstatement, greater complexity, significant judgment, recurring deficiencies, or other unpredictability. Because the inspection process changes over time and firms’ circumstances can change between inspections, the PCAOB warns that inspection results are not necessarily comparable across years or across firms. The report also notes that the firm may have taken remedial actions after the deficiencies were identified, such as performing additional procedures, advising issuer management about possible financial statement or ICFR changes, or taking steps to prevent reliance on prior audit reports.

This is a public PCAOB inspection report for Marcum LLP, headquartered in New York, New York, covering the firm’s 2024 inspection and issued June 25, 2025. The PCAOB reviewed 26 issuer audits with fiscal years ending in 2023 and evaluated selected portions of those audits as well as elements of the firm’s system of quality control. The report is not itself a new rulemaking document, but it is a regulatory finding about audit quality and compliance with PCAOB standards, rules, and other applicable professional requirements.

The PCAOB found that 21 of the 26 reviewed audits were serious enough to be included in Part I.A, meaning the deficiencies were significant enough that, in the PCAOB’s view, Marcum had not obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence to support its audit opinion(s) on the issuer’s financial statements and/or internal control over financial reporting at the time the opinions were issued. The most common problems in these Part I.A audits involved testing controls over or substantive testing of revenue and related accounts, goodwill and intangible assets, and long-lived assets; the PCAOB specifically noted recurring deficiencies in how the firm performed substantive procedures to address risks of material misstatement, tested estimates, and tested data or reports used in substantive testing.

The report also identifies Part I.B deficiencies, which are other noncompliance issues with PCAOB standards or rules that did not rise to the level of unsupported audit opinions. These included deficiencies related to consideration of fraud, engagement quality review, audit committee communications, risk assessment, management communications, critical audit matters, the audit report itself, and Form AP. In addition, the report lists Part I.C independence issues, including audit committee pre-approval, financial relationships, partner rotation, and tax services provided to persons in financial reporting oversight roles. The report expressly states that inclusion of a deficiency does not automatically mean the issuer’s financial statements are materially misstated, that a material weakness in ICFR exists, that the Board concluded the firm lacked objectivity and impartiality, or that the firm has not already addressed the deficiency.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the PCAOB is signaling elevated risk in Marcum’s audit methodology and independence practices, especially around revenue, estimates, and audit evidence reliability. There are no explicit remediation deadlines, effective dates, monetary penalties, or mandated corrective actions in the excerpt provided, but the inspection findings are significant because they may affect regulatory scrutiny of the firm’s issuer audits, its quality control remediation efforts, and any issuer or audit committee decision-making regarding engagement oversight, independence monitoring, and audit evidence standards.

rows.summary:
This is a PCAOB public inspection report dated June 25, 2025 covering Forvis Mazars, LLP’s 2024 inspection, based on 14 issuer audits with fiscal years generally ending in 2023. The PCAOB’s review was limited to portions of selected audits and also included an evaluation of elements of the firm’s system of quality control. The report is an inspection finding, not a new rule, but it identifies areas where the PCAOB believes the firm did not fully comply with applicable auditing, independence, and professional requirements.

The most significant findings are in Part I.A: 10 of the 14 audits reviewed were placed in this category because the deficiencies were serious enough that the PCAOB believed the firm, at the time it issued its audit reports, had not obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence to support its opinion(s) on the issuer’s financial statements and/or internal control over financial reporting (ICFR). The report says these deficiencies primarily involved testing controls and/or substantive testing of allowance for credit losses, business combinations, revenue, and related accounts. The most common issues were failures in testing the design or operating effectiveness of selected controls, inadequate testing of estimates, insufficient testing of data or reports used in substantive procedures, and failure to identify controls related to significant accounts or relevant assertions.

Part I.B identifies other PCAOB standard/rule compliance problems that were not framed as unsupported-opinion issues. These related to audit committee communications, the firm’s audit report, and consideration of fraud. Part I.C identifies one independence-related issue, specifically involving audit committee pre-approval. The report emphasizes that inclusion of a deficiency does not automatically mean the issuer’s financial statements are materially misstated, that undisclosed material weaknesses in ICFR exist, or that the PCAOB concluded the firm was not objective and impartial throughout the engagement period.

For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that the PCAOB expects stronger audit evidence around high-risk areas such as allowance for credit losses, business combinations, and revenue, and better execution of control testing, estimate testing, and reliance on system-generated data/reports. The report does not state a remediation deadline or impose a direct penalty in the text provided, but it serves as a formal regulatory signal that the firm’s audit methodology, documentation, and independence governance were deficient in multiple engagements during the 2024 inspection cycle.

The PCAOB says those deficiencies primarily involved the firm’s substantive testing of revenue, business combinations, warrants, and equity. In two audits, the inspection work was tied to the issuer restating its financial statements to correct misstatements, and the firm revised and reissued its audit report on those financial statements.

The Part I.B deficiencies concerned audit-process and standards issues, specifically retention of audit documentation, engagement quality review, audit committee communications, auditor tenure, and critical audit matters. The Part I.C independence issues related to audit committee pre-approval and financial relationships. rows.summary:
The PCAOB’s May 22, 2025 2024 inspection report on Crowe LLP (Chicago) describes the firm’s compliance with PCAOB standards, rules, and other applicable professional requirements in audits of issuers, based on review of 17 issuer audits with fiscal years ending in 2023. The report’s most serious findings are in Part I.A: three of the 17 audits reviewed contained deficiencies significant enough that the PCAOB believed Crowe had **not obtained sufficient appropriate audit evidence** to support its audit opinions on the issuer financial statements and/or internal control over financial reporting at the time the opinions were issued. The principal problem areas were Crowe’s **testing of controls over, and substantive testing of, the allowance for credit losses**.  

The report says the most common Part I.A issues involved failures in testing the **design or operating effectiveness of controls selected for testing**, failures to test controls over the **accuracy and completeness of data or reports** used in operating controls, and deficiencies in testing an **estimate**. For compliance purposes, this signals heightened risk around audit evidence and control testing for credit loss estimation processes, especially where the firm relies on system-generated reports or data inputs. The report also cautions that a Part I.A deficiency does not automatically mean the issuer’s financial statements were materially misstated or that an undisclosed material weakness existed, but it does mean the PCAOB concluded the audit evidence was insufficient for the issued opinion.  

Part I.B identifies other PCAOB standards/rule violations that did not rise to the level of unsupported opinions. In 2024, those deficiencies related to **consideration of fraud, retention of audit documentation, audit committee communications, and risk assessment**. These are important compliance points because they indicate weaknesses in audit planning, documentation discipline, governance communications, and fraud/risk procedures, even where the PCAOB did not conclude the opinion was unsupported.  

Part I.C identifies apparent independence violations tied to **audit committee pre-approval**. For a compliance team, that means the report also raises issues around ensuring required audit committee authorization procedures were followed before audit services were performed. The report notes that inclusion of a deficiency in Part I.C does not necessarily mean the PCAOB concluded the firm was not objective and impartial, but it does indicate a potential failure to comply with independence-related pre-approval requirements.  

No specific remediation deadline or monetary penalty is stated in the excerpt provided; the report is an inspection finding document rather than an enforcement order. However, the inspection date is **May 22, 2025**, and the audited periods reviewed were **fiscal years ending in 2023**, so the compliance significance is immediate for any Crowe audit clients and for firms with similar control-testing and audit committee approval processes.

Our selection of audits for review does not necessarily constitute a representative sample of the firm’s total population of issuer audits. rows.summary:
This PCAOB public inspection report covers CBIZ CPAs P.C. (formerly Mayer Hoffman McCann P.C.), headquartered in New York, and was issued May 22, 2025 as PCAOB Release No. 104-2025-092. The Board inspected the firm’s audits of public companies for 2024, selecting two issuer audits for review, both involving fiscal years ending in 2022, and also evaluated elements of the firm’s system of quality control. The report emphasizes that the inspection used a risk-based selection process, focused only on portions of the selected audits rather than full engagements, and therefore the findings are limited to the specific audit areas reviewed rather than a determination about all of the firm’s audit work.

The overview section shows the firm’s public-company audit footprint and inspection sample changed from the prior inspection year: in 2024 the firm had 22 total issuer audit clients as principal auditor, compared with 37 in 2021; the report also lists 1 total engagement partner on issuer audit work in 2024 and 15 in 2021. The firm had 2 audits reviewed in 2024, both principal-auditor audits, with 0 integrated audits of financial statements and ICFR reviewed; in the comparable 2021 inspection, 4 audits were reviewed, including 2 integrated audits. The report states that 1 of the 2 reviewed audits in 2024 had Part I.A deficiencies, resulting in a 50% deficiency rate, versus 3 of 4 audits and a 75% deficiency rate in the prior inspection.

For compliance purposes, the most important practical point is that a Part I.A deficiency means PCAOB inspectors concluded the audit opinion was unsupported in the specific area(s) reviewed, but the report also notes that this does not necessarily mean the firm failed to remediate the issue afterward; remediation may include additional audit work, informing management that financial statements or ICFR reporting must be changed, or taking steps to prevent reliance on the prior audit reports. The report also makes clear that the inspection findings are not a representative sample of all of the firm’s issuer audits, and the results are not directly comparable across years because the inspection scope, risk focus, firm circumstances, and standards can change. While the excerpt provided does not include the substantive Part I findings, the report as a whole signals that CBIZ’s public-company audit practice was subject to PCAOB scrutiny and had at least one unsupported-opinion deficiency in the 2024 inspection cycle, which should be considered in any internal quality control or vendor oversight review.

rows.summary:
This PCAOB report is the Board’s **first inspection of KPMG’s Hong Kong practice** and covers the firm’s 2024 work on audits of public companies; the inspection was conducted with the **China Securities Regulatory Commission, the Ministry of Finance of the PRC, and Hong Kong’s Accounting and Financial Reporting Council**. The PCAOB states that it reviewed **three issuer audits** and certain elements of the firm’s **quality control system**, using a **risk-based selection approach** rather than a full-scope review, so the findings apply only to the portions of the audits actually inspected and are **not a representative sample** of all KPMG audits. KPMG’s 2024 issuer-audit footprint in the report was small: **1 issuer audit client where KPMG was principal auditor**, **15 issuer audits where it was not principal auditor**, and **12 engagement partners** on issuer audit work.

From a compliance perspective, the most important point is that the inspection found **deficiencies in 2 of the 3 audits reviewed**, meaning **67%** of the reviewed audits had Part I.A deficiencies. The report says these deficiencies were serious enough to be categorized as **“Audits with Unsupported Opinions,”** which indicates the PCAOB believed the audit work did not provide sufficient support for the opinions issued on those engagements. The report also notes there were **other instances of non-compliance with PCAOB standards or rules** and a separate section on **independence**, plus observations related to the firm’s **quality control** system; however, the excerpt provided does not include the specific findings in those sections.

The report is dated **May 22, 2025** and is a **public version** of the inspection report; parts were omitted under **Sections 104(g)(2) and 105(b)(5)(A) of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002**, which is standard for PCAOB public releases. The inspection overview also emphasizes that any deficiency listed in Part I does **not automatically mean the firm failed to remedy the issue**, because the PCAOB notes that firms often perform **remedial actions after the deficiency is identified**. For compliance teams, the practical takeaway is that KPMG Hong Kong was subject to PCAOB inspection oversight in 2024, that the inspection identified material audit-quality concerns in a majority of the reviewed engagements, and that any company relying on KPMG Hong Kong for PCAOB-regulated audit work should treat this report as a signal to scrutinize auditor oversight, independence, and audit-quality remediation closely.

We selected for review one audit of an issuer with a fiscal year ending in 2023. For the issuer audit selected, we reviewed a portion of the audit. We also evaluated elements of the firm’s system of quality control. 2024 Inspection Approach In selecting issuer audits for review, we use a risk-based method of selection. We make selections based on (1) our internal evaluation of audits we believe have a heightened risk of material misstatement, including those with challenging audit areas, and (2) other risk-based characteristics, including issuer and firm considerations. In certain situations, we may select all of the firm’s issuer audits for review. When we review an audit, we do not review every aspect of the audit. Rather, we generally focus our attention on audit areas we believe to be of greater complexity, areas of greater significance or with a heightened risk of material misstatement to the issuer’s financial statements, and areas of recurring deficiencies. We may also select some audit areas for review in a manner designed to incorporate unpredictability. Our selection of audits for review does not necessarily constitute a representative sample of the firm’s total population of issuer audits. Additionally, our inspection findings are specific to the particular portions of the issuer audits reviewed. They are not an assessment of all of the firm’s audit work or of all of the audit procedures performed for the audits reviewed. This PCAOB public inspection report covers Yu Certified Public Accountant, P.C. for the 2024 inspection cycle and was issued on May 8, 2025. The PCAOB reviewed one issuer audit for a fiscal year ending in 2023, selected using its risk-based inspection methodology, and also evaluated elements of the firm’s system of quality control. The report makes clear that PCAOB inspection findings apply only to the portions of the audit reviewed and are not a full assessment of all audit work or all procedures performed on the engagement.

For the 2024 inspection year, the firm reported 5 total issuer audit clients for which it served as principal auditor and 1 total engagement partner on issuer audit work. The PCAOB reviewed 1 audit, and that audit was not an integrated audit of financial statements and internal control over financial reporting. The report shows no Part I.A deficiencies in the 2024 inspection, compared with 1 audit with Part I.A deficiencies in the prior inspection year shown in the historical data, meaning the percentage of audits with Part I.A deficiencies moved from 100% in the prior year to 0% in 2024.

The inspection approach described in the report emphasizes that PCAOB audit selections are risk-based and may focus on audits or areas with heightened risk of material misstatement, challenging audit areas, greater significance, recurring deficiencies, or other firm/issuer risk characteristics. The PCAOB also states that inspections do not necessarily produce a representative sample of all issuer audits, and the findings are specific to the reviewed portions of the audit, not to the firm’s overall audit practice.

From a compliance perspective, the document is a public PCAOB inspection report rather than a rulemaking or enforcement order, so it does not itself impose a new deadline, filing obligation, or numeric threshold on the firm. Its practical compliance significance is that it documents the firm’s current PCAOB inspection status, the scale of its issuer practice, and whether the inspected engagement had any reported Part I.A deficiencies; here, the public report indicates none for 2024.

This is a PCAOB 2024 inspection report for Ernst & Young Auditores Independentes S/S Ltda. in São Paulo, Brazil, issued May 8, 2025. The PCAOB reviewed three audits of issuers with fiscal years ending in 2023, using a risk-based selection process that focuses on higher-risk or more complex audit areas and does not represent a full review of all audit work. For the 2024 inspection, the firm had 7 issuer audit clients where it was the principal auditor, 49 issuer audits where it was not the principal auditor, and 150 total engagement partners on issuer audit work; the report compares this with 2021 figures of 13, 54, and 152, respectively.

The inspection found no Part I.A deficiencies, meaning the PCAOB did not identify any audits with unsupported opinions in the areas reviewed, and the percentage of reviewed audits with Part I.A deficiencies was 0%. The report also indicates that the PCAOB reviewed two integrated audits of financial statements and internal control over financial reporting (ICFR), and one additional audit where the firm was not the principal auditor. Because the inspection was limited to selected portions of selected audits, the findings apply only to the specific audit areas reviewed and are not a conclusion about all of the firm’s audit work.

The document also notes that the PCAOB evaluated elements of the firm’s system of quality control, but the excerpt provided does not include the detailed Part II quality control observations. For compliance purposes, the key takeaway is that this public report reflects the PCAOB’s 2024 inspection of the firm’s issuer-audit practice and confirms that no unsupported-opinion findings were reported in the inspected work, while still signaling that quality control was reviewed and may have additional observations elsewhere in the full report. The report also emphasizes that inspection selections are risk-based and may not be comparable year over year because the mix of audits, audit areas, and firm circumstances can change.

This PCAOB report is a 2024 inspection of Kronick Kalada Berdy & Co, P.C. (headquartered in Kingston, Pennsylvania), issued publicly on May 8, 2025 as PCAOB Release No. 104-2025-086. The PCAOB reviewed two issuer audits for fiscal years ending in 2022 and also evaluated elements of the firm’s system of quality control; the report explains that inspections are risk-based and limited to selected portions of selected audits, so the findings are not a full assessment of all audit work or all issuer audits performed by the firm.

For compliance purposes, the most important point is that the report is an inspection report, not a rulemaking change, and it identifies deficiencies in the firm’s audits and/or quality control rather than imposing new regulatory requirements on issuers. The firm had 7 total issuer audit clients in 2024, compared with 8 in the prior inspection year shown in the report; it had 1 engagement partner on issuer audit work in 2024, compared with 3 in the prior year. Two audits were reviewed in both years, and in 2024 both reviewed audits were principal-auditor engagements; none were integrated audits of financial statements and ICFR.

The report’s historical comparison shows that in the prior inspection year one of the two reviewed audits had a Part I.A deficiency, while in the 2024 inspection none of the reviewed audits had a Part I.A deficiency. Part I.A in PCAOB inspection reports refers to audits with unsupported opinions, so the absence of Part I.A deficiencies in 2024 indicates the PCAOB did not identify unsupported-opinion findings in the portion of the reviewed work. The report also states that the PCAOB focused on areas it considered higher risk, more complex, or more significant, and that inspection findings apply only to the portions of the audits actually reviewed.

No new deadlines, reporting dates, remediation deadlines, fees, or numeric thresholds are imposed on clients or audit firms in the excerpt provided beyond the inspection date and the historical audit-count statistics. The document is mainly a PCAOB oversight report for the firm’s audit practice, and any compliance relevance for a corporate team would be indirect: if Kronick Kalada Berdy & Co. is the company’s auditor or could be considered for engagement, this inspection report provides context on the PCAOB’s review results and the size and scope of the firm’s issuer-audit practice.

A-1 Crowe PR PSC, PCAOB Release No. 104-2024-163, October 24, 2024 | 2 2024 INSPECTION In the 2024 inspection of Crowe PR PSC, the Public Company Accounting Oversight Board (PCAOB) assessed the firm’s compliance with laws, rules, and professional standards applicable to the audits of public companies. We selected for review one audit of an issuer with a fiscal year ending in 2023. For the issuer audit selected, we reviewed a portion of the audit. We also evaluated elements of the firm’s system of quality control. 2024 Inspection Approach In selecting issuer audits for review, we use a risk-based method of selection. We make selections based on (1) our internal evaluation of audits we believe have a heightened risk of material misstatement, including those with challenging audit areas, and (2) other risk-based characteristics, including issuer and firm considerations. In certain situations, we may select all of the firm’s issuer audits for review. When we review an audit, we do not review every aspect of the audit. Rather, we generally focus our attention on audit areas we believe to be of greater complexity, areas of greater significance or with a heightened risk of material misstatement to the issuer’s financial statements, and areas of recurring deficiencies. We may also select some audit areas for review in a manner designed to incorporate unpredictability. Our selection of audits for review does not necessarily constitute a representative sample of the firm’s total population of issuer audits. Additionally, our inspection findings are specific to the particular portions of the issuer audits reviewed. They are not an assessment of all of the firm’s audit work or of all of the audit procedures performed for the audits reviewed. View the details on thescope of our inspections and our inspections procedures. Crowe PR PSC, PCAOB Release No. 104-2024-163, October 24, 2024 | 3 OVERVIEW OF THE 2024 INSPECTION AND HISTORICAL DATA BY INSPECTION YEAR The following information provides an overview of our 2024 inspection as well as data from the previous inspection. We use a risk-based method to select audits for review and to identify areas on which we focus our review. Because our inspection process evolves over time, it can, and often does, focus on a different mix of audits and audit areas from inspection to inspection and firm to firm. Further, a firm’s business, the applicable auditing standards, or other factors can change from the time of one inspection to the next. As a result of these variations, we caution that our inspection results are not necessarily comparable over time or among firms.
